title: Syntax and Semantics Meet in the “Middle”: Probing the Syntax-Semantics Interface of LMs Through Agentivity
abstract: Recent advances in large language models have prompted researchers to examine their abilities across a variety of linguistic tasks, but little has been done to investigate how models handle the interactions in meaning across words and larger syntactic forms—i.e. phenomena at the intersection of syntax and semantics. We present the semantic notion of agentivity as a case study for probing such interactions. We created a novel evaluation dataset by utilitizing the unique linguistic properties of a subset of optionally transitive English verbs. This dataset was used to prompt varying sizes of three model classes to see if they are sensitive to agentivity at the lexical level, and if they can appropriately employ these word-level priors given a specific syntactic context. Overall, GPT-3 text-davinci-003 performs extremely well across all experiments, outperforming all other models tested by far. In fact, the results are even better correlated with human judgements than both syntactic and semantic corpus statistics. This suggests that LMs may potentially serve as more useful tools for linguistic annotation, theory testing, and discovery than select corpora for certain tasks.

title: Higher-order Comparisons of Sentence Encoder Representations
abstract: Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) is a technique developed by neuroscientists for comparing activity patterns of different measurement modalities (e.g., fMRI, electrophysiology, behavior). As a framework, RSA has several advantages over existing approaches to interpretation of language encoders based on probing or diagnostic classification: namely, it does not require large training samples, is not prone to overfitting, and it enables a more transparent comparison between the representational geometries of different models and modalities. We demonstrate the utility of RSA by establishing a previously unknown correspondence between widely-employed pretrained language encoders and human processing difficulty via eye-tracking data, showcasing its potential in the interpretability toolbox for neural models.
specific_phenomena: Syntactic complexity (Yngve scores,), word frequency, and lexical ambiguity
experimental_materials_comment: Dundee eye-tracking corpus (Kennedy et al., 2003)
interp_method: Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)
main_findings: The study using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) to compare pre-trained language models (BERT-large and ELMo) with human eye-tracking data found that sentences that are more difficult for humans to process correspond to greater divergence in LM layer representations. Specifically, longer human gaze fixations were strongly associated with higher disagreement both between layers within BERT and between BERT and ELMo, indicating instability in sentence representations. Syntactic complexity, measured by Yngve scores, emerged as a key factor driving this effect, with intermediate BERT layers showing the strongest encoding of syntax. This creates a tripartite relationship: sentences high in syntactic complexity produce longer human fixation times and greater LM layer disagreement. Other factors such as word frequency showed moderate correlations, while lexical ambiguity had little impact on either human processing difficulty or LM representational divergence.

title: Morphosyntactic probing of multilingual BERT models
abstract: We introduce an extensive dataset for multilingual probing of morphological information in language models (247 tasks across 42 languages from 10 families), each consisting of a sentence with a target word and a morphological tag as the desired label, derived from the Universal Dependencies treebanks. We find that pre-trained Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa) learn features that attain strong performance across these tasks. We then apply two methods to locate, for each probing task, where the disambiguating information resides in the input. The first is a new perturbation method that “masks” various parts of context; the second is the classical method of Shapley values. The most intriguing finding that emerges is a strong tendency for the preceding context to hold more information relevant to the prediction than the following context.

main_findings: research on multilingual language models (mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa) reveals that these models acquire substantial morphosyntactic knowledge during pre-training, effectively using syntactic context for predicting features like Case, Gender, Number, and Tense. A key finding is the directional asymmetry in contextual information: the preceding (left) context is generally about 40% more informative than the following (right) context, reflecting progressive left-to-right feature spread, which arises from linguistic structure rather than model bias. Perturbation experiments confirmed this, while typological exceptions (e.g., SOV languages like Hindi showing right-context dominance) demonstrate the models’ sensitivity to grammatical regularities. Overall, the target word itself is the most informative, pre-trained features give high performance exceeding baselines, and XLM-RoBERTa generally outperforms mBERT, particularly in case and tense tasks. Aggregating results by morphosyntactic tags (POS or Tag) provides clearer generalization patterns than by language, showing that different linguistic categories rely variably on target forms and context.

title: How does the pre-training objective affect what large language models learn about linguistic properties?
abstract: Several pre-training objectives, such as masked language modeling (MLM), have been proposed to pre-train language models (e.g. BERT) with the aim of learning better language representations. However, to the best of our knowledge, no previous work so far has investigated how different pre-training objectives affect what BERT learns about linguistics properties. We hypothesize that linguistically motivated objectives such as MLM should help BERT to acquire better linguistic knowledge compared to other non-linguistically motivated objectives that are not intuitive or hard for humans to guess the association between the input and the label to be predicted. To this end, we pre-train BERT with two linguistically motivated objectives and three non-linguistically motivated ones. We then probe for linguistic characteristics encoded in the representation of the resulting models. We find strong evidence that there are only small differences in probing performance between the representations learned by the two different types of objectives. These surprising results question the dominant narrative of linguistically informed pre-training.

main_findings: The study found that the type of pre-training objective has surprisingly little impact on a language model’s (LM’s) syntactic knowledge. Using BERT-BASE models pre-trained with both linguistically motivated objectives (e.g., Masked Language Modeling, S+R) and non-linguistically motivated objectives (e.g., First Char, ASCII, Random), the researchers evaluated nine probing tasks, focusing on three syntactic tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst, BShift). Results showed that non-linguistically motivated objectives often performed as well as—or even better than—linguistically motivated ones, while only the fully Random objective consistently underperformed. For instance, First Char and ASCII outperformed MLM on TreeDepth, and S+R surpassed MLM on TopConst. These findings suggest that, regardless of objective, LMs acquire similar linguistic capabilities, likely driven more by pre-training data and model size than by the specific pre-training task, with models primarily learning word co-occurrence patterns rather than task-specific linguistic rules.

title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models.
specific_phenomena: word order: Swapping n-grams and phrase
experimental_materials_comment: sentences from the English Penn Treebank
interp_method: swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original
main_findings: Studies of BERT and its variants reveal that these language models encode hierarchical syntactic knowledge, showing sensitivity to phrase structure that emerges across network layers. Representational analyses using controlled word and phrase swaps demonstrate that distortions are smaller within valid phrases and larger when swaps break phrasal boundaries, with verb phrases causing greater distortion than noun phrases. Sensitivity increases with syntactic distance and across deeper layers, as larger-scale perturbations affect later layers and attention shifts from local to more distant syntactic dependencies. This syntactic awareness is linked to the encoding of complex linguistic information, where distortions correlate with impairment in parse tree reconstruction and boundary saliency in deeper layers. Importantly, these effects persist even when controlling for surface-level word co-occurrence statistics, confirming that BERT’s syntactic sensitivity reflects genuine hierarchical structure rather than mere statistical patterns.

title: Naturalistic Causal Probing for Morpho-Syntax
abstract: Probing has become a go-to methodology for interpreting and analyzing deep neural models in natural language processing. However, there is still a lack of understanding of the limitations and weaknesses of various types of probes. In this work, we suggest a strategy for input-level intervention on naturalistic sentences. Using our approach, we intervene on the morpho-syntactic features of a sentence, while keeping the rest of the sentence unchanged. Such an intervention allows us to causally probe pre-trained models. We apply our naturalistic causal probing framework to analyze the effects of grammatical gender and number on contextualized representations extracted from three pre-trained models in Spanish: the multilingual versions of BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT-2. Our experiments suggest that naturalistic interventions lead to stable estimates of the causal effects of various linguistic properties. Moreover, our experiments demonstrate the importance of naturalistic causal probing when analyzing pre-trained models.

main_findings: the research investigates how Language Models (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-2) encode and use morpho-syntactic features like grammatical gender and number, using naturalistic causal probing rather than traditional correlational methods. It finds that causal estimates of syntactic knowledge are robust, stable across datasets, and more reliable than template-based or naïve correlational approaches, with the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) predicting changes in representations under interventions. Gender and number are largely linearly encoded, often along a single principal dimension, capturing substantial variance in contextualized representations. Conventional correlational probes are shown to overestimate syntactic knowledge and fail on counterfactually augmented data due to sensitivity to spurious correlations. The causal effects of morpho-syntax vary across word types, aligning more strongly between nouns and adjectives than determiners. Finally, the study reveals causal gender biases in tasks like adjective prediction, with models such as RoBERTa showing predictable gendered associations, though effects differ depending on the syntactic role of the word and syncretism in adjectives.

title: Probe-Less Probing of BERT’s Layer-Wise Linguistic Knowledge with Masked Word Prediction
abstract: The current study quantitatively (and qualitatively for an illustrative purpose) analyzes BERT’s layer-wise masked word prediction on an English corpus, and finds that (1) the layerwise localization of linguistic knowledge primarily shown in probing studies is replicated in a behavior-based design and (2) that syntactic and semantic information is encoded at different layers for words of different syntactic categories. Hypothesizing that the above results are correlated with the number of likely potential candidates of the masked word prediction, we also investigate how the results differ for tokens within multiword expressions.
specific_phenomena: POS match, word match, and POS match without word match
experimental_materials_comment: corpus of web reviews written in English:  STREUSLE 4.4 (Schneider et al., 2018; Schneider and Smith, 2015)
Mechanistic_method: Behavioral Probing (layer-wise masked word prediction), feeding intermediate layers directly to the classification layer
interp_method: nan
main_findings: investigated how syntactic knowledge is encoded in BERT using a behavior-based, layer-wise masked word prediction probe, revealing that such knowledge is primarily localized in lower to middle layers, consistent with prior structure-based findings and classical NLP pipeline analogies. Using POS match metrics, the researchers found that syntactic ability peaks in lower layers (expected layer ≈ 3.68) while semantic knowledge spreads across higher layers. Contributions also vary by syntactic category: lower layers encode particles (PARTs) more strongly (expected layer ≈ 1.80), whereas proper nouns (PROPNs) rely on middle to higher layers (≈ 6.68). Open versus closed word classes further modulate layer-wise encoding, highlighting category-specific variability. For tokens in Multiword Expressions (MWEs), POS match peaks at higher layers than average, likely because semantic information is needed to predict the POS sequences in these constrained contexts (e.g., NOUNs in MWEs: 4.48 vs. all NOUNs: 3.98), showing that syntax interacts with semantics in complex ways across layers.

title: Probing for Constituency Structure in Neural Language Models
abstract: In this paper, we investigate to which extent contextual neural language models (LMs) implicitly learn syntactic structure. More concretely, we focus on constituent structure as represented in the Penn Treebank (PTB). Using standard probing techniques based on diagnostic classifiers, we assess the accuracy of representing constituents of different categories within the neuron activations of a LM such as RoBERTa. In order to make sure that our probe focuses on syntactic knowledge and not on implicit semantic generalizations, we also experiment on a PTB version that is obtained by randomly replacing constituents with each other while keeping syntactic structure, i.e., a semantically ill-formed but syntactically well-formed version of the PTB. We find that 4 pretrained transfomer LMs obtain high performance on our probing tasks even on manipulated data, suggesting that semantic and syntactic knowledge in their representations can be separated and that constituency information is in fact learned by the LM. Moreover, we show that a complete constituency tree can be linearly separated from LM representations.
specific_phenomena: constituent structur
experimental_materials_comment: English Penn Treebank data (PTB, Marcus et al.,1993),  two modified versions of the PTB with semantically nonsensical sentences that have the same syntactic structure as the original data.
interp_method: ensure that the probing classifier captures syntactic properties and not semantic properties
main_findings: Research on contextual neural language models (LMs) such as RoBERTa, BERT, XLNet, and DistilBERT shows that these models implicitly learn and encode syntactic structure, particularly constituency structure, which is often linearly separable at the levels of model, layer, and neuron. Probing experiments reveal that full constituency trees can be reconstructed with high accuracy (e.g., RoBERTa achieving 82.6% F1), and this syntactic knowledge is largely independent of semantics, as models retain strong performance even on semantically nonsensical but syntactically well-formed data. Diagnostic tasks further confirm fine-grained syntactic competence, with high accuracy in LCA prediction and chunking tasks, while analysis across layers and neurons shows that syntax is concentrated in middle layers and distributed across a subset of neurons. Token representation strategies, like concatenation, improve predictions, and different LMs, though similar in overall syntactic performance, encode constituency structure differently, reflecting varying implicit generalizations based on training data and objectives.

title: Hyperbolic Embedding for Finding Syntax in BERT
abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing have improved our understanding of what kind of linguistic knowledge is encoded in modern word representations. For example, methods for testing the ability to extract syntax trees from a language model architecture were developed by Hewitt and Manning (2019)-they project word vectors into Euclidean subspace in such a way that the corresponding squared Euclidean distance approximates the tree distance between words in the syntax tree. This work proposes a method for assessing whether embedding word representations in hyperbolic space can better reflect the graph structure of syntax trees. We show that the tree distance between words in a syntax tree can be approximated well by the hyperbolic distance between corresponding word vectors.
specific_phenomena: graph structure of syntax trees: whether embedding word representations in hyperbolic space can better reflect the graph structure of syntax trees
experimental_materials_comment: English Universal Dependencies dataset
interp_method: purpose of the performed experiments is to show that the usual (non-squared) Poincar distances can encode tree distances, methods were able to recover syntactic knowledge from word representation space.
main_findings: The research demonstrates that hyperbolic geometry provides an effective representation of syntactic knowledge in BERT, with hyperbolic distances closely approximating tree distances in syntax structures. By embedding word representations into the Poincaré ball using Gnomonic and Hyperboloid mappings, the study successfully recovered syntactic information from BERT layers, achieving competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art probes. Specifically, these methods outperformed the Structural probe in average Spearman correlation (Hyperboloid: 83.93, Gnomonic: 83.79 vs. Structural: 80.94) and achieved comparable UUAS scores, with particular advantages in lower-dimensional embeddings. Importantly, the work highlights that hyperbolic distances themselves—not their squares—directly reflect syntax tree distances, enhancing interpretability. Experiments were conducted on the English Universal Dependencies dataset and evaluated using UUAS and DSpr.

title: Probing BERT in Hyperbolic Spaces
abstract: Recently, a variety of probing tasks are proposed to discover linguistic properties learned in contextualized word embeddings. Many of these works implicitly assume these embeddings lay in certain metric spaces, typically the Euclidean space. This work considers a family of geometrically special spaces, the hyperbolic spaces, that exhibit better inductive biases for hierarchical structures and may better reveal linguistic hierarchies encoded in contextualized representations. We introduce a Poincare probe, a structural probe projecting these embeddings into a Poincare subspace with explicitly defined hierarchies. We focus on two probing objectives: (a) dependency trees where the hierarchy is defined as head-dependent structures; (b) lexical sentiments where the hierarchy is defined as the polarity of words (positivity and negativity). We argue that a key desideratum of a probe is its sensitivity to the existence of linguistic structures. We apply our probes on BERT, a typical contextualized embedding model. In a syntactic subspace, our probe better recovers tree structures than Euclidean probes, revealing the possibility that the geometry of BERT syntax may not necessarily be Euclidean. In a sentiment subspace, we reveal two possible meta-embeddings for positive and negative sentiments and show how lexically-controlled contextualization would change the geometric localization of embeddings. We demonstrate the findings with our Poincare probe via extensive experiments and visualization. Our results can be reproduced at this https URL.
specific_phenomena: explore the limit of BERT embeddings: negation,
experimental_materials_comment: Penn Treebank dataset (Marcus & Marcinkiewicz, 1993)
interp_method: recover syntax trees in a strict notion
main_findings: The study of syntactic knowledge in BERT using the Poincaré probe reveals that BERT’s embeddings may reside in a hyperbolic rather than Euclidean space, with the Poincaré probe outperforming Euclidean probes in reconstructing syntax trees, especially for deeper trees, longer edges, and longer sentences. The optimal hyperbolic curvature is around -1, and the probe more accurately captures hierarchical structures, placing root words near the origin and organizing words by syntactic depth. The Poincaré probe is sensitive to linguistic structure without being a general-purpose parser, as it does not inflate scores for embeddings lacking syntactic information. Both probes indicate that syntactic information is primarily localized in the middle layers of BERT (around layer 7), earlier than semantic features like sentiment, suggesting that hyperbolic geometry better models BERT’s encoding of hierarchical syntactic structure.

title: Analysing Syntactic and Semantic Features in Pre-trained Language Models in a Fully Unsupervised Setting
abstract: Transformer-based pre-trained language models (PLMs) have been used in all NLP tasks and resulted in a great success. This has led to the question of whether we can transfer this knowledge to syntactic or semantic parsing in a completely unsupervised setting. In this study, we leverage PLMs as a source of external knowledge to perform a fully unsupervised parser model for semantic, constituency and dependency parsing. We analyse the results for English, German, French, and Turkish to understand the impact of the PLMs on different languages for syntactic and semantic parsing. We visualize the attention layers and heads in PLMs for parsing to understand the information that can be learned throughout the layers and the attention heads in the PLMs both for different levels of parsing tasks. The results obtained from dependency, constituency, and semantic parsing are similar to each other, and the middle layers and the ones closer to the final layers have more syntactic and semantic information.

main_findings: finds that transformer-based pre-trained language models (PLMs) encode both syntactic and semantic information primarily in their middle to final layers, with lower layers generally less informative except in certain cases like Turkish or GPT-2 for semantic parsing. Analysis of attention heads shows that top heads usually carry more syntactic information, though exceptions exist for Turkish due to shorter sentences. Across parsing tasks—dependency, constituency, and semantic—the layer patterns are similar, but unsupervised dependency parsing is consistently harder than the other tasks, while semantic and constituency parsing perform comparably well. Sentence length impacts performance, with shorter sentences being parsed more accurately, as longer sentences make it harder to capture distant relationships. Overall, multilingual PLMs outperform auto-regressive models like GPT and GPT-2, which struggle due to their unidirectional context processing.

title: Controlling the Imprint of Passivization and Negation in Contextualized Representations
abstract: Contextualized word representations encode rich information about syntax and semantics, alongside specificities of each context of use. While contextual variation does not always reflect actual meaning shifts, it can still reduce the similarity of embeddings for word instances having the same meaning. We explore the imprint of two specific linguistic alternations, namely passivization and negation, on the representations generated by neural models trained with two different objectives: masked language modeling and translation. Our exploration methodology is inspired by an approach previously proposed for removing societal biases from word vectors. We show that passivization and negation leave their traces on the representations, and that neutralizing this information leads to more similar embeddings for words that should preserve their meaning in the transformation. We also find clear differences in how the respective features generalize across datasets.
syntactic_phenomena: Argument Structure and other Constructions, negation and NPIs
specific_phenomena: passivization and negation,
experimental_materials_comment:
using a dataset automatically created with the templates proposed by Prasad et al. (2019)
and SICK (Sentences Involving Compositional Knowledge) dataset (Marelli et al., 2014b).
interp_method:
iteratively (1) training a linear classifie to predict zi from xi, followed by (2) projecting xi on the null-space of the classifier, using a projection matrix PN (W ) such that W (PN (W )x) = 0 ∀x, where W is the weight matrix of the classifier, and N (W ) is its null-space. Through the projection step in each iteration, the information detected
by the trained linear classifier is removed from the representation. The procedure continues until the attempt to train a linear classifier on the projected data becomes unsuccessful
main_findings: finds that contextualized word representations from BERT and Neural Machine Translation (MT) encoders strongly encode syntactic and semantic information, with transformations like passivization and negation leaving clear, detectable traces. These traces are robust enough that classifiers can reliably distinguish sentence variants, and visualizations show near-linear separation of verb and noun representations across active/passive forms. However, these transformations also distort word similarity, which can be effectively mitigated using Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP), reducing variant-specific information while preserving core semantic content. Comparisons between models reveal that MT encoders generalize these transformation features better than BERT: cleaned MT representations transfer well across datasets and grammatical categories, while BERT embeddings retain dataset- and category-specific signals, limiting their generalization. Overall, the findings highlight both the richness of syntactic encoding in LMs and the differential impact of training objectives on feature generalizability.

title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
abstract: Recent work has found evidence that Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, is capable of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that some aspects of its representations are shared cross-lingually. To better understand this overlap, we extend recent work on finding syntactic trees in neural networks’ internal representations to the multilingual setting. We show that subspaces of mBERT representations recover syntactic tree distances in languages other than English, and that these subspaces are approximately shared across languages. Motivated by these results, we present an unsupervised analysis method that provides evidence mBERT learns representations of syntactic dependency labels, in the form of clusters which largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy. This evidence suggests that even without explicit supervision, multilingual masked language models learn certain linguistic universals.
specific_phenomena: syntactic tree distances in languages other than English
languages_tested_comment: 11 languages: Arabic, Chinese, Czech, English, Farsi, Finnish, French, German, Indonesian, Latvian, and Spanish
experimental_materials_comment: probe the model on trees encoded in the Universal Dependencies v2 formalism (Nivre et al.,2020)
interp_method: structual probe (hewitt manning 2019),  enable zero-shot transfer across languages to successfully recover syntax:  probe is able to pick up on features that are jointly encoded in M-BERT across language
main_findings: Research on Multilingual BERT (mBERT) shows that the model encodes rich syntactic knowledge across languages, even without explicit linguistic supervision. Using structural probes, researchers identified a syntactic subspace within mBERT representations that effectively recovers tree structures, particularly in the 7th and 8th layers, and is localized to a relatively small portion of the 768-dimensional representation. This subspace is cross-lingually robust, allowing probes trained on one language—or on combined multilingual data—to recover syntax in other languages, with the degree of subspace overlap strongly correlating with transfer performance. Moreover, mBERT spontaneously forms clusters corresponding to universal grammatical relations, largely aligning with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, and even making finer-grained distinctions, such as differentiating prenominal vs. postnominal adjectives, types of determiners, or negative adverbial modifiers. These findings highlight mBERT’s capacity to capture both language-specific and cross-lingual syntactic universals.

title: Investigating Language Relationships in Multilingual Sentence Encoders Through the Lens of Linguistic Typology
abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model’s ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that the models encode. In this article, we investigate these questions by leveraging knowledge from the field of linguistic typology, which studies and documents structural and semantic variation across languages. We propose methods for separating language-specific subspaces within state-of-the-art multilingual sentence encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM, and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological, and syntactic structure. Moreover, we investigate how typological information about languages is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies. In addition, we propose a simple method to study how shared typological properties of languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models—M-BERT and XLM-R. The results provide insight into their information-sharing mechanisms and suggest that these linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically similar languages in these models.
specific_phenomena: Linguistic Typology, 25 wals features
languages_tested_comment: Bulgarian (bul), French (fra), Spanish (spa), German (deu), Greek (ell), Russian (rus), Turkish (tur), Arabic (ara), Vietnamese (vie), Thai (tha), Chinese (zho), Hindi (hin), Swahili (swa), Swedish (swe) and Urdu (urd)
experimental_materials_comment:
10,000 random sentences from the Tatoeba corpora, 25 WALS features used for probing along with their correpsonding WALS codes and
categories
interp_method: propose a set of 25 language-level probing task to  test whether it is possible to successfully separate language-specific subspaces within multilingual encoders by the linguistic typological properties of the languages
main_findings: Multilingual sentence encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM, and XLM-R) exhibit notable strengths in capturing syntactic and word order properties, particularly through their language-specific components, which reliably encode features like the order of subject, object, and verb, adposition-noun phrase order, negation, and pronoun distinctions. However, they struggle with predicting certain features, such as Subject-Verb order when no dominant order exists and question formation properties. Model performance varies: M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM in distinguishing languages across broader linguistic properties, likely due to greater reliance on typological organization. The localization of syntactic information differs by pretraining objective—cross-lingual models (LASER, XLM) store typological properties in lower layers, which diminish in higher layers as representations become more language-agnostic, whereas monolingual models (M-BERT, XLM-R) maintain stable, less localizable typological information across all layers. Additionally, M-BERT and XLM-R encode typological features jointly across languages, evidenced by the deterioration in probing task performance for multiple languages sharing the same feature when a language’s specific information is removed, indicating systematic and shared encoding of syntactic properties.

title: Correlating Neural and Symbolic Representations of Language
abstract: Analysis methods which enable us to better understand the representations and functioning of neural models of language are increasingly needed as deep learning becomes the dominant approach in NLP. Here we present two methods based on Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Tree Kernels (TK) which allow us to directly quantify how strongly the information encoded in neural activation patterns corresponds to information represented by symbolic structures such as syntax trees. We first validate our methods on the case of a simple synthetic language for arithmetic expressions with clearly defined syntax and semantics, and show that they exhibit the expected pattern of results. We then our methods to correlate neural representations of English sentences with their constituency parse trees.
specific_phenomena: tree depth, tree kernel is an estimate of similarity between two syntax trees based on the number of tree fragments they share
experimental_materials_comment: use the 2,002 sentences corresponding to the development section of the EWT Universal Dependencies (Silveira et al., 2014), plus 200 sentences from the training section as reference sentenceswhen fitting RSAREGRESS .
interp_method: RSA, TreeKernels: an alternative approach (to diagnostic classifiers probing= based on correlating neural representations of sentences and structured symbolic representations commonly used in linguistics
main_findings: The analysis of InferSent and BERT regarding syntactic knowledge using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Tree Kernels revealed that both models encode substantial syntactic information, significantly surpassing simple baselines like random models or bag-of-words. Their sensitivity to syntactic structure depends on the strictness of structure matching, with strict matching (λ=1) showing clear syntactic encoding only in trained models, while RSAREGRESS detects moderate correlations even in untrained models and BoW representations. In BERT, syntactic information is most prominent in intermediate layers (layers 15–22), with later layers focusing more on non-syntactic aspects. Training plays a crucial role, as trained models exhibit stronger correlations with syntactic structures than untrained models, which can even show negative correlations, highlighting that learning is necessary to overcome initially misleading activation patterns.

title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT’s attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT’s attention.
specific_phenomena: dependency Syntax, Direct object, Noun modifiers, Possessive pronouns, Passive auxiliary verbs, prepositions,coreferent HEAD analysis
experimental_materials_comment: 1000 Wikipedia segments, each segment consists of at most 128 tokens corresponding to two consecutive paragraphs of Wikipedia
interp_method: we propose an attention-based probing classifier that takes attention maps as input. The classifier achieves 77 UAS at dependency parsing, showing BERT’s attention captures a substantial amount about syntax
main_findings: Analysis of BERT’s attention mechanisms reveals that the model captures substantial syntactic knowledge, with individual attention heads specializing in specific linguistic relations—such as determiners, direct objects, passive auxiliaries, possessives, and objects of prepositions—achieving high accuracy without explicit syntactic supervision. Overall, combining attention maps with word embeddings in an attention-based probing classifier attains a 77 UAS, showing that BERT’s attention encodes significant syntactic structure comparable to vector-based probes. Beyond linguistic specialization, general attention patterns emerge: some heads focus on fixed positional offsets, others exhibit broad, high-entropy attention akin to a bag-of-vectors, many attend heavily to the [SEP] token as a “no-op,” and heads within the same layer often behave similarly, forming functional clusters.

title: Probing for Predicate Argument Structures in Pretrained Language Models
abstract: Thanks to the effectiveness and wide availability of modern pretrained language models (PLMs), recently proposed approaches have achieved remarkable results in dependency- and span-based, multilingual and cross-lingual Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). These results have prompted researchers to investigate the inner workings of modern PLMs with the aim of understanding how, where, and to what extent they encode information about SRL. In this paper, we follow this line of research and probe for predicate argument structures in PLMs. Our study shows that PLMs do encode semantic structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate, and also provides insights into the correlation between predicate senses and their structures, the degree of transferability between nominal and verbal structures, and how such structures are encoded across languages. Finally, we look at the practical implications of such insights and demonstrate the benefits of embedding predicate argument structure information into an SRL model.
model_name_comment: BERT (base-cased), RoBERTa (base), multilingual BERT (base) and XLM-RoBERTa (base)
specific_phenomena: argument structure of a predicate (encoded in contextual representation?)
experimental_materials_comment: verbal predicate instances of the English training datasets provided as part of the CoNLL-2009 shared task for dependency-based SRL (Hajiˇc et al.,2009).
interp_method: nan
main_findings: investigates how Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) encode Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) information, particularly Predicate Argument Structures (PASs), revealing that semantic knowledge is distributed non-uniformly across layers: predicate senses are encoded relatively evenly, favoring top layers slightly, while roleset information concentrates in middle layers. Verbal and nominal predicates are represented differently, highlighting challenges in transferring knowledge between them. Using a weighted average of all layers for probing captures more semantic information than relying on top layers alone, and multilingual PLMs show similar layer distributions for PASs across English and Chinese, supporting cross-lingual transfer potential. These insights improved SRL system performance when integrated via multi-task learning. In parallel, the study contextualizes these findings with prior probing research showing that PLMs encode syntactic knowledge hierarchically: lower layers capture lexical information, upper layers sentence-level structure, and distances between syntactic constituents are represented, effectively “rediscovering” the classical NLP pipeline.

title: Identifying Elements Essential for BERT’s Multilinguality
abstract: It has been shown that multilingual BERT (mBERT) yields high quality multilingual representations and enables effective zero-shot transfer. This is surprising given that mBERT does not use any crosslingual signal during training. While recent literature has studied this phenomenon, the reasons for the multilinguality are still somewhat obscure. We aim to identify architectural properties of BERT and linguistic properties of languages that are necessary for BERT to become multilingual. To allow for fast experimentation we propose an efficient setup with small BERT models trained on a mix of synthetic and natural data. Overall, we identify four architectural and two linguistic elements that influence multilinguality. Based on our insights, we experiment with a multilingual pretraining setup that modifies the masking strategy using VecMap, i.e., unsupervised embedding alignment. Experiments on XNLI with three languages indicate that our findings transfer from our small setup to larger scale settings.
specific_phenomena: word order
fine_tuning_materials: finetune the pretrained models on English XNLI (3 epochs, batch size 32, learning rate 2e-
experimental_materials_comment: nan
interp_method: nan
main_findings: investigates the factors that enable multilingual BERT (mBERT) to produce cross-lingual representations, emphasizing both architectural and linguistic contributions. A central finding is the critical role of word order: experiments with inverted word order in a synthetic language show that disrupting word order nearly destroys multilinguality, highlighting that similar word order across languages is necessary. This aligns with architectural insights, particularly the importance of shared position embeddings, as language-specific position embeddings significantly reduce multilinguality, likely due to mismatches between word positions and their embeddings. Analysis on real-world XNLI data further supports this, showing a moderate correlation between word-order similarity and zero-shot performance. Beyond word order, the study identifies six key elements for multilinguality: four architectural—limited parameters, shared position embeddings, shared special tokens, and the standard masking strategy—and two linguistic—word order similarity and comparability of training corpora. Additionally, multilinguality emerges late in training, but a proposed knn-replace masking strategy accelerates and strengthens cross-lingual alignment.

title: Analyzing Individual Neurons in Pre-trained Language Models
abstract: While a lot of analysis has been carried to demonstrate linguistic knowledge captured by the representations learned within deep NLP models, very little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We carry outa neuron-level analysis using core linguistic tasks of predicting morphology, syntax and semantics, on pre-trained language models, with questions like: i) do individual neurons in pre-trained models capture linguistic information? ii) which parts of the network learn more about certain linguistic phenomena? iii) how distributed or focused is the information? and iv) how do various architectures differ in learning these properties? We found small subsets of neurons to predict linguistic tasks, with lower level tasks (such as morphology) localized in fewer neurons, compared to higher level task of predicting syntax. Our study also reveals interesting cross architectural comparisons. For example, we found neurons in XLNet to be more localized and disjoint when predicting properties compared to BERT and others, where they are more distributed and coupled.
specific_phenomena: POS tagging, syntax tagging and chunking
experimental_materials_comment: POS-tagging using the Penn TreeBank (Marcus et al., 1993), syntax tagging (CCG supertagging)7 using CCGBank (Hockenmaier, 2006), syntactic chunking using CoNLL 2000 shared task dataset (Tjong Kim Sang and Buchholz, 2000), and semantic tagging using the Parallel Meaning Bank data (Abzianidze et al., 2017).
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, neuron ranking algorithm (intervention-based component through ablation study)
interp_method: logistic regression classifier with elastic-net regularization (Zou and Hastie, 2005)
main_findings: analyzed individual neurons in pre-trained language models (ELMo, T-ELMo, BERT, XLNet) on linguistic tasks, focusing on syntax through Syntactic Chunking and CCG Supertagging. It found that higher-level syntactic tasks require more neurons than lower-level tasks, with CCG Supertagging needing up to a third of the network’s neurons, indicating distributed and redundant representations. Linguistic knowledge is increasingly localized in higher layers: lower layers capture word-level information, middle layers support simpler syntactic tasks like Chunking, and final layers dominate for complex tasks like CCG. Architectural differences also affect representation: BERT distributes syntactic knowledge broadly across layers, whereas XLNet localizes neurons more exclusively to specific syntactic properties, allowing easier isolation and interpretation of neuron function.

title: Discourse structure interacts with reference but not syntax in neural language models
abstract: Language models (LMs) trained on large quantities of text have been claimed to acquire abstract linguistic representations. Our work tests the robustness of these abstractions by focusing on the ability of LMs to learn interactions between different linguistic representations. In particular, we utilized stimuli from psycholinguistic studies showing that humans can condition reference (i.e. coreference resolution) and syntactic processing on the same discourse structure (implicit causality). We compared both transformer and long short-term memory LMs to find that, contrary to humans, implicit causality only influences LM behavior for reference, not syntax, despite model representations that encode the necessary discourse information. Our results further suggest that LM behavior can contradict not only learned representations of discourse but also syntactic agreement, pointing to shortcomings of standard language modeling.
specific_phenomena:
discourse structure, determined by implicit causality
verbs, could be acquired; IC verb biase
experimental_materials_comment: stimuli from a human experiment conducted in Ferstl et al. (2011), which asked participants to give continuations to sentence fragments
interp_method: model behavior (e.g., probability assigned to possible next words) and model representation (e.g., similarity between hidden representations)
main_findings: finds that while language models (LMs) encode certain syntactic and discourse information, they fail to integrate abstract linguistic knowledge, specifically implicit causality (IC), with syntactic processing. Unlike humans, who adjust both referential and syntactic comprehension based on discourse structure, LMs only show IC effects on reference but not on relative clause (RC) attachment, instead favoring local noun agreement. LSTM models did not develop any IC-based distinctions in RC attachment and consistently aligned representations with the lower noun. Transformer models (TransformerXL, GPT-2 XL) represented IC contrasts in earlier layers, but this knowledge was largely lost or misrepresented in the final layers, leading to behavior dominated by locality preferences despite encoded syntactic cues like number agreement. These results suggest that although LMs can represent abstract syntactic contrasts, they struggle to utilize discourse-informed syntactic knowledge, calling into question the robustness of their abstract linguistic representations.

title: Amnesic Probing: Behavioral Explanation with Amnesic Counterfactuals
abstract: A growing body of work makes use of probing in order to investigate the working of neural models, often considered black boxes. Recently, an ongoing debate emerged surrounding the limitations of the probing paradigm. In this work, we point out the inability to infer behavioral conclusions from probing results, and offer an alternative method that focuses on how the information is being used, rather than on what information is encoded. Our method, Amnesic Probing, follows the intuition that the utility of a property for a given task can be assessed by measuring the influence of a causal intervention that removes it from the representation. Equipped with this new analysis tool, we can ask questions that were not possible before, for example, is part-of-speech information important for word prediction? We perform a series of analyses on BERT to answer these types of questions. Our findings demonstrate that conventional probing performance is not correlated to task importance, and we call for increased scrutiny of claims that draw behavioral or causal conclusions from probing results.
model_name_comment: BERT, masked vs. the non-masked version, BERT- BASE -uncased
specific_phenomena: is part-of-speech information important for word prediction
experimental_materials_comment: English UD Treebank (McDonald et al., 2013) for c-pos, f-pos, and dep; and English OntoNotes (Weischedel et al., 2013) for ner, phrase start, and phrase end. For training, we use 100,000 random tokens from those datasets
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques (Amnesic Probing, using Iterative Null-space Projection)
interp_method: Amnestic probing, LM accuracy: Word prediction accuracy. Kullback-Leibler Divergence
main_findings: the study using Amnesic Probing on BERT-BASE-UNCASED investigated the influence of syntactic knowledge on word prediction by selectively removing linguistic properties such as dependency labels, fine- and coarse-grained POS tags, and phrase boundaries. Results showed that dependency labels and fine-grained POS tags are highly important, causing major drops in accuracy when removed, while coarse POS is moderately important, and phrase markers are largely unimportant, sometimes even slightly improving performance. Removing coarse POS affected closed-class words like conjunctions, determiners, and particles far more than open-class words like nouns and verbs, indicating POS is crucial for predicting function words. Layer-wise analysis revealed that POS information is most critical in upper layers (layers 11–12), whereas phrase markers peak in middle layers (layers 5–7), and the recoverability of POS information varies across layers, being more recoverable in lower layers for non-masked inputs but less so for masked inputs. Overall, the study highlights that BERT relies heavily on certain syntactic features, especially for predicting function words, and that their importance and recoverability vary systematically across the network’s layers.

title: Is Supervised Syntactic Parsing Beneficial for Language Understanding Tasks? An Empirical Investigation
abstract: Traditional NLP has long held (supervised) syntactic parsing necessary for successful higher-level semantic language understanding (LU). The recent advent of end-to-end neural models, self-supervised via language model- ing (LM), and their success on a wide range of LU tasks, however, questions this belief. In this work, we empirically investigate the usefulness of supervised parsing for seman- tic LU in the context of LM-pretrained trans- former networks. Relying on the established fine-tuning paradigm, we first couple a pre- trained transformer with a biaffine parsing head, aiming to infuse explicit syntactic knowl- edge from Universal Dependencies treebanks into the transformer. We then fine-tune the model for LU tasks and measure the effect of the intermediate parsing training (IPT) on downstream LU task performance. Results from both monolingual English and zero-shot language transfer experiments (with intermedi- ate target-language parsing) show that explicit formalized syntax, injected into transformers through IPT, has very limited and inconsistent effect on downstream LU performance. Our results, coupled with our analysis of transform- ers’ representation spaces before and after in- termediate parsing, make a significant step to- wards providing answers to an essential ques- tion: how (un)availing is supervised parsing for high-level semantic natural language un- derstanding in the era of large neural models?
specific_phenomena: dependency parsing (as an intermediate training task), Hans dataset
fine_tuning_materials: fine-tune transformers for two types of LU tasks: (1) se- quence classification (SEQC) tasks, where a se- quence of text needs to be assigned a discrete la- bel; and (2) multiple choice classification (MCC) tasks where we need to select the correct an- swer between two or more options for a given a premise and/or question
experimental_materials_comment: Universal Dependencies treebanks that we use for our intermediate parsing training and evaluation of our biaffine dependency parsers. The UD tree-banks v.2.5
Mechanistic_method: Intermediate Parsing Training, centered kernel alignment (linear)
interp_method: interme-diate parsing training (IPT) based on a state-of-the-art-level dependency parser, indicate that explicitsyntax, at least in our extensive experiments, pro-vides negligible impact on LU tasks
main_findings: Research on syntactic knowledge in transformer-based language models like BERT and RoBERTa shows that explicitly injecting syntactic information via supervised parsing (e.g., Intermediate Parsing Training with Universal Dependencies) has limited and inconsistent benefits for downstream language understanding tasks. Monolingual English experiments reveal negligible gains, even when model parameters are preserved, likely due to a mismatch between the syntactic structures provided and the structural knowledge useful for LU tasks. Probing analyses indicate that these models already encode substantial latent syntax through self-supervised pretraining, capturing hierarchical structures, parts-of-speech, and dependencies sufficient to reconstruct trees, making explicit syntax largely redundant. While IPT can sometimes yield modest zero-shot transfer gains in multilingual models, most improvements are attributable to exposure to additional target-language data rather than the injected syntactic signal itself. Overall, transformers implicitly acquire the necessary structural inductive biases during pretraining, suggesting that supervised parsing adds little value for high-resource languages in high-level language understanding.

title: BERT syntactic transfer: A computational experiment on Italian, French and English languages
abstract: This paper investigates the ability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) language model to transfer syntactic knowledge cross-lingually, verifying if and to which extent syntactic dependency relationships learnt in a language are maintained in other languages. In detail, the main contributions of this paper are: (i) an analysis of the cross-lingual syntactic transfer capability of mBERT model; (ii) a detailed comparison of cross-language syntactic transfer among languages belonging to different branches of the Indo-European languages, namely English, Italian and French, which present very different syntactic constructions; (iii) a study on the transferability of a syntactic phenomenon peculiar of Italian language, namely the pronoun dropping (pro-drop), also known as omissibility of the subject. To this end, a structural probe devoted to reconstruct the dependency parse tree of a sentence has been exploited, representing the input sentences with the contextual embeddings from mBERT layers. The results of the experimental assessment have shown a transfer of syntactic knowledge of the mBERT model among these languages. Moreover, the behaviour of the probe in the transition from pro-drop to non-pro-drop languages and vice versa has proven to be more effective in case of languages sharing a common linguistic matrix. The possibility of transferring syntactical knowledge, especially in the case of specific phenomena, meets both a theoretical need and can have important practical implications in syntactic tasks, such as dependency parsing.
specific_phenomena:
Italian pronoun dropping (focused on the specific null-subject phenomenon, which is peculiar of Italian language and not present in English and French)
syntactic dependency relationships learnt in a language are maintained in other languages (approximation of dependency relationships in sentences)
experimental_materials_comment: Parallel Universal Dependencies (PUD) (Zeman et al., 2017)  parallel treebanks created for the CoNLL 2017 shared task on Multilingual Parsing from Raw Text to Universal Dependencies, containing, among the others, parallel English–French–Italian sentences, manually translated and annotated
interp_method: structural probe (adapted the one from hewitt and Manning 2019) to reconstruct the dependency parse tree of a sentence, a cross-lingual test on an aligned and parallel annotated treebank.
main_findings: the study on multilingual BERT (mBERT) reveals that the model effectively encodes and transfers syntactic knowledge across languages, showing cross-lingual performance comparable to monolingual benchmarks. This transferability is most pronounced in the middle-to-upper layers of the Transformer, with structural probes successfully reconstructing dependency parse trees from contextual embeddings. Cross-lingual performance correlates with linguistic proximity: Romance languages (Italian-French) exhibit higher transfer accuracy than typologically distant pairs (English-Italian). Additionally, mBERT captures language-specific phenomena such as pro-drop, correctly handling subject omission in Italian and transferring subject agreement knowledge across languages, demonstrating robust encoding of both universal and language-specific syntactic structures.

title: Assessing BERT’s ability to learn Italian syntax: a study on null-subject and agreement phenomena
abstract: The work presented in this paper investigates the ability of BERT neural language model pretrained in Italian to embed syntactic dependency relationships into its layers, by approximating a Dependency Parse Tree. To this end, a structural probe, namely a supervised model able to extract linguistic structures from a language model, has been trained leveraging the contextual embeddings from the layers of BERT. An experimental assessment has been performed using an Italian version of BERT-base model and a set of datasets for Italian labelled with Universal Dependencies formalism. The results, achieved using standard metrics of dependency parsers, have shown that a knowledge of the Italian syntax is embedded in central-upper layers of the BERT model, according to what observed in literature for the English case. In addition, the probe has been also used to experimentally evaluate the BERT model behaviour in case of two specific syntactic phenomena in Italian, namely null-subject and subject-verb-agreement, showing better performance than an Italian state-of-the-art parser. These findings can open a path for the development of new hybrid approaches, exploiting the probe to integrate or improve limits or weaknesses in analysing articulated constructions of Italian syntax, traditionally complex to be parsed.
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Agreement and feature-checking
specific_phenomena: extract hierarchical syntactic information that approximates a Dependency Parse Tree, Subject‑verb agreement, null-subject phenomenon,
experimental_materials_comment: three Italian datasets which provide an annotated treebank; Italian Stanford Dependency Treebank (ISDT), Venice Italian Treebank (VIT), Italian PUD test set version of the Parallel Universal Dependencies (PUD)
interp_method: syntactic probe
main_findings: investigated how Italian syntactic knowledge is represented in the BERT language model, focusing on general syntax as well as the complex phenomena of null-subject clauses and Subject-Verb Agreement (SVA). It found that Italian syntactic information is primarily embedded in the middle-to-upper layers of BERT, with layer 7 achieving the highest performance (over 80% sUAS) in structural probing tasks, supporting the hierarchical view of linguistic representation in the model. For null-subject phenomena, the probe significantly outperformed the state-of-the-art Italian parser, accurately reconstructing hierarchical structures even in sentences with noncanonical word order. For SVA, the probe achieved performance comparable to the parser but showed greater robustness to long-distance dependencies and multiple agreement attractors, correctly linking subjects and verbs in complex sentences where traditional parsers often fail. Overall, the findings highlight BERT’s ability to encode both general syntactic knowledge and challenging Italian-specific syntactic patterns.

title: Deep Clustering of Text Representations for Supervision-Free Probing of Syntax
abstract: We explore deep clustering of multilingual text representations for unsupervised model interpretation and induction of syntax. As these representations are high-dimensional, out-of-the-box methods like K-means do not work well. Thus, our approach jointly transforms the representations into a lower-dimensional cluster-friendly space and clusters them. We consider two notions of syntax: Part of Speech Induction (POSI) and Constituency Labelling (CoLab) in this work. Interestingly, we find that Multilingual BERT (mBERT) contains surprising amount of syntactic knowledge of English; possibly even as much as English BERT (E-BERT). Our model can be used as a supervision-free probe which is arguably a less-biased way of probing. We find that unsupervised probes show benefits from higher layers as compared to supervised probes. We further note that our unsupervised probe utilizes E-BERT and mBERT representations differently, especially for POSI. We validate the efficacy of our probe by demonstrating its capabilities as a unsupervised syntax induction technique. Our probe works well for both syntactic formalisms by simply adapting the input representations. We report competitive performance of our probe on 45-tag English POSI, state-of-the-art performance on 12-tag POSI across 10 languages, and competitive results on CoLab. We also perform zero-shot syntax induction on resource impoverished languages and report strong results.
specific_phenomena: part of speech induction (POSI) and constituency labelling (CoLab)
fine_tuning_materials: In the joint representation learning and clustering stage, we finetune the encoder fθ trained in the pretraining stage to minimize a clustering loss LKL. The goal of this step is to learn a latent space that is amenable to clusterin
experimental_materials_comment: 45-tag Penn Treebank Wall Street Journal (WSJ)dataset (Marcus, Santorini, and Marcinkiewicz 1993) andmultilingual 12-tag datasets drawn from the universal depen-dencies project (Nivre et al. 2016)
interp_method: "deep clustering": new clustering-based approach to probe contextualized text representations
main_findings: The study reveals that BERT models, particularly Multilingual BERT (mBERT), encode substantial syntactic knowledge, with mBERT often matching or surpassing English BERT (E-BERT) in unsupervised tasks like Part-of-Speech Induction (POSI) and Constituency Labelling (CoLab). Using the unsupervised SyntDEC probe, researchers found that syntactic information is predominantly captured in higher layers of BERT, with mBERT and E-BERT showing different layer utilization patterns, and unsupervised gains more evenly distributed across layers compared to supervised probes. mBERT also encodes morphological information and demonstrates superior fine-grained syntactic distinction, especially for nouns, numerals, and pronouns, though verb distinctions remain challenging. Additionally, mBERT exhibits strong zero-shot crosslingual capabilities, allowing English-trained clusters to transfer effectively to typologically distant languages, highlighting both its general syntactic knowledge and crosslingual robustness.

title: The Low-Dimensional Linear Geometry of Contextualized Word Representations
abstract: Black-box probing models can reliably extract linguistic features like tense, number, and syntactic role from pretrained word representations. However, the manner in which these features are encoded in representations remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of the linear geometry of contextualized word representations in ELMO and BERT. We show that a variety of linguistic features (including structured dependency relationships) are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces. We then refine this geometric picture, showing that there are hierarchical relations between the subspaces encoding general linguistic categories and more specific ones, and that low-dimensional feature encodings are distributed rather than aligned to individual neurons. Finally, we demonstrate that these linear subspaces are causally related to model behavior, and can be used to perform fine-grained manipulation of BERT’s output distribution.
specific_phenomena: syntactic categories, roles, and relations: Pos, dependency label prediction, dependency edge prediction
experimental_materials_comment: 3 groups of sentences from the dataset of Marvin and Linzen (2018) designed to test BERT’s predictions at subject–verb agreement
interp_method: We say the representations encode the task if there exists a probe g(R) that predicts f (W ) according to a score S(g(R), f (W )), which we choose to be held-out accuracy. The use of an expressive model downstream of the projected representation disentangles questions about representation geom- etry from the questions about probe capacity con- sidered in previous work
main_findings: investigates how contextualized word representations in language models like ELMo and BERT encode linguistic and syntactic knowledge, revealing that such information is stored in low-dimensional linear subspaces that are hierarchically organized and causally related to model behavior. Simple syntactic features like part-of-speech tags and dependency labels can be captured in very compact subspaces (often <10 dimensions), while relational features like dependency edges require slightly higher dimensions, and non-linguistic controls generally do not exhibit this low-dimensional structure. These subspaces are distributed rather than neuron-aligned, meaning the relevant information is spread across multiple neurons rather than concentrated in individual ones, with deeper layers showing more distributed encodings. Hierarchically, broader syntactic categories contain smaller subspaces for fine-grained distinctions, and interventions show these subspaces are causally significant: selectively ablating minimal “noun” or “verb” subspaces disrupts BERT’s subject–verb agreement predictions without affecting coarse syntactic knowledge, demonstrating that very small, targeted subspaces carry crucial syntactic information.

title: How effective is BERT without word ordering? Implications for language understanding and data privacy
abstract: Ordered word sequences contain the rich structures that define language. However, it’s often not clear if or how modern pretrained language models utilize these structures. We show that the token representations and self-attention activations within BERT are surprisingly resilient to shuffling the order of input tokens, and that for several GLUE language understanding tasks, shuffling only minimally degrades performance, e.g., by 4% for QNLI. While bleak from the perspective of language understanding, our results have positive implications for cases where copyright or ethics necessitates the consideration of bag-of-words data (vs. full documents). We simulate such a scenario for three sensitive classification tasks, demonstrating minimal performance degradation vs. releasing full language sequences.

title: A Structural Probe for Finding Syntax in Word Representations
abstract: Recent work has improved our ability to detect linguistic knowledge in word representations. However, current methods for detecting syntactic knowledge do not test whether syntax trees are represented in their entirety. In this work, we propose a structural probe, which evaluates whether syntax trees are embedded in a linear transformation of a neural network’s word representation space. The probe identifies a linear transformation under which squared L2 distance encodes the distance between words in the parse tree, and one in which squared L2 norm encodes depth in the parse tree. Using our probe, we show that such transformations exist for both ELMo and BERT but not in baselines, providing evidence that entire syntax trees are embedded implicitly in deep models’ vector geometry.
specific_phenomena: tree depth evaluation metrics

main_findings: Studies using structural probes reveal that language models like ELMo and BERT implicitly encode full syntactic parse trees within their word representation spaces. By applying simple linear transformations, researchers found that the geometry of these embeddings reflects key syntactic relationships: the squared L2 distance between transformed word vectors approximates their tree distance (i.e., the number of edges between them), and the squared L2 norm corresponds to each word’s depth in the parse tree. These properties—absent in baseline models—demonstrate that BERT and ELMo capture global and hierarchical syntax in a compact, low-rank subspace. Quantitatively, BERT (especially BERTLARGE) outperforms ELMo in syntactic encoding accuracy, with middle layers showing the strongest representation of syntactic structure.

title: Bird’s Eye: Probing for Linguistic Graph Structures with a Simple Information-Theoretic Approach
abstract: NLP has a rich history of representing our prior understanding of language in the form of graphs. Recent work on analyzing contextualized text representations has focused on hand-designed probe models to understand how and to what extent do these representations encode a particular linguistic phenomenon. However, due to the inter-dependence of various phenomena and randomness of training probe models, detecting how these representations encode the rich information in these linguistic graphs remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose a new information-theoretic probe, Bird’s Eye, which is a fairly simple probe method for detecting if and how these representations encode the information in these linguistic graphs. Instead of using model performance, our probe takes an information-theoretic view of probing and estimates the mutual information between the linguistic graph embedded in a continuous space and the contextualized word representations. Furthermore, we also propose an approach to use our probe to investigate localized linguistic information in the linguistic graphs using perturbation analysis. We call this probing setup Worm’s Eye. Using these probes, we analyze the BERT models on its ability to encode a syntactic and a semantic graph structure, and find that these models encode to some degree both syntactic as well as semantic information; albeit syntactic information to a greater extent.
specific_phenomena: dependency syntax (Marcus et al., 1993; De Marn- effe et al., 2006) and a more semantic formalism, AMR (Banarescu et al., 2013).

interp_method: Bird’s Eye Probe: probing for Syntactic and Semantic Graph Structures, Worm's Eye Probe (see abstract)
main_findings: The experiments using Bird’s Eye and Worm’s Eye information-theoretic probes show that BERT strongly captures syntactic structure, encoding syntax more effectively than semantics. The Bird’s Eye probe revealed that both BERT-base and BERT-large achieve high Mutual Information Gap (MIG) scores for syntactic structures (especially dependency syntax), outperforming non-contextual models like GloVe and ELMo-0, while scoring lower for semantic representations. Syntactic information is most prominent in BERT’s lower and middle layers, decreasing in upper layers. The Worm’s Eye probe further showed that BERT effectively encodes localized syntactic features, particularly proper nouns (NNP) and adjectives (JJ), while plural nouns (NNS) are less well represented. For dependency relations, prepositional modifiers (prep), objects of prepositions (pobj), and noun compound modifiers (nn) are strongly encoded, whereas nominal subject (nsubj) relations are weakest.

title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformer-based model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

It also showed that the amount of both syntactic and semantic information handled by the heads vary from layer to layer, sometimes showing that the last layer contributes much less especially with large models
main_findings: Analyses of attention heads in transformer-based language models (GPT, GPT-2, BERT, ELECTRA) reveal that syntactic knowledge is distributed across layers, with lower and mid-layers primarily responsible for encoding syntactic and surface-level information such as tree depth and constituent structure, while higher layers tend to focus more on semantic aspects. Mid-layer heads often specialize in syntactic tasks like subject number and coordinate inversion, indicating a syntactic–semantic progression through the network. Importantly, individual attention heads rarely specialize exclusively in syntax or semantics; instead, they capture both types of information in a balanced manner, though their relative contributions vary across layers and model sizes. Performance analyses show that internal layers often yield better representations for syntactic probing than the final layer, and constructing embeddings from top-performing attention heads significantly boosts accuracy—demonstrating that syntactic knowledge is both distributed and localized within specific, high-value attention heads.

title: Exploring Span Representations in Neural Coreference Resolution
abstract: In coreference resolution, span representations play a key role to predict coreference links accurately. We present a thorough examination of the span representation derived by applying BERT on coreference resolution (Joshi et al., 2019) using a probing model. Our results show that the span representation is able to encode a significant amount of coreference information. In addition, we find that the head-finding attention mechanism involved in creating the spans is crucial in encoding coreference knowledge. Last, our analysis shows that the span representation cannot capture non-local coreference as efficiently as local coreference.

fine_tuning_materials: fine-tuned on the coreference resolution task (i.e., on OntoNotes annotations) using 128 wordpieces for BERT-base and 384 wordpieces for BERT-large. The fine-tuned model is trained using split OntoNotes documents where each segment non-overlaps and is fed as a separate instance
