main_findings: demonstrates that span representations derived from BERT, especially when fine-tuned for coreference resolution on OntoNotes, encode substantial coreference information, with simple probing models achieving over 90% accuracy in predicting mention-span coreference. Fine-tuning markedly improves this encoding, though the models struggle with long-range coreference, showing decreased performance as the distance between mentions increases. A key finding is the crucial role of the head-finding attention mechanism, which identifies the head word within spans and significantly drives coreference prediction; ablation of this mechanism causes the largest performance drops. Span-width embeddings also contribute meaningfully, indicating the model leverages span size information, while boundary representations (first and last wordpieces) contribute minimally. Overall, the study highlights that BERT fine-tuned for coreference resolution relies heavily on internal span structure—linked to syntactic representation—to encode coreference knowledge effectively.

title: From General Language Understanding to Noisy Text Comprehension
abstract: Obtaining meaning-rich representations of social media inputs, such as Tweets (unstructured and noisy text), from general-purpose pre-trained language models has become challenging, as these inputs typically deviate from mainstream English usage. The proposed research establishes effective methods for improving the comprehension of noisy texts. For this, we propose a new generic methodology to derive a diverse set of sentence vectors combining and extracting various linguistic characteristics from latent representations of multi-layer, pre-trained language models. Further, we clearly establish how BERT, a state-of-the-art pre-trained language model, comprehends the linguistic attributes of Tweets to identify appropriate sentence representations. Five new probing tasks are developed for Tweets, which can serve as benchmark probing tasks to study noisy text comprehension. Experiments are carried out for classification accuracy by deriving the sentence vectors from GloVe-based pre-trained models and Sentence-BERT, and by using different hidden layers from the BERT model. We show that the initial and middle layers of BERT have better capability for capturing the key linguistic characteristics of noisy texts than its latter layers. With complex predictive models, we further show that the sentence vector length has lesser importance to capture linguistic information, and the proposed sentence vectors for noisy texts perform better than the existing state-of-the-art sentence vectors.

main_findings: The study on BERT’s linguistic comprehension, particularly with noisy text like Tweets, found that BERT effectively captures syntactic information, primarily within its middle layers (Region 2). Consistent with earlier research on standard English, the model encodes syntax strongly, with specific attention heads aligning to linguistic structures such as syntax trees and coreference. When tested on syntactic probing tasks—Bigram Shift (BShift) and Tree Depth (TreeDepth)—the best performance came from vectors generated in the middle layers, while shallow layers contributed less. Optimal performance varied by classifier: Logistic Regression favored vectors from all layers, while MLPs performed best using layers 1, 5, and 9. Compared to GloVe and Word2Vec, BERT’s sentence vectors achieved superior accuracy, confirming its robustness in representing syntactic features even in unstructured, noisy language. Overall, syntactic cues are most effectively captured in BERT’s initial and middle regions, rather than its top layers.

title: Spying on Your Neighbors: Fine-grained Probing of Contextual Embeddings for Information about Surrounding Words
abstract: Although models using contextual word embeddings have achieved state-of-the-art results on a host of NLP tasks, little is known about exactly what information these embeddings encode about the context words that they are understood to reflect. To address this question, we introduce a suite of probing tasks that enable fine-grained testing of contextual embeddings for encoding of information about surrounding words. We apply these tasks to examine the popular BERT, ELMo and GPT contextual encoders, and find that each of our tested information types is indeed encoded as contextual information across tokens, often with near-perfect recoverability—but the encoders vary in which features they distribute to which tokens, how nuanced their distributions are, and how robust the encoding of each feature is to distance. We discuss implications of these results for how different types of models break down and prioritize word-level context information when constructing token embeddings.

main_findings: the study finds that contextual embeddings from language models like BERT, ELMo, and GPT encode rich syntactic information, prioritizing abstract linguistic features over specific word identities. Noun number is robustly represented across all tokens, with bidirectional models (BERT and ELMo) maintaining strong encoding for both subjects and objects, while GPT reliably encodes subject number across subsequent tokens. Verb features are encoded less strongly, though the causative-inchoative alternation is consistently captured. Importantly, these syntactic representations are resilient to increased linear distance between words, indicating hierarchical sentence-level awareness, with deeper transformer models (BERT, GPT) showing more distance robustness than the shallower ELMo. Architectural nuances affect encoding patterns: bidirectional models distribute contextual information more selectively and encode features like number and animacy strongly, while GPT, being unidirectional, emphasizes earlier context over later context, reflecting differences in information prioritization and syntactic sensitivity.

title: Do Neural Language Models Show Preferences for Syntactic Formalisms?
abstract: Recent work on the interpretability of deep neural language models has concluded that many properties of natural language syntax are encoded in their representational spaces. However, such studies often suffer from limited scope by focusing on a single language and a single linguistic formalism. In this study, we aim to investigate the extent to which the semblance of syntactic structure captured by language models adheres to a surface-syntactic or deep syntactic style of analysis, and whether the patterns are consistent across different languages. We apply a probe for extracting directed dependency trees to BERT and ELMo models trained on 13 different languages, probing for two different syntactic annotation styles: Universal Dependencies (UD), prioritizing deep syntactic relations, and Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD), focusing on surface structure. We find that both models exhibit a preference for UD over SUD — with interesting variations across languages and layers — and that the strength of this preference is correlated with differences in tree shape.

main_findings: examined how well neural language models, specifically BERT and ELMo, capture syntactic structure according to Universal Dependencies (UD), emphasizing deep syntax, versus Surface-Syntactic UD (SUD), which emphasizes surface structure. Overall, both models showed a clear preference for UD across most languages, with BERT peaking around layer 7 and ELMo around layer 2–3. This preference is strongly linked to tree properties, particularly lower tree height in UD, and is most pronounced for function words (e.g., adpositions, auxiliaries, determiners), where UD’s strategy of directly connecting content words yields higher accuracy. Multilingual analysis revealed that languages rich in function words (e.g., Chinese, Hebrew, Hindi) favored UD, while agglutinative languages (e.g., Basque, Finnish, Turkish) showed minimal or reversed preference. BERT consistently outperformed ELMo due to its larger, deeper architecture, and experiments with fully supervised parsers indicated that SUD is not inherently harder to learn, confirming that the models’ UD preference reflects their internal syntactic biases rather than treebank difficulty.

title: Classifier Probes May Just Learn from Linear Context Features
abstract: Classifiers trained on auxiliary probing tasks are a popular tool to analyze the representations learned by neural sentence encoders such as BERT and ELMo. While many authors are aware of the difficulty to distinguish between “extracting the linguistic structure encoded in the representations” and “learning the probing task,” the validity of probing methods calls for further research. Using a neighboring word identity prediction task, we show that the token embeddings learned by neural sentence encoders contain a significant amount of information about the exact linear context of the token, and hypothesize that, with such information, learning standard probing tasks may be feasible even without additional linguistic structure. We develop this hypothesis into a framework in which analysis efforts can be scrutinized and argue that, with current models and baselines, conclusions that representations contain linguistic structure are not well-founded. Current probing methodology, such as restricting the classifier’s expressiveness or using strong baselines, can help to better estimate the complexity of learning, but not build a foundation for speculations about the nature of the linguistic structure encoded in the learned representations.
specific_phenomena: syntactic dependency parsing
experimental_materials_comment: based on the English Web Treebank data set from the Universal Dependencies (UD) project (Nivre et al., 2018)
interp_method: simple classifier trained on these models’ representations can reconstruct the words in the context of single tokens with surprisingly high accuracy. Based on this observation, we propose to evaluate probes with regard to the context-only hypothesis: That the probing classifier learns the task based on linear context information alone
main_findings: Recent analyses of language model (LM) representations, particularly in BERT and ELMo, reveal that much of their apparent syntactic knowledge may instead reflect encoding of linear context rather than deeper linguistic structure. Token embeddings contain substantial information about neighboring words, enabling high accuracy in predicting nearby tokens, which can explain strong performance on many probing tasks without requiring genuine syntactic understanding. The Context-Only Hypothesis formalizes this, asserting that probes may rely solely on adjacent word information, challenging the reliability of standard probing methods and common baselines, which often cannot distinguish true syntactic knowledge from simple context memorization. Experiments restricting probe expressiveness or training data further show that uncontextualized embeddings sometimes outperform contextualized layers in syntactic tasks, undermining previous interpretations of a “pipeline” of linguistic processing across layers. Instead, layer-wise performance may largely reflect the layer’s capacity to capture local versus broader linear context, offering a context-driven, rather than linguistically structural, explanation for prior findings.

title: Test Harder than You Train: Probing with Extrapolation Splits
abstract: Previous work on probing word representations for linguistic knowledge has focused on interpolation tasks. In this paper, we instead analyse probes in an extrapolation setting, where the inputs at test time are deliberately chosen to be ‘harder’ than the training examples. We argue that such an analysis can shed further light on the open question whether probes actually decode linguistic knowledge, or merely learn the diagnostic task from shallow features. To quantify the hardness of an example, we consider scoring functions based on linguistic, statistical, and learning-related criteria, all of which are applicable to a broad range of NLP tasks. We discuss the relative merits of these criteria in the context of two syntactic probing tasks, part-of-speech tagging and syntactic dependency labelling. From our theoretical and experimental analysis, we conclude that distance-based and hard statistical criteria show the clearest differences between interpolation and extrapolation settings, while at the same time being transparent, intuitive, and easy to control.
specific_phenomena: part-of-speech (POS) tagging and syntactic dependency labelling.
experimental_materials_comment: English Web Treebank (EWT) as released by the Universal Dependencies project (Nivre et al., 2020) (v2.5). More specif- ically, we extract our examples from two 1,000- sentence sets Strain and Stest, randomly sampled from the training and the development section of the EWT, respectively.
interp_method: enriching probing experiments with automated extrapolation setups can be a valu- able supplement to standard probing methods, as it gives us an instrument to test the generalisation ca- pability of the probe, and thereby the robustness of the features it use
main_findings: examines how well BERT’s contextualized representations encode syntactic knowledge under extrapolation conditions, where probes are trained on “easy” examples and tested on “hard” ones, focusing on POS tagging (T1) and dependency labeling (T2). Overall, the LM shows limited but non-random generalization, with substantially lower accuracy than standard interpolation setups, and performance varying with the hardness criterion. Structural criteria like arc length for T2 and most frequent tag for T1 were most informative: short arcs or less frequent tags sharply reduced extrapolation accuracy, highlighting that early layers rely on word-specific information while higher layers encode more generalizable patterns. Sentence length was largely uninformative, while learning-based criteria (speed of learning, sample-specific loss) also revealed generalization limits but were less interpretable. The study concludes that automated extrapolation probing provides a useful framework to test probes’ generalization and exposes where LMs fail to leverage abstract syntactic knowledge, with arc length and most frequent tag being the clearest indicators of these limits.

title: Where Does Linguistic Information Emerge in Neural Language Models? Measuring Gains and Contributions across Layers
abstract: Probing studies have extensively explored where in neural language models linguistic information is located. The standard approach to interpreting the results of a probing classifier is to focus on the layers whose representations give the highest performance on the probing task. We propose an alternative method that asks where the task-relevant information emerges in the model. Our framework consists of a family of metrics that explicitly model local information gain relative to the previous layer and each layer’s contribution to the model’s overall performance. We apply the new metrics to two pairs of syntactic probing tasks with different degrees of complexity and find that the metrics confirm the expected ordering only for one of the pairs. Our local metrics show a massive dominance of the first layers, indicating that the features that contribute the most to our probing tasks are not as high-level as global metrics suggest.

main_findings: the study on linguistic information distribution in language models, particularly syntactic knowledge, highlights a distinction between global and local metrics, revealing different insights about where and how information is stored. Global metrics, which measure overall usable information, indicate that the middle layers of BERT contain the most syntactic knowledge, with a weakly supported hierarchy where grandparent prediction peaks slightly later than parent prediction. In contrast, local metrics, which measure layer-wise information gain, show that the earliest layers dominate, suggesting that most new, useful syntactic features emerge very shallowly, and the expected parent–grandparent hierarchy is largely absent when considering maximum local gains. However, fine-grained local metrics like Emergent Information (EMI) do partially confirm the hierarchy, with early layers contributing more to parent predictions than to grandparent predictions. Overall, these findings reveal that information localization is highly sensitive to the evaluation method and that the observed patterns are not robust across languages or BERT variants, emphasizing the need for careful metric selection when probing linguistic hierarchies.

title: Decoding BERT’s Internal Processing of Garden-Path Structures through Attention Maps
abstract: Recent advancements in deep learning neural models, such as BERT, have demonstrated remarkable performance in natural language processing tasks, yet understanding their internal processing remains a challenge. This study employs the method of examining attention maps to uncover the internal processing of BERT, specifically when dealing with garden-path sentences. The analysis focuses on BERT's utilization of linguistic cues, such as transitivity, plausibility, and the presence of a comma, and evaluates its capacity for reanalyzing misinterpretations. The results revealed that BERT exhibits human-like syntactic processing by attending to the presence of a comma, showing sensitivity to transitivity, and reanalyzing misinterpretations, despite initially lacking sensitivity to plausibility. By concentrating on attention maps, the present study provides valuable insights into the inner workings of BERT and contributes to a deeper understanding of how advanced neural language models acquire and process complex linguistic structures.
specific_phenomena: manifestation of the garden-path effect (caused by subject-object ambiguity) and in the employment of transitivity and plausibility
experimental_materials_comment: a total of 48 garden-path sentences, distinguished by the incorporation of two distinct linguistic cues: transitivity and plausibility, with each represented in 24 instances. These sentences are characterized by an initial subject-object ambiguity, a structural feature that generates temporary processing difficulties.
Mechanistic_method: behavioral approach, Attention Analysis (Attention Maps, Attention Weights)
interp_method: nan
main_findings: investigated BERT’s syntactic processing using attention maps, focusing on garden-path sentences and the use of linguistic cues. It found that BERT exhibits human-like syntactic behavior, initially misinterpreting ambiguous structures due to the garden-path effect but successfully reanalyzing them to recover correct subject-verb dependencies. Attention to the direct object (dobj) relation increased in longer sentences and transitive contexts, reflecting sensitivity to structural cues, while attention to the subject-verb (nsubj) relation remained stable, indicating reliable recovery of the main clause structure. BERT showed strong sensitivity to transitivity but little sensitivity to plausibility in the examined attention head, suggesting that semantic cues may be processed by other heads or aggregated elsewhere. Overall, the findings reveal that BERT can internally track complex syntactic dependencies and utilize structural information to resolve ambiguities, paralleling human sentence processing.

title: (AL)BERT Down the Garden Path: Psycholinguistic Experiments for Pre-trained Language Models
abstract: This study compared the syntactic capabilities of several neural language models (LMs) including Transformers (BERT / ALBERT) and LSTM and investigated whether they exhibit human-like syntactic representations through a targeted evaluation approach, a method to evaluate the syntactic processing ability of LMs using sentences designed for psycholinguistic experiments. By employing garden- path structures with several linguistic manipulations, whether LMs detect temporary ungrammaticality and use a linguistic cue such as plausibility, transitivity, and morphology is assessed. The results showed that both Transformers and LSTM exploited several linguistic cues for incremental syntactic processing, comparable to human syntactic processing. They differed, however, in terms of whether and how they use each linguistic cue. Overall, Transformers had a more human-like syntactic representation than LSTM, given their higher sensitivity to plausibility and ability to retain information from previous words. Meanwhile, the number of parameters does not seem to undermine the performance of LMs, contrary to what was predicted in previous studies. Through these findings, this research sought to contribute to a greater understanding of the syntactic processing of neural language models as well as human language processing

main_findings: found that ALBERT, BERT, and LSTM language models exhibit human-like incremental syntactic processing, particularly in detecting temporary ungrammaticality in garden-path sentences and using linguistic cues such as transitivity, morphology, clausal boundaries, and relative clauses. All models were highly sensitive to transitivity and morphological cues, showing stronger garden-path effects in transitive or morphologically ambiguous contexts, whereas sensitivity to plausibility was weaker and only significant in the largest Transformer models (bert-large, albert-xxlarge). While no major architecture-wide differences were statistically significant, Transformers generally displayed more human-like syntactic representations than LSTMs, retaining information over longer sentences and showing greater sensitivity to plausibility, unlike LSTMs, which lost prior word information as sentence length increased. Finally, a larger number of parameters did not impair performance; in fact, the largest models performed best in plausibility-sensitive tasks, suggesting parameter count can enhance syntactic and semantic sensitivity.

title: Empirical Linguistic Study of Sentence Embeddings
abstract: The purpose of the research is to answer the question whether linguistic information is retained in vector representations of sentences. We introduce a method of analysing the content of sentence embeddings based on universal probing tasks, along with the classification datasets for two contrasting languages. We perform a series of probing and downstream experiments with different types of sentence embeddings, followed by a thorough analysis of the experimental results. Aside from dependency parser-based embeddings, linguistic information is retained best in the recently proposed LASER sentence embeddings.

main_findings: The study on the retention of syntactic knowledge in language model (LM) sentence embeddings found that models explicitly trained for dependency parsing, particularly COMBO-based embeddings, retained linguistic information most accurately across nearly all compositional probing tasks (e.g., TreeDepth, Passive, Tense, SubjNum, ObjNum), likely aided by an “information leak” from using similar parsing architectures. Among general-purpose embeddings, LASER demonstrated the strongest performance, excelling in 17 of 22 task-language pairs, likely due to its training on massive multilingual corpora despite its relatively simple BiLSTM architecture. Additional observations include that MEAN-pooled embeddings generally outperform MAX-pooled variants, and model performance shows high cross-linguistic consistency, with English and Polish yielding similar relative results. The study emphasizes a compositional approach to syntactic probing, focusing on tasks like passive voice, tense, tree depth, top dependency structures, and grammatical number, highlighting that embeddings capture syntactic properties reliably even across typologically diverse languages.

title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious—i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model’s representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.
specific_phenomena: grammatical number
experimental_materials_comment: Linzen et al.’s (2016) number agreement dataset, which consists of sentences extracted from Wikipedia. In this dataset, each sentence has been labeled with the po- sition of the cue and target, along with their gram- matical number.
interp_method: perform analyses using independent sets of representations for nouns and verbs; as well as a mixed set which merges both of them. Further, verbs are masked when performing the number agreement task, so their representations differ from those of unmasked verbs. Ergo, we analyze both unmasked and masked tokens at the target verb’s position—which for simplicity we call verbs and masked verbs, respectively. This leaves us with four probed cat- egories: nouns, verbs, masked-verbs, and mixed
main_findings: investigates how BERT encodes and uses grammatical number to solve subject–verb number agreement, revealing three key findings. First, BERT employs a linear functional encoding of number, confirmed by amnesic probing showing that erasing this information directly impairs task performance. Second, the encoding is disjoint for nouns and verbs, with separate subspaces for each category, as interventions targeting one do not affect the other. Third, the transfer of number information from subject to verb occurs mainly between BERT’s 3rd and 8th layers and is largely indirect, passing through other tokens in the sentence, though the noun remains the core source of number information. Overall, the study highlights that BERT’s handling of grammatical number is both linear and functionally distinct across lexical categories, with a layered, syntactically mediated mechanism for information transfer.

title: Universal Dependencies According to BERT: Both More Specific and More General
abstract: This work focuses on analyzing the form and extent of syntactic abstraction captured by BERT by extracting labeled dependency trees from self-attentions. Previous work showed that individual BERT heads tend to encode particular dependency relation types. We extend these findings by explicitly comparing BERT relations to Universal Dependencies (UD) annotations, showing that they often do not match one-to-one. We suggest a method for relation identification and syntactic tree construction. Our approach produces significantly more consistent dependency trees than previous work, showing that it better explains the syntactic abstractions in BERT. At the same time, it can be successfully applied with only a minimal amount of supervision and generalizes well across languages.

We use another PUD treebanks from the CoNLL 2017 Shared Task for evaluation of mBERT in all languages (Nivre et al., 2017)3.

main_findings: Research on syntactic knowledge in BERT and mBERT reveals that syntactic information is both localized in specific attention heads and distributed across multiple heads, with combining these heads into ensembles substantially improving dependency relation extraction. While BERT’s latent syntax diverges systematically from standard Universal Dependencies (UD) annotations—requiring modifications for phenomena like copulas, expletives, and coordination—these adjustments improve accuracy, particularly for nominal subjects. Some heads are multipurpose, capturing multiple syntactic relations, and mBERT demonstrates cross-lingual consistency in encoding relations, especially subjects. For dependency tree extraction, head ensembles yield more consistent and accurate trees, requiring minimal supervision (as few as 10 annotated sentences), though performance is lower for SOV languages compared to SVO languages, likely reflecting corpus composition in mBERT’s pre-training. Overall, the findings highlight that BERT’s attention heads encode rich, partially language-independent syntactic knowledge that can be effectively leveraged with minimal annotation and careful head selection.

title: Introducing Orthogonal Constraint in Structural Probes
abstract: With the recent success of pre-trained models in NLP, a significant focus was put on interpreting their representations. One of the most prominent approaches is structural probing (Hewitt and Manning, 2019), where a linear projection of word embeddings is performed in order to approximate the topology of dependency structures. In this work, we introduce a new type of structural probing, where the linear projection is decomposed into 1. iso-morphic space rotation; 2. linear scaling that identifies and scales the most relevant dimensions. In addition to syntactic dependency, we evaluate our method on two novel tasks (lexical hypernymy and position in a sentence). We jointly train the probes for multiple tasks and experimentally show that lexical and syntactic information is separated in the representations. Moreover, the orthogonal constraint makes the Structural Probes less vulnerable to memorization.
specific_phenomena: Dependency Syntax , Position in a Sentence
experimental_materials_comment: test sentences from Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank (Silveira et al., 2014).
interp_method: introduction of an orthogonal constraint: he sufficient rank of a transformation is learned during the optimization. The rank regularization is a prerequisite to disentangle the information encoded by the probe (Section 5.2
main_findings: The analysis of BERT large cased using Orthogonal Structural Probes (OSP) reveals that syntactic knowledge, particularly dependency syntax, is effectively captured in the model and can be reliably probed. OSPs achieve high correlations for dependency depth (0.858) and distance (0.842), comparable to standard probes but more resistant to memorizing random structures. Syntactic information is primarily concentrated in the mid-to-upper layers (Layer 16–17) and is stored in low-rank, focal subspaces (137–189 dimensions within a 1024-dimensional embedding), often orthogonal to lexical information, indicating a clear separation of syntactic and lexical representations. Dependency syntax overlaps substantially with positional information, suggesting structural cues are partially encoded through word order. OSPs can also be applied to parsing, achieving a UAS of 77.51% by jointly probing for dependency distance and depth, demonstrating that the representations contain sufficient structural information for practical extraction tasks.

title: Probing via Prompting
abstract: Probing is a popular approach to understand what linguistic information is contained in the representations of pre-trained language models. However, the mechanism of selecting the probe model has recently been subject to intense debate, as it is not clear if the probes are merely extracting information or modelling the linguistic property themselves. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel model-free approach to probing via prompting, which formulates probing as a prompting task. We conduct experiments on five probing tasks and show that PP is comparable or better at extracting information than diagnostic probes while learning much less on its own. We further combine the probing via prompting approach with pruning to analyze where the model stores the linguistic information in its architecture. Finally, we apply the probing via prompting approach to examine the usefulness of a linguistic property for pre-training by removing the heads that are essential to it and evaluating the resulting model’s performance on language modeling.

main_findings: Analysis of BERT large cased using Orthogonal Structural Probes (OSP) reveals that syntactic knowledge, particularly dependency syntax, is effectively captured and localized in mid-to-upper layers (especially Layer 16–17), with high Spearman correlations for dependency depth (0.858) and distance (0.842) comparable to Standard Structural Probes, but with less vulnerability to memorizing random structures. Syntactic information is stored in relatively low-dimensional, focal subspaces (137–189 of 1024 dimensions) that are largely orthogonal to lexical information, while dependency depth subspaces are largely contained within dependency distance subspaces. There is partial overlap with positional information, suggesting that relative word positions contribute to syntactic inference. Finally, OSPs can be applied to dependency parsing, achieving a 77.51% Unlabeled Attachment Score, demonstrating that the representations encode dependency structures sufficiently for extraction.

title: How is BERT surprised? Layerwise detection of linguistic anomalies
abstract: Transformer language models have shown remarkable ability in detecting when a word is anomalous in context, but likelihood scores offer no information about the cause of the anomaly. In this work, we use Gaussian models for density estimation at intermediate layers of three language models (BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet), and evaluate our method on BLiMP, a grammaticality judgement benchmark. In lower layers, surprisal is highly correlated to low token frequency, but this correlation diminishes in upper layers. Next, we gather datasets of morphosyntactic, semantic, and commonsense anomalies from psycholinguistic studies; we find that the best performing model RoBERTa exhibits surprisal in earlier layers when the anomaly is morphosyntactic than when it is semantic, while commonsense anomalies do not exhibit surprisal at any intermediate layer. These results suggest that language models employ separate mechanisms to detect different types of linguistic anomalies.

main_findings: investigates how Transformer language models (BERT, RoBERTa, XLNet) detect and process morphosyntactic anomalies using a Gaussian model (GM) to measure layerwise surprisal. The study finds that morphosyntactic anomalies trigger high surprisal in earlier layers (e.g., layers 3–4 in RoBERTa) compared to semantic anomalies, indicating that LMs process syntactic information before semantic or commonsense content. The GM approach achieves high accuracy on morphosyntactic tasks, particularly with RoBERTa, and shows model-dependent sensitivity: BERT and XLNet detect mainly morphosyntactic anomalies, while semantic and commonsense anomalies elicit later or minimal surprisal. Semantic violations appear at later layers (layers 9+), and commonsense anomalies rarely produce high surprisal. Additionally, lower-layer surprisal is influenced by token frequency, with rarer tokens producing higher surprisal. Overall, the findings highlight that LMs internally distinguish anomaly types hierarchically, with syntactic structure assessed early in intermediate layers, a pattern consistent with prior probing studies.

title: Linguistic Knowledge and Transferability of Contextual Representations
abstract: Contextual word representations derived from large-scale neural language models are successful across a diverse set of NLP tasks, suggesting that they encode useful and transferable features of language. To shed light on the linguistic knowledge they capture, we study the representations produced by several recent pretrained contextualizers (variants of ELMo, the OpenAI transformer language model, and BERT) with a suite of seventeen diverse probing tasks. We find that linear models trained on top of frozen contextual representations are competitive with state-of-the-art task-specific models in many cases, but fail on tasks requiring fine-grained linguistic knowledge (e.g., conjunct identification). To investigate the transferability of contextual word representations, we quantify differences in the transferability of individual layers within contextualizers, especially between recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers. For instance, higher layers of RNNs are more task-specific, while transformer layers do not exhibit the same monotonic trend. In addition, to better understand what makes contextual word representations transferable, we compare language model pretraining with eleven supervised pretraining tasks. For any given task, pretraining on a closely related task yields better performance than language model pretraining (which is better on average) when the pretraining dataset is fixed. However, language model pretraining on more data gives the best results.

main_findings: Contextual Word Representations (CWRs) derived from language models encode strong but uneven syntactic knowledge. Linear probes show that CWRs effectively capture basic and general syntax—including part-of-speech tagging, syntactic roles, chunking, and dependency relations—often rivaling specialized models and demonstrating stronger syntactic than semantic encoding. However, they struggle with fine-grained and hierarchical syntax, such as identifying conjuncts or predicting a word’s higher-level ancestors in phrase-structure trees, indicating that such detailed syntactic structures are not fully represented. When additional task-specific contextualization is added, performance improves substantially, suggesting that while the information is learnable, it is not explicitly encoded in pretrained representations. Layerwise analyses reveal that LSTM-based models (e.g., ELMo) store the most transferable features in lower layers, while Transformer models (e.g., BERT) distribute syntactic knowledge more evenly, with mid-layers offering the highest generality.

title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT’s representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT’s representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT’s representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

main_findings: Research on BERT’s syntactic knowledge shows that the model transitions from encoding linear information in its lower layers to hierarchical linguistic structure in its higher layers. Diagnostic classifiers revealed that while early layers capture positional word information, later layers abstract and represent syntactic relationships, enabling generalization to complex constructions such as identifying the main auxiliary or subject noun. However, performance declines in cases involving ambiguous structures like possessives, suggesting reliance on local rather than fully global syntactic cues. Diagnostic attention analyses using a “confusion score” further showed that BERT’s attention is sensitive but imperfect in modeling syntactic dependencies such as subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora: it partially captures grammatical structure but remains influenced by distractor phrases, indicating incomplete hierarchical sensitivity. Overall, BERT encodes increasingly abstract and structurally relevant syntactic information across layers, though its representations fall short of human-like grammatical precision.

title: Predicting Inductive Biases of Pre-Trained Models
abstract: Most current NLP systems are based on a pre-train-then-fine-tune paradigm, in which a large neural network is first trained in a self-supervised way designed to encourage the network to extract broadly-useful linguistic features, and then fine-tuned for a specific task of interest. Recent work attempts to understand why this recipe works and explain when it fails. Currently, such analyses have produced two sets of apparently-contradictory results. Work that analyzes the representations that result from pre-training (via "probing classifiers") finds evidence that rich features of linguistic structure can be decoded with high accuracy, but work that analyzes model behavior after fine-tuning (via "challenge sets") indicates that decisions are often not based on such structure but rather on spurious heuristics specific to the training set. In this work, we test the hypothesis that the extent to which a feature influences a model's decisions can be predicted using a combination of two factors: The feature's "extractability" after pre-training (measured using information-theoretic probing techniques), and the "evidence" available during fine-tuning (defined as the feature's co-occurrence rate with the label). In experiments with both synthetic and natural language data, we find strong evidence (statistically significant correlations) supporting this hypothesis.

main_findings: The research reconciles conflicting findings about large language models’ (LMs) syntactic knowledge by showing that the key factor determining whether an LM relies on genuine structural features or spurious heuristics is the relative extractability of those features after pre-training. While probing studies show that models like BERT and T5 encode rich syntactic information, challenge-set results reveal that fine-tuned models often ignore this knowledge, defaulting to easier heuristics. The study demonstrates that this discrepancy arises because fine-tuned models preferentially use features that are easier to extract from their internal representations. Using prequential Minimum Description Length (MDL) as a measure of extractability, the authors find a strong correlation between the ratio of a target feature’s extractability (e.g., syntactic dependency) to that of a spurious one (e.g., lexical overlap) and model behavior across tasks like subject-verb agreement and filler-gap dependencies. When syntactic features are at least as extractable as surface ones, models naturally adopt the correct structural generalization, even with minimal fine-tuning data; otherwise, they remain trapped by heuristics. Thus, fine-tuning success depends less on data quantity and more on how pre-training shapes the inductive bias through relative feature accessibility.

title: Probing Across Time: What Does RoBERTa Know and When?
abstract: Models of language trained on very large corpora have been demonstrated useful for natural language processing. As fixed artifacts, they have become the object of intense study, with many researchers “probing” the extent to which they acquire and readily demonstrate linguistic abstractions, factual and commonsense knowledge, and reasoning abilities. Recent work applied several probes to intermediate training stages to observe the developmental process of a large-scale model (Chiang et al., 2020). Following this effort, we systematically answer a question: for various types of knowledge a language model learns, when during (pre)training are they acquired? Using RoBERTa as a case study, we find: linguistic knowledge is acquired fast, stably, and robustly across domains. Facts and commonsense are slower and more domain-sensitive. Reasoning abilities are, in general, not stably acquired. As new datasets, pretraining protocols, and probes emerge, we believe that probing-across-time analyses can help researchers understand the complex, intermingled learning that these models undergo and guide us toward more efficient approaches that accomplish necessary learning faster.

main_findings: The "probing across time" analysis of RoBERTa reveals that linguistic knowledge, particularly syntax, is acquired rapidly, robustly, and stably early in pretraining, in contrast to factual, commonsense, or reasoning knowledge, which is slower or unstable. Using both structural LKT probes and behavioral BLIMP probes, the study found that RoBERTa achieves most of its syntactic learning (about 97% of performance improvement) within roughly 20% of total training steps, with minimal sensitivity to domain or corpus size variations. This rapid acquisition of linguistic knowledge also aligns with downstream task performance, as simpler benchmarks like CoLA and SST-2 reach near-maximal performance even earlier, highlighting that core syntactic capabilities emerge early and reliably during pretraining.

title: Have Attention Heads in BERT Learned Constituency Grammar?
abstract: With the success of pre-trained language models in recent years, more and more researchers focus on opening the “black box” of these models. Following this interest, we carry out a qualitative and quantitative analysis of constituency grammar in attention heads of BERT and RoBERTa. We employ the syntactic distance method to extract implicit constituency grammar from the attention weights of each head. Our results show that there exist heads that can induce some grammar types much better than baselines, suggesting that some heads act as a proxy for constituency grammar. We also analyze how attention heads’ constituency grammar inducing (CGI) ability changes after fine-tuning with two kinds of tasks, including sentence meaning similarity (SMS) tasks and natural language inference (NLI) tasks. Our results suggest that SMS tasks decrease the average CGI ability of upper layers, while NLI tasks increase it. Lastly, we investigate the connections between CGI ability and natural language understanding ability on QQP and MNLI tasks.

main_findings: examined how BERT and RoBERTa encode syntactic knowledge, specifically constituency grammar, in their attention heads and how this relates to NLU performance. Using the syntactic distance method to extract implicit constituency trees, the researchers found that pre-trained models only partially learn constituency grammar, with attention heads performing slightly better than right-branching baselines but effectively inducing certain phrase types like NP, PP, ADJP, and ADVP. CGI ability varies by layer: higher layers in BERT and middle layers in RoBERTa show stronger abilities. Fine-tuning affects this ability differently depending on the task: NLI tasks generally enhance CGI in higher layers, improving phrase induction, while SMS tasks decrease it, and overall improvements in parsing are modest. In terms of NLU performance, BERT’s attention heads with higher CGI ability are more critical for tasks like QQP and MNLI, whereas in RoBERTa the relationship is weaker and task-dependent. These findings suggest that while some syntactic knowledge is present and useful, explicit formalized syntax may not be strictly necessary for NLU in these models.

title: From Balustrades to Pierre Vinken: Looking for Syntax in Transformer Self-Attentions
abstract: We inspect the multi-head self-attention in Transformer NMT encoders for three source languages, looking for patterns that could have a syntactic interpretation. In many of the attention heads, we frequently find sequences of consecutive states attending to the same position, which resemble syntactic phrases. We propose a transparent deterministic method of quantifying the amount of syntactic information present in the self-attentions, based on automatically building and evaluating phrase-structure trees from the phrase-like sequences. We compare the resulting trees to existing constituency treebanks, both manually and by computing precision and recall.
specific_phenomena: Constituency tree generated by our tree extraction algorithm from the attention matrices of the ende encoder , attention balustrades, seem to capture syntactic structures
experimental_materials_comment: MT
Mechanistic_method: Feature Visualization ( heatmaps of self-attention weights), inguistically uninformed tree extraction algorithm
interp_method: transparent linguistically uninformed algorithm for extracting constituency trees from the balusters, compared the resulting trees with standard syntactic parse trees, and showed that syntax is indeed captured
main_findings: the analysis of the Transformer NMT encoder reveals that its self-attention mechanism captures substantial syntactic knowledge, evidenced both qualitatively and quantitatively. Qualitatively, recurring “balustrade” patterns in attention matrices—vertical sequences spanning subwords—often correspond to syntactic phrases and nested structures, suggesting implicit constituency representations. Quantitatively, a linguistically uninformed algorithm extracting binary constituency trees from these patterns achieved F1 scores 6–13 points higher than uninformed baselines across English, German, and French, with better performance for German and French due to flatter syntactic structures. This syntactic knowledge is localized in a subset of attention heads—typically one-third of heads in the first layer and portions of the last layers—whose selective use further boosts tree quality by 3–10 points. However, the encoder captures only partial syntactic structures relevant to translation, and its representations may not fully align with classical syntactic trees.

title: Probing Tasks Under Pressure
abstract: Probing tasks are frequently used to evaluate whether the representations of Neural Language Models (NLMs) encode linguistic information. However, it is still questioned if probing classification tasks really enable such investigation or they simply hint for surface patterns in the data. We present a method to investigate this question by comparing the accuracies of a set of probing tasks on gold and automatically generated control datasets. Our results suggest that probing tasks can be used as reliable diagnostic methods to investigate the linguistic information encoded in NLMs representations.

main_findings: The study investigating linguistic competence in an Italian BERT using probing tasks found that the model largely relies on implicit linguistic knowledge when predicting authentic linguistic features, as evidenced by higher accuracy for gold feature values compared to automatically altered controls. The model could discriminate between real and manipulated features, indicating it goes beyond surface patterns, though length-constrained controls slightly improved predictions due to superficial similarities. In terms of syntactic knowledge, features related to sentence tree structure and subordination were predicted most accurately, but this likely reflects BERT’s encoding of sentence length rather than purely abstract syntactic understanding. Other syntactic features were predicted with low accuracy, and top-ranked features often acted as proxies for sentence length, such as syntactic root distribution, verbal heads, and sentence boundary punctuation. Overall, the findings suggest that while Italian BERT encodes linguistic competence, its syntactic predictions are heavily influenced by length-related cues rather than fully abstract structural knowledge.

title: Testing the Effectiveness of the Diagnostic Probing Paradigm on Italian Treebanks
abstract: The outstanding performance recently reached by neural language models (NLMs) across many natural language processing (NLP) tasks has steered the debate towards understanding whether NLMs implicitly learn linguistic competence. Probes, i.e., supervised models trained using NLM representations to predict linguistic properties, are frequently adopted to investigate this issue. However, it is still questioned if probing classification tasks really enable such investigation or if they simply hint at surface patterns in the data. This work contributes to this debate by presenting an approach to assessing the effectiveness of a suite of probing tasks aimed at testing the linguistic knowledge implicitly encoded by one of the most prominent NLMs, BERT. To this aim, we compared the performance of probes when predicting gold and automatically altered values of a set of linguistic features. Our experiments were performed on Italian and were evaluated across BERT’s layers and for sentences with different lengths. As a general result, we observed higher performance in the prediction of gold values, thus suggesting that the probing model is sensitive to the distortion of feature values. However, our experiments also showed that the length of a sentence is a highly influential factor that is able to confound the probing model’s predictions.

main_findings: the study applied diagnostic probing to BERT’s Italian representations and found that the model reliably encodes linguistic knowledge, especially syntactic information, as probes performed better on authentic feature values than on altered controls. For standard-length sentences (10–30 tokens), dependency relations and parts of speech were best encoded in early layers, complex syntactic patterns like subject–object order emerged in middle layers, and verbal predicate complexity was weakly represented across layers. Sentence length strongly influenced probing outcomes: features related to syntactic structure and subordination were sensitive to length, suggesting reliance on length as a proxy, while subject–object order was less affected. Analyses of very short (≤9 tokens) and long (31–100 tokens) sentences confirmed these patterns, with short sentences showing higher mastery of structural and ordering features, and long sentences exhibiting similar hierarchical encoding as standard sentences, indicating BERT’s syntactic knowledge is robust across sentence lengths but varies in depth depending on feature type and complexity.

title: Linguistic Profiling of a Neural Language Model
abstract: In this paper we investigate the linguistic knowledge learned by a Neural Language Model (NLM) before and after a fine-tuning process and how this knowledge affects its predictions during several classification problems. We use a wide set of probing tasks, each of which corresponds to a distinct sentence-level feature extracted from different levels of linguistic annotation. We show that BERT is able to encode a wide range of linguistic characteristics, but it tends to lose this information when trained on specific downstream tasks. We also find that BERT’s capacity to encode different kind of linguistic properties has a positive influence on its predictions: the more it stores readable linguistic information of a sentence, the higher will be its capacity of predicting the expected label assigned to that sentence.

main_findings: The study on BERT’s linguistic knowledge, using 68 sentence-level probing tasks across lexical, morpho-syntactic, and syntactic properties, shows that pre-trained BERT encodes a broad range of linguistic features, which positively impact downstream tasks like NLI. While fine-tuning on specific tasks can reduce the precision of general linguistic knowledge—particularly in higher layers—BERT’s middle layers robustly capture syntactic information, including word order, subordination, and verbal predicate structures. Global and local tree structures are especially well encoded, though sensitivity to sentence length varies across features. Notably, performance differs even within the same syntactic group, with some dependency relations predicted more accurately than others. Layerwise clustering revealed that BERT does not strictly separate syntactic and morphological features, instead forming mixed clusters reflecting hierarchical sentence properties. Crucially, sentences correctly classified in NLI tend to be longer and more complex, indicating that BERT’s deeper syntactic knowledge contributes directly to downstream task success.

title: Contextual and Non-Contextual Word Embeddings: an in-depth Linguistic Investigation
abstract: In this paper we present a comparison between the linguistic knowledge encoded in the internal representations of a contextual Language Model (BERT) and a contextual-independent one (Word2vec). We use a wide set of probing tasks, each of which corresponds to a distinct sentence-level feature extracted from different levels of linguistic annotation. We show that, although BERT is capable of understanding the full context of each word in an input sequence, the implicit knowledge encoded in its aggregated sentence representations is still comparable to that of a contextual-independent model. We also find that BERT is able to encode sentence-level properties even within single-word embeddings, obtaining comparable or even superior results than those obtained with sentence representations.

main_findings: the study on syntactic knowledge in BERT reveals that, compared to non-contextual models like Word2vec, BERT effectively encodes syntactic information both in aggregated sentence representations and in single-word embeddings. BERT’s sentence-level representations show particular strength in capturing syntactic properties, with aggregation methods such as Sum performing best for syntactic features, while Mean works well for other tasks; yet, overall linguistic knowledge in BERT’s aggregated embeddings is comparable to Word2vec. Remarkably, BERT’s single-word embeddings also encode sentence-level syntax, often outperforming Word2vec and sometimes approaching the performance of aggregated embeddings, with the last token being the most informative for syntactic probing. Layer-wise analysis indicates that BERT’s ability to encode linguistic properties peaks around layer -8, declining in higher layers where task-specific information dominates, reflecting a trade-off between general syntactic knowledge and task-focused representations.

title: Italian Transformers Under the Linguistic Lens
abstract: In this paper we present an in-depth investigation of the linguistic knowledge encoded by the transformer models currently available for the Italian language. In particular, we investigate whether and how using different architectures of probing models affects the performance of Italian transformers in encoding a wide spectrum of linguistic features. Moreover, we explore how this implicit knowledge varies according to different textual genres.

main_findings: The investigation into the syntactic knowledge encoded by Italian Language Models (LMs) using probing tasks revealed several key findings. The study, using 82 probing features across nine groups, examined various aspects of syntactic knowledge such as parsed tree structures, element order, syntactic relations, subordination, and verbal predicate structures. The choice of probing model architecture significantly impacted performance, with Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) models outperforming Linear Support Vector Regression (SVR), especially on complex tasks. Different transformer models like BERT-based variants showed varying performance on specific syntactic tasks, with GePpeTto excelling in syntactic dependencies and GilBERTo in tree structure prediction. Layerwise analysis revealed that syntactic knowledge, such as subject/object order and subordination, improved progressively across layers. Additionally, model performance varied by textual genre, with social media language and interrogative sentences posing significant challenges due to their non-canonical structures.

title: Asking without Telling: Exploring Latent Ontologies in Contextual Representations
abstract: The success of pretrained contextual encoders, such as ELMo and BERT, has brought a great deal of interest in what these models learn: do they, without explicit supervision, learn to encode meaningful notions of linguistic structure? If so, how is this structure encoded? To investigate this, we introduce latent subclass learning (LSL): a modification to classifier-based probing that induces a latent categorization (or ontology) of the probe’s inputs. Without access to fine-grained gold labels, LSL extracts emergent structure from input representations in an interpretable and quantifiable form. In experiments, we find strong evidence of familiar categories, such as a notion of personhood in ELMo, as well as novel ontological distinctions, such as a preference for fine-grained semantic roles on core arguments. Our results provide unique new evidence of emergent structure in pretrained encoders, including departures from existing annotations which are inaccessible to earlier methods.

main_findings: the study using Latent Subclass Learning (LSL) to analyze Language Models (LMs) like BERT and ELMo reveals that these models capture meaningful linguistic structures, including both semantic and syntactic knowledge. The LSL method identifies stable latent ontologies within the models, demonstrating their ability to categorize linguistic concepts, such as personhood, dates, and organizations, as well as distinguishing finer semantic categories, like small and large cardinal numbers. The study also uncovers syntactic knowledge, showing that LMs group syntactic elements into clusters corresponding to phrase structure (e.g., complete clauses and subject-taking phrases) and dependency relations (e.g., verb arguments, left- and right-heads, and punctuation). These findings suggest that LMs encode fundamental syntactic and semantic structures, which align with established linguistic categories, offering evidence of the models' capacity to learn and transfer such knowledge across tasks.

title: A Tale of a Probe and a Parser
abstract: Measuring what linguistic information is encoded in neural models of language has become popular in NLP. Researchers approach this enterprise by training “probes”—supervised models designed to extract linguistic structure from another model’s output. One such probe is the structural probe (Hewitt and Manning, 2019), designed to quantify the extent to which syntactic information is encoded in contextualised word representations. The structural probe has a novel design, unattested in the parsing literature, the precise benefit of which is not immediately obvious. To explore whether syntactic probes would do better to make use of existing techniques, we compare the structural probe to a more traditional parser with an identical lightweight parameterisation. The parser outperforms structural probe on UUAS in seven of nine analysed languages, often by a substantial amount (e.g. by 11.1 points in English). Under a second less common metric, however, there is the opposite trend—the structural probe outperforms the parser. This begs the question: which metric should we prefer?
specific_phenomena: UUAS: Syntactic Distance. Tree Extraction, converting from syntactic distance to a syntactic tree representation

main_findings: investigated the syntactic knowledge encoded in multilingual BERT using two lightweight probing approaches—a Structural Probe and a Structured Perceptron Parser—across nine diverse languages. Results showed that conclusions about BERT’s syntax heavily depend on the evaluation metric: the parser outperformed the probe on the Undirected Unlabeled Attachment Score (UUAS), capturing more tree structure, while the probe excelled on Distance Spearman Correlation (DSpr), which measures pairwise distances. Post-processing the parser’s predictions largely closed this gap, indicating that differences were partly due to metric alignment rather than the model itself. The findings highlight that probe design strongly influences the interpretation of LM syntax, with traditional parser-like probes being highly effective under standard metrics like UUAS, suggesting that probing methods should closely reflect the structure of the tasks they aim to measure.

title: RuSentEval: Linguistic Source, Encoder Force!
abstract: The success of pre-trained transformer language models has brought a great deal of interest on how these models work, and what they learn about language. However, prior research in the field is mainly devoted to English, and little is known regarding other languages. To this end, we introduce RuSentEval, an enhanced set of 14 probing tasks for Russian, including ones that have not been explored yet. We apply a combination of complementary probing methods to explore the distribution of various linguistic properties in five multilingual transformers for two typologically contrasting languages – Russian and English. Our results provide intriguing findings that contradict the common understanding of how linguistic knowledge is represented, and demonstrate that some properties are learned in a similar manner despite the language differences.
model_name_comment: M-BERT, XLM-R, MiniLm, Labse, M-Bart only Bert encoder

experimental_materials_comment: Russian Wikipedia articles2 and news cor- pora such as Lenta.ru3 and the news segment of Taiga corpus (Shavrina and Shapovalova, 2017)

main_findings: the study on syntactic knowledge in multilingual language models (LMs) across Russian and English revealed both cross-linguistic similarities and model-specific differences in how syntax is represented. Overall, surface and syntactic properties are learned similarly across languages, with most models storing syntactic information in middle or higher layers, though M-BART and LABSE challenge the assumption that syntax is confined to the middle layers. For hierarchical structure (TreeDepth), M-BART encodes this knowledge primarily in middle-to-higher layers (7–12), while other models like M-BERT, XLM-R, and MiniLM distribute it around layers 5–7. For sensitivity to incorrect word order (NShift/BShift), LABSE peaks at lower-to-middle layers (2–8), whereas most other models concentrate this knowledge in middle-to-higher layers. These differences highlight model-specific behavior: M-BART localizes syntactic properties at higher layers, while LABSE shows unique lower-layer sensitivity for word order tasks. Overall, these findings indicate that syntax and semantics are represented variably across layers depending on model architecture and pre-training, underscoring the complexity and diversity of transformer-based representations.

title: Morph Call: Probing Morphosyntactic Content of Multilingual Transformers
abstract: The outstanding performance of transformer-based language models on a great variety of NLP and NLU tasks has stimulated interest in exploration of their inner workings. Recent research has been primarily focused on higher-level and complex linguistic phenomena such as syntax, semantics, world knowledge and common-sense. The majority of the studies is anglocentric, and little remains known regarding other languages, specifically their morphosyntactic properties. To this end, our work presents Morph Call, a suite of 46 probing tasks for four Indo-European languages of different morphology: Russian, French, English and German. We propose a new type of probing tasks based on detection of guided sentence perturbations. We use a combination of neuron-, layer- and representation-level introspection techniques to analyze the morphosyntactic content of four multilingual transformers, including their understudied distilled versions. Besides, we examine how fine-tuning on POS-tagging task affects the probing performance.
specific_phenomena: nominal morphosyntactic features of Number, Case, Person, and Gender.

interp_method: 46 probing tasks:  detection of guided sentence perturbations
main_findings: uses the Morph Call probing suite to examine how multilingual transformer language models (LMs) encode syntactic knowledge in English, French, German, and Russian, primarily through perturbation tasks that manipulate sentence structure. The study finds that sensitivity to syntactic perturbations (e.g., stop-word or article removal) is mostly concentrated in the lower-to-middle layers [3–8], whereas inflectional knowledge (subject-predicate agreement) is stored higher [5–12]. Syntactic perturbations are generally easier for the models to detect, with XLM-R showing the highest sensitivity across languages. The distribution of syntactic knowledge varies by language morphology—English shows more uniform layer distribution, while morphologically rich languages localize it more—and fine-tuning, such as for POS tagging, can shift where perturbation sensitivity is most pronounced, often increasing toward the output layers. Overall, LMs capture syntactic structure reliably and detectably, often more so than inflectional features.

title: Is German secretly a Slavic language? What BERT probing can tell us about language groups
abstract: In the light of recent developments in NLP, the problem of understanding and interpreting large language models has gained a lot of urgency. Methods developed to study this area are subject to considerable scrutiny. In this work, we take a closer look at one such method, the structural probe introduced by Hewitt and Manning (2019). We run a series of experiments involving multiple languages, focusing principally on the group of Slavic languages. We show that probing results can be seen as a reflection of linguistic classification, and conclude that multilingual BERT learns facts about languages and their groups.
specific_phenomena: syntactic tree distances in languages
languages_tested_comment: Belarusian Chinese Croatian Czech English Finnish French German Indonesian Latvian Lithuanian Polish Russian Slovak Slovene Spanish Ukrainian
experimental_materials_comment: manually annotated dependency trees – from the Universal Dependencies project (Nivre et al., 2017)
interp_method: based on the structural probing method introduced in Hewitt and Manning (2019) and applied to a multilingual setting in Chi et al. (2020)
main_findings: the study using structural probing on multilingual BERT (mBERT) revealed that the model’s embedding space encodes significant syntactic knowledge reflecting real-world linguistic classifications, particularly dependency syntax. By applying a structural probe and measuring syntax recall with UUAS, the researchers found that pre-training is crucial: mBERT’s embeddings naturally separated language families, such as Slavic versus non-Slavic languages, whereas a randomized baseline failed to show any meaningful structure. Within Slavic languages, the model correctly identified internal syntactic relationships, while German emerged as the closest non-Slavic language and Finnish the most distant, aligning with known linguistic typologies. Probes trained on the same language achieved the highest recall, though scores varied across languages, and robust conclusions required at least 5,000 annotated sentences. Overall, the findings demonstrate that mBERT implicitly captures syntactic patterns consistent with established linguistic facts through its pre-training.

title: Subspace Chronicles: How Linguistic Information Emerges, Shifts and Interacts during Language Model Training
abstract: Representational spaces learned via language modeling are fundamental to Natural Language Processing (NLP), however there has been limited understanding regarding how and when during training various types of linguistic information emerge and interact. Leveraging a novel information theoretic probing suite, which enables direct comparisons of not just task performance, but their representational subspaces, we analyze nine tasks covering syntax, semantics and reasoning, across 2M pre-training steps and five seeds. We identify critical learning phases across tasks and time, during which subspaces emerge, share information, and later disentangle to specialize. Across these phases, syntactic knowledge is acquired rapidly after 0.5% of full training. Continued performance improvements primarily stem from the acquisition of open-domain knowledge, while semantics and reasoning tasks benefit from later boosts to long-range contextualization and higher specialization. Measuring cross-task similarity further reveals that linguistically related tasks share information throughout training, and do so more during the critical phase of learning than before or after. Our findings have implications for model interpretability, multi-task learning, and learning from limited data.

In addition, we use English Twee- bank v2 (Liu et al., 2018) for DEP, and TweetEval (Rosenthal et al., 2017) for SENTI.

main_findings: syntactic knowledge in language models emerges extremely rapidly, with core abilities like Parts-of-Speech (POS) tagging and syntactic dependencies (DEP) showing steep gains within the first 1k–10k training steps, a critical learning phase during which POS performance largely stabilizes, especially for closed-class words. While foundational syntax is acquired early, later training stages continue to refine and specialize representations, improving DEP performance, compressing POS information, and enhancing long-range contextualization, particularly for complex dependencies and open-domain categories like nouns. Subspace analyses reveal that syntactic tasks initially share representational space with related tasks, including coreference resolution, but later disentangle and specialize, often converging in the model’s middle layers. These dynamics imply that substantial syntactic competence arises after minimal pre-training, enabling efficient fine-tuning for downstream tasks, though tasks requiring longer-range syntax, like DEP, benefit from continued training up to full pre-training.

title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models’ subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.
