main_findings: Causal analysis of subject-verb agreement in language models (LMs) using the Natural Indirect Effect (NIE) method revealed that both multilingual (XGLM, mBERT) and monolingual BERT-based models exhibit two distinct layer-wise patterns for number agreement, differentiating short-range (adjacent) and long-range (non-adjacent) dependencies, with patterns largely consistent across languages in multilingual models. The study found variable neuron overlap, with autoregressive LMs (ALMs, e.g., XGLM) showing significant cross-lingual neuron sharing, while masked LMs (MLMs, e.g., mBERT) primarily share neurons across structures within a language, suggesting an abstract representation of syntactic agreement alongside structure-specific specialization. Neuron sparsity differs by architecture, with MLMs having more sparse syntax neurons and behavioral analyses underestimating their syntactic sensitivity due to interference from other neurons. Overall, ALMs encode syntactic agreement more robustly than MLMs, exhibiting greater neuron overlap, consistent layer-wise effects, and a higher proportion of agreement-sensitive neurons, likely influenced by their left-to-right processing versus the fill-in-the-blank objective of MLMs.

title: Exploring the Role of BERT Token Representations to Explain Sentence Probing Results
abstract: Several studies have been carried out on revealing linguistic features captured by BERT. This is usually achieved by training a diagnostic classifier on the representations obtained from different layers of BERT. The subsequent classification accuracy is then interpreted as the ability of the model in encoding the corresponding linguistic property. Despite providing insights, these studies have left out the potential role of token representations. In this paper, we provide a more in-depth analysis on the representation space of BERT in search for distinct and meaningful subspaces that can explain the reasons behind these probing results. Based on a set of probing tasks and with the help of attribution methods we show that BERT tends to encode meaningful knowledge in specific token representations (which are often ignored in standard classification setups), allowing the model to detect syntactic and semantic abnormalities, and to distinctively separate grammatical number and tense subspaces.
specific_phenomena: grammatical number and tense information
experimental_materials_comment: set of sentence-level probing tasks from SentEval (Conneau and Kiela, 2018): several single-sentence evaluation tasks. Each task provides 100k instances for training and 10k for test, all balanced across target classes
interp_method: diagnostic classifier and incorporating attribution methods
main_findings: An in-depth gradient-based attribution analysis of BERT reveals how syntactic and morphological knowledge is encoded at the token level. Intermediate layers generally capture syntactic phenomena, but specific tokens, especially endings like ##s and ##ed, play a critical role in encoding grammatical number and tense, with BERT distinguishing plural nouns from third-person verbs in higher-layer subspaces. For word-level abnormalities, such as in the Bi-gram Shift task, BERT’s representations of inverted tokens show increased attribution and altered self-attention patterns, with changes localized to the shifted words. At the phrasal level, as in Coordination Inversion, BERT encodes structural oddities primarily in the representations of coordinators like "and" or "but," with minimal impact on surrounding words, highlighting that both local and phrasal syntactic anomalies are captured through focused, token-specific subspaces.

title: Refining Targeted Syntactic Evaluation of Language Models
abstract: Targeted syntactic evaluation of subject-verb number agreement in English (TSE) evaluates language models’ syntactic knowledge using hand-crafted minimal pairs of sentences that differ only in the main verb’s conjugation. The method evaluates whether language models rate each grammatical sentence as more likely than its ungrammatical counterpart. We identify two distinct goals for TSE. First, evaluating the systematicity of a language model’s syntactic knowledge: given a sentence, can it conjugate arbitrary verbs correctly? Second, evaluating a model’s likely behavior: given a sentence, does the model concentrate its probability mass on correctly conjugated verbs, even if only on a subset of the possible verbs? We argue that current implementations of TSE do not directly capture either of these goals, and propose new metrics to capture each goal separately. Under our metrics, we find that TSE overestimates systematicity of language models, but that models score up to 40% better on verbs that they predict are likely in context.

experimental_materials_comment: minimal ling. pairs, S/V number agreement TSE templates from Marvin and Linzen (2018) and BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020
interp_method: measuring systematicity and likely behavior of model:  two minimal pair evaluations, equally-weighted and model-weighted syntactic evaluation
main_findings: refines Targeted Syntactic Evaluation (TSE) for subject-verb number agreement and distinguishes between a language model’s systematicity—its ability to correctly conjugate arbitrary verbs—and its likely behavior—the probability of generating a correct verb in context. Using two new metrics, Equally-Weighted (EW) for systematicity and Model-Weighted (MW) for likely behavior, the research finds that standard TSE overestimates systematicity, as EW evaluations across a large set of verbs reveal substantial drops in performance for unlikely verbs, sometimes by up to 40%. Conversely, MW scores show that LMs reliably produce correct conjugations for likely verbs, with high accuracy especially when sampling is restricted to higher-probability verbs. Overall, LMs demonstrate strong performance in contextually probable verb conjugations but significant weaknesses in systematic syntactic ability across arbitrary or low-probability verbs.

title: The Rediscovery Hypothesis: Language Models Need to Meet Linguistics
abstract: There is an ongoing debate in the NLP community whether modern language models contain linguistic knowledge, recovered through so-called probes. In this paper, we study whether linguistic knowledge is a necessary condition for the good performance of modern language models, which we call the rediscovery hypothesis. In the first place, we show that language models that are significantly compressed but perform well on their pretraining objectives retain good scores when probed for linguistic structures. This result supports the rediscovery hypothesis and leads to the second contribution of our paper: an information-theoretic framework that relates language modeling objectives with linguistic information. This framework also provides a metric to measure the impact of linguistic information on the word prediction task. We reinforce our analytical results with various experiments, both on synthetic and on real NLP tasks in English.
specific_phenomena: POS, NER,
experimental_materials_comment:
standard benchmark dataset OntoNotes 5.0 (Weischedel et al., 2013) using the jiant toolkit (Pruksachatkun et al., 2020);
English UD (Silveira et al., 2014) u
interp_method: nan
main_findings: Research on syntactic knowledge in Language Models (LMs) shows strong support for the rediscovery hypothesis, indicating that LMs naturally acquire linguistic knowledge during pretraining, especially in English. Experiments demonstrate that pruning affects complex syntactic tasks (like constituency parsing) more than simpler tasks (like POS tagging), and that entire syntax trees can be extracted from deep model embeddings using structural probing. Syntactic knowledge is acquired early in training—often before semantic knowledge—with tasks like POS tagging, dependency parsing, and constituency parsing reaching peak performance within 30–60 epochs, reflecting a pipeline similar to classical NLP. Information-theoretic analyses confirm that syntactic properties, particularly fine-grained POS tags, are highly interdependent with underlying text and are essential for optimal LM performance, as their removal causes a larger performance drop than removing semantic information like NER labels. Distribution analyses further show that syntactic knowledge is spread across tokens, with rare tokens more affected by pruning, highlighting the interplay between memorization and learned linguistic structure.

title: Does BERT Rediscover a Classical NLP Pipeline?
abstract: Does BERT store surface knowledge in its bottom layers, syntactic knowledge in its middle layers, and semantic knowledge in its upper layers? In re-examining Jawahar et al. (2019) and Tenney et al.’s (2019a) probes into the structure of BERT, we have found that the pipeline-like separation that they asserted lacks conclusive empirical support. BERT’s structure is, however, linguistically founded, although perhaps in a way that is more nuanced than can be explained by layers alone. We introduce a novel probe, called GridLoc, through which we can also take into account token positions, training rounds, and random seeds. Using GridLoc, we are able to detect other, stronger regularities that suggest that pseudo-cognitive appeals to layer depth may not be the preferable mode of explanation for BERT’s inner workings.
syntactic_phenomena: Hierarchical structure, POS, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena:
tree depth, POS Const Deps Ent SRL Coref SPR Relns;
10 probing tasks at 3 linguistic levels: • surface tasks: sentence length (SL) and word content (WC);  • syntactic tasks: bigram shift (BS), tree depth (TD) and top constituent (TC); • and semantic tasks: tense, subject number (SN), object number (ON), semantic odd man out (SOMO) and coordination inversion (CI).
experimental_materials_comment: 10 tasks in SentEval (Conneau and Kiela, 2018)
interp_method: GridLoc: more complete picture of where task specific knowledge resides, by breaking down the probe’s attention weight across both token positions and layers, as well as across random seeds and training iterations
main_findings: studies on BERT’s syntactic knowledge challenge the traditional view that its layers function as a classical NLP pipeline (surface → syntax → semantics). Reassessing prior probing work and introducing the GridLoc attention-based probe, researchers found that syntactic and semantic information are inseparable across layers, peaking mostly between layers 6–9, with only surface features clearly concentrated in lower layers. GridLoc further revealed that syntactic knowledge is distributed in parallel with semantic knowledge rather than occupying dedicated layers. Notably, the Tree Depth task exposed a unique anomaly: attention varies by token position and part-of-speech (POS), with nouns, prepositions, and punctuation mapping to different layers, indicating that BERT organizes linguistic information in a fine-grained, non-pipeline manner, where different aspects of the same linguistic level spread across layers rather than following a sequential processing hierarchy.

title: Using Roark-Hollingshead Distance to Probe BERT’s Syntactic Competence
abstract: Probing BERT’s general ability to reason about syntax is no simple endeavour, primarily because of the uncertainty surrounding how large language models represent syntactic structure. Many prior accounts of BERT’s agility as a syntactic tool (Clark et al., 2013; Lau et al., 2014; Marvin and Linzen, 2018; Chowdhury and Zamparelli, 2018; Warstadt et al., 2019, 2020; Hu et al., 2020) have therefore confined themselves to studying very specific linguistic phenomena, and there has still been no definitive answer as to whether BERT “knows” syntax. The advent of perturbed masking (Wu et al., 2020) would then seem to be significant, because this is a parameter-free probing method that directly samples syntactic trees from BERT’s embeddings. These sampled trees outperform a right-branching baseline, thus providing preliminary evidence that BERT’s syntactic competence bests a simple baseline. This baseline is underwhelming, however, and our reappraisal below suggests that this result, too, is inconclusive. We propose RH Probe, an encoder-decoder probing architecture that operates on two probing tasks. We find strong empirical evidence confirming the existence of important syntactic information in BERT, but this information alone appears not to be enough to reproduce syntax in its entirety. Our probe makes crucial use of a conjecture made by Roark and Holling-shead (2008) that a particular lexical annotation that we shall call RH distance is a sufficient encoding of unlabelled binary syntactic trees, and we prove this conjecture.
specific_phenomena: Tree Integrity, usage of POS and RH distance information
experimental_materials_comment: Constituency trees  from the Penn Treebank (PTB) (Marcus et al., 1994).
interp_method:
RH Probe, an encoder-decoder probing architecture that operates on two probing tasks;  measure of the syntactic distance between a token ti and its predecessor ti−1, a lexicalized measure, a sequence of which encodes the structure of certain constituency trees.
an abla- tive probe observes the classifier’s performance decrease when an input source is removed from training; and an “attack” probe observes its perfor- mance decrease after input features are obscured through randomization during testing (after a noise- free training).
main_findings: The study using the Roark-Hollingshead (RH) Probe demonstrates that BERT encodes significant syntactic knowledge, but this knowledge alone is incomplete and insufficient to fully reconstruct syntax. Ablation experiments show that language model embeddings provide useful parsing information, yet their syntactic knowledge is disjoint from traditional representations like RH sequences and POS tags, which, when added, substantially boost performance. The study also finds that model size or complexity does not guarantee more syntactic information, as smaller models sometimes outperform larger ones. Attack probes reveal that BERT’s embeddings are heavily weighted and highly extractable, making them more influential than formally sufficient RH distance features for downstream classifiers. Overall, the research highlights that while BERT contains syntactic information, effective syntax reconstruction benefits from both external structural features and the extractability advantage of higher-quality LMs, with the RH Probe offering a novel framework for analyzing these interactions.

title: Joint processing of linguistic properties in brains and language models
abstract: Language models have been shown to be very effective in predicting brain recordings of subjects experiencing complex language stimuli. For a deeper understanding of this alignment, it is important to understand the alignment between the detailed processing of linguistic information by the human brain versus language models. In NLP, linguistic probing tasks have revealed a hierarchy of information processing in neural language models that progresses from simple to complex with an increase in depth. On the other hand, in neuroscience, the strongest alignment with high-level language brain regions has consistently been observed in the middle layers. These findings leave an open question as to what linguistic information actually underlies the observed alignment between brains and language models. We investigate this question via a direct approach, in which we eliminate information related to specific linguistic properties in the language model representations and observe how this intervention affects the alignment with fMRI brain recordings obtained while participants listened to a story. We investigate a range of linguistic properties (surface, syntactic and semantic) and find that the elimination of each one results in a significant decrease in brain alignment across all layers of a language model. These findings provide direct evidence for the role of specific linguistic information in the alignment between brain and language models, and opens new avenues for mapping the joint information processing in both systems.
specific_phenomena: syntactic properties i.e. Top Constituents (tests for the sequence of top-level constituents in the syntactic tree. This is a 20-class classification task) and Tree Depth, Sentence Length Tense, Subject Number, Object Number
experimental_materials_comment: details of tasks are mentioned in Conneau et al. (2018)
interp_method: remove a linguistic property from the pretrained BERT representations, we use a ridge regression method in which the probing task label is considered as input and the word features are the target
main_findings: found that syntactic knowledge, particularly Tree Depth and Top Constituents, plays a critical role in aligning language model (BERT and GPT-2) representations with fMRI recordings of human brain activity. Removing these syntactic properties led to a substantial drop in brain alignment across all layers, with the largest effects observed in the middle to late layers, where BERT typically encodes hierarchical linguistic information. Top Constituents primarily drove the middle-layer “bump” in alignment across all language regions, especially the Inferior Frontal Gyrus (IFG), while Tree Depth had stronger effects on temporal regions (ATL, PTL) and frontal areas (IFG, MFG), including sub-regions IFSp and IFJa. Voxel-wise analyses confirmed these effects were localized to canonical left-hemisphere language regions. Overall, these findings highlight that syntactic information is essential for LMs to mirror human neural patterns of language comprehension.

title: Exploratory Model Analysis Using Data-Driven Neuron Representations
abstract: Probing classifiers have been extensively used to inspect whether a model component captures specific linguistic phenomena. This top-down approach is, however, costly when we have no probable hypothesis on the association between the target model component and phenomena. In this study, aiming to provide a flexible, exploratory analysis of a neural model at various levels ranging from individual neurons to the model as a whole, we present a bottom-up approach to inspect the target neural model by using neuron representations obtained from a massive corpus of text. We first feed massive amount of text to the target model and collect sentences that strongly activate each neuron. We then abstract the collected sentences to obtain neuron representations that help us interpret the corresponding neurons; we augment the sentences with linguistic annotations (e.g., part-of-speech tags) and various metadata (e.g., topic and sentiment), and apply pattern mining and clustering techniques to the augmented sentences. We demonstrate the utility of our method by inspecting the pre-trained BERT. Our exploratory analysis reveals that i) specific phrases and domains of text are captured by individual neurons in BERT, ii) a group of neurons simultaneously capture the same linguistic phenomena, and iii) deeper-level layers capture more specific linguistic phenomena.
specific_phenomena: POS
fine_tuning_materials: training set in Sentiment140 (Go et al., 2009) that annotates the sentences with polarity labels (positive and negative)
experimental_materials_comment: such as Wikipedia and BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015)
Mechanistic_method: bottom-up, example-based exploratory analysis using data-driven neuron representations
interp_method:
Data-Driven Inspection of Neuron; collected 10K sentences corresponding to each neuron, and identified the common linguistic phenomena in those sentences by using frequent pattern mining.
bottom-up, exploratory analysis method to uncover what specific linguistic phenomena individual neurons in neural NLP models, such as BERT, respond to. Using large-scale text and data mining, the method identifies linguistic signatures—recurring patterns that activate certain neurons
main_findings: The study conducted a bottom-up, exploratory analysis of the pre-trained BERT model to uncover the specific linguistic phenomena captured by individual neurons, using large text corpora and pattern mining without prior assumptions. It found that neurons are highly specialized, with some responding to concrete phrases, domains, or parts of speech, and that groups of neurons often cooperate to represent similar phenomena, particularly in deeper layers. Focusing on syntactic knowledge, the study identified neurons selective for specific POS tags, such as nouns and verbs, with distinct activation patterns. Across layers, selectively responsive POS neurons were concentrated in deeper layers of pre-trained BERT, contrasting with randomly initialized models and highlighting a divergence from top-down probing results that suggest lower layers handle POS tasks best; this indicates that deep neurons capture highly specific structural information, while top-down methods may detect more uniform, less selective POS responses.

title: Cross-linguistic Comparison of Linguistic Feature Encoding in BERT Models for Typologically Different Languages
abstract: Though recently there have been an increased interest in how pre-trained language models encode different linguistic features, there is still a lack of systematic comparison between languages with different morphology and syntax. In this paper, using BERT as an example of a pre-trained model, we compare how three typologically different languages (English, Korean, and Russian) encode morphology and syntax features across different layers. In particular, we contrast languages which differ in a particular aspect, such as flexibility of word order, head directionality, morphological type, presence of grammatical gender, and morphological richness, across four different tasks.
model_name_comment: BERT-base-cased, RuBERT (Kuratov and Arkhipov, 2019), BERT-Kor-base model
specific_phenomena:
Word Order, Morphological features, inflection vs agglutination, Long-distance agreementdataset provided by Stanovsky et al. (2019)
gender marking
interp_method: bigram shift (BShift) probing task introduced by Conneau et al. (2018)
main_findings: Research on BERT-based models (BERT-Base Cased and RuBERT) shows that Transformer layers encode syntactic knowledge in a way roughly aligned with classic NLP pipelines, with middle layers primarily handling syntax parsing and complex syntactic relations. Language typology significantly affects how syntax is encoded: Russian, with its rich morphology and relatively free word order, requires more layers than English or Korean to achieve optimal syntactic performance. In word order sensitivity tasks, RuBERT outperforms BERT-Base at middle and higher layers due to morphological cues binding words together, while Korean models show near-perfect accuracy with morphology-based tokenization, highlighting awareness of agglutination. For long-distance agreement, models initially rely on semantic co-occurrence, but higher layers increasingly encode abstract hierarchical structure, with Russian benefiting from its complex morphology to better capture long-distance syntactic dependencies, showing that both morphology and layer depth critically influence syntactic encoding.

title: The Heads Hypothesis: A Unifying Statistical Approach Towards Understanding Multi-Headed Attention in BERT
abstract: Multi-headed attention heads are a mainstay in transformer-based models. Different methods have been proposed to classify the role of each attention head based on the relations between tokens which have high pair-wise attention. These roles include syntactic (tokens with some syntactic relation), local (nearby tokens), block (tokens in the same sentence) and delimiter (the special [CLS], [SEP] tokens). There are two main challenges with existing methods for classification: (a) there are no standard scores across studies or across functional roles, and (b) these scores are often average quantities measured across sentences without capturing statistical significance. In this work, we formalize a simple yet effective score that generalizes to all the roles of attention heads and employs hypothesis testing on this score for robust inference. This provides us the right lens to systematically analyze attention heads and confidently comment on many commonly posed questions on analyzing the BERT model. In particular, we comment on the co-location of multiple functional roles in the same attention head, the distribution of attention heads across layers, and effect of fine-tuning for specific NLP tasks on these functional roles. The code is made publicly available at https://github.com/iitmnlp/heads-hypothesis
specific_phenomena: nsubj, dobj, amod and advmod (syntactic heads), syntactic role
fine_tuning_materials: GLUE, MRPC, QNLI, QQP and SST-2 tasks
experimental_materials_comment: 1000 input sequences (num sents) from the standard test sets of the 4 GLUE tasks for all our analysis experiments. We use open-source library spaCy for dependency parsing;
Mechanistic_method: unifying statistical approach (classify the functional roles of attention heads)
interp_method: we formalize a simple yet effective score that generalizes to all the roles of attention heads and employs hypothesis testing on this score for robust inference
main_findings: analysis of BERT’s attention heads revealed that syntactic knowledge is primarily captured by heads that attend to syntactically related tokens, with fine-grained roles such as nsubj, dobj, amod, and advmod. Syntactic heads show a strong overlap with local heads, with 42–89% co-occurrence, reflecting that many syntactic relations are local, and correlations between local and syntactic attention patterns are high. Across BERT’s 12 layers, syntactic heads are most prevalent in the middle layers (6–8), where multi-functional heads are also concentrated, while the last layers contain few syntactic or multi-skilled heads. Fine-tuning on GLUE tasks has minimal impact on early and middle layers but causes the final layers to specialize in general token-level attention without strong syntactic bias. Overall, the findings highlight that syntactic information is largely captured indirectly through local attention, is concentrated in middle layers, and exhibits stability through fine-tuning except in the top layers.

title: Deep Subjecthood: Higher-Order Grammatical Features in Multilingual BERT
abstract: We investigate how Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encodes grammar by examining how the high-order grammatical feature of morphosyntactic alignment (how different languages define what counts as a “subject”) is manifested across the embedding spaces of different languages. To understand if and how morphosyntactic alignment affects contextual embedding spaces, we train classifiers to recover the subjecthood of mBERT embeddings in transitive sentences (which do not contain overt information about morphosyntactic alignment) and then evaluate them zero-shot on intransitive sentences (where subjecthood classification depends on alignment), within and across languages. We find that the resulting classifier distributions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of their training languages. Our results demonstrate that mBERT representations are influenced by high-level grammatical features that are not manifested in any one input sentence, and that this is robust across languages. Further examining the characteristics that our classifiers rely on, we find that features such as passive voice, animacy and case strongly correlate with classification decisions, suggesting that mBERT does not encode subjecthood purely syntactically, but that subjecthood embedding is continuous and dependent on semantic and discourse factors, as is proposed in much of the functional linguistics literature. Together, these results provide insight into how grammatical features manifest in contextual embedding spaces, at a level of abstraction not covered by previous work.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: morphosyntactic
languages_tested_comment: 24: Basque, Chinese, Croatian, Czech, English, Estonian, Farsi, Finnish, French, German, Hebrew, Hindi, Indonesian, Japanese, Latin, Latvian, Norwegian, Polish, Russian, Serbian, Slovak, Slovene, Spanish, Urdu
experimental_materials_comment: train a subjecthood classifier, data points are extracted from the Universal Dependencies treebanks (Nivre et al., 2016): we use the dependency parse informa- tion to determine whether each noun is an A or an O, and if it is either we pass the whole sen- tence through mBERT and take the contextual em- bedding corresponding to the noun.
interp_method: nan
main_findings: Research on Multilingual BERT (mBERT) shows that the model encodes high-order grammatical features such as morphosyntactic alignment, representing grammatical roles like subjecthood in a continuous space strongly influenced by semantics. Experiments reveal that classifiers trained on mBERT embeddings can reliably distinguish transitive agents (A) from objects (O), particularly in higher layers, and that these representations reflect the morphosyntactic biases of the training languages, including nominative-accusative and ergative patterns. Subjecthood representations are transferable across languages, supporting zero-shot cross-lingual predictions, and alignment biases generalize coherently interlingually. Importantly, subjecthood is not purely structural: embeddings for passive subjects occupy intermediate positions between agents and objects, and semantic factors like animacy and grammatical case strongly modulate classification, showing that mBERT integrates both syntactic and semantic cues in encoding grammatical roles.

with lexical semantics in the internal language system of models

Our experiments rest on comparing the grammatical subjecthood of a noun in a sentence (as annotated in the English GUM and EWT UD treebanks) with the type-level (fixed embedding) subjecthood
main_findings: Research on BERT’s syntactic knowledge shows that the model resolves grammatical roles (subject vs. object) by combining lexical biases with contextual information, particularly fine-grained word order. Probing classifiers reveal that for prototypical sentences—where lexical semantics align with grammatical roles—subjecthood is encoded from the earliest layers, while in non-prototypical sentences, type-level biases dominate early layers and syntactic knowledge only emerges in later layers, indicating that contextual cues can override lexical expectations. Moreover, word order independently influences grammatical representations: swapping subject and object roles in identical word distributions allows probes to accurately recover subjecthood, demonstrating BERT’s sensitivity to syntactic structure. Finally, fine-grained positional information is essential in difficult, non-prototypical cases, as simple heuristics like word primacy fail to produce correct grammatical embeddings, highlighting the model’s reliance on detailed syntactic ordering rather than general sentence position.

title: Do Attention Heads in BERT Track Syntactic Dependencies?
abstract: We investigate the extent to which individual attention heads in pretrained transformer language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, implicitly capture syntactic dependency relations. We employ two methods---taking the maximum attention weight and computing the maximum spanning tree---to extract implicit dependency relations from the attention weights of each layer/head, and compare them to the ground-truth Universal Dependency (UD) trees. We show that, for some UD relation types, there exist heads that can recover the dependency type significantly better than baselines on parsed English text, suggesting that some self-attention heads act as a proxy for syntactic structure. We also analyze BERT fine-tuned on two datasets---the syntax-oriented CoLA and the semantics-oriented MNLI---to investigate whether fine-tuning affects the patterns of their self-attention, but we do not observe substantial differences in the overall dependency relations extracted using our methods. Our results suggest that these models have some specialist attention heads that track individual dependency types, but no generalist head that performs holistic parsing significantly better than a trivial baseline, and that analyzing attention weights directly may not reveal much of the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.
model_name_comment: BERT- large-cased and uncased, and RoBERTa, fine-tuned: CoLA-BERT and MNLI-BERT
specific_phenomena: dependency trees from the attention weights for a given layer and head
fine_tuning_materials: Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA; Warstadt et al., 2019b) and MNLI to investigate the impact of fine-tuning on a syntax-related task (CoLA) and a semantic-related task (MNLI) on the structure of attention weights and resultant extracted dependency relations. We refer to these fine-tuned models as CoLA-BERT and MNLI-BERT respectively
experimental_materials_comment: English Parallel Universal Dependencies (PUD) treebank from the CoNLL 2017 shared task (Zeman et al.,2018)
interp_method: two methods for extracting dependency relations from the attention heads of Transformer-based models; Maximum Attention Weights, Maximum Spanning Tree
main_findings: Studies on BERT and RoBERTa reveal that while certain individual attention heads, termed "specialist heads," reliably capture specific syntactic dependencies such as nsubj, obj, and to a lesser extent conj, the models struggle to form complete syntactic trees from attention weights, with methods like Maximum Spanning Tree (MST) failing to meaningfully outperform simple baselines. This indicates a gap between the syntactic knowledge these models encode and what can be directly extracted from attention patterns. Fine-tuning impacts this selectively: semantics-oriented fine-tuning (MNLI) improves long-distance clausal dependencies but slightly reduces short-distance accuracy, while syntax-oriented fine-tuning (CoLA) has minimal effect, and overall attention patterns remain largely stable. These findings highlight that attention weights reveal only part of the models’ syntactic knowledge, which may be richer than direct extraction suggests.

title: The Architectural Bottleneck Principle
abstract: In this paper, we seek to measure how much information a component in a neural network could extract from the representations fed into it. Our work stands in contrast to prior probing work, most of which investigates how much information a model's representations contain. This shift in perspective leads us to propose a new principle for probing, the architectural bottleneck principle: In order to estimate how much information a given component could extract, a probe should look exactly like the component. Relying on this principle, we estimate how much syntactic information is available to transformers through our attentional probe, a probe that exactly resembles a transformer's self-attention head. Experimentally, we find that, in three models (BERT, ALBERT, and RoBERTa), a sentence's syntax tree is mostly extractable by our probe, suggesting these models have access to syntactic information while composing their contextual representations. Whether this information is actually used by these models, however, remains an open question.
specific_phenomena: probe the ability to reconstruct a syntax tree; dependency trees from the attention weights for a given layer and head,
experimental_materials_comment: universal dependencies’ (UD) treebanks (Zeman et al., 2020), treebanks: English EWT (Silveira et al., 2014); Basque BDT (Aduriz et al., 2003); Turkish IMST (Sulubacak et al., 2016); Tamil TTB (Ramasamy and Žabokrtský, 2012)
interp_method: how much information its components could extract. We then quantify this amount using V-information. Evaluating the attention mechanism of popular transformer language model
main_findings: demonstrates that transformer-based language models (LMs) like BERT, ALBERT, and RoBERTa have a high potential to extract syntactic information from sentences, as measured by the Architectural Bottleneck Principle and attentional probes. Using V-information, the study found that these models could access roughly 85% of syntactic information in English sentences, with similar trends across other languages, and that this information is most extractable in the middle layers. Importantly, this syntactic knowledge emerges from pretraining rather than being inherent to the architecture. However, while attention heads could use this information, the study shows they do not actually compute weights resembling syntax trees, leaving the question of actual usage open. Methodologically, the study also highlights that simpler structural probes underestimate LMs’ potential, as the attentional probe recovered more syntactic information than previous baseline methods.

title: Information-Theoretic Probing for Linguistic Structure
abstract: The success of neural networks on a diverse set of NLP tasks has led researchers to question how much these networks actually “know” about natural language. Probes are a natural way of assessing this. When probing, a researcher chooses a linguistic task and trains a supervised model to predict annotations in that linguistic task from the network’s learned representations. If the probe does well, the researcher may conclude that the representations encode knowledge related to the task. A commonly held belief is that using simpler models as probes is better; the logic is that simpler models will identify linguistic structure, but not learn the task itself. We propose an information-theoretic operationalization of probing as estimating mutual information that contradicts this received wisdom: one should always select the highest performing probe one can, even if it is more complex, since it will result in a tighter estimate, and thus reveal more of the linguistic information inherent in the representation. The experimental portion of our paper focuses on empirically estimating the mutual information between a linguistic property and BERT, comparing these estimates to several baselines. We evaluate on a set of ten typologically diverse languages often underrepresented in NLP research—plus English—totalling eleven languages. Our implementation is available in https://github.com/rycolab/info-theoretic-probing.
specific_phenomena: word-level POS tag labeling
experimental_materials_comment: POS and dependency labeling, using the universal POS tag (Petrov et al., 2012) and dependency label information from the Uni-versal Dependencies 2.5
interp_method: propose an information-theoretic operational-ization of probing that defines it as the task of esti-mating conditional mutual information.
main_findings: investigated multilingual BERT’s syntactic knowledge using an information-theoretic probing framework, focusing on Part-of-Speech (POS) and dependency labeling across eleven typologically diverse languages. Theoretically, contextualized embeddings cannot contain more information about a word-level syntactic task than the original sentence, so probing primarily reflects the language rather than the embeddings. Optimal probes should maximize performance to tightly estimate mutual information, and control functions were introduced to measure the gain of contextual embeddings over type-level baselines. For POS labeling, most information was already captured by type-level embeddings, with BERT providing only modest gains (under 9%) in five languages, highlighting the dominance of lexical information. Dependency labeling showed universal but still modest improvements (up to 12%), indicating some context-sensitive syntactic knowledge but limited additional information beyond simple embeddings. Overall, BERT encodes substantial syntactic information but rarely exceeds type-level baselines by more than 12%, suggesting future research should focus on the ease of extraction of syntactic knowledge rather than mere presence.

title: Pareto Probing: Trading Off Accuracy for Complexity
abstract: The question of how to probe contextual word representations in a way that is principled and useful has seen significant recent attention. In our contribution to this discussion, we argue, first, for a probe metric that reflects the trade-off between probe complexity and performance: the Pareto hypervolume. To measure complexity, we present a number of parametric and non-parametric metrics. Our experiments with such metrics show that probe’s performance curves often fail to align with widely accepted rankings between language representations (with, e.g., non-contextual representations outperforming contextual ones). These results lead us to argue, second, that common simplistic probe tasks such as POS labeling and dependency arc labeling, are inadequate to evaluate the properties encoded in contextual word representations. We propose full dependency parsing as an example probe task, and demonstrate it with the Pareto hypervolume. In support of our arguments, the results of this illustrative experiment conform closer to accepted rankings among contextual word representations.
specific_phenomena: tasks are part-of-speech labeling (POSL; Hewitt and Liang, 2019;Belinkov et al., 2017) and dependency arc labeling (DAL; Tenney et al., 2019a,b; Voita and Titov,2020).

interp_method: new approach to probing, treating it as a bi-objective optimization problem. It has no single optimal solution, but can be analyzed—under the lens of Pareto efficiency— to arrive on a set of optimal solutions
main_findings: investigates how the methodology of probing language models (LMs) affects conclusions about their syntactic knowledge, introducing Pareto Probing, which evaluates probes based on a trade-off between accuracy and complexity. It finds that simplistic metrics or toy tasks like POSL and DAL can misleadingly suggest that non-contextual embeddings (one-hot, fastText) outperform contextual ones (BERT, RoBERTa), because these tasks are shallow and primarily reflect word identity rather than deep syntax. In contrast, harder tasks like full dependency parsing reveal a substantial advantage for contextual representations, demonstrating that they encode significantly more syntactic knowledge than non-contextual embeddings. Overall, the study emphasizes that both probe complexity and task difficulty critically shape conclusions, and that meaningful assessments require challenging tasks and Pareto-optimal probes to avoid misleading results.

title: How Do BERT Embeddings Organize Linguistic Knowledge?
abstract: Several studies investigated the linguistic information implicitly encoded in Neural Language Models. Most of these works focused on quantifying the amount and type of information available within their internal representations and across their layers. In line with this scenario, we proposed a different study, based on Lasso regression, aimed at understanding how the information encoded by BERT sentence-level representations is arrange within its hidden units. Using a suite of several probing tasks, we showed the existence of a relationship between the implicit knowledge learned by the model and the number of individual units involved in the encodings of this competence. Moreover, we found that it is possible to identify groups of hidden units more relevant for specific linguistic properties.

main_findings: the investigation into BERT embeddings reveals that the model implicitly encodes syntactic knowledge, with the complexity of a linguistic feature influencing both the number of hidden units involved and their organization across layers. Using Lasso regression probing tasks, the study found that complex sentence-wide features—such as the depth of the syntactic tree, dependency link lengths, and prepositional chain counts—rely on a larger set of units and become more distributed in higher layers, particularly when using [CLS] token representations. In contrast, simpler word-level features like POS or dependency labels require fewer units and remain more localized. Clustering analyses showed that BERT organizes linguistic features coherently across layers, with related features forming identifiable clusters, suggesting a linguistically meaningful and structured embedding space that scales with feature complexity.

title: Multilingual Probing of Deep Pre-Trained Contextual Encoders
abstract: Encoders that generate representations based on context have, in recent years, benefited from adaptations that allow for pre-training on large text corpora. Earlier work on evaluating fixed-length sentence representations has included the use of ‘probing’ tasks, that use diagnostic classifiers to attempt to quantify the extent to which these encoders capture specific linguistic phenomena. The principle of probing has also resulted in extended evaluations that include relatively newer word-level pre-trained encoders. We build on probing tasks established in the literature and comprehensively evaluate and analyse – from a typological perspective amongst others – multilingual variants of existing encoders on probing datasets constructed for 6 non-English languages. Specifically, we probe each layer of a multiple monolingual RNN-based ELMo models, the transformer-based BERT’s cased and uncased multilingual variants, and a variant of BERT that uses a cross-lingual modelling scheme (XLM).
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Agreement and feature-checking, Hierarchical structure
specific_phenomena:

Sentence length, word count, tree depth, bigram shift,subject number, object number, coordination inversion, (semantic:) odd man out, tense prediction

main_findings: comprehensive evaluation of multilingual pre-trained contextual encoders using syntactic probing tasks—such as Tree Depth, Bigram Shift, Subject Number, Object Number, and Coordination Inversion—revealed key insights into how different architectures retain linguistic knowledge. Recurrent models like ELMo generally outperform transformer-based models (BERT, XLM) on lower-level syntactic phenomena, while transformers show performance drops on tasks like Word Count, Tree Depth, and Bigram Shift, though ELMo notably improves on BiShift when using contextualized representations. Cross-lingual models like XLM tend to underperform compared to monolingual or multilingual transformers due to a trade-off between universal representations and language-specific syntactic retention, whereas BERT better preserves surface and syntactic information. Language-specific morphological cues affect subject and object number retention, with French and Spanish easier to probe due to plural articles enhancing representations, unlike English, German, or Russian. Additional analyses show BERT’s attention heads and layers encode syntactic structures corresponding to dependency syntax, with some layer hierarchies aligning with classical NLP pipelines. Finally, task-specific findings include German retaining Coordination Inversion information relatively well, and modifications using dependency trees for tasks like CoordInv and TreeDepth showed minimal impact on performance.

title: Visualizing and Measuring the Geometry of BERT
abstract: Transformer architectures show significant promise for natural language processing. Given that a single pretrained model can be fine-tuned to perform well on many different tasks, these networks appear to extract generally useful linguistic features. A natural question is how such networks represent this information internally. This paper describes qualitative and quantitative investigations of one particularly effective model, BERT. At a high level, linguistic features seem to be represented in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces. We find evidence of a fine-grained geometric representation of word senses. We also present empirical descriptions of syntactic representations in both attention matrices and individual word embeddings, as well as a mathematical argument to explain the geometry of these representations.
specific_phenomena: investigate whether attention matrices encode syntactic features ( existence of a dependency relation between two token,which type of dependency relation exists between two tokens) . Second, we provide a simple mathematical analysis of the tree embeddings that they found :Geometry of parse tree embeddings
languages_tested_comment: English, French, German, Spanish, Russian, Turkish and Finnish
experimental_materials_comment:
corpus of parsed sentences from the Penn Treebank.This dataset has the constituency grammar for the sentences, which was translated to a dependency grammar using the PyStanfordDependencies library;
data on different word senses, collected all sentences used in the introductions to English-language Wikipedia articles
interp_method: use an attention probe, an analog of edge probing: goal is to classify a given relation between the two tokens. If a linear model achieves reliable accuracy, it seems reasonable to say that the model-wide attention vector encodes that relation
main_findings: research on syntactic knowledge in BERT shows that the model encodes grammatical information both in its attention matrices and context embeddings. Attention probes reveal that dependency relations between tokens can be predicted with high accuracy, indicating that specific directions in attention space correspond to particular syntactic relations. Context embeddings geometrically represent entire dependency parse trees using a “Pythagorean embedding,” where squared Euclidean distances between word vectors reflect tree distances, capturing both standard grammatical relations and additional quantitative nuances. Furthermore, syntax and semantics are represented in largely separate, orthogonal subspaces within context embeddings, allowing BERT to encode multiple linguistic features simultaneously while maintaining their distinction. Overall, these findings demonstrate that BERT internally organizes syntax in a structured, mathematically interpretable way, complementing its semantic representations.

title: From BERT‘s Point of View: Revealing the Prevailing Contextual Differences
abstract: Though successfully applied in research and industry large pretrained language models of the BERT family are not yet fully understood. While much research in the field of BERTology has tested whether specific knowledge can be extracted from layer activations, we invert the popular probing design to analyze the prevailing differences and clusters in BERT’s high dimensional space. By extracting coarse features from masked token representations and predicting them by probing models with access to only partial information we can apprehend the variation from ‘BERT’s point of view’. By applying our new methodology to different datasets we show how much the differences can be described by syntax but further how they are to a great extent shaped by the most simple positional information.
specific_phenomena: ordered Part-of-Speech tags
experimental_materials_comment: SemCor&OMSTI noun-synsets, SemCor&OMSTI person.n.01, cctweets-random, cctweets-activist
interp_method: invert the probingdesign to instead predict features of the represen-tative space itself. From masked token representa-tions we extract clusters and principal componentsof contextual information and explore their natureby probing models that receive as input detangledtypes of information. We thus paint a picture of thedissimilarities and groupings within a dataset fromBERT’s point of view, thereby expanding existingprobing methodology by a crucial perspective
main_findings: The analysis of layer activations in language models like BERT and DeBERTa, using an inverted probing design with Bag-of-Words (BOW), Part-of-Speech (POS), and positional inputs, reveals that syntactic knowledge is the strongest descriptor of contextual representations, with POS models outperforming or matching BOW models and providing substantial gains over position-only models. However, positional information plays a surprisingly dominant role, often explaining half or more of the POS model’s performance, suggesting models rely on “shortcut” features rather than fully exploiting syntactic cues. Dataset-specific analyses confirmed genuine syntactic distinctions, such as differentiating synsets or detecting patterns like tokens followed by an apostrophe, which POS models captured almost perfectly while BOW models failed. These findings underscore that while language models encode sophisticated syntactic information, correlations between syntax, semantics, and position make it easy to overestimate their capabilities, highlighting the need for caution when interpreting model sophistication.

title: Analyzing Encoded Concepts in Transformer Language Models
abstract: We propose a novel framework ConceptX, to analyze how latent concepts are encoded in representations learned within pre-trained lan-guage models. It uses clustering to discover the encoded concepts and explains them by aligning with a large set of human-defined concepts. Our analysis on seven transformer language models reveal interesting insights: i) the latent space within the learned representations overlap with different linguistic concepts to a varying degree, ii) the lower layers in the model are dominated by lexical concepts (e.g., affixation) and linguistic ontologies (e.g. Word-Net), whereas the core-linguistic concepts (e.g., morphology, syntactic relations) are better represented in the middle and higher layers, iii) some encoded concepts are multi-faceted and cannot be adequately explained using the existing human-defined concepts.
model_name_comment: bert-base-uncased, berta-base-cased, RoBERTa, XLNet, and ALBERT, multilingual-bert-cased (mBERT), XLM-RoBERT
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Argument Structure and other Constructions, Hierarchical structure, POS, word order
specific_phenomena: Syntactic: Chunking tags (Tjong Kim Sang and Buchholz, 2000) and CCG super-tags (Hockenmaier, 2006), Lexical Concepts: Ngrams, Affixes, Casing, First and the Last Word (in a sentence),  Morphology and Semantics: POS tags (Marcus et al 1993)
experimental_materials_comment: subset of WMT News 20182 (359M tokens) dataset. We randomly selected 250k sentences from the dataset (≈5M tokens) to train clustering model,  final: 25k word types with 10 contexts per word
interp_method: ConceptX, a novel framework foranalyzing the encoded concepts within deep NLPmodels. Our method uses unsupervised clusteringto discover latent concepts within the contextual-ized representations and then aligned these con-cepts with a suite of human-defined concepts togenerate explanations for them
main_findings: The analysis of syntactic knowledge in transformer language models (LMs) using the ConceptX framework revealed that syntactic concepts, as core-linguistic elements alongside morphology and semantics, are predominantly encoded in the middle to higher layers of the models, peaking around layers 7–10, with a decline in the final layers for some models like XLNet and mBERT. Specific syntactic tasks, such as Chunking and CCG super-tagging, showed relatively low alignment with encoded concepts (7% and 14%, respectively), indicating that models do not fully capture the human-defined syntactic hierarchy. This contrasts with lexical concepts and linguistic ontologies, which are better represented in initial layers and decline in higher layers. Additionally, multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R exhibited stronger layer-wise representation of core-linguistic concepts, likely due to the diversity of languages in training enhancing their acquisition of syntactic and morphological knowledge.

title: LMFingerprints: Visual Explanations of Language Model Embedding Spaces through Layerwise Contextualization Scores
abstract: Language models, such as BERT, construct multiple, contextualized embeddings for each word occurrence in a corpus. Understanding how the contextualization propagates through the model's layers is crucial for deciding which layers to use for a specific analysis task. Currently, most embedding spaces are explained by probing classifiers; however, some findings remain inconclusive. In this paper, we present LMFingerprints, a novel scoring‐based technique for the explanation of contextualized word embeddings. We introduce two categories of scoring functions, which measure (1) the degree of contextualization, i.e., the layerwise changes in the embedding vectors, and (2) the type of contextualization, i.e., the captured context information. We integrate these scores into an interactive explanation workspace. By combining visual and verbal elements, we provide an overview of contextualization in six popular transformer‐based language models. We evaluate hypotheses from the domain of computational linguistics, and our results not only confirm findings from related work but also reveal new aspects about the information captured in the embedding spaces. For instance, we show that while numbers are poorly contextualized, stopwords have an unexpected high contextualization in the models' upper layers, where their neighborhoods shift from similar functionality tokens to tokens that contribute to the meaning of the surrounding sentences.
model_name_comment: BERT-base-uncased, mBERT-base-multilingual-uncased, roberta-base, gpt2, xlnet-base-cased, xlm-mlm-en-2048
specific_phenomena: POS tagging, syntactic Similarity: Same POS tag, Same previous POS tag, Same next POS tag s
experimental_materials_comment: corpus of 800 unique sentences sourced from the RTE-1, RTE-2, and RTE-3 datasets, which are originally intended for Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks. These sentences, derived from the news domain, cover diverse content and were initially presented as sentence pairs. For the purposes of this study, they were separated into individual sentences.
interp_method: a novel scoring method and interactive visualization to analyze how transformer models contextualize word embeddings.
main_findings: the study on syntactic knowledge in language models, particularly BERT, shows that syntactic information is distributed hierarchically across layers: basic features like POS tags are captured in early layers (layers 3–4), complex syntactic structures such as dependency patterns are most prominent in middle layers (layers 6–9), and semantic information tends to reside in upper layers, confirming the traditional NLP pipeline. Using novel scoring functions that measure token similarity based on POS tags and neighboring POS structures, the analysis revealed that BERT and BERT-multilingual models encode n-gram syntactic patterns primarily in middle layers, while models like RoBERTa and GPT-2 capture such patterns differently, often in upper layers, and XLNet shows weaker POS similarity. Additionally, function words (stopwords) are highly contextualized in upper layers, reflecting surrounding semantic content, whereas numbers remain relatively context-insensitive, retaining similarity to other numbers across layers. Overall, the results refine previous findings by detailing which layers encode different levels of syntactic knowledge and highlighting model-specific differences in syntactic and functional token representations.

title: A multilabel approach to morphosyntactic probing
abstract: We propose using a multilabel probing task to assess the morphosyntactic representations of multilingual word embeddings. This tweak on canonical probing makes it easy to explore morphosyntactic representations, both holistically and at the level of individual features (e.g., gender, number, case), and leads more naturally to the study of how language models handle co-occurring features (e.g., agreement phenomena). We demonstrate this task with multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2018), training probes for seven typologically diverse languages: Afrikaans, Croatian, Finnish, Hebrew, Korean, Spanish, and Turkish. Through this simple but robust paradigm, we verify that multilingual BERT renders many morphosyntactic features simultaneously extractable. We further evaluate the probes on six held-out languages: Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slovenian, Tagalog, and Yoruba. This zero-shot style of probing has the added benefit of revealing which cross-linguistic properties a language model recognizes as being shared by multiple languages.
specific_phenomena: extract (166) features like POS, number, gender, case, tense, and language-specific morphological categories (e.g., Finnish infinitives).
languages_tested_comment: Afrikaans, Croatian, Finnish, Hewbrew, Korean, Spanish, Turkish, Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slobenian, Tagalog, Yoruba
experimental_materials_comment: Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks: multilabel probing using morphologically annotated corpora from UD. Table A1 summarizes the datasets for the monolingual and multilingual experiments and Table A2 for the crosslingual experiments
interp_method: Monolingual probing (probes trained and tested on individual languages), Multilingual probing (probes trained on combined training data from multiple languages), Crosslingual transfer (zero-shot evaluation of probes trained on other languages)
main_findings: investigates how multilingual BERT (mBERT) encodes morphosyntactic knowledge using a novel multilabel probing task, revealing that mBERT robustly represents a wide range of morphosyntactic features, with the sixth layer consistently yielding the most informative embeddings across diverse languages. The multilabel paradigm captures co-occurring grammatical features, as exemplified by Hebrew determiners, showing that the model can infer covert grammatical markers from overt cues. Cross-linguistic evaluation indicates that mBERT encodes some universal categories, like nouns and verbs, cohesively, while others, like adjectives or features with variable distribution, are represented more diffusely, with structural similarities between languages facilitating transfer. Finally, multilingual probes, though slightly less accurate than monolingual ones, provide more selective and expressive diagnostics, especially for features that are consistently represented across languages, highlighting the trade-off between memorization and extraction in probing mBERT’s linguistic knowledge.

title: Probing for Referential Information in Language Models
abstract: Language models keep track of complex information about the preceding context – including, e.g., syntactic relations in a sentence. We investigate whether they also capture information beneficial for resolving pronominal anaphora in English. We analyze two state of the art models with LSTM and Transformer architectures, via probe tasks and analysis on a coreference annotated corpus. The Transformer outperforms the LSTM in all analyses. Our results suggest that language models are more successful at learning grammatical constraints than they are at learning truly referential information, in the sense of capturing the fact that we use language to refer to entities in the world. However, we find traces of the latter aspect, too.
model_name_comment: TransformerXL (Dai et al., 2019),  AWD-LSTM (Merity et al., 2017)
syntactic_phenomena: Binding and coreference, POS, Agreement and feature-checking
specific_phenomena: anaphora resolution, annotated coreference chains/antecedent for POS tag, number/gender agreement
experimental_materials_comment: OntoNotes 5.0 (Weischedel et al., 2013)
interp_method: probe for referen- tial information encoded in language models, on two linguistic levels (morphosyntax, semantics) and two kinds of context: local (around one para- graph of context), and global (document context)
main_findings: demonstrates that language models (LMs), specifically AWD-LSTM and TransformerXL, are highly proficient at capturing syntactic knowledge, or morphosyntax, even without explicit training. The models robustly encode grammatical constraints, such as pronoun-antecedent agreement in gender and number, and correctly identify nominal elements as antecedents with high accuracy (e.g., TransformerXL identified mentions in 92.6% of cases). Transformers consistently outperform LSTMs by about 10% in probe tasks, though both architectures show similar morphosyntactic behavior. While LMs exhibit some recency bias, the Transformer’s attention mechanism mitigates this effect, allowing it to reference more distant antecedents. Overall, the hidden layers of these models strongly encode grammatical information, which can be effectively extracted using simple linear probes, confirming that LMs capture formal linguistic properties far better than semantico-referential content.

title: A Latent-Variable Model for Intrinsic Probing
abstract: The success of pre-trained contextualized representations has prompted researchers to analyze them for the presence of linguistic information. Indeed, it is natural to assume that these pre-trained representations do encode some level of linguistic knowledge as they have brought about large empirical improvements on a wide variety of NLP tasks, which suggests they are learning true linguistic generalization. In this work, we focus on intrinsic probing, an analysis technique where the goal is not only to identify whether a representation encodes a linguistic attribute but also to pinpoint where this attribute is encoded. We propose a novel latent-variable formulation for constructing intrinsic probes and derive a tractable variational approximation to the log-likelihood. Our results show that our model is versatile and yields tighter mutual information estimates than two intrinsic probes previously proposed in the literature. Finally, we find empirical evidence that pre-trained representations develop a cross-lingually entangled notion of morphosyntax.

specific_phenomena: English–Number, Portuguese–Gender and Noun Class, Polish–Tense, Russian–Voice, Arabic–Case, Finnish–Tense
languages_tested_comment: English, Portuguese, Polish, Russian, Arabic, Finnish

We estimate our probes’ parameters using the UD training set
interp_method: Intrinsic Probing:  new method for training intrinsic probes using a subset-valued latent variable, with variational inference for marginalization. Two variational families—Poisson and conditional Poisson sampling—are proposed to model the posterior over subsets
main_findings: m-BERT shares the same informative neurons across multiple languages for expressing certain morphosyntactic features, such as number. Languages like Russian, Polish, Portuguese, English, and Arabic show statistically significant overlap in their top 30 most informative neurons for this feature. This suggests that m-BERT encodes a cross-lingually entangled representation of morphosyntax, likely enhanced between typologically similar languages.

title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.
specific_phenomena: Definiteness, Comparison, Possession, Aspect, Polarity, Number, Animacy, Mood, Gender, Person, POS, Case, Tense, Finiteness
experimental_materials_comment: 43 treebanks from Universal Dependencies 2.1 (UD; Nivre et al., 2017), which contain sentences annotated with morphosyntactic information in a wide array of languages
interp_method: latent-variable model recently proposed by Sta´nczak et al. (2022) for intrinsic probing
main_findings: probes trained on different languages read the same concepts from the same neurons in smaller-scale masked language models such as mBERt syntax is encoded in similar ways across lan guages (Chi et al., 2020; Stanczak et al., 2022), though these rely on correlational methods based on dependency parsing, which introduce confounds and may not rely on syntactic information per se. shows that multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R share neurons that encode morphosyntactic features across languages, especially among typologically similar ones. The extent of neuron overlap varies by feature type and language, increasing with pretraining data size but decreasing in larger models. These findings support the idea of cross-lingual generalization through shared representations and suggest that encouraging neuron overlap could improve zero-shot transfer to low-resource languages

title: BERT Rediscovers the Classical NLP Pipeline
abstract: Pre-trained text encoders have rapidly advanced the state of the art on many NLP tasks. We focus on one such model, BERT, and aim to quantify where linguistic information is captured within the network. We find that the model represents the steps of the traditional NLP pipeline in an interpretable and localizable way, and that the regions responsible for each step appear in the expected sequence: POS tagging, parsing, NER, semantic roles, then coreference. Qualitative analysis reveals that the model can and often does adjust this pipeline dynamically, revising lower-level decisions on the basis of disambiguating information from higher-level representations.
model_name_comment: BERT base uncased and BERT large uncased
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, POS, Binding and coreference, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: part-of-speech (POS), constituents (Consts.), dependencies (Deps.), entities, semantic role labeling (SRL), coreference (Coref.), semantic proto-roles (SPR; Reisinger et al., 2015), and relation classification (SemEval)

main_findings: "learns" familiar order of linguistic operations, observe that in general, syntactic information is more localizable, with weights related to syntactic tasks tending to be concentrated on a few layers (high K(s) and K(∆)), while information related to semantic tasks is generally spread across the entire network, individual examples show that BERT can resolve information out-of-order, using high-level cues to inform lower-level tasks. This suggests that BERT models complex hierarchical language structures and interactions between them.

title: Probing the SpanBERT Architecture to interpret Scientific Domain Adaptation Challenges for Coreference Resolution
abstract: Coreference Resolution is a challenging problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that aims at clustering all references of the same entity or event. This requires both syntactic and semantic understanding of the text. A strong coreference resolution model is essential for achieving good performance in several downstream NLP tasks such as Question-Answering, Information Extraction etc. SpanBERT (Joshi et al. 2020) has achieved state of the art performance in coreference resolution on the OntoNotes dataset (Pradhan et al. 2012). However it still has several challenges when performing coreference resolution on documents involving multiple domain speciﬁc entities and events. In this paper we have highlighted these issues with SpanBERT-Base (pre-trained coreference model) in scientiﬁc domain adaptation. Our detailed experiments have been performed on the Sci-ERC scientiﬁc abstract dataset (Luan et al. 2018), where we analyse the encoder attention and probe the coarse-to-ﬁne head network to interpret the short comings of SpanBERT. This has lead to interesting ﬁndings that showed: 1) While we observed that the syntactic behaviour is captured appropriately, the self-attention mechanism in the encoder layers of SpanBERT struggles to capture domain speciﬁc semantic concepts, 2) Inferior mention spans are picked in the top mention spans list due to poor mention scores even though better candidate key mention spans exist, and 3) Even by increasing the hyperparameter λ from 0.4 to 1 and 2, there is insigniﬁ-cant improvement in both N key ∩ response and response coreference cluster scores across 5 different evaluation metrics.
specific_phenomena: Coreference resolution
experimental_materials_comment: SciERC scientific abstract dataset (Luan et al. 2018), 500 annotated scientific domain abstracts
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Encoder Attention Analysis, Feature Visualization (Attention)
interp_method: looking at Encoder attention, Identification of Mentions, Mention scores, Antecedent scores and Coreference Cluster
main_findings: While it is observed that the syntactic behaviour is captured appropriately, the self-attention mechanism in the encoder layers of SpanBERT struggles to capture domain speciﬁc semantic concepts, and there is insigni-cant improvement in both N key ∩ response and response coreference cluster scores across 5 different evaluation metrics: performance of SpanBERT on coreference resolution in scientific texts, revealing that while it captures syntactic structure well, it struggles with semantic understanding in the scientific domain. This semantic weakness hinders its effectiveness in resolving coreference. The authors suggest improvements such as using more robust tokenization methods (e.g., BPE-Dropout or SentencePiece) to handle out-of-vocabulary words, and employing advanced fine-tuning techniques to prevent catastrophic forgetting during domain adaptation

title: Using Integrated Gradients to explain Linguistic Acceptability learnt by BERT
abstract: BERT has been a breakthrough in language understanding by leveraging the multi-head self-attention mechanism in its architecture. To the best of our knowledge this work is the first to leverage Layer Integrated Gradients Attribution Scores (LIGAS) to explain the Linguistic Acceptability criteria that are learnt by BERT on the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA) benchmark dataset. Our experiments on 5 different categories of sentences lead to the following interesting findings: 1) LIGAS for Linguistically Acceptable (LA) sentences are significantly smaller in comparison to Linguistically Unacceptable (LUA) sentences, 2) There are specific subtrees of the Constituency Parse Tree (CPT) for LA and LUA sentences which contribute larger LIGAS, 3) Across the different categories of sentences we observed around 88% to 100% of the Correctly classified sentences had positive LIGAS, indicating a strong positive relationship to the prediction confidence of the model, and 4) Around 57% of the Misclassified sentences had positive LIGAS, which we believe can become correctly classified sentences if the LIGAS are parameterized in the loss function of the model.
syntactic_phenomena: Argument Structure and other Constructions, Binding and coreference, Agreement and feature-checking

title: When Does Syntax Mediate Neural Language Model Performance? Evidence from Dropout Probes
abstract: Recent causal probing literature reveals when language models and syntactic probes use similar representations. Such techniques may yield “false negative” causality results: models may use representations of syntax, but probes may have learned to use redundant encodings of the same syntactic information. We demonstrate that models do encode syntactic information redundantly and introduce a new probe design that guides probes to consider all syntactic information present in embeddings. Using these probes, we find evidence for the use of syntax in models where prior methods did not, allowing us to boost model performance by injecting syntactic information into representations.
model_name_comment: bert-base-uncased, fintuned on  QA, NLI, NLI-HANS
syntactic_phenomena: Argument Structure and other Constructions, Agreement and feature-checking

Each suite includes sentence templates that require syntactic interpretation to resolve meaning—for example, determining who was tall or who had an object. The goal is to assess whether models rely on syntax causally, not just statistically, to interpret ambiguous structures accurately.
interp_method: Dropout Probe: . At training time, the dropout layer masks a random subset of the input; the mask itself changes with every training batch; neural probing architecture for generating useful causal analysis of trained language models. Our technical contribution — adding a dropout layer before probes — was inspired by a theory of redundant syntactic encodings in models.
main_findings: showed that 1) models encoded syntactic information redundantly, 2) dropout probes, unlike stan- dard probes, revealed that QA models used syntactic representations causally, and 3) by injecting syntactic information at test time in syntactically- challenging domains, we could increase model per- formance without retraining.

title: What if This Modified That? Syntactic Interventions with Counterfactual Embeddings
abstract: Neural language models exhibit impressive performance on a variety of tasks, but their in- ternal reasoning may be difficult to understand. Prior art aims to uncover meaningful proper- ties within model representations via probes, but it is unclear how faithfully such probes portray information that the models actually use. To overcome such limitations, we pro- pose a technique, inspired by causal analy- sis, for generating counterfactual embeddings within models. In experiments testing our technique, we produce evidence that suggests some BERT-based models use a tree-distance- like representation of syntax in downstream prediction tasks.
specific_phenomena: Coordination Ambiguity, NP/Z (Noun Phrase / Zero) Ambiguity, Relative Clause (RC) Attachment Ambiguity, NP/VP (Noun Phrase / Verb Phrase) Attachment Ambiguity
fine_tuning_materials: already fine-tuned on the SQuAD dataset, and referred to the model as QA (Wolf et al., 2019; Rajpurkar et al., 2016)
