NP/Z Corpus (Mask model): 60 ambiguous sentences inspired by psycholinguistic studies, like “When the dog scratched the vet [MASK] ran.”      Relative Clause (RC) Corpus (QA model): 192 sentences with relative clause ambiguities, such as “The tall man and short woman who were happy saw the dog.”      NP/VP Attachment Corpus (QA model): 144 sentences testing prepositional phrase attachment, e.g., “The girl saw the boy with the telescope.”
interp_method: a new technique using counterfactual embeddings and causal analysis to investigate how neural language models like BERT internally reason.  The goal is to determine not just what linguistic information models encode (which traditional probes show), but what information they actually use for downstream tasks •Technique Developed: A gradient-based algorithm is proposed to generate "counterfactual embeddings" by manipulating internal model representations (embeddings) according to specific syntactic principles (e.g., changing a sentence's implied parse). This differs from previous causal analysis methods that modify input data or ablate parts of embeddings
main_findings:
pretrained BERT model does use representations of syntax causally (i.e., model outputs change when using different syntactic interpretations), the authors find that a BERT model fine-tuned on a question answering task does not show similar behavior. Identifying causal mechanisms in models is impor tant not only for fairness and robustness measures, but also for improving model performance. 
•Key Finding 1 (Mask Model): Experiments showed that the standard BERT model, trained on masked word prediction tasks, does leverage features of syntax in predicting masked words. Specifically, distance-based syntactic representations (like word distances in a parse tree) appear to be used, while depth-based manipulations had little effect. Multi-layered non-linear distance probes performed better at eliciting these changes than simpler linear probes •Key Finding 2 (QA Model): In contrast, a BERT model fine-tuned for question-answering does not appear to use the syntactic information detected by the probes in its downstream predictions. This suggests fine-tuning for specific tasks might reduce the alignment between model and human representations of language •Implications for Probe Design: The results contribute to the debate on probe design, suggesting that more complex, multi-layered probes can be advantageous in revealing model behavior, challenging the prior notion that simpler probes are always preferable

title: Data-driven Cross-lingual Syntax: An Agreement Study with Massively Multilingual Models
abstract: Massively multilingual models such as mBERT and XLM-R are increasingly valued in Natural Language Processing research and applications, due to their ability to tackle the uneven distribution of resources available for different languages. The models’ ability to process multiple languages relying on a shared set of parameters raises the question of whether the grammatical knowledge they extracted during pre-training can be considered as a data-driven cross-lingual grammar. The present work studies the inner workings of mBERT and XLM-R in order to test the cross-lingual consistency of the individual neural units that respond to a precise syntactic phenomenon, that is, number agreement, in five languages (English, German, French, Hebrew, Russian). We found that there is a significant overlap in the latent dimensions that encode agreement across the languages we considered. This overlap is larger (a) for long- vis-à-vis short-distance agreement and (b) when considering XLM-R as compared to mBERT, and peaks in the intermediate layers of the network. We further show that a small set of syntax-sensitive neurons can capture agreement violations across languages; however, their contribution is not decisive in agreement processing.
specific_phenomena: Number agreement,  subject-verb agreement: Simple agreement (referred to as short-distance agreement) • Long-distance VP-coordination (referred to as long-distance agreement)
languages_tested_comment: English, German, French, Russian, and Hebrew
experimental_materials_comment: CLAMS dataset (Mueller et al. 2020), a cross-linguistic resource for the syntactic evaluation of word prediction models ("CLAMS includes subject-verb agreement challenge sets for English, French, German, Hebrew and Russian, generated from grammars we develop.")
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Linguistic Correlation Analysis, Activation Patching (Ablation)
interp_method: Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA), which is a supervised technique based on linear classification, to identify the neural units most relevant to the number agreement task
main_findings: investigating the cross-lingual consistency of individual neurons responding to syntactic phenomena: models contain language-neutral and language-specific components, with certain neurons consistently responding to syntactic features in multiple languages. Cross-lingual consistency is stronger in more complex syntactic structures, and XLM-R shows better cross-lingual alignment than mBERT. The results suggest that these multilingual models use shared structural resources for grammar across languages, supporting the idea that they generalize beyond surface linguistic differences. However, the study focuses only on number agreement;

title: The Better Your Syntax, the Better Your Semantics? Probing Pretrained Language Models for the English Comparative Correlative
abstract: Construction Grammar (CxG) is a paradigm from cognitive linguistics emphasising the connection between syntax and semantics. Rather than rules that operate on lexical items, it posits constructions as the central building blocks of language, i.e., linguistic units of different granularity that combine syntax and semantics. As a first step towards assessing the compatibility of CxG with the syntactic and semantic knowledge demonstrated by state-of-the-art pretrained language models (PLMs), we present an investigation of their capability to classify and understand one of the most commonly studied constructions, the English comparative correlative (CC). We conduct experiments examining the classification accuracy of a syntactic probe on the one hand and the models’ behaviour in a semantic application task on the other, with BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa as the example PLMs. Our results show that all three investigated PLMs are able to recognise the structure of the CC but fail to use its meaning. While human-like performance of PLMs on many NLP tasks has been alleged, this indicates that PLMs still suffer from substantial shortcomings in central domains of linguistic knowledge.

title: Frequency Effects on Syntactic Rule Learning in Transformers
abstract: Pre-trained language models perform well on a variety of linguistic tasks that require symbolic reasoning, raising the question of whether such models implicitly represent abstract symbols and rules. We investigate this question using the case study of BERT’s performance on English subject–verb agreement. Unlike prior work, we train multiple instances of BERT from scratch, allowing us to perform a series of controlled interventions at pre-training time. We show that BERT often generalizes well to subject–verb pairs that never occurred in training, suggesting a degree of rule-governed behavior. We also find, however, that performance is heavily influenced by word frequency, with experiments showing that both the absolute frequency of a verb form, as well as the frequency relative to the alternate inflection, are causally implicated in the predictions BERT makes at inference time. Closer analysis of these frequency effects reveals that BERT’s behavior is consistent with a system that correctly applies the SVA rule in general but struggles to overcome strong training priors and to estimate agreement features (singular vs. plural) on infrequent lexical items.
specific_phenomena: English subject–verb number agreement (using a targeted syntactic evaluation framework)
experimental_materials_comment: natural sentences, which are gener-lly both syntactically and semantically coherent (23,298 sentences from Wikipedia),and (2) nonce sentences (following Gulordava et al.2018) which are grammatically valid but not nec-essarily semantically coherent (compiled a list of 200 nouns, 336 verbs, and 56 sen-tential contexts—sentence templates where we re-move the original subject and verb—such that anygiven (noun, verb, sentential context) triplet yieldsa grammatically correct nonce sentence)
interp_method: use probing  to attribute different types of SVA errors to specific underlying mechanisms within BERT: 2 probes were used: one tested whether embeddings at masked verb positions contained enough information to infer subject number, and the other tested whether verb embeddings encoded number features. Results showed that BERT's performance strongly depends on verb frequency—more frequent verbs lead to better agreement encoding. While BERT appears to represent the SVA rule, it often defaults to more common verb forms in cases of frequency imbalance, even when it has access to the correct features.
main_findings: whether BERT handles subject–verb agreement (SVA) using abstract rule-like representations or item-specific patterns. Findings suggest BERT does encode the correct SVA rule but struggles with low-frequency verbs due to noisy or insufficient training data. Errors often arise not from a lack of grammatical knowledge but from biased priors favoring more frequent verb forms. BERT also fails to apply rules when frequency-based preferences conflict with grammatical expectations.

title: Explaining pretrained language models' understanding of linguistic structures using construction grammar
abstract: Construction Grammar (CxG) is a paradigm from cognitive linguistics emphasizing the connection between syntax and semantics. Rather than rules that operate on lexical items, it posits constructions as the central building blocks of language, i.e., linguistic units of different granularity that combine syntax and semantics. As a first step toward assessing the compatibility of CxG with the syntactic and semantic knowledge demonstrated by state-of-the-art pretrained language models (PLMs), we present an investigation of their capability to classify and understand one of the most commonly studied constructions, the English comparative correlative (CC). We conduct experiments examining the classification accuracy of a syntactic probe on the one hand and the models' behavior in a semantic application task on the other, with BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa as the example PLMs. Our results show that all three investigated PLMs, as well as OPT, are able to recognize the structure of the CC but fail to use its meaning. While human-like performance of PLMs on many NLP tasks has been alleged, this indicates that PLMs still suffer from substantial shortcomings in central domains of linguistic knowledge.

title: A Non-Linear Structural Probe
abstract: fine-tuning is performed for the dependency parsing task; • Multilingual BERT (mBERT) is fine-tuned on a specific source language chosen for the transfer experiment,  data used for fine-tuning for the dependency parsing task is from Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks (version 2.8)

languages_tested_comment: Basque, English, Finnish, Korean, Tamil, Turkish
experimental_materials_comment: data from the Universal Dependencies 2.4 Treebank, which includes sentences annotated with dependency trees. It covered six typologically diverse languages, using up to 12,000 training sentences per language, split into 80% training, 10% development, and 10% test sets.
interp_method: builds on the Linear Structural Probe (Hewitt & Manning, 2019), which learns a linear transformation to predict syntactic distances between word pairs based on dependency trees. To improve on this, the authors introduce kernelized, non-linear probes that use functions like polynomial, RBF (Gaussian), and sigmoid kernels. These allow for more expressive modeling of non-linear relationships in contextual embeddings without increasing model complexity. The RBF kernel consistently outperformed the linear baseline across six typologically diverse languages, indicating that syntactic knowledge in BERT is non-linearly encoded.
main_findings: syntactic information may be encoded non-linearly in the representations produced by BERT. We hypothe- size that this is true due to the similarity of the RBF kernel and BERT’s self-attention layers.

title: Probing for Understanding of English Verb Classes and Alternations in Large Pre-trained Language Models
abstract: We investigate the extent to which verb alternation classes, as described by Levin (1993), are encoded in the embeddings of Large Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) such as BERT, RoBERTa, ELECTRA, and DeBERTa using selectively constructed diagnostic classifiers for word and sentence-level prediction tasks. We follow and expand upon the experiments of Kann et al. (2019), which aim to probe whether static embeddings encode frame-selectional properties of verbs. At both the word and sentence level, we find that contextual embeddings from PLMs not only outperform non-contextual embeddings, but achieve astonishingly high accuracies on tasks across most alternation classes. Additionally, we find evidence that the middle-to-upper layers of PLMs achieve better performance on average than the lower layers across all probing tasks.
specific_phenomena: Causative-Inchoative Alternation – Verbs like break can be both transitive and intransitive, but others like cut cannot.  Spray-Load Class – Verbs like spray allow both "theme on location" and "location with theme" constructions, unlike pour.  Dative Alternation – Involves variation in argument structure for verbs like give (e.g., "gave a book to her" vs. "gave her a book").  There-Insertion Alternation – Tests verbs' compatibility with existential constructions like "There is a cat on the roof".  Understood-Object Alternation – Involves verbs where the object can be omitted but still understood (e.g., "She eats").
experimental_materials_comment: dataset created by Kann et al. (2019). One is the Lexical Verb frame Alternations dataset (LaVA), and  Frames and Alternations of Verbs (FAVA), the other dataset, is a corpus of 9413 semi-automatically generated sentences formed from the verbs in LaVA along with human grammaticalityjudgments.
interp_method:
use simple, selective logistic regression classifiers trained on precomputed PLM embeddings—either verb-level (averaged token embeddings from grammatical sentences) or sentence-level (averaged hidden states across all layers). These classifiers then predict verb class membership or sentence grammaticality
 control task, besides the linear probe (Logistic Regression), they also compare its selectivity against more complex classifiers: a Multi-layer Perceptron with 1-hidden layer (MLP-1) and an MLP with 2-hidden layers (MLP-2). The conclusion from the control task was that the linear probe (Logistic Regression) was a good choice for their linguistic task because it achieved higher selectivity without a substantial loss in accuracy compared to the MLP models
main_findings: models encode syntactic knowledge about English verb alternation classes. Their contextual embeddings outperform static embeddings (like GloVe) in both word- and sentence-level tasks, achieving high accuracy and Matthews correlation coefficients. Middle-to-upper layers of PLMs contain the richest syntactic information. ELECTRA performs best overall, likely due to its discriminator-based pretraining. The use of simple logistic regression probes—validated as selective and reliable—confirms that this knowledge is genuinely embedded in the models, not just extracted by complex classifiers.

title: Cross-Linguistic Syntactic Difference in Multilingual BERT: How Good is It and How Does It Affect Transfer?
abstract: Multilingual BERT (mBERT) has demonstrated considerable cross-lingual syntactic ability, whereby it enables effective zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of syntactic knowledge. The transfer is more successful between some languages, but it is not well understood what leads to this variation and whether it fairly reflects difference between languages. In this work, we investigate the distributions of grammatical relations induced from mBERT in the context of 24 typologically different languages. We demonstrate that the distance between the distributions of different languages is highly consistent with the syntactic difference in terms of linguistic formalisms. Such difference learnt via self-supervision plays a crucial role in the zero-shot transfer performance and can be predicted by variation in morphosyntactic properties between languages. These results suggest that mBERT properly encodes languages in a way consistent with linguistic diversity and provide insights into the mechanism of cross-lingual transfer.

interp_method: The study utilized a parser with a deep biaffine attention mechanism on top of mBERT for dependency parsing, following the setup of Wu and Dredze (2019). This setup involved training a linear model to predict POS tags on the source side (the language being fine-tuned on) and applying it to the target languages to avoid introducing external cross-lingual information. Subtracting the embeddings of head-dependent word pairs to derive syntactic representations. Using a simple linear classifier to predict grammatical relations from these representations.
main_findings: Grammatical relations are recoverable from mBERT’s embeddings, particularly from layers 7 and 8, where relation-specific clusters emerge. Probing is less effective for morphologically rich languages (e.g., Turkish, Finnish) and those using CJK tokenization (e.g., Chinese, Korean), likely due to tokenization issues. syntactic differences learned during pretraining significantly influence zero-shot transfer performance in tasks like dependency parsing. Fine-tuning on a source language improves task-specific alignment between source and target languages, but it can also distort the broader syntactic structure learned during pretraining—especially for typologically distant languages. Additionally, variation in morphosyntactic properties from the WALS, particularly word order features, strongly predicts the syntactic differences learned by mBERT. Using these properties, the researchers built a model that successfully identified optimal source languages for transfer tasks, enabling better zero-shot performance without exhaustive experimentation.

title: Perturbed Masking: Parameter-free Probing for Analyzing and Interpreting BERT
abstract: By introducing a small set of additional parameters, a probe learns to solve specific linguistic tasks (e.g., dependency parsing) in a supervised manner using feature representations (e.g., contextualized embeddings). The effectiveness of such probing tasks is taken as evidence that the pre-trained model encodes linguistic knowledge. However, this approach of evaluating a language model is undermined by the uncertainty of the amount of knowledge that is learned by the probe itself. Complementary to those works, we propose a parameter-free probing technique for analyzing pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT). Our method does not require direct supervision from the probing tasks, nor do we introduce additional parameters to the probing process. Our experiments on BERT show that syntactic trees recovered from BERT using our method are significantly better than linguistically-uninformed baselines. We further feed the empirically induced dependency structures into a downstream sentiment classification task and find its improvement compatible with or even superior to a human-designed dependency schema.
specific_phenomena: dependency trees (recover syntactic trees)
experimental_materials_comment: two datasets from SemEval 2014  (Pontiki et al., 2014),
interp_method: Perturbed Masking technique into the masked language modeling (MLM) objective to measure the impact a word xj has on predicting another word xi (Sec 2.2) and then induce the global linguistic properties (e.g., depen-dency trees) from this inter-word information
main_findings: a parameter-free probing method to complement existing approaches for interpreting BERT. Their results support prior findings that BERT naturally encodes rich syntactic information, learned through self-supervised training on plain text. e.g., results reinforce those of (Hewitt andManning, 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Jawahar et al., 2019; Tenney et al., 2019b,a)

title: Disentangling Representations of Text by Masking Transformers
abstract: Representations from large pretrained models such as BERT encode a range of features into monolithic vectors, affording strong predictive accuracy across a range of downstream tasks. In this paper we explore whether it is possible to learn disentangled representations by identifying existing subnetworks within pretrained models that encode distinct, complementary aspects. Concretely, we learn binary masks over transformer weights or hidden units to uncover subsets of features that correlate with a specific factor of variation; this eliminates the need to train a disentangled model from scratch for a particular task. We evaluate this method with respect to its ability to disentangle representations of sentiment from genre in movie reviews, toxicity from dialect in Tweets, and syntax from semantics. By combining masking with magnitude pruning we find that we can identify sparse subnetworks within BERT that strongly encode particular aspects (e.g., semantics) while only weakly encoding others (e.g., syntax). Moreover, despite only learning masks, disentanglement-via-masking performs as well as — and often better than —previously proposed methods based on variational autoencoders and adversarial training.

title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope
abstract: Large pretrained language models like BERT, after fine-tuning to a downstream task, have achieved high performance on a variety of NLP problems. Yet explaining their decisions is difficult despite recent work probing their internal representations. We propose a procedure and analysis methods that take a hypothesis of how a transformer-based model might encode a linguistic phenomenon, and test the validity of that hypothesis based on a comparison between knowledge-related downstream tasks with downstream control tasks, and measurement of cross-dataset consistency. We apply this methodology to test BERT and RoBERTa on a hypothesis that some attention heads will consistently attend from a word in negation scope to the negation cue. We find that after fine-tuning BERT and RoBERTa on a negation scope task, the average attention head improves its sensitivity to negation and its attention consistency across negation datasets compared to the pre-trained models. However, only the base models (not the large models) improve compared to a control task, indicating there is evidence for a shallow encoding of negation only in the base models.

title: Probing language identity encoded in pre-trained multilingual models: a typological view
abstract: Pre-trained multilingual models have been extensively used in cross-lingual information processing tasks. Existing work focuses on improving the transferring performance of pre-trained multilingual models but ignores the linguistic properties that models preserve at encoding time—“language identity”. We investigated the capability of state-of-the-art pre-trained multilingual models (mBERT, XLM, XLM-R) to preserve language identity through language typology. We explored model differences and variations in terms of languages, typological features, and internal hidden layers. We found the order of ability in preserving language identity of whole model and each of its hidden layers is: mBERT > XLM-R > XLM. Furthermore, all three models capture morphological, lexical, word order and syntactic features well, but perform poorly on nominal and verbal features. Finally, our results show that the ability of XLM-R and XLM remains stable across layers, but the ability of mBERT fluctuates severely. Our findings summarize the ability of each pre-trained multilingual model and its hidden layer to store language identity and typological features. It provides insights for later researchers in processing cross-lingual information.

Layer-wise, mBERT showed peak syntactic encoding in middle layers, while XLM and XLM-R were more stable across layers.

title: What does Chinese BERT learn about syntactic knowledge?
abstract: Pre-trained language models such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) have been applied to a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks and obtained significantly positive results. A growing body of research has investigated the reason why BERT is so efficient and what language knowledge BERT is able to learn. However, most of these works focused almost exclusively on English. Few studies have explored the language information, particularly syntactic information, that BERT has learned in Chinese, which is written as sequences of characters. In this study, we adopted some probing methods for identifying syntactic knowledge stored in the attention heads and hidden states of Chinese BERT. The results suggest that some individual heads and combination of heads do well in encoding corresponding and overall syntactic relations, respectively. The hidden representation of each layer also contained syntactic information to different degrees. We also analyzed the fine-tuned models of Chinese BERT for different tasks, covering all levels. Our results suggest that these fine-turned models reflect changes in conserving language structure. These findings help explain why Chinese BERT can show such large improvements across many language-processing tasks.

Two high-level semantic tasks—Natural Language Inference (NLI) using the OCNLI dataset and Question Matching (CQ) using the LCQMC dataset—produced NLI-BERT and CQ-BERT

main_findings: Chinese BERT encodes substantial syntactic knowledge across its architecture. While no single attention head captures full sentence structure, individual heads—especially in middle layers (5–9)—effectively represent specific dependency relations. Collectively, all heads enable strong sentence parsing. Unique Chinese constructions like bèi (被) and baˇ (把) are well encoded in middle layers, while aspectual particles (-zhe, -le, -guò) are captured in lower layers, indicating a layer-wise split between structural and lexical knowledge. Positional proximity boosts performance, with near-perfect accuracy for adjacent dependencies. In hidden states, the final layer (12) holds the most syntactic information, though lower layers may lack full structural encoding. Fine-tuning affects this knowledge: POS tagging enhances syntax, NLI erodes it, and tasks like word segmentation or question matching preserve or mildly impact it.

title: Systematic testing of three Language Models reveals low language accuracy, absence of response stability, and a yes-response bias
abstract: Humans are universally good in providing stable and accurate judgments about what forms part of their language and what not. Large Language Models (LMs) are claimed to possess human-like language abilities; hence, they are expected to emulate this behavior by providing both stable and accurate answers, when asked whether a string of words complies with or deviates from their next-word predictions. This work tests whether stability and accuracy are showcased by GPT-3/text-davinci-002, GPT-3/text-davinci-003, and ChatGPT, using a series of judgment tasks that tap on 8 linguistic phenomena: plural attraction, anaphora, center embedding, comparatives, intrusive resumption, negative polarity items, order of adjectives, and order of adverbs. For every phenomenon, 10 sentences (5 grammatical and 5 ungrammatical) are tested, each randomly repeated 10 times, totaling 800 elicited judgments per LM (total n = 2,400). Our results reveal variable above-chance accuracy in the grammatical condition, below-chance accuracy in the ungrammatical condition, a significant instability of answers across phenomena, and a yes-response bias for all the tested LMs. Furthermore, we found no evidence that repetition aids the Models to converge on a processing strategy that culminates in stable answers, either accurate or inaccurate. We demonstrate that the LMs’ performance in identifying (un)grammatical word patterns is in stark contrast to what is observed in humans (n = 80, tested on the same tasks) and argue that adopting LMs as theories of human language is not motivated at their current stage of development.

Targe Language Models (LMs), their underlying syntactic knowledge is limited and unreliable. When prompted to make explicit grammaticality judgments, LMs perform only slightly above chance—especially struggling with ungrammatical sentences—and exhibit a strong bias toward accepting all sentences as grammatical. Their responses are unstable, often varying when the same sentence is repeated, and they show no consistent improvement with repetition, unlike humans. These findings challenge claims that LMs can serve as models of human linguistic competence and highlight the lack of transparency around how their language abilities are engineered. revealing a stark absence of response stability and a bias toward yes-responses. Our results raise the question of how knowledge of language in LMs is engineered to have specific characteristics that are absent from human performance.

title: Large language models are better than theoretical linguists at theoretical linguistics
abstract: Large language models are better than theoretical linguists at theoretical linguistics, at least in the domain of verb argument structure; explaining why (for example), we can say both The ball rolled and Someone rolled the ball, but not both The man laughed and *Someone laughed the man. Verbal accounts of this phenomenon either do not make precise quantitative predictions at all, or do so only with the help of ancillary assumptions and by-hand data processing. Large language models, on the other hand (taking text-davinci-002 as an example), predict human acceptability ratings for these types of sentences with correlations of around r = 0.9, and themselves constitute theories of language acquisition and representation; theories that instantiate exemplar-, input- and construction-based approaches, though only very loosely. Indeed, large language models succeed where these verbal (i.e., non-computational) linguistic theories fail, precisely because the latter insist – in the service of intuitive interpretability – on simple yet empirically inadequate (over)generalizations.
specific_phenomena: causative constructions. It examines the models’ ability to distinguish between intransitive-inchoative (e.g., "The ball rolled"), transitive-causative (e.g., "Someone rolled the ball"), and periphrastic causatives (e.g., "Someone made the man laugh"). it explores whether LLMs can infer argument structure privileges for novel verbs in a way similar to humans. similar syntactic patterns apply to other constructions like datives, locatives, passives, and verbal un-prefixation

(2020), and asked to rate their grammatical acceptability on a 5-point scale. In a separate "wug" test using davinci-002, novel verbs were introduced, and the model's surprisal (as a proxy for acceptability) was measured when these verbs appeared in transitive versus periphrastic causative forms

main_findings: LLms are better than theoretical linguists at theoretical linguistics; at least in the domain that we know something about: learning and representing verbs’ argument structure privileges. The phenomenon is that while – for example – some English verbs can occur in both the intransitive-inchoative (1) and transitive-causative construction (2), others can appear in the former (3) but not the latter (4), and instead form only periphrastic causatives with make (5). particularly text-davinci-002, excel at predicting human judgments about verb argument structure, outperforming traditional linguistic theories. The model showed strong correlations (up to r = 0.92) with human acceptability ratings for both transitive and periphrastic causative constructions. The authors argue that LLMs function as explicit, data-driven theories of language acquisition, learning syntactic patterns through distributional learning across vast linguistic input. Remarkably, the models also generalized well to novel verbs in a “wug” test, using semantic cues to prefer appropriate syntactic constructions. findings underscore the LLMs' capacity to abstract and apply nuanced syntactic knowledge, even to unfamiliar linguistic items.

title: Prompting is not a substitute for probability measurements in large language models
abstract: Prompting is now a dominant method for evaluating the linguistic knowledge of large language models (LLMs). While other methods directly read out models’ probability distributions over strings, prompting requires models to access this internal information by processing linguistic input, thereby implicitly testing a new type of emergent ability: metalinguistic judgment. In this study, we compare metalinguistic prompting and direct probability measurements as ways of measuring models’ linguistic knowledge. Broadly, we find that LLMs’ metalinguistic judgments are inferior to quantities directly derived from representations. Furthermore, consistency gets worse as the prompt query diverges from direct measurements of next-word probabilities. Our findings suggest that negative results relying on metalinguistic prompts cannot be taken as conclusive evidence that an LLM lacks a particular linguistic generalization. Our results also highlight the value that is lost with the move to closed APIs where access to probability distributions is limited.

title: Auxiliary task demands mask the capabilities of smaller language models
abstract: Developmental psychologists have argued about when cognitive capacities such as language understanding or theory of mind emerge. These debates often hinge on the concept of "task demands" -- the auxiliary challenges associated with performing a particular evaluation -- that may mask the child’s underlying ability. The same issues arise when measuring the capacities of language models (LMs): performance on a task is a function of the model's underlying knowledge, combined with the model’s ability to interpret and perform the task given its available resources. Here, we show that for analogical reasoning, reflective reasoning, word prediction, and grammaticality judgments, evaluation methods with greater task demands yield lower performance than evaluations with reduced demands. This "demand gap" is most pronounced for models with fewer parameters and less training data. Our results illustrate that LM performance should not be interpreted as a direct indication of intelligence (or lack thereof), but as a reflection of capacities seen through the lens of researchers' design choices.

title: Language models align with human judgments on key grammatical constructions
abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) make human-like linguistic generalizations? Dentella et al. (2023) ("DGL") prompt several LLMs ("Is the following sentence grammatically correct in English?") to elicit grammaticality judgments of 80 English sentences, concluding that LLMs demonstrate a "yes-response bias" and a "failure to distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences". We re-evaluate LLM performance using well-established practices and find that DGL's data in fact provide evidence for just how well LLMs capture human behaviors. Models not only achieve high accuracy overall, but also capture fine-grained variation in human linguistic judgments.

main_findings: LLMs demonstrate strong, human-like syntactic generalization, especially when evaluated using minimal-pair analysis instead of metalinguistic prompts. This improved method revealed near-ceiling performance across most syntactic phenomena, with the exception of center embedding, where both LLMs and humans struggled. The models' surprisal-based scores reliably predicted human grammaticality judgments, and newer models like GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4 even outperformed humans on some tasks. The study also revisited the earlier-reported yes-response bias and found it largely absent in updated models.

title: Assessing BERT’s Syntactic Abilities
abstract: I assess the extent to which the recently introduced BERT model captures English syntactic phenomena, using (1) naturally-occurring subject-verb agreement stimuli; (2) “coloreless green ideas” subject-verb agreement stimuli, in which content words in natural sentences are randomly replaced with words sharing the same part-of-speech and inflection; and (3) manually crafted stimuli for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora phenomena. The BERT model performs remarkably well on all cases.

title: Can language models capture syntactic associations without surface cues? A case study of reflexive anaphor licensing in English control constructions
abstract: In this work, we examine a Transformer-based LM, namely Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) (Radford et al., 2019), which is trained only on surface strings, to see whether or not the model makes correct predictions about the agree- ment patterns of reflexive pronouns in subject and object control constructions. Our findings show that GPT-2 struggles with subject control construc- tions such as (2), but does quite well on object con- trol constructions such as (3). One reason might be that the model tries to associate the anaphor with the closest noun phrase. Moreover, while we find that a model with a larger number of parame- ters shows higher accuracy on the tasks related to subject control constructions, performance remains below chance and the model does not mimic human behavior.

title: BLiMP: The Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for English
abstract: We introduce The Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs (BLiMP),1 a challenge set for evaluating the linguistic knowledge of language models (LMs) on major grammatical phenomena in English. BLiMP consists of 67 individual datasets, each containing 1,000 minimal pairs—that is, pairs of minimally different sentences that contrast in grammatical acceptability and isolate specific phenomenon in syntax, morphology, or semantics. We generate the data according to linguist-crafted grammar templates, and human aggregate agreement with the labels is 96.4%. We evaluate n-gram, LSTM, and Transformer (GPT-2 and Transformer-XL) LMs by observing whether they assign a higher probability to the acceptable sentence in each minimal pair. We find that state-of-the-art models identify morphological contrasts related to agreement reliably, but they struggle with some subtle semantic and syntactic phenomena, such as negative polarity items and extraction islands.

All tested models, including GPT-2, fall short of human performance, with GPT-2 performing best but still 8 points below humans. While neural LMs acquire robust knowledge of some syntactic phenomena like ellipsis and control/raising, and perform well on morpho-syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor agreement), they struggle with more abstract or complex constructions such as island effects, argument structure, NPI licensing, and quantifiers. Models also show reliance on surface cues, with performance affected by intervening material or attractor nouns. The findings suggest that more data helps with easier phenomena, but hard syntactic challenges like extraction islands and NPIs show little improvement, even with large training data, highlighting limitations in LMs’ syntactic generalization.

title: When Do You Need Billions of Words of Pretraining Data?
abstract: NLP is currently dominated by general-purpose pretrained language models like RoBERTa, which achieve strong performance on NLU tasks through pretraining on billions of words. But what exact knowledge or skills do Transformer LMs learn from large-scale pretraining that they cannot learn from less data? We adopt four probing methods---classifier probing, information-theoretic probing, unsupervised relative acceptability judgment, and fine-tuning on NLU tasks---and draw learning curves that track the growth of these different measures of linguistic ability with respect to pretraining data volume using the MiniBERTas, a group of RoBERTa models pretrained on 1M, 10M, 100M and 1B words. We find that LMs require only about 10M or 100M words to learn representations that reliably encode most syntactic and semantic features we test. A much larger quantity of data is needed in order to acquire enough commonsense knowledge and other skills required to master typical downstream NLU tasks. The results suggest that, while the ability to encode linguistic features is almost certainly necessary for language understanding, it is likely that other forms of knowledge are the major drivers of recent improvements in language understanding among large pretrained models.
specific_phenomena:
Classifier Probing and Minimum Description Length (MDL) Probing: part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and constituency parsing. 
BLIMP, agreement phenomena such as anaphor agreement, determiner-noun agreement, and subject-verb agreement (typically learned early); wh-dependencies like filler-gap dependencies and island effects (learned later); and additional syntactic categories including argument structure, binding, control/raising, and ellipsis. BLiMP also covers harder or mixed phenomena that involve both syntactic and semantic elements, such as irregular forms, negative polarity item (NPI) licensing, and quantifiers
experimental_materials_comment: BLiMP Suite consists of 67 tasks made up of minimal sentence pairs that differ by a single edit to test contrasts in grammatical acceptability—covering phenomena such as agreement (e.g., anaphor, determiner-noun, subject-verb) and wh-dependencies (e.g., filler-gap, island effects). In contrast, the Edge Probing Suite includes ten controlled tasks designed to evaluate how well syntactic and semantic features can be extracted from model representations,
interp_method: adopt four probing methods—classifier probing, information-theoretic probing, unsupervised relative acceptability judgment, and fine-tuning on NLU tasks
main_findings: syntactic knowledge is acquired early during language model pretraining, with models like MiniBERTas and RoBERTaBASE requiring only 10M–100M words to reliably encode core syntactic features. Evidence from classifier probing on the Edge Probing Suite indicates that tasks such as part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and constituency parsing reach about 90% of their performance improvements with just 10M words. Minimum Description Length (MDL) probing supports this, showing earlier and more efficient encoding of syntactic features compared to semantic ones. In BLiMP, individual grammatical phenomena show varying learning curves: agreement phenomena (e.g., anaphor agreement, subject-verb agreement) are learned fastest (1M–10M words), while wh-dependencies (e.g., filler-gap, island effects) are harder and learned later (up to 100M words). Other syntactic aspects like argument structure, binding, ellipsis, and control/raising are also acquired within the 10M–100M range. However, quantifiers remain challenging, never being effectively learned—even with 30B words—due to their reliance on subtle semantics and pragmatics. Importantly, the acquisition of syntactic knowledge precedes the learning of commonsense reasoning and complex NLU task performance, which require far more data (1B–30B words), suggesting that while syntactic structure forms a foundational layer, higher-level language understanding depends on broader and later-learned capabilities.

title: A Systematic Assessment of Syntactic Generalization in Neural Language Models
abstract: While state-of-the-art neural network models continue to achieve lower perplexity scores on language modeling benchmarks, it remains unknown whether optimizing for broad-coverage predictive performance leads to human-like syntactic knowledge. Furthermore, existing work has not provided a clear picture about the model properties required to produce proper syntactic generalizations. We present a systematic evaluation of the syntactic knowledge of neural language models, testing 20 combinations of model types and data sizes on a set of 34 English-language syntactic test suites. We find substantial differences in syntactic generalization performance by model architecture, with sequential models underperforming other architectures. Factorially manipulating model architecture and training dataset size (1M-40M words), we find that variability in syntactic generalization performance is substantially greater by architecture than by dataset size for the corpora tested in our experiments. Our results also reveal a dissociation between perplexity and syntactic generalization performance.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Dependency parsing and constituency, Argument Structure and other Constructions, Hierarchical structure, Binding and coreference,  Ellipsis and filler-gap dependencies, POS, Negation and NPIs
specific_phenomena: including number agreement, argument structure, hierarchical structure, c-command, anaphoric relations, binding principles (A, B, C), locality constraints, clausal embedding, thematic roles, T→C movement, passives, wh-movement, island constraints, and part-of-speech distinctions. These are tested through six core syntactic circuits: Agreement (subject-verb number agreement), Licensing (negative polarity item and reflexive pronoun licensing), Garden-Path Effects (main verb/reduced relative and NP/Z ambiguities), Gross Syntactic Expectation (subordination structures), Center Embedding (recursive nesting of clauses), and Long-Distance Dependencies (filler-gap dependencies and cleft constructions). Robustness is further tested with versions of some suites containing irrelevant modifiers to assess whether models maintain syntactic generalizations in more complex contexts.
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic training data and controlled syntactic test suites. For training, they used subsets of English newswire text from the BLLIP 1987–89 corpus in four sizes (1M, 5M, 14M, 42M tokens), tokenized with the Penn Treebank tokenizer, along with pre-trained models trained on up to 2B tokens. For evaluation, they used 34 psycholinguistically inspired test suites—33 adapted from prior work and one novel (Cleft)—designed to probe specific syntactic phenomena through minimal sentence variations across controlled conditions. These test suites, grouped into six “syntactic circuits” (Agreement, Licensing, Garden-Path Effects, Gross Syntactic Expectation, Center Embedding, Long-Distance Dependencies), cover phenomena like subject-verb agreement, negative polarity item licensing, reflexives, subordination, filler-gap dependencies, and more. The materials were informed by theoretical linguistics (e.g. Carnie, 2012) and target 16 key syntactic phenomena, with some suites including added distractors to test robustness
interp_method: The test suites are divided into 6 syntactic circuits, based on the type of algorithm required to successfully process each construction;our approach does not involve fine-tuning, but rather assesses what syntactic knowledge is induced from the language modeling objective alone.
main_findings:
systematic evaluation of the syntactic knowledge of neural language models, hierarchical inductive biases appear to support human-like syntactic generalizations in small-data settings
Our circuit-level analysis reveals consistent failure on Licensing but inconsistent behavior on other circuits, suggesting that different syntactic circuits make use of different underlying processing capacities. In
addition to the insight these results provide about neural NLP systems, they also bear on questions central to cognitive science and linguistics, putting lower bounds on what syntactic knowledge can be acquired from string input alone; syntactic generalization in neural language models is more influenced by model architecture than by training data size, revealing a clear dissociation between perplexity and syntactic ability. While models trained on large datasets achieved low perplexity, this did not reliably translate to better syntactic performance. Instead, architecture (inductive bias) had a stronger impact, with some Transformer models achieving strong syntactic generalization (SG) scores even with far less data. The research also showed circuit-level variation, where different syntactic phenomena (e.g., Licensing, Agreement, Garden-Paths) depended on distinct processing capacities—Licensing, in particular, posed challenges across most models. Additionally, robustness to syntactically irrelevant modifiers varied by model, with models like GPT-2-XL showing strong stability. Overall, the findings emphasize that broad performance metrics like perplexity miss important aspects of syntactic knowledge, and that targeted evaluation is essential for understanding language models' linguistic competence.

title: Cross-Linguistic Syntactic Evaluation of Word Prediction Models
abstract: A range of studies have concluded that neural word prediction models can distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences with high accuracy. However, these studies are based primarily on monolingual evidence from English. To investigate how these models’ ability to learn syntax varies by language, we introduce CLAMS (Cross-Linguistic Assessment of Models on Syntax), a syntactic evaluation suite for monolingual and multilingual models. CLAMS includes subject-verb agreement challenge sets for English, French, German, Hebrew and Russian, generated from grammars we develop. We use CLAMS to evaluate LSTM language models as well as monolingual and multilingual BERT. Across languages, monolingual LSTMs achieved high accuracy on dependencies without attractors, and generally poor accuracy on agreement across object relative clauses. On other constructions, agreement accuracy was generally higher in languages with richer morphology. Multilingual models generally underperformed monolingual models. Multilingual BERT showed high syntactic accuracy on English, but noticeable deficiencies in other languages.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: investigates subject-verb agreement across various syntactic configurations—such as across prepositional phrases, relative clauses, and coordinated verb phrases—while also addressing structure-sensitive phenomena like reflexive anaphora, negative polarity item licensing, reduced relative clauses, and sentential complements in English-specific evaluations
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli, such as those employed in the CLAMS (Cross-Linguistic Syntactic Evaluation of Word Prediction Models, Mueller et al., ACL 2020) dataset, are systematically constructed to isolate specific syntactic phenomena—particularly subject-verb agreement
interp_method: The study uses the CLAMS dataset—a controlled, cross-linguistic benchmark focused on subject-verb agreement—to eliminate confounds found in natural language corpora and ensure that models are tested on core syntactic understanding, not memorized patterns.
main_findings: mBERT's syntactic abilities are inconsistent across languages. While it performs well on English subject-verb agreement tasks, its performance drops significantly in languages like Hebrew and Russian, even on simpler constructions. This is attributed to vocabulary limitations, script-related biases, and challenges with subword tokenization in morphologically rich languages. In contrast, monolingual English BERT consistently outperforms mBERT on English syntactic tasks, highlighting the trade-off in generalization versus specialization across languages.

title: Are Transformers a Modern Version of ELIZA? Observations on French Object Verb Agreement
abstract: Many recent works have demonstrated that unsupervised sentence representations of neural networks encode syntactic information by observing that neural language models are able to predict the agreement between a verb and its subject. We take a critical look at this line of research by showing that it is possible to achieve high accuracy on this agreement task with simple surface heuristics, indicating a possible flaw in our assessment of neural networks' syntactic ability. Our fine-grained analyses of results on the long-range French object-verb agreement show that contrary to LSTMs, Transformers are able to capture a non-trivial amount of grammatical structure.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: French object-verb agreement, a syntactic phenomenon requiring number and gender agreement between a preceding object and a past participle—posing challenges due to non-adjacency and attractors like auxiliary verbs. They also reference subject-verb agreement and long-distance agreement as common tasks for evaluating syntactic encoding in neural networks. Additionally, they discuss context-free patterns and minimize the impact of anaphora resolution by limiting test complexity.
experimental_materials_comment: The original test set was derived from the French Gutenberg corpus and Universal Dependency treebanks, focusing on simpler syntactic patterns while avoiding complex anaphora. To better isolate syntactic understanding, the authors created manipulated test sets, including:      Heuristic-categorized sets, grouped by how easily surface-level cues could predict agreement;      A nonce set, replacing content words with syntactically matched nonsense words to remove lexical biases;      A mirror set, balancing singular/plural distributions to reduce frequency bias;      A permuted set, with scrambled prefixes to test reliance on word order;      And distance-based analyses to measure model performance across varying syntactic distances between the object and verb.     These tools were designed to probe whether models rely on true syntactic understanding or superficial patterns.
interp_method: nan
main_findings: perform well on French object past-participle agreement, only Transformers demonstrate genuine syntactic understanding. LSTMs rely heavily on surface heuristics and their accuracy collapses on harder, structure-sensitive cases. Transformers, by contrast, maintain high performance even when lexical cues are removed (nonce test), class frequency is balanced (mirror test), or surface heuristics fail, indicating they encode abstract, hierarchical syntactic structure. However, word order remains crucial to their success, suggesting their syntactic ability is deeply tied to sequence information.

title: A computational psycholinguistic evaluation of the syntactic abilities of Galician BERT models at the interface of dependency resolution and training time
abstract: This paper explores the ability of Transformer models to capture subject- verb and noun-adjective agreement dependencies in Galician. We conduct a series of word prediction experiments in which we manipulate dependency length together with the presence of an attractor noun that acts as a lure. First, we evaluate the over- all performance of the existing monolingual and multilingual models for Galician. Secondly, to observe the effects of the training process, we compare the different de- grees of achievement of two monolingual BERT models at different training points. We also release their checkpoints and propose an alternative evaluation metric. Our results confirm previous findings by similar works that use the agreement prediction task and provide interesting insights into the number of training steps required by a Transformer model to solve long-distance dependencies

The evaluations were conducted using a specialized dataset by Garcia and Crespo-Otero (2022), featuring thousands of gender- and number-balanced sentences in Galician. To ensure fair evaluation, all masked target words appeared in the model vocabularies, and a novel metric (Probability Distance accuracy) was used to assess syntactic discrimination in semantically plausible contexts.
interp_method: Targeted Syntactic Evaluation (TSE), inspired by psycholinguistic studies, and centered on a Word Prediction Task to assess syntactic understanding. They also introduce a new evaluation metric, Probability Distance (PD accuracy), which measures the confidence gap between correct and incorrect alternatives, offering a more fine-grained assessment than standard binary accuracy
main_findings: Galician BERT models can resolve syntactic agreement dependencies, though with varying accuracy: BERT-base performs best, while Bertinho-small is least accurate. Noun-adjective agreement is generally easier for models than subject-verb agreement. All models are vulnerable to interference from attractor nouns, especially in longer dependencies, with less accurate models more affected. Attraction effects are also more severe for subject-verb dependencies. Training data size plays a crucial role in performance—more so than training time—with larger corpora yielding better results. Model initialization from mBERT helps early learning, but complex structures still cause instability, particularly for Check-base. The study also highlights that the proposed Probability Distance (PD accuracy) metric offers a more nuanced assessment of syntactic knowledge than traditional 0–1 accuracy, revealing that models often show weaker, less confident preferences even when correct.

title: Grokking of Hierarchical Structure in Vanilla Transformers
abstract: For humans, language production and comprehension is sensitive to the hierarchical structure of sentences. In natural language processing, past work has questioned how effectively neural sequence models like transformers capture this hierarchical structure when generalizing to structurally novel inputs. We show that transformer language models can learn to generalize hierarchically after training for extremely long periods -- far beyond the point when in-domain accuracy has saturated. We call this phenomenon \emph{structural grokking}. On multiple datasets, structural grokking exhibits inverted U-shaped scaling in model depth: intermediate-depth models generalize better than both very deep and very shallow transformers. When analyzing the relationship between model-internal properties and grokking, we find that optimal depth for grokking can be identified using the tree-structuredness metric of \citet{murty2023projections}. Overall, our work provides strong evidence that, with extended training, vanilla transformers discover and use hierarchical structure.
specific_phenomena: Dyck Language Modeling (Dyck-LM), Question Formation, Tense Inflection
experimental_materials_comment: controlled, synthetic datasets to test whether transformer models can generalize using hierarchical syntactic rules. The 3 tasks—Dyck Language Modeling, Question Formation, and Tense Inflection—are carefully constructed so that both hierarchical and non-hierarchical rules can explain the training data, but only hierarchical rules succeed on novel test cases. This setup isolates the model's structural generalization abilities. The authors acknowledge that all datasets are based on context-free grammars.
Mechanistic_method: Tree Projections, Weight Norms and Attention Sparsity, structural grokking
interp_method: structural grokking, where transformer language models begin to generalize hierarchically to novel inputs—but only after extensive training, well beyond the saturation of in-domain accuracy. To analyze and predict this, they introduce the functional tree-structuredness metric (tscore), which uniquely correlates with successful structural grokking and reflects the emergence of tree-like internal computations in models that achieve hierarchical generalization
main_findings: transformers can learn syntactic structure, but doing so depends on training duration, model depth, and emergent tree-like internal representations: LMs) can acquire syntactic (hierarchical) knowledge—but only under specific conditions:  Structural Grokking: Transformers can learn to generalize hierarchically, even to novel structures, but only after prolonged training, well beyond the point when in-domain accuracy saturates.    Evidence Across Tasks: On tasks like Dyck Language Modeling, Question Formation, and Tense Inflection, models gradually shift from memorization to true generalization, demonstrating hierarchical understanding.    Inverted U-Shaped Depth Effect: Intermediate-depth models (not too shallow or deep) are best at hierarchical generalization. Both very shallow and very deep models typically fail to grok structure.     Tree-Structuredness Predicts Success: Models that succeed at hierarchical generalization exhibit high functional tree-structuredness, suggesting they internally compute using syntactic-like structure. However, all models induce approximate syntax, even if only some generalize successfully.    Extended Training Crucial: Early stopping harms hierarchical generalization, as grokking only occurs late in training—e.g., accuracy on novel structures can improve from ~40% to ~90% if training continues.

title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models
abstract: Language models demonstrate both quantitative improvement and new qualitative capabilities with increasing scale. Despite their potentially transformative impact, these new capabilities are as yet poorly characterized. In order to inform future research, prepare for disruptive new model capabilities, and ameliorate socially harmful effects, it is vital that we understand the present and near-future capabilities and limitations of language models. To address this challenge, we introduce the Beyond the Imitation Game benchmark (BIG-bench). BIG-bench currently consists of 204 tasks, contributed by 450 authors across 132 institutions. Task topics are diverse, drawing problems from linguistics, childhood development, math, common-sense reasoning, biology, physics, social bias, software development, and beyond. BIG-bench focuses on tasks that are believed to be beyond the capabilities of current language models. We evaluate the behavior of OpenAI's GPT models, Google-internal dense transformer architectures, and Switch-style sparse transformers on BIG-bench, across model sizes spanning millions to hundreds of billions of parameters. In addition, a team of human expert raters performed all tasks in order to provide a strong baseline. Findings include: model performance and calibration both improve with scale, but are poor in absolute terms (and when compared with rater performance); performance is remarkably similar across model classes, though with benefits from sparsity; tasks that improve gradually and predictably commonly involve a large knowledge or memorization component, whereas tasks that exhibit "breakthrough" behavior at a critical scale often involve multiple steps or components, or brittle metrics; social bias typically increases with scale in settings with ambiguous context, but this can be improved with prompting.
