Key evaluation metrics include exact string match, multiple choice grade, expected calibration error, and Brier score. To assess scaling behavior, the benchmark introduces two heuristics: Linearity (L), which tracks consistent improvement with scale, and Breakthroughness (B), indicating tasks where performance jumps only after reaching a critical model size
main_findings: LMs improve with scale, their syntactic knowledge remains limited and brittle, especially when tasks require precise rule-based reasoning or grammatical transformations. Key syntactic evaluations—like Dyck languages (nested dependencies), syntax-sensitive dependencies, and tasks probing morphological understanding—show that models can capture some hierarchical structure and general grammar, but often fail under controlled, fine-grained syntactic tests. Tasks like gender_inclusive_sentences_german reveal that models struggle with exact string-level grammatical edits, despite improving on broader overlap metrics like ROUGE. Overall, although syntactic performance improves quantitatively with size, it lacks robustness, exhibits high sensitivity to input phrasing, and often plateaus below human-level performance, revealing fundamental gaps in structural language understanding

title: Can Transformers Process Recursive Nested Constructions, Like Humans?
abstract: Recursive processing is considered a hallmark of human linguistic abilities. A recent study evaluated recursive processing in recurrent neural language models (RNN-LMs) and showed that such models perform below chance level on embedded dependencies within nested constructions – a prototypical example of recursion in natural language. Here, we study if state-of-the-art Transformer LMs do any better. We test eight different Transformer LMs on two different types of nested constructions, which differ in whether the embedded (inner) dependency is short or long range. We find that Transformers achieve near-perfect performance on short-range embedded dependencies, significantly better than previous results reported for RNN-LMs and humans. However, on long-range embedded dependencies, Transformers’ performance sharply drops below chance level. Remarkably, the addition of only three words to the embedded dependency caused Transformers to fall from near-perfect to below-chance performance. Taken together, our results reveal how brittle syntactic processing is in Transformers, compared to humans.
model_name_comment: GPT2, GPT2-Medium, GPT2-Large and GPT-XL, RoBERTa, RoBERTa-Large,  English LSTM-LM,
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Dependency parsing and constituency
specific_phenomena: include nested constructions, recursive processing, embedded dependencies, long-range dependencies, grammatical agreement, number-agreement tasks, subject-verb dependencies, prepositional phrase-induced dependency lengthening, and the Markedness Effect.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli designed to test language models’ ability to handle recursive nested constructions and grammatical agreement, specifically through two types of number-agreement tasks: Short-Nested Constructions, where subject and verb in the nested clause were adjacent (e.g., "The keys that the man holds are..."), and Long-Nested Constructions, where a prepositional phrase (e.g., "near the cabinet") was inserted into the nested clause to create a long-range dependency (e.g., "The keys that the man near the cabinet holds are..."). These tasks targeted number agreement as a probe for hierarchical syntactic processing and were included in the BIG-bench benchmark
interp_method: Model performance is assessed by comparing the probabilities assigned to correct vs. incorrect verb forms in both embedded and main clause contexts
main_findings: Transformers, especially models like GPT-2 XL, perform near-perfectly on short-range nested dependencies, surpassing both RNN-based models and human performance. However, their performance collapses on long-nested dependencies—those with minimally inserted prepositional phrases—dropping below chance levels and revealing a brittleness in syntactic generalization. Despite their greater scale and training data, Transformers share RNNs’ difficulty with recursive, structure-sensitive tasks, especially within inner embedded dependencies. Notably, all models exhibited a grammatical agreement bias known as the Markedness Effect, making more errors with singular subjects than plural ones, aligning with human patterns in English. Results for Italian Transformer models were weaker, suggesting under-training. Overall, while Transformers excel at simple hierarchical structures, they struggle with deeper recursion

title: Can language models handle recursively nested grammatical structures? A case study on comparing models and humans
abstract: How should we compare the capabilities of language models (LMs) and humans? I draw inspiration from comparative psychology to highlight some challenges. In particular, I consider a case study: processing of recursively nested grammatical structures. Prior work suggests that LMs cannot handle these structures as reliably as humans can. However, the humans were provided with instructions and training, while the LMs were evaluated zero-shot. I therefore match the evaluation more closely. Providing large LMs with a simple prompt -- substantially less content than the human training -- allows the LMs to consistently outperform the human results, and even to extrapolate to more deeply nested conditions than were tested with humans. Further, reanalyzing the prior human data suggests that the humans may not perform above chance at the difficult structures initially. Thus, large LMs may indeed process recursively nested grammatical structures as reliably as humans. This case study highlights how discrepancies in the evaluation can confound comparisons of language models and humans. I therefore reflect on the broader challenge of comparing human and model capabilities, and highlight an important difference between evaluating cognitive models and foundation models.
specific_phenomena: recursively nested grammatical structures; these include center-embedding, where phrases are inserted within others in a way that increases complexity, and embedding depth, which reflects the number of nested layers in a sentence. They distinguish between inner dependencies (grammatical links within the embedded parts) and outer dependencies (the main clause agreement), and highlight the role of distractors like plural prepositional phrases that can interfere with correct agreement. Also discussed are subject-verb agreement across different distances, the concept of Merge from generative grammar (combining elements into hierarchical structures), structural priming (reusing recently encountered syntactic forms),
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli to evaluate language models' syntactic abilities, focusing on center-embedded, recursively nested grammatical structures, which are rare in written and nearly absent in spoken language. These stimuli test subject-verb agreement across both inner and outer dependencies within such complex sentences, using forced-choice tasks between singular and plural verb forms. Sentences were categorized by number (e.g., SSS, PSP), with the PSP condition proving most difficult. To simulate human-like exposure, models were primed with grammatically correct prompt sentences using a non-overlapping lexicon. Complexity was further increased by adding plural prepositional phrases or deeper embeddings. While humans were tested with Italian stimuli, models were evaluated on English versions, introducing structural and morphological differences.
interp_method: simple prompting (even with just two or eight examples)
main_findings: and the roles of recurrence and attention in neural models. They also mention the competence-performance distinction; Chinchilla, can process recursively nested grammatical structures and subject-verb agreement more effectively than previously thought. While earlier studies suggested LMs underperformed humans—especially on complex inner dependencies like the PSP condition—this study shows that simple prompting (even with just two or eight examples) enables LMs to outperform humans, even in the most difficult conditions. Chinchilla also generalized to deeper embeddings and more distractors beyond what humans were tested on, still maintaining strong performance. Both large (70B) and smaller (7B) LMs outperformed humans on outer dependencies as well. Additionally, the study reanalyzes human performance and suggests that humans may also require training effects, challenging the assumption of innate syntactic competence. These results support the idea that emergent syntactic capabilities in LMs arise from domain-general learning and are highly sensitive to evaluation context, much like human experimental setups. Prompting acts similarly to structural priming, helping LMs recognize grammatical patterns without needing explicit recursive structure built in

title: Can neural networks acquire a structural bias from raw linguistic data?
abstract: We evaluate whether BERT, a widely used neural network for sentence processing, acquires an inductive bias towards forming structural generalizations through pretraining on raw data. We conduct four experiments testing its preference for structural vs. linear generalizations in different structure-dependent phenomena. We find that BERT makes a structural generalization in 3 out of 4 empirical domains---subject-auxiliary inversion, reflexive binding, and verb tense detection in embedded clauses---but makes a linear generalization when tested on NPI licensing. We argue that these results are the strongest evidence so far from artificial learners supporting the proposition that a structural bias can be acquired from raw data. If this conclusion is correct, it is tentative evidence that some linguistic universals can be acquired by learners without innate biases. However, the precise implications for human language acquisition are unclear, as humans learn language from significantly less data than BERT.
syntactic_phenomena: Binding and coreference, negation and NPIs
specific_phenomena: subject-auxiliary inversion (requiring fronting the structurally highest auxiliary), reflexive binding (dependent on a structural c-command relationship), negative polarity item (NPI) licensing (requiring structural c-command from negation, though BERT failed to show a structural bias here), and verb tense detection in embedded clauses, used to test BERT’s capacity for novel structural generalization. Additionally, subject-verb agreement, wh-dependencies, and broader grammatical acceptability judgments are mentioned
experimental_materials_comment: fine-tuning and testing used semi-automatically generated stimuli based on a simple context-free grammar and a hand-crafted lexicon. This data supported a "poverty of the stimulus" design, where BERT was trained on examples ambiguous between structural and linear generalizations, then tested on disambiguating minimal pairs across tasks like subject-auxiliary inversion, reflexive binding, NPI licensing, and verb tense detection
interp_method: poverty of the stimulus design," an experimental paradigm where BERT is fine-tuned on data that is deliberately ambiguous between structural and linear generalizations. The model’s inductive biases are then tested by evaluating its performance on held-out examples that clearly disambiguate between these competing generalizations. This approach is used to assess whether BERT’s unsupervised pretraining leads to a structural bias, and the authors reference it as a refinement of similar prior efforts in evaluating syntactic learning in neural networks.
main_findings: findings suggest that BERT can acquire structural syntactic biases from raw linguistic data, challenging the idea that such biases must be innate. Using a "poverty of the stimulus" design, researchers showed that BERT consistently favored structural over linear generalizations in three out of four syntactic tasks: subject-auxiliary inversion, reflexive binding, and verb tense detection in embedded clauses—all with high accuracy. However, BERT failed to make a structural generalization in negative polarity item (NPI) licensing, instead displaying a linear bias, a pattern that aligns with known human processing illusions. These results imply that hierarchical language structure can, at least in part, be learned from data without explicit supervision. While this does not directly translate to human language acquisition—given BERT’s massive training data and different learning mechanisms—it challenges claims that raw input is too impoverished to support such learning. Limitations remain, such as the possibility of surface-feature confounds, but overall, the study strengthens the case that self-supervised models like BERT can internalize significant syntactic structure.

title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. Our findings are fourfold. BERT’s phrasal representation captures the phrase-level information in the lower layers. The intermediate layers of BERT compose a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, starting with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle followed by semantic features at the top. BERT requires deeper layers while tracking subject-verb agreement to handle long-term dependency problem. Finally, the compositional scheme underlying BERT mimics classical, tree-like structures.
specific_phenomena: phrase-level information (or span-level information), Compositional, Tree-Like Structures, Sensitivity to word order (BShift)    ◦ Depth of the syntactic tree (TreeDepth)    ◦ Sequence of top-level constituents in the syntax tree (TopConst) • Dependency Relationships: determiner-noun dependencies (e.g., "the keys", "the cabinet", "the table") ◦ Subject-verb dependencies (e.g., "keys" and "are") ◦ Predicate-argument structure appears to be partly modeled
experimental_materials_comment: Phrase-level information was examined using span representations from BERT applied to the CoNLL 2000 chunking dataset. Compositional structure was probed via Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) trained on SNLI premise sentences. Subject-verb agreement was tested using controlled stimuli from Linzen et al. (2016), focusing on cases with multiple intervening nouns. To explore hierarchical linguistic encoding, the authors used ten probing tasks from Conneau et al. (2018), targeting syntactic features like word order (BShift), tree depth (TreeDepth), and top-level constituent sequence (TopConst). Finally, a dependency tree case study analyzed BERT’s attention patterns on the sentence "The keys to the cabinet are on the table" to illustrate its syntactic modeling capabilities
interp_method: probing tasks (from Conneau et al., 2018) via the SentEval toolkit to assess encoded linguistic features. t-SNE and k-means clustering were applied to span representations from BERT to analyze phrasal syntax, showing that lower layers better encode phrase-level information. Subject-verb agreement was treated as a proxy task using stimuli from Linzen et al. (2016) to test sensitivity to syntactic dependencies. To probe compositionality, Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) revealed that BERT's representations mimic tree-like structures. Finally, dependency tree induction from BERT’s self-attention weights, using the Chu-Liu-Edmonds algorithm, illustrated how BERT captures syntactic dependencies like determiner-noun and subject-verb relations.
main_findings: BERT acquires a hierarchical organization of linguistic information through unsupervised pretraining: surface features are captured in lower layers, syntactic features such as tree depth, constituent order, and subject-verb agreement emerge in middle layers, and semantic features dominate the higher layers. Phrase-level structure is best represented in the lower layers but diminishes in the upper ones, while deeper layers are needed to resolve long-distance dependencies. Despite relying solely on attention mechanisms and lacking explicit syntactic modules, BERT’s internal representations exhibit compositional, tree-like structures, closely resembling classical syntactic theory.

title: Parsing as Pretraining
abstract: Recent analyses suggest that encoders pretrained for language modeling capture certain morpho-syntactic structure. However, probing frameworks for word vectors still do not report results on standard setups such as constituent and dependency parsing. This paper addresses this problem and does full parsing (on English) relying only on pretraining architectures – and no decoding. We first cast constituent and dependency parsing as sequence tagging. We then use a single feed-forward layer to directly map word vectors to labels that encode a linearized tree. This is used to: (i) see how far we can reach on syntax modelling with just pretrained encoders, and (ii) shed some light about the syntax-sensitivity of different word vectors (by freezing the weights of the pretraining network during training). For evaluation, we use bracketing F1-score and las, and analyze in-depth differences across representations for span lengths and dependency displacements. The overall results surpass existing sequence tagging parsers on the ptb (93.5%) and end-to-end en-ewt ud (78.8%).
specific_phenomena: constituent parsing abilities, such as identifying and labeling phrase spans of varying lengths, detecting specific phrase types (e.g., noun phrases and verb phrases), and capturing unary branches; and dependency parsing abilities, including recognizing signed distances between heads and dependents (dependency displacements), identifying specific dependency relations (like 'det', 'nsubj', 'obj', 'root'), and correctly assigning head terms.
experimental_materials_comment: English Penn Treebank (PTB) for evaluating constituent parsing . The PTB is a widely used corpus derived from natural text. • EN-EWT UD treebank (v2.2) for evaluating dependency parsing. This is also a corpus of naturalistic English text.
interp_method: describe their approach as "casting both (full) constituent and dependency parsing as pretraining from language modelling". This involves reducing constituent and dependency parsing to a sequence labeling task, where a single feed-forward layer directly maps word vectors to labels that encode a linearized tree
main_findings: pretrained LMs like BERT inherently encode rich syntactic knowledge, especially for constituent structures. Even without fine-tuning, BERT's contextualized embeddings demonstrate strong syntax sensitivity, accurately identifying complex and infrequent phrase spans. BERT outperforms ELMO and non-contextual embeddings in modeling syntactic structure, particularly in constituent parsing, though it is somewhat less effective for dependency relations. These findings suggest that constituent structure aligns more naturally with what BERT learns during pretraining, and that syntax is deeply embedded in its representations—even without task-specific decoders

title: Are Pre-trained Language Models Aware of Phrases? Simple but Strong Baselines for Grammar Induction
abstract: With the recent success and popularity of pre-trained language models (LMs) in natural language processing, there has been a rise in efforts to understand their inner workings. In line with such interest, we propose a novel method that assists us in investigating the extent to which pre-trained LMs capture the syntactic notion of constituency. Our method provides an effective way of extracting constituency trees from the pre-trained LMs without training. In addition, we report intriguing findings in the induced trees, including the fact that pre-trained LMs outperform other approaches in correctly demarcating adverb phrases in sentences.
model_name_comment: BERT (Devlin et al., 2019)• GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019)• RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019b)• XLNet (Yang et al., 2019)
specific_phenomena: Subordinate Clauses (SBAR), Noun Phrases (NP), Verb Phrases (VP), Prepositional Phrases (PP), Adjective Phrases (ADJP), Adverb Phrases (ADVP); They also investigated the right-branching nature of English syntax
experimental_materials_comment: WSJ Penn Treebank (PTB): Used as the primary source of gold-standard human-annotated constituency trees. Standard split: sections 2–21 for training, 22 for validation, and 23 for testing. MNLI (Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference): Originally for inference tasks, but used here to evaluate parsers. Constituency trees were automatically generated, not human-annotated. Evaluation used both MNLI dev sets; 40,000 training sentences were sampled for validation. Preprocessing: Followed Kim et al. (2019a) with exceptions—no lowercasing, numbers preserved, and punctuation removed in MNLI, which may have inadvertently favored right-branching structures.
Mechanistic_method: Probing Technique (Structured Probes, linear), Attention Analysis (attention head analysis)
interp_method: method facilitates the derivation of constituency trees from pre-trained language models without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. It is inspired by the observation that Transformer-based LMs exhibit syntactic structure, particularly in their attention distributions, akin to constituency grammar. The core of their approach leverages the existing "concept of Syntactic Distance"
main_findings: pre-trained language models (LMs), such as BERT, GPT-2, RoBERTa, and XLNet, encode syntactic knowledge resembling constituency grammar. Attention patterns often reflect constituent structure, with words within the same phrase sharing attention behaviors. Pre-trained LMs outperform randomly initialized models in grammar induction tasks, indicating that syntactic knowledge is acquired during language modeling. They show strength in identifying smaller phrases like adjective and adverb phrases and some capacity for noun phrases, but struggle with right-branching biases typical of English syntax. Attention distributions, particularly from middle layers, are a key source of syntactic information and outperform hidden states for parsing. Among models, XLNet and GPT-2 exhibit the most robust syntactic awareness, likely due to their training objectives.

title: Inducing Syntactic Trees from BERT Representations
abstract: We use the English model of BERT and explore how a deletion of one word in a sentence changes representations of other words. Our hypothesis is that removing a reducible word (e.g. an adjective) does not affect the representation of other words so much as removing e.g. the main verb, which makes the sentence ungrammatical and of "high surprise" for the language model. We estimate reducibilities of individual words and also of longer continuous phrases (word n-grams), study their syntax-related properties, and then also use them to induce full dependency trees.
specific_phenomena: examined word reducibility—how easily a word can be omitted without harming sentence integrity—as a syntactic signal in BERT representations. They found that reducibility correlates with syntactic structure, particularly with dependency tree position: leaf and child nodes are more reducible than parents and roots, allowing leaf identification with 74.5% accuracy. Reducibility also varied by POS tags, with adjectives and adverbs being more reducible than verbs. The syntactic root was often the least reducible word (34–46% of cases), and dependency edge directions could be predicted (70.6% accuracy) by assuming parents are less reducible than their children
experimental_materials_comment: English sentences from the development set of the EWT English treebank (UD 2.3), filtered to include only words in BERT's vocabulary, and analyzed them using BERT-Large (uncased). Though not using traditional "controlled stimuli," they conducted controlled manipulations—such as deleting individual words or phrases—to compute reducibility scores and probe syntactic structure. These tests examined correlations between reducibility and dependency tree structure, POS tags, syntactic roots, and edge directions, enabling a structured investigation of syntactic properties using naturalistic data.
interp_method: stimating reducibility from BERT representations, they define it clearly: it involves measuring the average change in BERT representations of remaining words when a word or phrase is removed from a sentence. This change—quantified via Euclidean distance—is called the reducibility score. Based on these scores, they introduce two dependency tree-building algorithms: Algorithm D, which recursively builds projective trees using headed brackets and reducibility, and Algorithm R, a modified right-branching baseline that enforces a constraint where parents must be less reducible than their children, with the least reducible word as the root.
main_findings: BERT representations encode a notion of “reducibility”—the degree to which removing a word or phrase changes the sentence’s internal representations—which correlates strongly with syntactic structure. They find that leaf nodes and child nodes in dependency trees are more reducible than parents or roots, that roots tend to be the least reducible words, and that dependency edge direction can be inferred by assuming parents are less reducible than children. Using this, they propose Algorithms D and R to induce dependency trees directly from BERT, achieving strong results without any syntactic supervision. Additionally, POS-related patterns emerge, with adjectives and adverbs being highly reducible, and verbs less so, aligning with traditional linguistic expectations. Overall, they show that BERT implicitly encodes syntactic structure through reducibility, which can be operationalized to recover grammatical relationships.

title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models Using Minimal Pairs
abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel “decoding probing” method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the brain and its representations as “neural activations”, we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers’ representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.
specific_phenomena: using the BLiMP dataset: Argument Structure, Ellipsis, Filler Gap Dependency, Island Effects
experimental_materials_comment: use the BLiMP dataset, which provides 67 tasks across 12 syntactic and morphosyntactic phenomena. Each task includes 1,000 sentence pairs differing by a single, grammatically significant change (e.g., argument structure, ellipsis, filler-gap dependencies, island effects
interp_method: "decoding probing" This method is inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies and uses the Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs (BLiMP) to investigate the internal linguistic characteristics of neural language models layer by layer. The approach treats the language model as a "brain" and its representations as "neural activations" to decode grammaticality labels from intermediate layers' representations
main_findings: 1. Intermediate layers in LMs capture abstract syntax: Self-supervised models like GPT-2 XL encode abstract syntactic structures primarily in their intermediate layers, unlike simpler models such as GloVe and RNNs.2. Syntactic grammaticality is captured early and robustly: Syntactic information is reliably encoded in the first third of GPT-2 XL’s layers and remains distributed throughout later layers, with only a slight drop in performance.3. Sentence complexity affects depth of syntactic learning: As syntactic complexity increases, deeper layers are required to capture grammatical information, showing a linear relationship between tree depth and layer depth.4. Syntax is easier to learn than morphology or semantics: Syntax requires fewer layers to model (≈14 in GPT-2 XL) than morphology (≈16) or semantics-syntax interface (≈20), confirming that syntactic features are learned earlier. 5. ELMo exhibits strong syntactic performance: Despite being RNN-based, ELMo performs nearly on par with GPT-2 XL on syntactic tasks, though it falls behind in morphology and semantic tasks. 6. Attention heads encode syntactic features differently from embeddings: In Transformers like GPT-2 XL, attention matrices and hidden embeddings both encode syntax, but:    Attention outperforms on syntax and semantics-syntax tasks.    No clear layer-wise accumulation is observed in attention patterns, unlike embeddings.    Some attention heads specialize and contribute more to syntactic representation than others.

title: Acceptability Judgements via Examining the Topology of Attention Maps
abstract: The role of the attention mechanism in encoding linguistic knowledge has received special interest in NLP. However, the ability of the attention heads to judge the grammatical acceptability of a sentence has been underexplored. This paper approaches the paradigm of acceptability judgments with topological data analysis (TDA), showing that the geometric properties of the attention graph can be efficiently exploited for two standard practices in linguistics: binary judgments and linguistic minimal pairs. Topological features enhance the BERT-based acceptability classifier scores by 8%-24% on CoLA in three languages (English, Italian, and Swedish). By revealing the topological discrepancy between attention maps of minimal pairs, we achieve the human-level performance on the BLiMP benchmark, outperforming nine statistical and Transformer LM baselines. At the same time, TDA provides the foundation for analyzing the linguistic functions of attention heads and interpreting the correspondence between the graph features and grammatical phenomena. We publicly release the code and other materials used in the experiments.
model_name_comment: En-BERT-base, It-BERT-base, Sw-BERT-base, XLM-R-base, and RoBERTa-base.
specific_phenomena: across the CoLA/ITACoLA and BLiMP benchmarks include: simple syntax, argument structure (including prepositional phrase arguments), argument alternations, complement clauses, infinitival constructions (to-VP), question constructions (e.g., wh-movement, embedded questions), adjuncts, determiners (e.g., negative polarity, comparatives), auxiliaries and modals, binding, noun and adjective structures, predicate structures, general sentence-level syntax, anaphor agreement, control and raising, determiner-noun agreement, ellipsis, filler-gap dependencies, island effects, NPI licensing, quantifiers, and subject-verb agreement.
fine_tuning_materials: Fine-tuning and evaluation of the BERT-based/XLM-R acceptability classifiers. Each model is fine-tuned for 4 epochs
experimental_materials_comment: COLA (Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability): This English benchmark contains sentences derived from linguistic textbooks, ITACOLA: Similar to COLA, this Italian benchmark also contains sentences from linguistic textbooks, BLIMP (Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs), Naturalistic Language:     ◦ DALAJ (Data for Linguistic Acceptability Judgments for Swedish): In contrast to COLA and ITACOLA, DALAJ includes L2-written sentences . These sentences often feature morphological violations or incorrect word choices
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques (Representation Topology Divergence), individual attention heads analysis
interp_method: topological data analysis (TDA): They clarify that "TDA provides the foundation for analyzing the linguistic functions of attention heads and interpreting the correspondence between the graph features and grammatical phenomena". Within this framework, they also introduce and utilize: • Representation Topology Divergence (RTD) as a scoring function, particularly effective for discriminating between linguistic minimal pairs.• H0M (the average length of bars), which is a feature derived from barcodes obtained through TDA, used for both acceptability classification and scoring minimal pairs.
main_findings: topological features of attention maps in Transformer LMs (like BERT and RoBERTa) can be used to judge syntactic acceptability, offering insights into the syntactic knowledge encoded in attention mechanisms. Using Topological Data Analysis (TDA), the authors demonstrate that persistent graph features from attention heads capture various grammatical phenomena, such as morphological agreement, argument structure, complement clauses, and infinitival constructions. These topological features improve acceptability classification performance—sometimes to human-level accuracy on minimal pair tasks (e.g., BLiMP). The study also finds that ensembles of attention heads are more effective than individual heads for capturing complex syntactic phenomena like phrasal movement and island effects, and that higher-layer heads contribute more to syntax-sensitive judgments. While topology-based methods struggle with lexical-specific cues and abstract semantics, they offer compelling evidence that attention structure encodes grammatical acceptability in a topologically meaningful way

title: Picking BERT’s Brain: Probing for Linguistic Dependencies in Contextualized Embeddings Using Representational Similarity Analysis
abstract: As the name implies, contextualized representations of language are typically motivated by their ability to encode context. Which aspects of context are captured by such representations? We introduce an approach to address this question using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA). As case studies, we investigate the degree to which a verb embedding encodes the verb's subject, a pronoun embedding encodes the pronoun's antecedent, and a full-sentence representation encodes the sentence's head word (as determined by a dependency parse). In all cases, we show that BERT's contextualized embeddings reflect the linguistic dependency being studied, and that BERT encodes these dependencies to a greater degree than it encodes less linguistically-salient controls. These results demonstrate the ability of our approach to adjudicate between hypotheses about which aspects of context are encoded in representations of language.
syntactic_phenomena: Argument Structure and other Constructions, Binding and coreference, Dependency parsing and constituency
specific_phenomena: 1) Verb's Subject Encoding — whether a verb’s embedding encodes its subject more than unrelated nouns; 2) Pronoun's Antecedent Encoding — whether pronoun embeddings reflect their antecedents, distinguishing between reflexives and pronominals; and (3) Sentence's Head Word Encoding — whether full-sentence embeddings encode the main verb as the syntactic head, consistent with dependency grammar.
experimental_materials_comment: synthetically generated, controlled stimuli, to probe BERT's syntactic representations. They constructed custom corpora using probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) to precisely isolate syntactic variables. These included (1) subject–verb agreement contexts with prepositional phrases and relative clauses, (2) coreference contexts contrasting reflexives and pronominals, and (3) sentence head structures using intransitive/transitive sentences with and without adjectives. Each corpus was carefully balanced for number agreement, lexical overlap, and semantic plausibility
interp_method: Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) as a core methodological tool to investigate the linguistic content of BERT’s contextualized embeddings. RSA allows them to compare BERT's internal representational geometry to custom-built hypothesis models that encode specific linguistic dependencies
main_findings: shown through Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA). Across three controlled experiments, the authors found that BERT is sensitive to grammatical structure beyond surface-level cues. Specifically, verbs encode their syntactic subjects more strongly than nearby non-argument nouns, even when the latter are linearly closer; pronoun embeddings are more similar to their syntactic antecedents than to non-antecedents, for both reflexives and pronominals; and full-sentence embeddings (via the [CLS] token) primarily represent the main verb, aligning with its role as the sentence head in dependency grammar. An unexpected finding was that in transitive sentences, the direct object had a greater impact on the sentence embedding than the subject. Overall, the results provide strong evidence that BERT’s embeddings reflect core syntactic structures, supporting its effectiveness on tasks involving linguistic dependencies like agreement and coreference.

title: Counterfactual Interventions Reveal the Causal Effect of Relative Clause Representations on Agreement Prediction
abstract: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language? We propose AlterRep, an intervention-based method to address this question. For any linguistic feature of a given sentence, AlterRep generates counterfactual representations by altering how the feature is encoded, while leaving in- tact all other aspects of the original representation. By measuring the change in a model’s word prediction behavior when these counterfactual representations are substituted for the original ones, we can draw conclusions about the causal effect of the linguistic feature in question on the model’s behavior. We apply this method to study how BERT models of different sizes process relative clauses (RCs). We find that BERT variants use RC boundary information during word prediction in a manner that is consistent with the rules of English grammar; this RC boundary information generalizes to a considerable extent across different RC types, suggesting that BERT represents RCs as an abstract linguistic category.
model_name_comment: BERT-base, BERT-large, BERT-medium, BERT-small, BERT-mini, and BERT-tiny
specific_phenomena: include subject-verb agreement across relative clauses—specifically unreduced object RCs, reduced object RCs, unreduced passive RCs, reduced passive RCs, and active subject RCs—as well as simple agreement, sentential complements, and RC constructions with number-matching nouns.
experimental_materials_comment: constructed two main types of datasets: one for generating counterfactual representations and identifying RC subspaces using lexically matched sentence templates across five RC types (ORC, ORRC, PRC, PRRC, SRC) and two control coordination structures; and another for measuring agreement prediction accuracy using a subset of the Marvin and Linzen (2018) dataset, augmented with passive RCs and focused on sentences with copular verbs.
Mechanistic_method: intervention-based approach (AlterRep, iterative Null Space Projection)
interp_method: AlterRep, an intervention-based approach that tests whether a language model uses a specific linguistic feature in a grammatically consistent way. AlterRep works by (1) creating counterfactual word representations that selectively modify how a linguistic feature (e.g., relative clause boundaries) is encoded, and (2) measuring how the model's word prediction behavior changes when these altered representations are used. By comparing this behavioral shift to expectations from linguistic theory, AlterRep reveals the causal impact of the feature. The authors applied it to analyze how BERT models use relative clause information in subject-verb agreement tasks
main_findings: BERT models use Relative Clause (RC) boundary information for subject-verb agreement in a way that aligns with English grammar. Using the AlterRep method, the authors show that modifying how RC boundaries are represented in context causally affects BERT’s verb number predictions: encoding the verb as inside the RC increases errors (agreeing with an attractor), while encoding it as outside reduces errors (agreeing with the main subject). Crucially, only middle layers in BERT variants (e.g., layers 5–8 in BERT-base) showed this causal effect, even though RC information could be detected in all layers via probing. The RC boundary representation was also shown to generalize across RC types, suggesting that BERT encodes RCs as an abstract syntactic category. The effects were specific: they did not appear in control sentences without RCs or with matching-number subjects, and random interventions had no effect, confirming the linguistic specificity of the causal influence.

title: Verb Conjugation in Transformers Is Determined by Linear Encodings of Subject Number
abstract: Deep architectures such as Transformers are sometimes criticized for having uninterpretable "black-box" representations. We use causal intervention analysis to show that, in fact, some linguistic features are represented in a linear, interpretable format. Specifically, we show that BERT's ability to conjugate verbs relies on a linear encoding of subject number that can be manipulated with predictable effects on conjugation accuracy. This encoding is found in the subject position at the first layer and the verb position at the last layer, but distributed across positions at middle layers, particularly when there are multiple cues to subject number.
specific_phenomena: Subject-verb agreement,  Grammatical number of third-person subjects and verb, Verb conjugation (conjugate third-person present-tense verbs), redundant cues to subject numbe
experimental_materials_comment: dataset from Ravfogel et al. (2021) consists of syntactically controlled sentences with a relative clause between the subject and verb, such as "The author that the teacher admires is happy." This controlled design allowed the researchers to isolate and compare the effect of redundant vs. non-redundant cues to subject number (e.g., "the author that admires the teachers" vs. "the author that the teachers admire"). This setup ensured that observed effects on verb agreement were due to linear encoding of subject number, rather than confounding factors like semantics or discourse.
interp_method: causal intervention analysis based on the framework proposed by Ravfogel et al. (2021), employing counterfactual interventions to manipulate BERT’s hidden vectors in order to test whether these changes causally affect verb conjugation behavior. Specifically, they used the iterative nullspace projection (INLP) method to identify the "number subspace"—a linear subspace hypothesized to encode grammatical number—and intervened by altering hidden vectors along this subspace to flip the encoded subject number
main_findings: BERT encodes subject number in a linear and interpretable subspace, which directly determines its verb conjugation behavior. Through causal interventions, researchers showed that flipping hidden vectors along this “number subspace” could reverse BERT’s agreement predictions—turning 91% correct conjugations into 85% incorrect ones—demonstrating the subspace’s causal role in syntactic decisions. This subject number encoding is dynamic across layers: it originates at the subject’s position in the embedding layer, becomes distributed in middle layers, and converges at the verb’s position in the final layers (10–12). The presence of redundant syntactic cues (like agreeing embedded verbs) causes broader distribution of number information across positions, while its absence centralizes it in the subject’s hidden vector. The number subspace is also shown to be specific and precise, affecting only number-related predictions without disrupting general language modeling. Overall, the study provides compelling evidence that BERT uses a fully interpretable, linear mechanism to perform subject-verb agreement

title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.
specific_phenomena: Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task, which reveals several syntactic phenomena that the model appears to process internally. These include: indirect object identification, subject-object distinction through repetition, duplicate token detection, syntactic repetition, positional information processing (especially relative token positions), token value-based filtering, pattern recognition via induction heads (e.g., [A][B]...[A] → [B]), and local token relationship tracking (e.g., copying info from a token to its immediate successor)
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli: pIOI dataset (based on 15 structured templates with randomly inserted single-token names), the pABC dataset (a control set with unrelated names for mean ablation), random token sequences (to test pattern recognition of specific heads), counterfactual datasets (to disentangle token and position signals), and adversarial examples (manipulating duplicate name occurrences to probe model weaknesses).
Mechanistic_method: Circuit analysis, path patching, activation patching, Activation Patching (Ablation), Attention Analysis (attention pattern analysis)
interp_method: use path patching as their main method for discovering the circuit, describing it as a causal intervention that extends causal mediation analysis to language models by systematically tracing influential components back from the logits. They also employ supporting techniques including embedding space projections, attention pattern analysis, activation patching, and knockouts (notably mean ablation) to further define circuit function and control for varying information
main_findings: uncovers a detailed, mechanistic circuit within GPT-2 small that enables it to perform the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task using a human-interpretable algorithm involving syntactic processing—such as identifying names, removing duplicates, and isolating the indirect object. This behavior is achieved through a coordinated circuit of 26 attention heads with specialized roles (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads, Duplicate Token Heads) that manipulate token identity and position information. The findings show GPT-2 exhibits a specific, structured form of syntactic understanding, though the circuit is not yet fully understood and shows sensitivity to adversarial examples exploiting its reliance on duplication detection

title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.
specific_phenomena: four variants of the subject-verb agreement task: Simple agreement, Agreement Within RC (Relative Clause), Agreement Across RC (Relative Clause), Agreement Across PP (Prepositional Phrase)
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli and naturalistic language depending on the task. For subject-verb agreement, they employed controlled contrastive sentence pairs (e.g., “The boy near the teacher has” vs. “The boys near the teacher have”) to probe syntactic phenomena like simple agreement, agreement within/across relative clauses (RCs), and prepositional phrases (PPs)—adapted from Finlayson et al. (2021). For more general or application-focused tasks, they used naturalistic data: the Bias in Bios (BiB) dataset for testing the SHIFT method on gender bias in profession classification, and The Pile corpus for unsupervised large-scale discovery of model behaviors by clustering LM activations to uncover human-counterintuitive patterns and corresponding sparse feature circuits.
Mechanistic_method: Dictionary Learning (Sparse Autoencoders), Attribution Patching, Integrated Gradients, Activation Patching (Ablation)
interp_method: Sparse feature circuits are causally implicated, human-interpretable subnetworks that explain specific behaviors in language models (LMs). The authors develop a scalable and fully unsupervised pipeline to automatically discover thousands of these circuits across various LM tasks. To leverage this interpretability for practical benefit, they introduce SHIFT (Sparse Human-Interpretable Feature Trimming)—a technique that improves LM classifier generalization by allowing humans to identify and remove irrelevant features from circuits, even without access to disambiguating data
main_findings: present sparse feature circuits as a powerful method for interpreting how language models (LMs), such as Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B, process syntactic structures, particularly subject-verb agreement. These circuits are small, human-interpretable causal graphs that outperform traditional neuron- or attention-based analyses in both interpretability and efficiency. Using an unsupervised discovery method, they identified distinct syntactic mechanisms, such as subject number tracking, verb form promotion, and the use of PP/RC boundary detectors and NP number trackers. These were shown to function similarly across syntactic constructions like relative clauses and prepositional phrases. Sparse circuits also revealed unexpected mechanisms, such as dual systems for handling infinitival object prediction, and demonstrated how compositional structures form from overlapping narrow features

title: Causal interventions expose implicit situation models for commonsense language understanding
abstract: Accounts of human language processing have long appealed to implicit ``situation models'' that enrich comprehension with relevant but unstated world knowledge. Here, we apply causal intervention techniques to recent transformer models to analyze performance on the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC), where a single context cue shifts interpretation of an ambiguous pronoun. We identify a relatively small circuit of attention heads that are responsible for propagating information from the context word that guides which of the candidate noun phrases the pronoun ultimately attends to. We then compare how this circuit behaves in a closely matched ``syntactic'' control where the situation model is not strictly necessary. These analyses suggest distinct pathways through which implicit situation models are constructed to guide pronoun resolution.
specific_phenomena: number agreement signaled by the verb
experimental_materials_comment: Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC) and Winogrande datasets, which feature sentences requiring commonsense reasoning to resolve ambiguous pronouns. These base sentences were then systematically modified to create four experimental conditions: (1) Context Cue (original Winograd-like pairs where a key word changes pronoun resolution), (2) Context+Syntax Cue (adds verb number agreement as an additional syntactic cue), (3) Syntax Only (masks out context to isolate syntactic effects via number agreement), and (4) Synonym Control (replaces context words with semantic equivalents to control for lexical bias). In total, they created 200 sentence pairs for the first three conditions and 400 for the synonym control, carefully editing the sentences to ensure valid agreement cues and consistent tokenization for model interventions
interp_method: causal intervention probe techniques, specifically a method called interchange interventions, to analyze how transformer models process information during tasks like pronoun resolution. These techniques fall under the broader category of causal probes, which aim to uncover interpretable mechanisms by manipulating intermediate model representations. Interchange interventions involve swapping hidden representations between two similar sentence contexts (e.g., Winograd pairs) to observe how such changes affect the model’s output, thereby revealing how and where contextual information influences predictions
main_findings: how transformer-based language models, particularly ALBERT, process language by examining their internal mechanisms for resolving ambiguous pronouns using either implicit world knowledge or explicit syntactic cues. The researchers find that LLMs learn distinct, non-overlapping circuits for handling context-dependent (situation model-based) and syntax-based pronoun resolution. Situation models, exemplified through the Winograd Schema Challenge, involve broader contextual integration across the sentence and are processed by a small circuit of attention heads early in the network. In contrast, syntactic resolution relies on localized effects between the verb and the masked pronoun, emerging around layer 7 and dominated by syntax-specific heads. While models like ALBERT and GPT-4 demonstrate strong performance, they still lag behind humans on commonsense tasks. The study also carefully controls for lexical biases, confirming that the observed mechanisms reflect genuine linguistic processing rather than artifacts of specific words or dataset imbalances.

title: Sudden Drops in the Loss: Syntax Acquisition, Phase Transitions, and Simplicity Bias in MLMs
abstract: Most interpretability research in NLP focuses on understanding the behavior and features of a fully trained model. However, certain insights into model behavior may only be accessible by observing the trajectory of the training process. We present a case study of syntax acquisition in masked language models (MLMs) that demonstrates how analyzing the evolution of interpretable artifacts throughout training deepens our understanding of emergent behavior. In particular, we study Syntactic Attention Structure (SAS), a naturally emerging property of MLMs wherein specific Transformer heads tend to focus on specific syntactic relations. We identify a brief window in pretraining when models abruptly acquire SAS, concurrent with a steep drop in loss. This breakthrough precipitates the subsequent acquisition of linguistic capabilities. We then examine the causal role of SAS by manipulating SAS during training, and demonstrate that SAS is necessary for the development of grammatical capabilities. We further find that SAS competes with other beneficial traits during training, and that briefly suppressing SAS improves model quality. These findings offer an interpretation of a real-world example of both simplicity bias and breakthrough training dynamics.
specific_phenomena: BLiMP: island Effects, Anaphor Agreement, S-selection, Argument Structure, Determiner Noun Agreement, Subject Verb Agreement, Ellipsis, Control Raising, Quantifiers, Irregular Forms, Npi Licensing, Binding, Filler Gap Dependency
fine_tuning_materials: Fine-tuning on GLUE
experimental_materials_comment: syntactic attention was assessed using parsed sentences from Penn Treebank and Wikipedia. To test grammatical knowledge, the BLiMP benchmark—comprised of 67 minimal-pair grammatical tests—was used, alongside fine-tuning on GLUE, a multi-task benchmark for natural language understanding
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Syntactic Attention Structure, causal interventions (syntactic regularizer)
interp_method: developmental analysis approach, which involves tracking the training trajectory of models to understand the emergence and evolution of interpretable behaviors. Key methods include measuring Syntactic Attention Structure (SAS) using a probe to assess attention-based parsing accuracy, and controlling SAS via a syntactic regularizer that adjusts attention toward syntactic neighbors. They identify breakthroughs (or phase transitions) by locating sharp changes in training metrics. For grammatical evaluation, they use BLiMP to test minimal-pair sentence preferences and also fine-tune on GLUE tasks to assess broader language understanding.
main_findings:
identified a syntax acquisition phase in the training of masked language models, characterized by sudden drops in loss and rapid improvements in syntactic capabilities. They observed two distinct phase transitions: a “structure onset” marked by a spike in
unlabelled dependency parsing accuracy, followed by a “capabilities onset” where the model shows an abrupt increase in performance on the BLiMP grammatical acceptability benchmark.

title: Deep learning can contrast the minimal pairs of syntactic data
abstract: The present work aims to assess the feasibility of using deep learning as a useful tool to investigate syntactic phenomena. To this end, the present study concerns three research questions: (i) whether deep learning can detect syntactically inappropriate constructions, (ii) whether deep learning’s acceptability judgments are accountable, and (iii) whether deep learning’s aspects of acceptability judgments are similar to human judgments. As a proxy for a deep learning language model, this study chooses BERT. The current paper comprises syntactically contrasted pairs of English sentences which come from the three test suites already available. The first one is 196 grammatical –ungrammatical minimal pairs from DeKeyser (2000). The second one is examples in four published syntax textbooks excerpted from Warstadt et al. (2019). The last one is extracted from Sprouse et al. (2013), which collects the examples reported in a theoretical linguistics journal, Linguistic Inquiry. The BERT models, base BERT and large BERT, are assessed by judging acceptability of items in the test suites with an evaluation metric, surprisal, which is used to measure how ‘surprised’ a model is when encountering a word in a sequence of words, i.e., a sentence. The results are analyzed in the two frameworks: directionality and repulsion. The results of directionality reveals that the two versions of BERT are overall competent at distinguishing ungrammatical sentences from grammatical ones. The statistical results of both repulsion and directionality also reveal that the two variants of BERT do not differ significantly. Regarding repulsion, correct judgments and incorrect ones are significantly different. Additionally, the repulsion of the first test suite, which is excerpted from the items for testing learners’ grammaticality judgments, is higher than the other test suites, which are excerpted from the syntax textbooks and published literature. This study compares BERT’s acceptability judgments with magnitude estimation results reported in Sprouse et al. (2013) in order to examine if deep learning’s syntactic knowledge is akin to human knowledge. The error analyses on incorrectly judged items reveal that there are some syntactic constructions that the two BERTs have trouble learning, which indicates that BERT’s acceptability judgments are distributed not randomly.
syntactic_phenomena: Negation and NPIs, Argument Structure and other Constructions, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: Reflexive pronouns (without any attractor), Negation, who the hell (in an interrogative sentence), Comparative correlatives, V-movement, Adjectives, Multiple quantifiers, Parallel structures, Voice, Verb subcategorization, Adverbial phrases (adjoining to VP), so serving as complement of a preposition, Omission of complementizer that, Determiners, VP ellipsis, Modality, Usage of likely, Reflexive pronouns (with an attractor), Adverbial phrases (general), VP fronting, who the hell (in a declarative sentence), there in interrogative sentences
experimental_materials_comment: controlled experimental design, as the materials were carefully selected or modified to isolate single syntactic contrasts. The researchers constructed three test suites: Test Suite I – 98 minimal pairs from DeKeyser (2000), originally used to assess English learners’ grammar, featuring strong syntactic contrasts. Test Suite II – Derived from the CoLA corpus (Warstadt et al., 2019), focusing on four syntax textbooks; pairs were manually constructed or filtered to ensure minimal contrasts. Test Suite III – Based on Sprouse et al. (2013) examples from Linguistic Inquiry (2001–2010), filtered and edited for pairwise syntactic comparison and computational compatibility.
interp_method: calculating surprisal scores for masked tokens in syntactically contrasted minimal pairs, and analyzing these scores using two key frameworks: directionality (whether BERT prefers grammatical over ungrammatical sentences) and repulsion (the surprisal gap between the two, reflecting constraint strength).
main_findings: assessed BERT’s syntactic competence by testing whether it could distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences, justify its acceptability judgments, and align with human intuitions. Using three controlled test suites composed of syntactic minimal pairs, the researchers found that both base and large BERT models performed well overall, with high accuracy in detecting ungrammatical constructions. BERT exhibited stronger “repulsion” (surprisal distance) when its judgments were correct, especially for harder syntactic constraints like number agreement, suggesting it captures a hierarchy of syntactic rules. However, error analysis revealed specific weaknesses in BERT's grasp of more complex or infrequent phenomena, such as reflexives with attractors, VP fronting, adverbial placement, and certain wh-constructions. Some of these errors may stem from biases in the training data. While BERT’s judgments partially aligned with human performance, particularly on difficult cases, the model still falls short of replicating full human syntactic knowledge,

title: Using Computational Models to Test Syntactic Learnability
abstract: We studied the learnability of English filler-gap dependencies and the “island” constraints on them by assessing the generalizations made by autoregressive (incremental) language models that use deep learning to predict the next word given preceding context. Using factorial tests inspired by experimental psycholinguistics, we found that models acquire not only the basic contingency between fillers and gaps, but also the unboundedness and hierarchical constraints implicated in the dependency. We evaluated a model’s acquisition of island constraints by demonstrating that its expectation for a filler-gap contingency is attenuated within an island environment. Our results provide empirical evidence against the argument from the poverty of the stimulus for this particular structure.
syntactic_phenomena: Ellipsis and filler-gap dependencies, Agreement and feature-checking, Binding and coreference, Dependency parsing and constituency
specific_phenomena: filler–gap licensing and wh-effects (both with and without gaps), syntactic islands (Complex Noun Phrase, Adjunct, Subject, Sentential Subject, Coordination, Left Branch, and Wh-Islands), subject–verb number agreement, the A-over-A principle, cyclicity, wh-extraction constraints, binding and relative clause dependencies, gender dependency as a control, and subject–auxiliary inversion
experimental_materials_comment: The controlled stimuli used in the study were carefully hand-crafted, psycholinguistics-style test items designed to isolate and test specific grammatical phenomena while minimizing semantic influence. The tests targeted filler–gap dependencies—including basic licensing, flexibility, hierarchy, and unboundedness—as well as a range of syntactic island constraints (Adjunct, CNP, Coordination, Left Branch, Sentential Subject, Subject, and Wh-Islands). Additionally, gender dependency controls were included using morphologically gendered noun–pronoun pairs to ensure that observed effects were syntactic
interp_method: nan
main_findings: RNNs and Transformers acquire sophisticated syntactic generalizations about English filler–gap dependencies and their associated island constraints, challenging the Argument from the Poverty of the Stimulus (APS). The models learned the basic licensing and flexibility of filler–gap structures, showed sensitivity to syntactic hierarchy (such as c-command), and processed unbounded dependencies across multiple embedding layers—demonstrating generalization beyond training data statistics. Critically, they also acquired selective syntactic island constraints, significantly attenuating wh-effects in ungrammatical island environments, while maintaining gender-based dependencies as a control. These effects were robust across most island types, with architectural differences (e.g., JRNN outperforming larger GPT models) proving more impactful than training data size. These findings suggest that general-purpose, weakly biased learners can develop rich syntactic knowledge from surface data alone, undermining the APS and prompting a shift in linguistic nativism debates toward cross-linguistic evidence rather than single-language learnability.

title: A closer look at the performance of neural language models on reflexive anaphor licensing
abstract: An emerging line of work uses psycholinguis- tic methods to evaluate the syntactic gener- alizations acquired by neural language mod- els (NLMs). While this approach has shown NLMs to be capable of learning a wide range of linguistic knowledge, confounds in the de- sign of previous experiments may have ob- scured the potential of NLMs to learn certain grammatical phenomena. Here we re-evaluate the performance of a range of NLMs on reflex- ive anaphor licensing. Under our paradigm, the models consistently show stronger evi- dence of learning than reported in previous work. Our approach demonstrates the value of well-controlled psycholinguistic methods in gaining a fine-grained understanding of NLM learning potential.1
syntactic_phenomena: Binding and coreference, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: reflexive anaphor licensing (RAL) governed by locality and c-command, using relative clause constructions, sentential complement constructions, and prepositional phrase constructions.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli—minimal pairs of sentences differing only at key points—to test neural language models’ understanding of reflexive anaphor licensing (RAL). Sentences followed a consistent structure (two noun phrases, a verb, and a reflexive) and were tested under three conditions: baseline (grammatical), distractor (grammatical with a distracting NP), and ungrammatical (licensing NP mismatched in number). High-frequency, lexically gendered nouns and common reflexive verbs were selected, with careful counterbalancing to avoid lexical confounds. The stimuli targeted two core syntactic constraints—LOCALITY and C-COMMAND—across three constructions: relative clauses (testing both constraints), sentential complements (testing LOCALITY), and prepositional phrases (testing C-COMMAND)
interp_method: nan
main_findings: NLMs can robustly acquire complex syntactic knowledge related to Reflexive Anaphor Licensing (RAL), particularly the constraints of LOCALITY and C-COMMAND, when tested with carefully controlled experimental designs. Large-vocabulary models (like BERT, Transformer-XL, JRNN) performed near ceiling on sentential complement constructions, strongly supporting their learning of LOCALITY. In relative clause constructions, which test both LOCALITY and C-COMMAND, these models also performed above chance, though results were less consistent due to potential linear proximity biases. In prepositional phrase constructions isolating C-COMMAND, all models except TinyLSTM performed well, highlighting sensitivity to structural relations. Improvements in test design—like avoiding unigram confounds and using lexically gendered nouns

title: Investigating BERT’s Knowledge of Language: Five Analysis Methods with NPIs
abstract: Though state-of-the-art sentence representation models can perform tasks requiring significant knowledge of grammar, it is an open question how best to evaluate their grammatical knowledge. We explore five experimental methods inspired by prior work evaluating pretrained sentence representation models. We use a single linguistic phenomenon, negative polarity item (NPI) licensing, as a case study for our experiments. NPIs like any are grammatical only if they appear in a licensing environment like negation (Sue doesn’t have any cats vs. *Sue has any cats). This phenomenon is challenging because of the variety of NPI licensing environments that exist. We introduce an artificially generated dataset that manipulates key features of NPI licensing for the experiments. We find that BERT has significant knowledge of these features, but its success varies widely across different experimental methods. We conclude that a variety of methods is necessary to reveal all relevant aspects of a model’s grammatical knowledge in a given domain.
