specific_phenomena: Negative Polarity Item (NPI) licensing, the environments tested were: Adverbs (ADV), Conditionals (COND), Determiner Negation (D-NEG), Sentential Negation (S-NEG), Only (ONLY), Quantifiers (QNT), Questions (QUES), Simple Questions (SMP-Q), and Superlatives (SUP). NPIs used were “any” and “ever,”
fine_tuning_materials: fine-tuned on the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference corpus (Williams et al., 2018); BERT fine-tuned on Combinatory Categorial Grammar Bank corpus (Hockenmaier and Steedman, 2007),
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli consisted of an artificially generated dataset targeting Negative Polarity Item (NPI) licensing, created using templates and over 1,000 annotated lexical items to manipulate key features like licensor presence and scope. This dataset covered nine NPI environments (e.g., Adverbs, Conditionals, Sentential Negation, Questions, Superlatives) and tested NPIs like "any" and "ever". BERT was also tested on 104 handcrafted NPI sentences from prior work. The naturalistic language came from the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA), a dataset of 10,000+ linguistically diverse, expert-curated sentences used to train BERT acceptability classifiers
interp_method: nan
main_findings: BERT consistently detects NPIs and licensors, but its grasp of licensor scope is weaker and more variable.;  Better at Presence, Weaker at Scope: It excels at identifying presence of NPIs/licensors, but struggles with whether the NPI is within scope, which requires deeper syntactic understanding.;  Evaluation Method Matters:;      Gradient Minimal Pair: Showed near-perfect performance but masked scope-related weaknesses due to ceiling effects.;      Absolute Minimal Pair, Cloze, Probing: Exposed gaps, especially in complex environments (e.g., superlatives, quantifiers, adverbs), and showed gradient rather than categorical behavior.;  Grammatical Knowledge is Gradient: BERT’s judgments aren’t binary like formal grammar but reflect probabilistic acceptability, aligning with usage-based theories.;  Extra Pretraining Doesn’t Help: Further pretraining on tasks like MNLI or CCG did not improve NPI performance and sometimes hurt it.;  Conclusion: BERT shows real but imperfect syntactic competence; multi-method evaluation is essential to uncover the true scope of its grammatical knowledge.

title: How much pretraining data do language models need to learn syntax?
abstract: Transformers-based pretrained language models achieve outstanding results in many well-known NLU benchmarks. However, while pretraining methods are very convenient, they are expensive in terms of time and resources. This calls for a study of the impact of pretraining data size on the knowledge of the models. We explore this impact on the syntactic capabilities of RoBERTa, using models trained on incremental sizes of raw text data. First, we use syntactic structural probes to determine whether models pretrained on more data encode a higher amount of syntactic information. Second, we perform a targeted syntactic evaluation to analyze the impact of pretraining data size on the syntactic generalization performance of the models. Third, we compare the performance of the different models on three downstream applications: part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing and paraphrase identification. We complement our study with an analysis of the cost-benefit trade-off of training such models. Our experiments show that while models pretrained on more data encode more syntactic knowledge and perform better on downstream applications, they do not always offer a better performance across the different syntactic phenomena and come at a higher financial and environmental cost.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Ellipsis and filler-gap dependencies, Hierarchical structure, Argument Structure and other Constructions, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: Agreement (Subject-Verb Number Agreement), Center Embedding (embedding phrases in a nested structure requiring stack-like processing), Garden-Path Effects (handling syntactic ambiguities from local/global parse mismatches), Gross Syntactic Expectation (distinguishing coordinate vs. subordinate clauses), Licensing (requiring elements like NPIs or reflexives to appear within the scope of licensors), and Long-Distance Dependencies (capturing syntactic relations across large tree depth, including Filler-Gap and Cleft constructions
fine_tuning_materials: 3 downstream tasks after pretraining: Part-of-Speech (PoS) tagging and dependency parsing (both using the Universal Dependencies 2.5 English EWT corpus), and paraphrase identification (using the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus). Models were fine-tuned with simple linear layers or a deep Bi-affine parser, trained for 3 epochs
experimental_materials_comment:
naturalistic: Universal Dependencies Corpus for English (UD 2.5 English EWT) is used. For paraphrase identification, the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC)
controlled: stimuli inspired by psycholinguistic methods to precisely evaluate syntactic abilities in language models, aiming to detect human-like syntactic representations. It employs the SyntaxGym toolkit and syntactic tests from Hu et al. (2020), organized into six circuits: Agreement, Center Embedding, Garden-Path Effects, Gross Syntactic Expectation, Licensing, and Long-Distance Dependencies.
interp_method: a combination of structural probing, targeted syntactic evaluations, and downstream task performance. Syntactic encoding is measured with Hewitt and Manning's structural probes, evaluating tree distance (UUAS, DSpr) and tree depth (Root %, NSpr). SyntaxGym and tests from prior work (e.g., Marvin & Linzen, Wilcox et al., Futrell et al.) are used to evaluate syntactic generalization across six syntactic circuits, including agreement, garden-path effects, and long-distance dependencies. For practical language understanding, the models are fine-tuned on PoS tagging, dependency parsing, and paraphrase detection tasks using datasets like UD 2.5 and MRPC
main_findings: The study found that while LMs (roberta suite) pretrained on larger datasets tend to encode more syntactic information—evidenced by structural probes like tree depth and distance—they do not consistently generalize better across all syntactic phenomena. Surprisingly, models trained on less data sometimes outperformed heavily pretrained counterparts on certain syntax test suites. Although larger models showed more robustness to modifiers and performed better on downstream tasks like PoS tagging, dependency parsing, and paraphrase identification, the gains were modest relative to the massive increase in data and compute. Moreover, perplexity did not reliably predict syntactic generalization, and high variability was observed even within model families

title: A Discerning Several Thousand Judgments: GPT-3 Rates the Article + Adjective + Numeral + Noun Construction
abstract: Knowledge of syntax includes knowledge of rare, idiosyncratic constructions. LLMs must overcome frequency biases in order to master such constructions. In this study, I prompt GPT-3 to give acceptability judgments on the English-language Article + Adjective + Numeral + Noun construction (e.g., “a lovely five days”). I validate the prompt using the CoLA corpus of acceptability judgments and then zero in on the AANN construction. I compare GPT- 3’s judgments to crowdsourced human judgments on a subset of sentences. GPT-3’s judgments are broadly similar to human judgments and generally align with proposed constraints in the literature but, in some cases, GPT-3’s judgments and human judgments diverge from the literature and from each other.
specific_phenomena: English Article + Adjective + Numeral + Noun (AANN) construction, non-standard article-noun agreement, adjective-numeral order inversion, modifier requirement, sensitivity to adjective and noun types, adjective order in double-adjective AANNs, verb agreement with AANN subjects, subject-verb number agreement, part of speech, syntactic dependencies, verb argument construction biases, and relative clause representations.
experimental_materials_comment: The study used controlled, synthetically generated stimuli, constructing sentences through systematic variation of templates involving adjective, numeral, and noun types (e.g., art, distance, human, object, temporal, and unit-like nouns; quantitative, qualitative, and "stubbornly distributive" adjectives; low-range numerals), and also included degenerate AANN variants; the GPT-3 prompt was validated using CoLA's curated sentence set
interp_method: nan
main_findings: GPT-3 demonstrates a strong grasp of the rare and grammatically idiosyncratic English AANN (Article + Adjective + Numeral + Noun) construction, aligning closely with human judgments in key areas. Both GPT-3 and humans rated the AANN form as acceptable and clearly distinguished it from degraded variants, though GPT-3’s preference patterns for those variants differed somewhat. GPT-3 also mirrored human sensitivity to how noun and adjective types affect AANN acceptability, showing reduced ratings for constructions with distributive adjectives. In verb agreement tests, GPT-3 generally preferred plural verbs for animate and count nouns and singular verbs for distance and temporal nouns, replicating linguistic literature. However, it failed to reflect attested preferences in adjective ordering within double-adjective AANN structures. Overall, GPT-3 appears to have learned nuanced syntactic patterns specific to this construction, even when they conflict with more general grammatical rules

title: Probing GPT-3’s Linguistic Knowledge on Semantic Tasks
abstract: GPT-3 has attracted much attention from both academia and industry. However, it is still unclear what GPT-3 has understood or learned especially in linguistic knowledge. Some studies have shown linguistic phenomena including negation and tense are hard to be recognized by language models such as BERT. In this study, we conduct probing tasks focusing on semantic information. Specifically, we investigate GPT-3’s linguistic knowledge on semantic tasks to identify tense, the number of subjects, and the number of objects for a given sentence. We also experiment with different prompt designs and temperatures of the decoding method. Our experiment results suggest that GPT-3 has acquired linguistic knowledge to identify certain semantic information in most cases, but still fails when there are some types of disturbance happening in the sentence. We also perform error analysis to summarize some common types of mistakes that GPT-3 has made when dealing with certain semantic information.
specific_phenomena: Subject Number, Object Number
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language drawn from the pre-existing SentEval dataset. They used three semantic probing tasks—Tense, Subject Number (SubjNum), and Object Number (ObjNum)—each originally containing over 100,000 examples, from which they randomly sampled 500 for computational efficiency. GPT-3 was evaluated on these tasks using specially designed prompts that varied in style: binary-choice "default" prompts and open-ended "general" prompts. Additionally, both zero-shot and few-shot conditions were tested, with few-shot prompts including two or five example questions.
interp_method: prompting
main_findings: evaluating GPT-3’s understanding of semantic information, particularly tense and number (singular/plural) of sentence elements, rather than syntactic knowledge. However, findings revealed that semantic processing in GPT-3 is often influenced by underlying syntactic structures. GPT-3 generally performed well on Tense and Subject Number (SubjNum) tasks, especially with clear binary-choice (default) prompts, but struggled more with Object Number (ObjNum), likely due to the increased syntactic complexity of identifying objects. Prompt design had a significant impact: general prompts often led to misinterpretation and irrelevant answers, while few-shot examples helped performance in more challenging tasks like ObjNum but sometimes confused the model in simpler ones. Variations in decoding temperature had minimal effect. Qualitative error analysis showed that GPT-3’s semantic judgments were disrupted by specific syntactic features such as quotation marks, adverbials, negation, and complex clauses.

title: Word Acquisition in Neural Language Models
abstract: We investigate how neural language models acquire individual words during training, extracting learning curves and ages of acquisition for over 600 words on the MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventory (Fenson et al., 2007). Drawing on studies of word acquisition in children, we evaluate multiple predictors for words’ ages of acquisition in LSTMs, BERT, and GPT-2. We find that the effects of concreteness, word length, and lexical class are pointedly different in children and language models, reinforcing the importance of interaction and sensorimotor experience in child language acquisition. Language models rely far more on word frequency than children, but, like children, they exhibit slower learning of words in longer utterances. Interestingly, models follow consistent patterns during training for both unidirectional and bidirectional models, and for both LSTM and Transformer architectures. Models predict based on unigram token frequencies early in training, before transitioning loosely to bigram probabilities, eventually converging on more nuanced predictions. These results shed light on the role of distributional learning mechanisms in children, while also providing insights for more human-like language acquisition in language models.
specific_phenomena: - "syntactic complexity", "sentence length and (for unidirectional models) lexical class."
experimental_materials_comment: 611 single-token words from the MacArthur-Bates CDI, tracking learning via surprisal across natural contexts. For human comparison, the study used Wordbank data on children's age of acquisition and computed predictors like word frequency and Mean Length of Utterance (MLU) from the CHILDES corpus of child-directed speech (7.5 million tokens).
interp_method: nan
main_findings: how LSTMs, BERT, and GPT-2 acquire individual words during training, framing LMs as exemplars of distributional learning—learning purely from language statistics. Word acquisition is found to be highly dependent on word frequency, with frequency accounting for over 90% of the variance in learning order for LMs, in stark contrast to just 1% in children. Using a surprisal-based threshold to define when a word is learned, the authors show that BERT and GPT-2 learn frequent function words early, whereas children typically begin with nouns and verbs, highlighting a key divergence between statistical and sensorimotor-driven learning. The study also uses Mean Length of Utterance (MLU) as a proxy for syntactic complexity, finding that words appearing in more complex syntactic contexts (i.e., longer utterances) are learned later by LMs—a pattern consistent with child language acquisition. While not focused on specific syntactic structures, the research connects word learning to syntax through both MLU and surprisal,

title: minicons: Enabling Flexible Behavioral and Representational Analyses of Transformer Language Models
abstract: We present minicons, an open source library that provides a standard API for researchers interested in conducting behavioral and representational analyses of transformer-based language models (LMs). Specifically, minicons enables researchers to apply analysis methods at two levels: (1) at the prediction level -- by providing functions to efficiently extract word/sentence level probabilities; and (2) at the representational level -- by also facilitating efficient extraction of word/phrase level vectors from one or more layers. In this paper, we describe the library and apply it to two motivating case studies: One focusing on the learning dynamics of the BERT architecture on relative grammatical judgments, and the other on benchmarking 23 different LMs on zero-shot abductive reasoning. minicons is available at this https URL

Mechanistic_method: behavioral approach, Probing Techniques, Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)
interp_method: nan
main_findings: case study on how BERT models acquire syntactic and linguistic knowledge during pretraining, using minimal pairs from the BLIMP benchmark to evaluate acceptability judgments across 12 linguistic phenomena. The authors tested 145 MultiBERT models (variants of bert-base-uncased trained with different seeds and checkpoints) using the minicons scorer module. They found that while most linguistic phenomena eventually converged to BERT-base performance, acquisition rates varied: number and gender agreement were learned early, argument structure and ellipsis mid-training, and island effects the slowest. Some phenomena, like ellipsis and irregular forms, showed signs of forgetting, while NPI licensing and binding were highly sensitive to initial weights. Notably, binding outperformed BERT-base, peaking at 87% accuracy

title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models’ learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.Leveraging these findings, we compare the relative performance on different phenomena at varying learning stages with simpler reference models. Results suggest that NLMs exhibit consistent “developmental” stages. Moreover, we find the learning trajectory to be approximately one-dimensional: given an NLM with a certain overall performance, it is possible to predict what linguistic generalizations it has already acquired. Initial analysis of these stages presents phenomena clusters (notably morphological ones), whose performance progresses in unison, suggesting a potential link between the generalizations behind them.
model_name_comment: train: GPT2small, GPT2tiny, TransformerXL; test: GPT2, TransformerXL, LSTM
specific_phenomena: Blimp; animate subject, drop argument, existential there, determiner-noun agreement, wh vs that with gap, causative constructions, principle A binding, and island-related dependencies,

interp_method: behavioral approach, inspired by psycholinguistics, to study Neural Language Models (NLMs) by analyzing their observed behavior over training—specifically, how their accuracy on 67 BLIMP challenges evolves. By tracking performance vectors, correlating them to measure model similarity, and applying spectral clustering to learning curves,
main_findings: This work adopts a behavioral approach to investigate the implicit linguistic representations learned by Neural Language Models (NLMs), revealing that they share consistent training dynamics and generalize in similar ways, particularly in the acquisition of syntactic knowledge: models initially rely on local, identity-based cues, gradually developing global, structural sensitivity—though performance on certain syntactic phenomena may degrade over time, and the internal learning trajectories often diverge from traditional linguistic categorizations.

title: BabyBERTa: Learning More Grammar With Small-Scale Child-Directed Language
abstract: Transformer-based language models have taken the NLP world by storm. However, their potential for addressing important questions in language acquisition research has been largely ignored. In this work, we examined the grammatical knowledge of RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) when trained on a 5M word corpus of language acquisition data to simulate the input available to children between the ages 1 and 6. Using the behavioral probing paradigm, we found that a smaller version of RoBERTa-base that never predicts unmasked tokens, which we term BabyBERTa, acquires grammatical knowledge comparable to that of pre-trained RoBERTa-base - and does so with approximately 15X fewer parameters and 6,000X fewer words. We discuss implications for building more efficient models and the learnability of grammar from input available to children. Lastly, to support research on this front, we release our novel grammar test suite that is compatible with the small vocabulary of child-directed input.

interp_method: holistic scoring to evaluate grammatical knowledge, a method that sums cross-entropy errors across entire sentences to compute a preference score for minimal pairs, They contrast this with MLM scoring (or pseudo-log-likelihood), which involves masking tokens individually and summing log-losses, but note that holistic scoring better reflects human-like grammatical judgment
main_findings: shows that small transformer models like BabyBERTa, when trained on child-directed speech with optimized strategies (notably no unmasking), can acquire syntactic knowledge nearly on par with much larger models trained on vastly more data(Roberta); key findings highlight the benefits of simplified and diverse input, the scaffolding effect of early child-directed language, and limitations in mastering complex syntactic phenomena such as NPI licensing, ellipsis, and island effects.

title: The Curious Case of Absolute Position Embeddings
abstract: Transformer language models encode the notion of word order using positional information. Most commonly, this positional information is represented by absolute position embeddings (APEs), that are learned from the pretraining data. However, in natural language, it is not absolute position that matters, but relative position, and the extent to which APEs can capture this type of information has not been studied. In this work, we observe that models trained with APE over-rely on positional information to the point that they break-down when subjected to sentences with shifted position information. Specifically, when models are subjected to sentences starting from a non-zero position (excluding the effect of priming), they exhibit noticeably degraded performance on zero- to full-shot tasks, across a range of model families and model sizes. Our findings raise questions about the efficacy of APEs to model the relativity of position information, and invite further introspection on the sentence and word order processing strategies employed by these models.
model_name_comment: RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), BART (Lewis et al.,2020), GPT2 (Radford et al., 2019) and OPT
specific_phenomena: Blimp, relative distances between words rather than relying solely on fixed, absolute positions
experimental_materials_comment: Controlled stimuli included datasets like BLiMP, which features expert-crafted sentence pairs targeting specific grammatical phenomena; COPA, composed of hand-crafted causal reasoning prompts; and WinoGrande, based on the Winograd Schema Challenge; naturalistic language datasets such as MRPC (paraphrase pairs from real news), ARC (grade-school science questions), and RTE (textual entailment from natural sources) consist of examples drawn from real-world language use. Two additional datasets—PIQA (physical commonsense) and CoLA (linguistic acceptability)—were included
interp_method: phase shift: This methodology involves right-shifting the absolute positions of all tokens in a sentence by a specific distance k, ensuring that the relative distances between tokens within the sentence are preserved, while only the absolute starting position changes. This allows the researchers to evaluate the model's sentence encodings at different positions within the context window, effectively emulating sub-window sentence representation and factoring out the influence of prior context
main_findings: transformer LMs that use Absolute Position Embeddings (APEs) exhibit a strong over-reliance on the absolute position of tokens, leading to significant drops in performance when sentences are shifted from the beginning of the input window. This sensitivity to "phase shifts" affects a wide range of tasks and model types, with autoregressive models like GPT2 and OPT showing greater degradation than masked language models such as RoBERTa. Models tend to perform best when inputs start at position zero, revealing a "zero-position bias." In-context learning (e.g., zero- and few-shot tasks) is also disrupted by these shifts, especially in larger models, likely due to data sparsity in positional coverage during training. Moreover, fine-tuning amplifies position-specific overfitting, and performance varies erratically with different starting positions, pointing to learned positional quirks. These findings indicate that Transformer LMs with APEs do not consistently encode syntactic structure or word order independently of position

title: Studying word order through iterative shuffling
abstract: As neural language models approach human performance on NLP benchmark tasks, their advances are widely seen as evidence of an increasingly complex understanding of syntax. This view rests upon a hypothesis that has not yet been empirically tested: that word order encodes meaning essential to performing these tasks. We refute this hypothesis in many cases: in the GLUE suite and in various genres of English text, the words in a sentence or phrase can rarely be permuted to form a phrase carrying substantially different information. Our surprising result relies on inference by iterative shuffling (IBIS), a novel, efficient procedure that finds the ordering of a bag of words having the highest likelihood under a fixed language model. IBIS can use any black-box model without additional training and is superior to existing word ordering algorithms. Coalescing our findings, we discuss how shuffling inference procedures such as IBIS can benefit language modeling and constrained generation.
model_name_comment: BERT-Base, GPT2-small;  Distil-GPT-2, GPT-2 Medium, GPT-2 Large, and GPT-2 XL
specific_phenomena: investigated is word order, focusing on its role in encoding meaning, its impact on sentence interpretation, its recoverability from unordered words, its connection to "true English syntax," and its cross-linguistic variability.
fine_tuning_materials: GLUE benchmark, the authors fine-tuned the BERT-Base model
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic English corpora—including the Penn Treebank, Yelp, Wikipedia, arXiv abstracts, OpenWebText, and the GLUE benchmark—to evaluate word order's role in meaning and NLP performance, supplemented by controlled stimuli such as illustrative sentence pairs, constrained generation prompts, and human evaluation samples
interp_method: Inference by Iterative Shuffling (IBIS) is a combinatorial optimization-based method designed to find the most likely word order of a bag of words under a fixed language model; it operates by permuting spans using k-opt moves (adapted from the Traveling Salesman Problem), can work with any black-box LM without retraining, outperforms traditional left-to-right generation approaches like beam search, and includes a heuristic that ranks and scores candidate permutations to improve search efficiency.
main_findings: word order in English encodes surprisingly little additional meaning beyond the bag of words, challenging the assumption that syntactic structure is essential for NLP tasks; using the IBIS procedure, they show that language models like BERT and GPT-2 can recover original word order from unordered inputs with high accuracy, and perform most NLP tasks—including textual entailment, similarity detection, and sentiment classification—almost as well using unordered inputs, though tasks like grammaticality judgment and anaphora resolution remain more sensitive to word order; this suggests LMs' dependence on order stems from training rather than necessity, and opens avenues for models that focus more on semantic content than syntactic form, with caveats regarding language-specificity

title: Should You Mask 15% in Masked Language Modeling?
abstract: Masked language models (MLMs) conventionally mask 15% of tokens due to the belief that more masking would leave insufficient context to learn good representations; this masking rate has been widely used, regardless of model sizes or masking strategies. In this work, we revisit this important choice of MLM pre-training. We first establish that 15% is not universally optimal, and larger models should adopt a higher masking rate. Specifically, we find that masking 40% outperforms 15% for BERT-large size models on GLUE and SQuAD. Interestingly, an extremely high masking rate of 80% can still preserve 95% fine-tuning performance and most of the accuracy in linguistic probing, challenging the conventional wisdom about the role of the masking rate. We then examine the interplay between masking rates and masking strategies and find that uniform masking requires a higher masking rate compared to sophisticated masking strategies such as span or PMI masking. Finally, we argue that increasing the masking rate has two distinct effects: it leads to more corruption, which makes the prediction task more difficult; it also enables more predictions, which benefits optimization. Using this framework, we revisit BERT’s 80-10-10 corruption strategy. Together, our results contribute to a better understanding of MLM pre-training.

main_findings: The study investigates the role of masking rates in Masked Language Models (MLMs), revealing that the commonly used 15% rate is not optimal across model sizes. Larger models like BERT-large perform better with higher masking rates (up to 40%), while smaller models benefit from lower rates. Surprisingly, even with very high masking rates (e.g., 80%), MLMs retain strong performance on downstream tasks and preserve most linguistic knowledge, as shown by BLiMP evaluations. While most syntactic phenomena remain robust, filler-gap dependencies and island effects degrade at high masking levels. The study also shows that optimal masking rates depend on the masking strategy (e.g., span or PMI masking requires lower rates than uniform masking), and introduces a useful distinction between corruption rate (how much context is masked) and prediction rate (how much is predicted), which have opposing effects on performance. Lastly, it finds that the standard 80-10-10 corruption strategy underperforms compared to simply replacing all masked tokens with [MASK], suggesting that pre-training can be more effective with simplified masking

title: Word Order Matters When You Increase Masking
abstract: Word order, an essential property of natural languages, is injected in Transformer-based neural language models using position encoding. However, recent experiments have shown that explicit position encoding is not always useful, since some models without such feature managed to achieve state-of-the art performance on some tasks. To understand better this phenomenon, we examine the effect of removing position encodings on the pre-training objective itself (i.e., masked language modelling), to test whether models can reconstruct position information from co-occurrences alone. We do so by controlling the amount of masked tokens in the input sentence, as a proxy to affect the importance of position information for the task. We find that the necessity of position information increases with the amount of masking, and that masked language models without position encodings are not able to reconstruct this information on the task. These findings point towards a direct relationship between the amount of masking and the ability of Transformers to capture order-sensitive aspects of language using position encoding.

experimental_materials_comment: use artificial languages rather than natural ones to precisely control experimental conditions and directly investigate how models use position information. They used data generated from a context-free grammar (CFG) with fixed rule probabilities, allowing access to the true probability distribution of sentence completions—something not feasible with natural language. The artificial language included morphological agreement and had a fixed word order, enabling targeted probing of syntactic and positional understanding. This controlled setup avoids confounds common in natural language and reduces computational cost, while allowing rigorous evaluation of model behavior.
interp_method: controlled experimental setup to evaluate how essential explicit position encoding is for masked language modeling (MLM). They compare two BERT variants—one with position embeddings and one without (NP)—across different masking levels. Using artificial language data (with known ordered and unordered true probability distributions), they measure how closely each model's predictions match these distributions using KL-divergence. This design lets them isolate and test the role of position information in syntactic learning, which would not be feasible with natural language data.
main_findings: Transformer-based language models rely increasingly on syntactic position information—especially word order and morphological agreement—as the amount of masking increases during pretraining. Using an artificial language with fixed word order, the researchers show that models like BERT (with explicit position encodings) can approximate true ordered language distributions across masking levels, while models without position encodings (like NP) fail under higher masking. This demonstrates that explicit position encodings are essential for capturing syntactic structure, particularly when more of the context is hidden. The study challenges the assumption that transformers can infer syntactic order from co-occurrence statistics alone, emphasizing that position encoding and masking rate critically shape the acquisition of syntactic knowledge.

title: Convolutions and Self-Attention: Re-interpreting Relative Positions in Pre-trained Language Models
abstract: In this paper, we detail the relationship between convolutions and self-attention in natural language tasks. We show that relative position embeddings in self-attention layers are equivalent to recently-proposed dynamic lightweight convolutions, and we consider multiple new ways of integrating convolutions into Transformer self-attention. Specifically, we propose composite attention, which unites previous relative position encoding methods under a convolutional framework. We conduct experiments by training BERT with composite attention, finding that convolutions consistently improve performance on multiple downstream tasks, replacing absolute position embeddings. To inform future work, we present results comparing lightweight convolutions, dynamic convolutions, and depthwise-separable convolutions in language model pre-training, considering multiple injection points for convolutions in self-attention layers.
model_name_comment: BERT-small models  that incorporated lightweight convolutions
specific_phenomena: Grammaticality judgments, evaluated using the CoLA task
fine_tuning_materials: GLUE
experimental_materials_comment: nan
Mechanistic_method: behavioral approach, manipulate model architecture (Architectural intervention), Feature Visualization
interp_method: Composite attention is a unified framework that combines fixed and dynamic lightweight convolutions to model relative position information in Transformers. It merges the benefits of fixed convolutions (as in Raffel et al., 2020) and dynamic ones (as in Shaw et al., 2018), offering both structured positional encoding and flexibility across tokens. Essentially, it reframes existing relative position embedding methods within a convolutional perspective, enhancing the model's ability to capture syntactic and positional cues.
main_findings: integration of convolutions into Transformer self-attention, revealing that relative position embeddings are mathematically equivalent to lightweight convolutions, particularly dynamic ones. Building on this, the authors introduce composite attention, a unified framework combining both fixed and dynamic lightweight convolutions, which outperforms standard BERT on various NLP tasks. Experiments show that convolutional variants consistently enhance model performance, especially for local syntactic tasks like grammaticality judgments (e.g., CoLA), where local position information is critical. The benefits are more pronounced in smaller models, and although additional convolutions help, there is a limit to useful local mixing. Overall, the findings emphasize that convolutions are effective substitutes for absolute position embeddings, improving syntactic sensitivity by capturing local dependencies crucial for natural language understanding

title: Word Order Does Matter and Shuffled Language Models Know It
abstract: Recent studies have shown that language models pretrained and/or fine-tuned on randomly permuted sentences exhibit competitive performance on GLUE, putting into question the importance of word order information. Somewhat counter-intuitively, some of these studies also report that position embeddings appear to be crucial for models’ good performance with shuffled text. We probe these language models for word order information and investigate what position embeddings learned from shuffled text encode, showing that these models retain a notion of word order information. We show this is in part due to a subtlety in how shuffling is implemented in previous work – before rather than after subword segmentation. Surprisingly, we find even Language models trained on text shuffled after subword segmentation retain some semblance of information about word order because of the statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities. Finally, we show that beyond GLUE, a variety of language understanding tasks do require word order information, often to an extent that cannot be learned through fine-tuning.
