main_findings: LMs, even when trained on shuffled text, can retain significant syntactic knowledge—particularly about word order—due largely to the influence of position embeddings. Shuffled models (like SHUF.N1) perform well on word order probing tasks, nearly matching models trained on unshuffled data (ORIG), and outperforming models without positional encodings (NOPOS). This highlights the crucial role of position embeddings in encoding word order. The retention of order information is partly explained by artifacts in the shuffling process, such as performing it before subword segmentation (which keeps word parts contiguous), accidental bigram overlap in short sentences, and genre-based sentence length cues. These factors allow models to capture local dependencies, often mimicking convolutional patterns through offset attention. While GLUE tasks show only minor performance drops for shuffled models, more syntax-sensitive benchmarks like SuperGLUE and WinoGrande reveal a larger gap, underscoring the importance of word order for complex reasoning and argument structure. Probing tasks also show shuffled models struggle with long-distance dependencies but maintain strength in local ones.

title: Masked Language Modeling and the Distributional Hypothesis: Order Word Matters Pre-training for Little
abstract: A possible explanation for the impressive performance of masked language model (MLM) pre-training is that such models have learned to represent the syntactic structures prevalent in classical NLP pipelines. In this paper, we propose a different explanation: MLMs succeed on downstream tasks almost entirely due to their ability to model higher-order word co-occurrence statistics. To demonstrate this, we pre-train MLMs on sentences with randomly shuffled word order, and show that these models still achieve high accuracy after fine-tuning on many downstream tasks—including tasks specifically designed to be challenging for models that ignore word order. Our models perform surprisingly well according to some parametric syntactic probes, indicating possible deficiencies in how we test representations for syntactic information. Overall, our results show that purely distributional information largely explains the success of pre-training, and underscore the importance of curating challenging evaluation datasets that require deeper linguistic knowledge.
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, POS, Agreement and feature-checking, Negation and NPIs
specific_phenomena: Dependency Parsing (DEP), Part-of-Speech tagging (POS), Dependency Arc Labeling (DAL), and SentEval tasks such as TreeDepth, TopConstituents, and BigramShift. Non-parametric probes, which assess model predictions directly without additional classifiers, include Agreement Attractors and the Marvin and Linzen (2018) stimuli, targeting fine-grained syntactic phenomena like subject-verb agreement across various clause structures, reflexives, and negative polarity items
fine_tuning_materials: General Language Understanding and Evaluation(GLUE) benchmark, the Paraphrase Adversaries from Word Scrambling (PAWS) dataset,
experimental_materials_comment: created permuted corpora, including M1 (fully shuffled), M2–M4 (shuffled n-grams), MUG (unigram-only frequency), MNP (no positional embeddings), and M512 (shuffled buffer of 512 tokens). They evaluated models using parametric syntactic probes (like dependency parsing, POS tagging, and SentEval tasks: TreeDepth, TopConstituents, BigramShift) and non-parametric probes based on minimal pairs, including datasets from Linzen et al., Gulordava et al., and Marvin and Linzen
interp_method: pre-training MLMs on permuted sentences with varying degrees of n-gram preservation (from fully shuffled to shuffled 4-grams), alongside constructing baseline models such as MUG (which uses only unigram frequencies), MNP (a RoBERTa model without positional embeddings), and MRI (a randomly initialized RoBERTa). These configurations allow them to isolate and assess the influence of word order, positional information, and co-occurrence statistics on model performance.
main_findings: contextual Word embeddings are surprisingly invariant to scrambling word order: MLMs like BERT and RoBERTa perform well, arguing that their success stems more from modeling higher-order word co-occurrence statistics than from learning syntactic structures. It finds that pre-training on shuffled sentences has only a minor effect on performance for many downstream tasks (e.g., GLUE, PAWS), highlighting the robustness of MLMs to disrupted word order. Positional embeddings remain crucial, even when natural word order is absent, and distributional priors alone allow randomized models to achieve strong performance. While syntactic probing shows that natural word order helps on tasks like dependency parsing, even shuffled models can perform reasonably well on many syntactic benchmarks, especially with parametric probes. However, non-parametric probes reveal clearer deficiencies in shuffled models’ syntactic knowledge. The study also shows that fine-tuning can help recover word order information, especially for tasks like CoLA, RTE, and PAWS, though naturally ordered pre-training offers consistent advantages in few-shot settings.

title: Word Frequency Does Not Predict Grammatical Knowledge in Language Models
abstract: Neural language models learn, to varying degrees of accuracy, the grammatical properties of natural languages. In this work, we investigate whether there are systematic sources of variation in the language models’ accuracy. Focusing on subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora, we find that certain nouns are systematically understood better than others, an effect which is robust across grammatical tasks and different language models. Surprisingly, we find that across four orders of magnitude, corpus frequency is unrelated to a noun’s performance on grammatical tasks. Finally, we find that a novel noun’s grammatical properties can be few-shot learned from various types of training data. The results present a paradox: there should be less variation in grammatical performance than is actually observed.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: subject-Verb Agreement (SVA) (VA Simple, SVA Subj.Rel.Clause, SVA Sent.Comp., SVA PP, SVA Obj.Rel.Clause.That, and SVA Obj.Rel.Clause.NoThat) and Reflexive Anaphora (RA) RA Simple, RA Sent.Comp., RA Obj.Rel.Clause.That, and RA Obj.Rel.Clause.NoThat
fine_tuning_materials: syntactic fine-tuning
experimental_materials_comment: template-based sentence construction, where lexical items (nouns, verbs, adjectives) were randomly sampled from WordNet and VerbNet to fill templates like “The 〈TargetNoun〉 〈Verb〉.” Each sentence had multiple variants (e.g., 2x2 or 2x2x2 setups) to manipulate grammaticality and number agreement between target and distractor nouns. For few-shot learning experiments, novel words like "wug" (singular) and "wuz" (plural) were introduced and fine-tuned using small sets of syntactically or semantically controlled stimuli
interp_method: minimal pair methodology
main_findings: LMs acquire grammatical knowledge about nouns in a systematic yet puzzling way. Performance on grammatical tasks like subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora varies consistently across different nouns, tasks, and models (e.g., GPT-2, Transformer-XL, and BERT), with two latent dimensions driving this variation. Surprisingly, a noun’s frequency in the training corpus does not predict how well its grammatical behavior is learned—challenging expectations from few-shot learning theories. The models can learn grammatical properties of novel nouns from minimal data, especially when exposed to syntactic cues or semantically informative contexts. However, purely semantic training was less reliable for inducing correct subject-verb agreement. These findings suggest that while LMs are capable of few-shot grammatical learning, their inconsistent performance across nouns cannot be explained by data availability alone, pointing instead to an unresolved "excess variation" in how syntactic information is represented.

title: Subject Verb Agreement Error Patterns in Meaningless Sentences: Humans vs. BERT
abstract: Both humans and neural language models are able to perform subject verb number agreement (SVA). In principle, semantics shouldn’t interfere with this task, which only requires syntactic knowledge. In this work we test whether meaning interferes with this type of agreement in English in syntactic structures of various complexities. To do so, we generate both semantically well-formed and nonsensical items. We compare the performance of BERT-base to that of humans, obtained with a psycholinguistic online crowdsourcing experiment. We find that BERT and humans are both sensitive to our semantic manipulation: They fail more often when presented with nonsensical items, especially when their syntactic structure features an attractor (a noun phrase between the subject and the verb that has not the same number as the subject). We also find that the effect of meaningfulness on SVA errors is stronger for BERT than for humans, showing higher lexical sensitivity of the former on this task.
specific_phenomena: Subject-Verb Agreement (SVA) with a focus on the principles of Structure Dependence (SD) and Meaning Independence (MI) across nine syntactic structures: (A) simple agreement, (B) sentential complement, (C) prepositional phrase, (D) subject relative clause, (E) short VP coordination, (F) object relative clause, (G) within object relative clause, (H) object relative clause (no "that"), and (I) within object relative clause (no "that")—with C, D, F, and H including attractors to test how linear distractors affect SVA judgments in both humans and BERT
experimental_materials_comment: subject-verb agreement with naturalistic language and controlled stimuli. The naturalistic items, called meaningful sentences (M&L data), were semantically well-formed and sampled from Marvin and Linzen (2018), with 30 sentences per syntactic structure. In contrast, the meaningless sentences (nonce items) were carefully generated to be semantically ill-formed by randomly filling syntactic templates with words of the correct part-of-speech, followed by manual filtering to ensure they remained uninterpretable. Both sentence types included syntactic constructions of varying complexity, including structures with attractors—intervening nouns of mismatched number—to test how meaning and syntax affect SVA errors in both humans and BERT.
interp_method: nan
main_findings: examined BERT-base's ability to handle subject-verb agreement (SVA) compared to human performance, focusing on the influence of semantics and syntax. Both humans and BERT performed worse on nonsensical (nonce) sentences, especially when attractors—intervening nouns with mismatched number—were present. However, BERT was more affected by meaninglessness and showed greater reliance on nearby attractors, indicating a stronger dependence on linear order rather than deeper syntactic structure. This challenges two linguistic principles: meaning independence (SVA should not rely on meaning) and structure dependence (SVA should be governed by hierarchical syntax). While BERT’s and humans’ error patterns correlated overall, they diverged in critical ways—BERT struggled more with attractors in meaningless contexts, while humans were more sensitive to structural complexity without attractors. These findings suggest that although BERT demonstrates some syntactic competence, it heavily relies on local context and semantics

title: Does BERT really agree ? Fine-grained Analysis of Lexical Dependence on a Syntactic Task
abstract: Although transformer-based Neural Language Models demonstrate impressive performance on a variety of tasks, their generalization abilities are not well understood. They have been shown to perform strongly on subject-verb number agreement in a wide array of settings, suggesting that they learned to track syntactic dependencies during their training even without explicit supervision. In this paper, we examine the extent to which BERT is able to perform lexically-independent subject-verb number agreement (NA) on targeted syntactic templates. To do so, we disrupt the lexical patterns found in naturally occurring stimuli for each targeted structure in a novel fine-grained analysis of BERT’s behavior. Our results on nonce sentences suggest that the model generalizes well for simple templates, but fails to perform lexically-independent syntactic generalization when as little as one attractor is present.
specific_phenomena: Number Agreement (NA) between subject and verb: Attraction Effects caused by intervening nouns with mismatched number; Hierarchical Constraints, where agreement depends on syntactic structure rather than linear word order; Sentential Complements, both with and without the complementizer "that"; Prepositional Phrases containing attractors; Subject and Object Relative Clauses, with and without "that"; Verb Phrase Coordination involving coordinated verbs; and the influence of Stative Verbs in complement clauses
experimental_materials_comment: 3 datasets to evaluate BERT's syntactic knowledge: M&L (Marvin & Linzen) — meaningful but controlled and unseen sentences designed to test syntax with limited semantics; WIKI — naturally occurring, meaningful sentences from Wikipedia, reflecting BERT's training data and allowing analysis of performance based on potential memorization; and NONCE — syntactically controlled but semantically meaningless sentences created by replacing content words while preserving structure, used to isolate syntactic ability and test lexically-independent generalization, especially under attraction effects
interp_method: nan
main_findings: BERT performs well on number agreement (NA) in simple syntactic contexts, its syntactic generalization is highly lexically dependent, particularly when attractors—intervening nouns of mismatched number—are present. BERT struggles with lexically-independent syntactic generalization in such cases, especially when the subject and verb are separated by hierarchically embedded phrases containing attractors, causing performance to drop to chance level on meaningless sentences. The model shows strong sensitivity to nearby lexical content, with performance significantly harmed by altering words close to the verb, even when those words are syntactically irrelevant. This suggests that BERT often relies on memorized lexical patterns and heuristics rather than abstract, hierarchical syntactic rules, performing better on familiar, naturally occurring (WIKI) sentences than on novel ones (M&L). However, in the absence of attractors, BERT maintains high NA accuracy—even on nonsensical inputs—indicating that pure syntactic competence is limited to simpler cases, and breaks down when syntactic complexity increases or semantic cues are removed.

title: Look at that! BERT can be easily distracted from paying attention to morphosyntax
abstract: Syntactic knowledge involves not only the ability to combine words and phrases, but also the capacity to relate different and yet truth-preserving structural variations (e.g. pas- sivization, inversion, topicalization, extraposi- tion, clefting, etc.), as well as the ability to in- fer that these syntactic variations all adhere to common morphosyntactic rules, like subject- verb agreement. Although there is some ev- idence that BERT has rich syntactic knowl- edge, our adversarial approach suggests that it is not deployed in a robust and linguistically appropriate way. English BERT can be tricked to miss even quite simple syntactic generaliza- tions, when compared with GPT-2, underscor- ing the need for stronger priors and for linguis- tically controlled experiments in evaluation.
model_name_comment: BERT base/large uncased,  GPT-2 (small and medium)
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: subject-verb agreement (both local and long-distance), paraphrasing, passivization, inversion, topicalization, extraposition, clefting (it-clefts and wh-clefts), subject/object extraction, clausal embedding, and subject-verb sequence ordering
fine_tuning_materials: Fine-tuned BERT on PAWS
experimental_materials_comment: Natural &controlled. Corpus-based extraction: Sentences or sentence components were drawn from parsed English corpora such as COCA, BNC, and Brown. attested linguistic material manipulated to form highly controlled and adversarial test cases: 6,000 sentence seeds, producing 28 variants each through controlled syntactic transformations (e.g., passivization, clefting, embedding).  5040 sentences by systematically manipulating:    Number inflection of the target subject (singular/plural).    Number inflection of attractor nouns (higher in structure).    Levels of clausal embedding (0–4). Target noun was always adjacent to the masked verb, making agreement easy if syntactic knowledge is properly used. Manually built 365 sentence pairs with 1–3 levels of clausal embedding
Mechanistic_method: Adversarial Testing, Probing Techniques (Structured Probes), Attention Flow analysis
interp_method: attention flow analysis using the maximum flow algorithm as a post-hoc technique
main_findings: BERT encodes rich syntactic representations, including the ability to model subject-verb agreement and syntax trees in its deeper layers, it fails to robustly and appropriately deploy this knowledge, especially in complex or distractor-heavy contexts. Across three experiments—local agreement, long-distance agreement, and syntactic paraphrasing—BERT was easily misled by surface-level features, showed poor generalization with rare or non-'be' verbs, and relied on shallow heuristics like lexical overlap or word order rather than true syntactic or semantic understanding. In contrast, GPT-2 demonstrated stronger, more resilient morphosyntactic abilities, consistently outperforming BERT and resisting interference from attractors. Overall, BERT's syntactic competence is brittle and heuristic-driven, suggesting that while it encodes grammatical structure, it often fails to use it in a linguistically meaningful way.

title: Accounting for Agreement Phenomena in Sentence Comprehension with Transformer Language Models: Effects of Similarity-based Interference on Surprisal and Attention
abstract: We advance a novel explanation of similarity-based interference effects in subject-verb and reflexive pronoun agreement processing, grounded in surprisal values computed from a pretrained large-scale Transformer model, GPT-2. Specifically, we show that surprisal of the verb or reflexive pronoun predicts facilitatory interference effects in ungrammatical sentences, where a distractor noun that matches in number with the verb or pronouns leads to faster reading times, despite the distractor not participating in the agreement relation. We review the human empirical evidence for such effects, including recent meta-analyses and large-scale studies. We also show that attention patterns (indexed by entropy and other measures) in the Transformer show patterns of diffuse attention in the presence of similar distractors, consistent with cue-based retrieval models of parsing. But in contrast to these models, the attentional cues and memory representations are learned entirely from the simple self-supervised task of predicting the next word.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: subject-verb agreement, reflexive pronoun agreement, similarity-based interference (facilitatory, inhibitory, proactive, and retroactive), dependency relations (like nsubj), agreement attraction errors, plural-singular asymmetry, and binding theory constraints in reflexive resolution.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli from prior human reading time studies to test agreement and interference effects in a 2×2 design (e.g., grammaticality × interference), while also conducting a preliminary analysis of naturalistic language from a Reddit corpus to examine whether similar interference-driven ungrammaticalities occur in real-world text.
Mechanistic_method: behavioral approach, Attention Analysis, Feature Visualization
interp_method: adopt Voita et al. (2019)’s method to identify attention heads specialized for specific syntactic dependencies (e.g., subject-verb and reflexive pronoun relations) using CoreNLP parsing and relative string positions. Conduct attention analyses using metrics like Attention Entropy and Attention to Target to assess how focused or dispersed attention is during sentence processing.
main_findings: GPT-2 captures key psycholinguistic effects through its internal mechanisms: It predicts facilitatory interference effects in subject-verb and reflexive pronoun agreement, mirroring human reading behavior via lower surprisal in ungrammatical but number-matching distractor conditions.    It shows no inhibitory interference effects, aligning with weak human evidence in grammatical distractor conditions.    Attention patterns in GPT-2 resemble cue-based retrieval, showing diffuse attention and reduced focus on grammatical targets in interfering contexts.    These effects emerge despite GPT-2 being trained solely on next-word prediction, suggesting that self-supervised learning naturally develops representations supporting syntactic processing and interference effects.    A preliminary naturalistic corpus analysis confirms that interfering distractors are more common than non-interfering ones in real-world agreement errors, though model behavior is not solely driven by frequency.

title: Does BERT agree? Evaluating knowledge of structure dependence through agreement relations
abstract: Learning representations that accurately model semantics is an important goal of natural language processing research. Many semantic phenomena depend on syntactic structure. Recent work examines the extent to which state-of-the-art models for pre-training representations, such as BERT, capture such structure-dependent phenomena, but is largely restricted to one phenomenon in English: number agreement between subjects and verbs. We evaluate BERT's sensitivity to four types of structure-dependent agreement relations in a new semi-automatically curated dataset across 26 languages. We show that both the single-language and multilingual BERT models capture syntax-sensitive agreement patterns well in general, but we also highlight the specific linguistic contexts in which their performance degrades.
specific_phenomena: structure-dependent agreement relations: subject-verb agreement, noun-determiner agreement, noun-attributive adjective agreement, and subject-predicate adjective agreement. These relations are assessed based on four morphosyntactic features—number, gender, case, and perso
languages_tested_comment: 26: Russian, Italian, French, Catalan, English, Dutch, Latin, Polish, Portuguese, Finnish, Romanian, Norwegian, Hindi, Croatian, Persian, Greek, Ukrainian, Swedish, Hebrew, Danish, Urdu, Basque, Turkish, Irish, Afrikaans, Armenian
experimental_materials_comment: semi-automatically curated naturalistic language data drawn from version 2.4 of the Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks; yielded nearly one million cloze examples. While the data was naturalistic, the evaluation itself used a refined cloze test to control for syntactic sensitivity and rule out effects from frequency or selectional preferences—thus combining natural input with a controlled evaluation
interp_method: cloze test: masking out one word in an agreement relation and asking BERT to predict the masked word
main_findings: BERT—both the English and multilingual versions—effectively models syntax-sensitive agreement patterns across 26 languages and four types of agreement relations (subject-verb, determiner, attributive adjective, and predicate adjective). BERT achieved over 90% accuracy on most agreement types and languages, with slightly weaker performance on subject-verb and predicate adjective relations. Performance declines when agreement dependencies are longer or more distractors are present, indicating some sensitivity to sentence complexity. Despite lacking explicit syntactic structure, BERT’s predictions reflect strong implicit syntactic knowledge, likely learned during pretraining. The study used a large cloze-style dataset with nearly one million examples and improved evaluation techniques to ensure results reflected syntactic understanding rather than word frequency or selectional preference. Overall, the findings suggest BERT captures structure-dependent agreement robustly across typologically diverse languages, though with some limitations under increased syntactic complexity.

title: Quantity doesn’t buy quality syntax with neural language models
abstract: Recurrent neural networks can learn to predict upcoming words remarkably well on average; in syntactically complex contexts, however, they often assign unexpectedly high probabilities to ungrammatical words. We investigate to what extent these shortcomings can be mitigated by increasing the size of the network and the corpus on which it is trained. We find that gains from increasing network size are minimal beyond a certain point. Likewise, expanding the training corpus yields diminishing returns; we estimate that the training corpus would need to be unrealistically large for the models to match human performance. A comparison to GPT and BERT, Transformer-based models trained on billions of words, reveals that these models perform even more poorly than our LSTMs in some constructions. Our results make the case for more data efficient architectures.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: simple subject-verb agreement, local number agreement, attractor constructions (involving subject relative clauses and prepositional phrases), object relative clauses (with and without overt relativizers), coordination constructions (short and long VP coordination), and reflexive anaphora requiring correct agreement between a reflexive pronoun and its antecedent.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli (from Marvin and Linzen, 2018) to evaluate the models' syntactic knowledge through minimal sentence pairs differing only in grammaticality.
interp_method: nan
main_findings: increasing model size and training data yields only limited gains in syntactic accuracy for language models. While basic local subject-verb agreement is learned quickly, more complex structures—like agreement across attractors, object relative clauses, coordination, and reflexive anaphora—remain challenging. Even large Transformer models like GPT and BERT, trained on billions of tokens, often performed no better or worse than smaller LSTMs, showing poor data efficiency. The results suggest that larger models and more data alone are insufficient for mastering syntax, and that external supervision or stronger inductive biases may be necessary for robust syntactic learning

title: Superglue: a stickier benchmark for general-purpose language understanding systems
abstract: In the last year, new models and methods for pretraining and transfer learning have driven striking performance improvements across a range of language understanding tasks. The GLUE benchmark, introduced a little over one year ago, offers a single-number metric that summarizes progress on a diverse set of such tasks, but performance on the benchmark has recently surpassed the level of non-expert humans, suggesting limited headroom for further research. In this paper we present SuperGLUE, a new benchmark styled after GLUE with a new set of more difficult language understanding tasks, a software toolkit, and a public leaderboard. SuperGLUE is available at https://super.gluebenchmark.com.
specific_phenomena: double negation, restrictivity, disjunction, and downward monotonicity
experimental_materials_comment: a mix of naturalistic text and controlled stimuli:  several tasks and diagnostic sets are expert-constructed to target specific syntactic phenomena and reasoning challenges. For instance, the Broad-Coverage Diagnostic (AXb) deliberately tests syntactic difficulties such as double negation, restrictivity, disjunction, and downward monotonicity, while Winogender (AXg) uses minimal sentence pairs to probe gender bias in coreference, a task deeply tied to syntactic understanding. Some tasks like COPA and MultiRC use handcrafted or structurally constrained examples to enforce causal or multi-sentence reasoning. Others, like WSC and WiC, embed syntactic challenges (e.g., anaphora, word sense disambiguation) within controlled formats despite using naturally sourced base texts.
interp_method: benchmark
main_findings: findings from SuperGLUE and related benchmarks highlight that while language models have made significant progress, they still exhibit major limitations in syntactic understanding. Models like BERT++ fall far short of human performance on tasks that demand deep syntactic reasoning, such as those in the GLUE diagnostic set, where they struggle with phenomena like restrictivity, downward monotonicity, and double negation. Tasks such as the Winograd Schema Challenge and Winogender further expose deficits in coreference resolution—an area heavily reliant on syntactic and semantic comprehension—where models often guess rather than truly resolve pronoun-antecedent relationships. Additionally, tasks like COPA, which require understanding causal and logical relationships embedded in syntax, reveal persistent weaknesses. Overall, these evaluations show that while LMs handle surface-level patterns well, they lack robust, generalizable syntactic knowledge and fail on linguistically complex tasks that require understanding structure and meaning beyond simple token co-occurrence.

title: Emergent linguistic structure in artificial neural networks trained by self-supervision
abstract: This paper explores the knowledge of linguistic structure learned by large artificial neural networks, trained via self-supervision, whereby the model simply tries to predict a masked word in a given context. Human language communication is via sequences of words, but language understanding requires constructing rich hierarchical structures that are never observed explicitly. The mechanisms for this have been a prime mystery of human language acquisition, while engineering work has mainly proceeded by supervised learning on treebanks of sentences hand labeled for this latent structure. However, we demonstrate that modern deep contextual language models learn major aspects of this structure, without any explicit supervision. We develop methods for identifying linguistic hierarchical structure emergent in artificial neural networks and demonstrate that components in these models focus on syntactic grammatical relationships and anaphoric coreference. Indeed, we show that a linear transformation of learned embeddings in these models captures parse tree distances to a surprising degree, allowing approximate reconstruction of the sentence tree structures normally assumed by linguists. These results help explain why these models have brought such large improvements across many language-understanding tasks.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: subject–verb agreement, dependency syntax: specific dependency types explored using attention probes include nominal subject, direct object, clausal complement, object of preposition, predeterminer, marker, passive auxiliary, and phrasal verb particle. addresses the model’s ability to identify the root of the sentence, compute parse depth, determine edge direction, and predict the label of the smallest phrasal constituent above a word. Additionally, it examines the model's understanding of reflexive anaphora and the ability to predict both the label of the dependency edge governing a word and the label of the edge governing its parent,
experimental_materials_comment: natural language corpora and controlled stimuli. For syntactic dependencies, attention heads and structural probes are assessed using the Penn Treebank's Wall Street Journal (WSJ) section, annotated with Stanford Dependencies.  Coreference resolution is evaluated with the CoNLL-2012 dataset, which contains annotations for anaphoric relationships among mentions. For other emergent linguistic properties like morphology, parts of speech, and semantics, analyses are conducted on representations derived from natural texts. Additionally, controlled stimuli—specifically constructed sentences—are used to test syntax sensitivity, particularly subject–verb agreement. These include intervening "attractor" nouns that challenge the model's ability to identify the true syntactic subject
interp_method: Attention Probes, which assess whether specific attention heads in BERT align with known linguistic relations by analyzing which words are attended to during processing, and Structural Probes, which test whether the internal vector representations of words encode syntactic tree structures by applying a linear transformation that approximates syntactic distances and depths.
main_findings: BERT displays strong sensitivity to syntax-dependent phenomena such as subject–verb agreement, even in the presence of distractor nouns, sometimes matching or surpassing human performance. This syntactic competence emerges through mechanisms like attention heads, some of which specialize in specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, subjects, phrasal particles), and structural probes, which reveal that BERT’s internal representations embed dependency tree structures with high fidelity. BERT achieves high accuracy in reconstructing parse tree distances, depths, and root identification, significantly outperforming baselines. These findings suggest that self-supervised objectives serve as powerful indirect supervision signals, allowing models to internalize syntactic structure

title: What do you learn from context? Probing for sentence structure in contextualized word representations
abstract: Contextualized representation models such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018a) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) have recently achieved state-of-the-art results on a diverse array of downstream NLP tasks. Building on recent token-level probing work, we introduce a novel edge probing task design and construct a broad suite of sub-sentence tasks derived from the traditional structured NLP pipeline. We probe word-level contextual representations from four recent models and investigate how they encode sentence structure across a range of syntactic, semantic, local, and long-range phenomena. We find that existing models trained on language modeling and translation produce strong representations for syntactic phenomena, but only offer comparably small improvements on semantic tasks over a non-contextual baseline.
model_name_comment: CoVe, ELMo, GPT2, and BERT-base-uncasd, BERT-large-uncased
specific_phenomena: POS tagging, constituent labeling, and dependency labeling
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language data from well-annotated corpora, such as OntoNotes 5.0, the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank, and SemEval 2010, for probing a range of syntactic and semantic tasks. include also controlled stimulus: the Definite Pronoun Resolution (DPR) dataset, based on the Winograd Schema Challenge, which targets difficult coreference cases requiring subtle semantic inference.
interp_method: edge probe approach: designed to be generic and can be applied to any task that can be represented as a labeled graph anchored to spans in a sentence
main_findings: The probe aims at measuring how well information about linguistic structure can be extracted from a pretrained encoder by decomposingstructured-prediction tasks into a common format, where a probing classifier receives spans and must predict a label such as aconstituent or relation type. Their results provided evidences corroborating that BERT model can represent the types of syntacticand semantic abstractions in an interpretable and localisable way, and that the regions responsible for each step appear this sequence:Part of Speech (PoS) tagging, parsing, Named Entity Recognition (NER), semantic roles and finally coreference.  investigates how contextualized word representations, such as ELMo, BERT, and GPT, encode syntactic structure and what improvements they bring over static embeddings. The findings show that these models strongly encode syntactic information, with models like ELMo achieving substantial performance gains on syntactic tasks (e.g., +25.4 F1 on constituents, +13.6 on dependencies). These gains are particularly strong for core semantic roles, which are tightly linked to syntax, but much weaker for purely semantic tasks, like semantic proto-role labeling. Most syntactic information appears to be local, as models using only a narrow context (±2 tokens) retain 80–90% of performance, though pretrained encoders still capture long-range dependencies more effectively than local baselines. The study also highlights that pretraining contributes over 70% of the performance improvements, though the model architecture alone can encode some syntactic patterns. Among models, BERT-large performs best, with intermediate layers contributing meaningfully to syntactic encoding when using scalar mixing. Overall, the results emphasize that contextual encoders prioritize and excel at capturing syntactic structure, especially over short spans, with more limited and variable improvements in purely semantic tasks.

title: Bert & family eat word salad: experiments with text understanding
abstract: In this paper, we study the response of large models from the BERT family to incoherent inputs that should confuse any model that claims to understand natural language. We define simple heuristics to construct such examples. Our experiments show that state-of-the-art models consistently fail to recognize them as ill-formed, and instead produce high confidence predictions on them. As a consequence of this phenomenon, models trained on sentences with randomly permuted word order perform close to state-of-the-art models. To alleviate these issues, we show that if models are explicitly trained to recognize invalid inputs, they can be robust to such attacks without a drop in performance.
specific_phenomena: word order and the recognition of well-formed vs. ill-formed inputs, sentence coherence
fine_tuning_materials: natural language inference (using MNLI and SNLI), paraphrase detection (using MRPC and QQP), and sentiment classification (using SST-2).
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic inputs come from standard NLP benchmarks like MNLI, SNLI, MRPC, QQP, and SST-2;  controlled stimuli as incoherent inputs intentionally engineered  (destructive transformations)
Mechanistic_method: behavioral approach, destructive transformations (gradient-based and statistical)
interp_method: destructive transformations—systematic perturbations that produce incoherent, "word salad" inputs—to test language models' ability to handle syntactically meaningless data. These transformations fall into three categories: lexical overlap-based (e.g., Sort, Reverse, Shuffle), which disrupt word order while preserving the bag-of-words; gradient-based (e.g., Drop, Repeat, Replace), which modify tokens based on their importance to the model’s output; and statistical (e.g., PBSMT), which generate nonsensical sequences using phrasal co-occurrence patterns. The purpose is to strip the input of meaningful linguistic structure, so that no valid label should remain, thereby evaluating whether models can recognize and respond appropriately to ill-formed language
main_findings: reveals a critical weakness in BERT-family language models regarding their understanding of syntactic structure, showing that despite high performance on standard benchmarks, these models consistently fail to recognize incoherent or ill-formed inputs as invalid. They often assign high-confidence predictions to meaningless sequences, such as alphabetically sorted or shuffled sentences, indicating a strong insensitivity to word order and syntactic disruption. Even when key label-bearing information is destroyed, models retain original predictions with high agreement and confidence, suggesting they rely on superficial patterns or spurious correlations rather than genuine syntactic understanding. This behavior is consistent across different architectures, pretraining tasks, and model sizes, and is not mitigated by standard calibration techniques. Surprisingly, models trained on meaningless, shuffled data perform nearly as well as those trained on coherent examples, further highlighting the models’ lack of reliance on syntactic form. These findings suggest that current models do not process language in a human-like, syntax-aware manner but instead exploit statistical regularities without truly grasping sentence structure or coherence.

title: Out of Order: How Important Is The Sequential Order of Words in a Sentence in Natural Language Understanding Tasks?
abstract: Do state-of-the-art natural language understanding models care about word order - one of the most important characteristics of a sequence? Not always! We found 75% to 90% of the correct predictions of BERT-based classifiers, trained on many GLUE tasks, remain constant after input words are randomly shuffled. Despite BERT embeddings are famously contextual, the contribution of each individual word to downstream tasks is almost unchanged even after the word's context is shuffled. BERT-based models are able to exploit superficial cues (e.g. the sentiment of keywords in sentiment analysis; or the word-wise similarity between sequence-pair inputs in natural language inference) to make correct decisions when tokens are arranged in random orders. Encouraging classifiers to capture word order information improves the performance on most GLUE tasks, SQuAD 2.0 and out-of-samples. Our work suggests that many GLUE tasks are not challenging machines to understand the meaning of a sentence.
specific_phenomena: GLUE, CoLA,  word-order
fine_tuning_materials: Glue, CoLA (Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability)
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language from standard NLU benchmarks (e.g., GLUE and SQuAD 2.0) and controlled stimuli, which are systematically manipulated versions of this data (e.g., shuffled n-grams, noun swaps, and synthetic CoLA-like examples) designed to test language models’ sensitivity to word order and syntactic structure while isolating specific linguistic effects
interp_method: finetuning the pretrained RoBERTa on a synthetic, CoLA-like task first, before finetuning the model on downstream tasks.• This synthetic task involves classifying a single sentence as "real" versus "fake," where "fake" sentences are created by swapping two random words in a real sentenc
main_findings: BERT-based language models often exhibit insensitivity to word order, relying instead on superficial lexical cues rather than deep syntactic understanding, especially across most GLUE tasks—except CoLA, where performance drops sharply with shuffled inputs, highlighting its unique sensitivity to syntax; furthermore, these models heavily depend on salient words and specific self-attention heads for tasks like sentiment analysis and sequence matching, and pretraining on syntactic tasks can enhance word-order awareness, though many models still behave similarly to bag-of-words systems despite their high benchmark scores

title: UnNatural Language Inference
abstract: Recent investigations into the inner-workings of state-of-the-art large-scale pre-trained Transformer-based Natural Language Understanding (NLU) models indicate that they appear to understand human-like syntax, at least to some extent. We provide novel evidence that complicates this claim: we find that state-of-the-art Natural Language Inference (NLI) models assign the same labels to permuted examples as they do to the original, i.e. they are invariant to random word-order permutations. This behavior notably differs from that of humans; we struggle to understand the meaning of ungrammatical sentences. To measure the severity of this issue, we propose a suite of metrics and investigate which properties of particular permutations lead models to be word order invariant. For example, in MNLI dataset we find almost all (98.7%) examples contain at least one permutation which elicits the gold label. Models are even able to assign gold labels to permutations that they originally failed to predict correctly. We provide a comprehensive empirical evaluation of this phenomenon, and further show that this issue exists in pre-Transformer RNN / ConvNet based encoders, as well as across multiple languages (English and Chinese). Our code and data are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/unlu.
syntactic_phenomena: POS, word order, negation and NPIs, Agreement and feature-checking, Dependency parsing and constituency, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: Word order, Agreement attraction phenomena, NPI (Negative Polarity Item) licensing, Phrasal boundaries and n-gram perturbation, POS, partial syntactic structure reconstruction from words alone
fine_tuning_materials: fine-tune RoBERTa on MNLI
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic NLI datasets (e.g., SNLI, MNLI, ANLI, OCNLI) and controlled syntactic manipulations (e.g., full word-order permutations, clumped permutations, POS-based analysis) to examine model sensitivity to syntax, including training on permuted data and human evaluation to contrast model and human responses to ungrammatical inputs.
interp_method:
word order metrics (Permutation Acceptance)for measuring NLI model performance at a large scale; insensitivity to word order: suite of metrics designed to quantify how often models still predict correct labels for permuted, ungrammatical sentences, revealing how much they rely (or fail to rely) on syntax.
 POS minitree signatures to explore whether models reconstruct abstract local syntactic structures from permuted inputs (e.g., POS tag patterns around words). A maximum entropy fine-tuning method is introduced to reduce word-order insensitivity. This involves increasing prediction uncertainty (entropy) on randomized training examples, encouraging the model to better distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical inputs
main_findings:
conclusions on word-order invariance  (thesis) NLI models focus on words more than word order, but can partially reconstruct syntactic information from words alone;
Analyzing Syntactic Structure Associated with Tokens: they are (perhaps noisily) reconstructing the original sentence from abstract, word-anchored information about common neighbors. syntax structure hypothesis. e, state-of-the-art language models—particularly those used in Natural Language Inference (NLI)—demonstrate a profound insensitivity to word order, a core aspect of syntax. These models often assign the same labels to severely permuted, ungrammatical sentences as to their grammatical counterparts, performing more like bag-of-words systems than syntactically aware interpreters. This word-order insensitivity persists across different architectures, languages, and even when models are trained on ungrammatical data. While there is some evidence that models capture abstract local syntactic cues—like part-of-speech neighborhoods—their syntactic knowledge is patchy and non-human-like. Human evaluations further highlight this gap: unlike models, human annotators struggle with permuted inputs, underscoring that high model accuracy does not equate to genuine syntactic understanding.

title: Syntactic Structure Distillation Pretraining For Bidirectional Encoders
abstract: Textual representation learners trained on large amounts of data have achieved notable success on downstream tasks; intriguingly, they have also performed well on challenging tests of syntactic competence. Given this success, it remains an open question whether scalable learners like BERT can become fully proficient in the syntax of natural language by virtue of data scale alone, or whether they still benefit from more explicit syntactic biases. To answer this question, we introduce a knowledge distillation strategy for injecting syntactic biases into BERT pretraining, by distilling the syntactically informative predictions of a hierarchical---albeit harder to scale---syntactic language model. Since BERT models masked words in bidirectional context, we propose to distill the approximate marginal distribution over words in context from the syntactic LM. Our approach reduces relative error by 2-21% on a diverse set of structured prediction tasks, although we obtain mixed results on the GLUE benchmark. Our findings demonstrate the benefits of syntactic biases, even in representation learners that exploit large amounts of data, and contribute to a better understanding of where syntactic biases are most helpful in benchmarks of natural language understanding.
model_name_comment: Student Model: BERT-bsae-cased, Teacher Model: Recurrent Neural Network Grammars (RNNGs)
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Dependency parsing and constituency, Hierarchical structure, Argument Structure and other Constructions, POS, Binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: hierarchical syntactic structures, grammaticality judgments, syntax-sensitive and non-local dependencies, subject-verb agreement with distractors, syntactic illicitness, argument-adjunct distinctions, phrase-structure and dependency parsing, phrase-structure non-terminals, semantic role labeling, coreference resolution, and CCG supertagging
fine_tuning_materials: syntax-sensitive benchmarks—notably CoLA, which tests linguistic acceptability and syntactic competence
experimental_materials_comment: benchmarks such as PTB, OntoNotes, and CoNLL for evaluation across tasks like parsing, SRL, and coreference resolution, illustrative examples (e.g., subject-verb agreement with distractors) that reflect the goals of controlled stimuli in probing specific syntactic phenomena
interp_method: structure distillation pretraining", a knowledge distillation strategy designed to inject syntactic biases into BERT during pretraining. This approach involves transferring the syntactically informative predictions of a hierarchical RNNG teacher into a BERT student model. The process is also described as a "structure distillation procedure" and a "new pretraining strategy" that enables BERT to learn from the approximate marginal word distributions generated by the syntactic language model. Models trained using this protocol are called structure-distilled BERTs
main_findings: highlighting the importance of syntactic information in tasks that are not explicitly syntactic in nature; highlight that explicit syntactic biases significantly improve LMs' syntactic competence, even at large scales. Injecting such biases into BERT via knowledge distillation from a hierarchical RNNG model boosts performance across six structured prediction tasks, including both syntactic (e.g., parsing, supertagging) and non-syntactic ones (e.g., SRL, coreference). Gains are especially strong in low-resource settings, showing improved sample efficiency. While this approach enhances performance on syntax-sensitive benchmarks like CoLA, it yields mixed results on the broader GLUE benchmark, suggesting that not all NLU tasks rely equally on syntactic knowledge. Overall, the results show that data scale alone is insufficient, and hierarchical syntactic inductive biases are valuable for more robust and sample-efficient language understanding.

title: Local Structure Matters Most: Perturbation Study in NLU
abstract: Recent research analyzing the sensitivity of natural language understanding models to word-order perturbations has shown that neural models are surprisingly insensitive to the order of words. In this paper, we investigate this phenomenon by developing order-altering perturbations on the order of words, subwords, and characters to analyze their effect on neural models’ performance on language understanding tasks. We experiment with measuring the impact of perturbations to the local neighborhood of characters and global position of characters in the perturbed texts and observe that perturbation functions found in prior literature only affect the global ordering while the local ordering remains relatively unperturbed. We empirically show that neural models, invariant of their inductive biases, pretraining scheme, or the choice of tokenization, mostly rely on the local structure of text to build understanding and make limited use of the global structure.
model_name_comment: CharBERT-Base, BiLSTMs, ConvNet, RoBERTa-Base, BART-Base, NPT Transformer (RoBERTa-Base architecture)

experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language from unaltered GLUE Benchmark datasets and controlled stimuli created by applying systematic perturbations to them. These perturbations—Full Shuffle, Phrase Shuffle, and Neighbor Flip—target word-, subword-, or character-level structures to disrupt global and/or local syntax to varying degrees.
interp_method: perturbation functions to systematically alter the order of text at different granularities—word, subword, and character levels—in order to analyze how neural language models respond to structural changes. The three main perturbation methods are: Full Shuffle, which randomly reorders all tokens at a given granularity, severely disrupting both local and global structure; Phrase Shuffle, which shuffles chunks of adjacent tokens, preserving some local coherence depending on a parameter (ρ); and Neighbor Flip, which swaps tokens with their immediate right neighbor based on a probability, subtly disrupting local structure while leaving global structure mostly intact. These functions were applied across multiple granularities and ρ values, generating 50 different perturbed versions of the GLUE Benchmark validation sets. To quantify the impact of these perturbations, the authors introduce three metrics: chrF-2 (to measure local structure preservation via character bigram overlap), Index Displacement Count (IDC) (to assess global disruption by tracking character position shifts), and Compression Rate (to estimate tokenization changes and out-of-vocabulary effects from local scrambling). These tools form the basis of their experimental framework for evaluating how language models rely on structural information.
main_findings: demonstrate that neural language models (LMs), regardless of their architecture (e.g., Transformers, RNNs, LSTMs), pretraining strategy, or tokenization method, rely predominantly on local structure—the relative positioning of characters or subwords—to build sentence representations and perform well on Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks. Through analyses involving both natural and finely scrambled inputs at word, subword, and character levels, the research shows that as long as local structures remain intact, models can maintain high performance, even when global structure—such as word order or syntactic well-formedness—is heavily disrupted. The strongest predictor of performance is the preservation of local coherence (measured by chrF-2), not the maintenance of absolute word positions (measured by IDC). This reliance on local structure holds consistently across model types and input granularities, suggesting that much of what is needed for NLU can be extracted without deep syntactic or global structural awareness. These results challenge the assumption that models truly depend on full syntactic structure and imply that even complex LMs often operate in a way that approximates a bag-of-words model, prioritizing local information over syntactic order.

title: Infusing finetuning with semantic dependencies
abstract: For natural language processing systems, two kinds of evidence support the use of text representations from neural language models “pretrained” on large unannotated corpora: performance on application-inspired benchmarks (Peters et al., , inter alia), and the emergence of syntactic abstractions in those representations (Tenney et al., , inter alia). On the other hand, the lack of grounded supervision calls into question how well these representations can ever capture meaning (Bender and Koller, ). We apply novel probes to recent language models— specifically focusing on predicate-argument structure as operationalized by semantic dependencies (Ivanova et al., )—and find that, unlike syntax, semantics is not brought to the surface by today’s pretrained models. We then use convolutional graph encoders to explicitly incorporate semantic parses into task-specific finetuning, yielding benefits to natural language understanding (NLU) tasks in the GLUE benchmark. This approach demonstrates the potential for general-purpose (rather than task-specific) linguistic supervision, above and beyond conventional pretraining and finetuning. Several diagnostics help to localize the benefits of our approach.
specific_phenomena: constituent and dependency labeling, syntactic parsing, and linguistic acceptability
fine_tuning_materials: finetuning of models like RoBERTa and SIFT is conducted on the GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation) benchmarks
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli (e.g., HANS and GLUE diagnostic sets) to evaluate language models; GLUE's diagnostic set (Wang et al., 2018) and the HANS diagnostic data (McCoy et al., 2019) are not used for finetuning. Instead, these are "artificially curated" datasets used for evaluating and analyzing the finetuned models' performance on specific linguistic phenomena, such as predicate-argument structure, logic, lexical semantics, and identifying reliance on superficial heuristics
interp_method: nan
main_findings: main findings highlight a shift in NLP from linguistically supervised modules to large-scale unsupervised pretraining, where models like BERT and RoBERTa learn language representations from raw text. Probing studies reveal that these pretrained language models implicitly capture syntactic structures, such as constituent and dependency relations, more effectively than semantic information like predicate-argument structures. For example, models show strong performance on syntactic tasks but perform poorly on semantic tasks, with significant performance gaps between finetuned and frozen models in semantic parsing. Surprisingly, larger models like RoBERTa-large do not consistently outperform smaller ones in structural probing, suggesting that size alone doesn't ensure deeper linguistic understanding. To address the models' semantic limitations, researchers introduced SIFT (Semantics-Infused Finetuning), which explicitly integrates semantic graphs into the finetuning process. SIFT consistently improves performance on NLU tasks, outperforming both RoBERTa baselines and syntax-infused models that incorporate Universal Dependencies. Overall, while pretrained LMs surface syntax well through pretraining, semantics require explicit modeling to meaningfully enhance downstream understanding.

title: Right for the wrong reasons: diagnosing syntactic heuristics in natural language inference
abstract: A machine learning system can score well on a given test set by relying on heuristics that are effective for frequent example types but break down in more challenging cases. We study this issue within natural language inference (NLI), the task of determining whether one sentence entails another. We hypothesize that statistical NLI models may adopt three fallible syntactic heuristics: the lexical overlap heuristic, the subsequence heuristic, and the constituent heuristic. To determine whether models have adopted these heuristics, we introduce a controlled evaluation set called HANS (Heuristic Analysis for NLI Systems), which contains many examples where the heuristics fail. We find that models trained on MNLI, including BERT, a state-of-the-art model, perform very poorly on HANS, suggesting that they have indeed adopted these heuristics. We conclude that there is substantial room for improvement in NLI systems, and that the HANS dataset can motivate and measure progress in this area

main_findings: The findings show that language models like BERT often rely on shallow, fallible syntactic heuristics—such as lexical overlap, subsequence, and constituent structure—to perform well on NLI tasks like MNLI, rather than genuinely understanding syntax or inference. This was exposed by the HANS dataset, where models performed near 0% on examples that invalidated these heuristics, despite high MNLI scores. Although BERT shows some sensitivity to syntax (e.g., word order), it still fails on basic syntactic distinctions like subject-object swaps, suggesting that its training data (not its architecture) fails to teach proper syntactic generalizations. However, augmenting training data with examples that explicitly counteract these heuristics significantly improves performance, indicating that models can learn to avoid such shortcuts when properly trained. Notably, human performance on HANS, while not perfect, is more balanced and less driven by the same syntactic biases that mislead models.

title: On the Evolution of Syntactic Information Encoded by BERT's Contextualized Representations
abstract: The adaptation of pretrained language models to solve supervised tasks has become a baseline in NLP, and many recent works have focused on studying how linguistic information is encoded in the pretrained sentence representations. Among other information, it has been shown that entire syntax trees are implicitly embedded in the geometry of such models. As these models are often fine-tuned, it becomes increasingly important to understand how the encoded knowledge evolves along the fine-tuning. In this paper, we analyze the evolution of the embedded syntax trees along the fine-tuning process of BERT for six different tasks, covering all levels of the linguistic structure. Experimental results show that the encoded syntactic information is forgotten (PoS tagging), reinforced (dependency and constituency parsing) or preserved (semantics-related tasks) in different ways along the fine-tuning process depending on the task.
syntactic_phenomena: POS, Dependency parsing and constituency, Hierarchical structure, Agreement and feature-checking
specific_phenomena: syntax trees, part-of-speech tagging, constituency parsing, dependency parsing, syntactic chunks and roles, phrase-level information, surface features, syntactic features, Universal Dependencies, syntactic relations, subject-verb agreement, tree distance, and tree depth.
fine_tuning_materials: naturalistic language corpora to fine-tune BERT
experimental_materials_comment: these include UD 2.5 EN EWT for PoS tagging and dependency parsing, Penn Treebank for constituency parsing, a multilingual UD benchmark for cross-linguistic dependency parsing, PTB SD 3.3.0, OntoNotes for semantic role labeling, SQuAD for question answering, and MRPC for paraphrase identification.
interp_method: uses the structural probe of Hewitt and Manning (2019) to analyze how syntactic information is embedded in BERT, specifically in the 7th layer of BERT-base (cased). This method evaluates the extent to which BERT’s vector space encodes syntax trees through two key analyses: tree distance evaluation (measuring parse tree distances using UUAS and DSpr) and tree depth evaluation (assessing depth using Root % and NSpr). The structural probe is central to tracking how syntactic knowledge evolves during fine-tuning for different NLP tasks.
main_findings: examines how BERT’s syntactic knowledge evolves during fine-tuning across various tasks using structural probes. It finds that syntactic information in BERT is not consistently preserved, but rather can be forgotten, reinforced, or maintained depending on the task. For morpho-syntactic tasks, such as Part-of-Speech (PoS) tagging, syntactic knowledge is forgotten, likely because these tasks rely more on local context than syntactic structure. In contrast, constituency and dependency parsing tasks reinforce and preserve syntactic information, aligning with their reliance on tree structures. For semantics-related tasks like Semantic Role Labeling (SRL), Question Answering (QA), and Paraphrase Identification, syntactic knowledge is generally preserved, though with some loss in certain metrics (e.g., UUAS), suggesting that global syntactic structure remains relevant even when not explicitly required. Overall, the study challenges the view that fine-tuning conservatively maintains linguistic representations, showing instead that syntactic knowledge in language models is highly task-sensitive.

title: The Importance of Being Recurrent for Modeling Hierarchical Structure
abstract: Recent work has shown that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can implicitly capture and exploit hierarchical information when trained to solve common natural language processing tasks (Blevins et al., 2018) such as language modeling (Linzen et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) and neural machine translation (Shi et al., 2016). In contrast, the ability to model structured data with non-recurrent neural networks has received little attention despite their success in many NLP tasks (Gehring et al., 2017; Vaswani et al., 2017). In this work, we compare the two architectures—recurrent versus non-recurrent—with respect to their ability to model hierarchical structure and find that recurrency is indeed important for this purpose. The code and data used in our experiments is available at https://github.com/ketranm/fan_vs_rnn
specific_phenomena: hierarchical structure as the overarching concept. It evaluates models on syntactic dependencies through a subject–verb agreement task, testing their ability to correctly model number agreement and remain robust in the presence of agreement attractors—intervening nouns with mismatched number that can obscure the true subject
experimental_materials_comment: subject–verb agreement task, based on Linzen et al. (2016), models predicted correct number agreement, with a 10,000-word vocabulary and rarer words replaced by part-of-speech tags.
interp_method: Transformer network as their non-recurrent model for this study and explicitly refer to it as Fully Attentional Network (FAN) to emphasize its characteristic of having full access to sequence history through attention
main_findings: evaluate syntactic dependencies, comparison of LSTM and Transformer architectures, found that the former slightly outperform Transformers on English subject-verb agreement; find that recurrent architectures like LSTMs are generally better than Fully Attentional Networks (FANs, Transformer-based) at capturing hierarchical syntactic structure, particularly in controlled tasks such as subject–verb agreement and logical inference. In both language modeling and explicitly supervised settings, LSTMs were more accurate and robust to syntactic difficulty factors like long subject–verb distances and multiple agreement attractors, and they generalized better to longer, unseen sequences when data was limited. This advantage is attributed to LSTMs’ sequential compression of history into a single evolving state, which seems to strengthen structural encoding, whereas FANs’ self-attention, despite direct access to all past tokens, was less effective at detecting certain dependencies. While this suggests recurrency is important for explicit syntactic generalization, the authors note that FANs and CNNs can still match or surpass LSTMs on large-scale tasks like machine translation, where efficiency and parallelism are critical.

title: Analyzing the Structure of Attention in a Transformer Language Model
abstract: The Transformer is a fully attention-based alternative to recurrent networks that has achieved state-of-the-art results across a range of NLP tasks. In this paper, we analyze the structure of attention in a Transformer language model, the GPT-2 small pretrained model. We visualize attention for individual instances and analyze the interaction between attention and syntax over a large corpus. We find that attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model, and that attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers. We also find that the deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships. Finally, we extract exemplar sentences that reveal highly specific patterns targeted by particular attention heads.
syntactic_phenomena: POS, Dependency parsing and constituency, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: POS tags (e.g., nouns, proper nouns, determiners), syntactic dependency relations (with different types like subjects, auxiliaries, conjunctions, determiners, expletives, and negations emphasized at varying layer depths), and fine-grained patterns such as entities, passive verbs, acronyms, nicknames, paired punctuation, and positional links like commas to preceding place names or noun phrase ends to their head nouns

Mechanistic_method: Feature Visualization, Attention Analysis (Attention Pattern Analysis)
interp_method: analysis of attention structure in a Transformer language model. Their approach combines multiple components: visualizing attention at different granularities (attention-head, model, and neuron views); aggregating attention patterns over a large corpus to measure attention to Part-of-Speech tags, syntactic dependency alignment, and mean attention distance; and extracting exemplar sentences to identify specific patterns captured by individual heads. offering both quantitative metrics and qualitative pattern discovery
main_findings: analysis of GPT-2 shows that its attention mechanism encodes rich syntactic knowledge in a structured, layer-dependent way. Middle layers align most strongly with syntactic dependency relations, especially for short-range dependencies, while deeper layers focus on more specific constructs and longer-range relationships. Attention targeting varies by dependency type—subjects appear more in deeper layers, while auxiliaries, determiners, and conjunctions are emphasized earlier. Part-of-speech targeting also follows a depth pattern, with lower layers specializing in low-level tags like determiners and deeper layers in higher-level tags like proper nouns. The deepest layers capture the longest-distance relationships, though attention distance varies widely between heads, sometimes concentrating on far but semantically linked words. Qualitative analysis reveals heads tuned to specific syntactic and semantic patterns, such as named entities, passive verbs, acronyms, punctuation pairs, and noun phrase structure—behaviors shaped by GPT-2’s left-to-right language modeling objective.

title: Cross-Lingual BERT Transformation for Zero-Shot Dependency Parsing
abstract: This paper investigates the problem of learning cross-lingual representations in a contextual space. We propose Cross-Lingual BERT Transformation (CLBT), a simple and efficient approach to generate cross-lingual contextualized word embeddings based on publicly available pre-trained BERT models (Devlin et al., 2018). In this approach, a linear transformation is learned from contextual word alignments to align the contextualized embeddings independently trained in different languages. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer parsing. Experiments show that our embeddings substantially outperform the previous state-of-the-art that uses static embeddings. We further compare our approach with XLM (Lample and Conneau, 2019), a recently proposed cross-lingual language model trained with massive parallel data, and achieve highly competitive results.

These pairs were used to learn the linear transformation within the CLBT approach. Specifically, 10,000 sentence pairs were used for each target language from the Europarl corpora,  SENSEVAL2 data: This dataset was employed for analysis to investigate the properties of contextualized representations before and after the linear transformation
interp_method: Cross-Lingual BERT Transformation (CLBT), describe CLBT as a simple and efficient approach designed to generate cross-lingual contextualized word embeddings using publicly available pre-trained BERT models. It works by learning a linear transformation from contextual word alignments to project contextualized embeddings, which were independently trained in different languages, into a shared semantic space. This method is also referred to as an "off-line approach"
main_findings: Cross-Lingual BERT Transformation (CLBT) enables highly effective zero-shot cross-lingual dependency parsing by projecting contextualized BERT embeddings into a shared semantic space through a simple, word sense–preserving linear transformation. CLBT outperforms prior state-of-the-art static embedding methods by 2.91% LAS while using vastly less parallel data and computation, and it scales quickly to new languages. Its success highlights that BERT embeddings—both monolingual and multilingual—encode rich, transferable contextual information crucial for syntactic analysis, including the ability to preserve word senses across languages and capture structural relations useful for parsing. The strong performance of mBERT, even without explicit cross-lingual supervision, further suggests that these models inherently encode implicit syntactic knowledge and cross-linguistic structural commonalities, which CLBT effectively aligns for accurate multilingual syntactic transfer.

title: Neural reality of argument structure constructions
abstract: In lexicalist linguistic theories, argument structure is assumed to be predictable from the meaning of verbs. As a result, the verb is the primary determinant of the meaning of a clause. In contrast, construction grammarians propose that argument structure is encoded in constructions (or form-meaning pairs) that are distinct from verbs. Two decades of psycholinguistic research have produced substantial empirical evidence in favor of the construction view. Here we adapt several psycholinguistic studies to probe for the existence of argument structure constructions (ASCs) in Transformer-based language models (LMs). First, using a sentence sorting experiment, we find that sentences sharing the same construction are closer in embedding space than sentences sharing the same verb. Furthermore, LMs increasingly prefer grouping by construction with more input data, mirroring the behavior of non-native language learners. Second, in a “Jabberwocky” priming-based experiment, we find that LMs associate ASCs with meaning, even in semantically nonsensical sentences. Our work offers the first evidence for ASCs in LMs and highlights the potential to devise novel probing methods grounded in psycholinguistic research.

In sentence-sorting experiments, larger and more data-rich LMs increasingly grouped sentences by shared construction rather than shared verb, mirroring patterns seen in more proficient human language learners, and this preference was consistent across multiple languages. In “Jabberwocky” priming experiments, LMs associated constructions with meaning even in semantically nonsensical sentences, showing sensitivity to word order and structural templates rather than relying solely on lexical cues. These results suggest LMs can interpret sentences based on general constructional patterns (e.g., transitive, ditransitive, caused-motion, resultative), reflecting a robust understanding of how syntactic configurations encode meaning—closely aligning with the construction grammar view over purely lexicalist accounts.

title: Lexical Semantics with Large Language Models: A Case Study of English 'break'
abstract: Large neural language models (LLMs) can be powerful tools for research in lexical semantics. We illustrate this potential using the English verb 'break', which has numerous senses and appears in a wide range of syntactic frames. We show that LLMs capture known sense distinctions and can be used to identify informative new sense combinations for further analysis. More generally, we argue that LLMs are aligned with lexical semantic theories in providing high-dimensional, contextually modulated representations, but LLMs' lack of discrete features and dependence on usage-based data offer a genuinely new perspective on traditional problems in lexical semantics.

A key pattern is the causative alternation, where break appears in both transitive (“The linguist broke the window”) and intransitive (“The window broke”) forms, linking to the unaccusativity hypothesis that treats intransitive subjects as underlying objects. Some senses are strictly transitive, while intransitive uses without particles are uniformly unaccusative; however, intransitive particle constructions vary, revealing that transitivity and unaccusativity are independent features. The study also distinguishes unergative uses, alongside causative and unaccusative constructions, and finds that probe models can classify them with high accuracy. The authors also mention using t-SNE visualizations as an investigative technique, but note that these have known distortions
main_findings: show that LLMs not only capture rich lexical semantics but also encode deep syntactic knowledge, as demonstrated through the English verb break. They model known sense distinctions, reveal new sense–syntax combinations, and strongly align with usage-based lexical semantic theories that view meaning as contextually modulated by morphosyntactic environment. Probing experiments reveal near-perfect accuracy in detecting construction types (e.g., causative, unaccusative, unergative), with the strongest signals in higher layers (e.g., layer 24 of RoBERTa-large), confirming robust encoding of argument structure. t-SNE visualizations show clear clustering by both meaning and syntactic frame, reinforcing this conclusion. Importantly, many model “errors” are theoretically revealing, uncovering nuanced cases where multiple readings or construction types coexist. These results suggest that LLMs provide a powerful, high-dimensional, usage-based lens for investigating the interaction between syntax and semantics, challenging traditional discrete-feature approaches in linguistic theory

title: Investigating Gender Bias in Language Models Using Causal Mediation Analysis
abstract: Many interpretation methods for neural models in natural language processing investigate how information is encoded inside hidden representations. However, these methods can only measure whether the information exists, not whether it is actually used by the model. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. The approach enables us to analyze the mechanisms that facilitate the flow of information from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. As a case study, we apply this methodology to analyzing gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias.
