Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are concentrated in specific components of the model that may exhibit highly specialized behavior.
model_name_comment: GPT2 small, medium, large, extra-large (xl), and a distilled model
specific_phenomena: gender bias analysis—relies on Winograd-style coreference resolution tasks
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli: Professions dataset—17 sentence templates combined with 169 professions rated for definitionality and stereotypicality, yielding 2,873 examples—and Winobias/Winogender datasets, which adapt Winograd-schema-style sentences to assess gender bias in coreference resolution.
interp_method: Causal mediation analysis is a methodology for interpreting neural NLP models by tracing how information flows from inputs to outputs through internal components, or “mediators,” such as neurons or attention heads. Proposed as a general framework beyond its gender bias case study, it addresses the limitations of methods like probing classifiers by establishing causal, rather than merely correlational, links between internal representations and model predictions.
main_findings: introduces a causal mediation analysis framework for interpreting Transformer language models, allowing researchers to trace how gender cues flow through specific internal components such as neurons and attention heads. The study finds that gender bias is learned during training, amplified in larger models, and highly concentrated in a small fraction of specialized components—particularly attention heads in middle layers and neurons in early layers. These components often take on distinct roles in bias propagation, a specialization that mirrors prior findings for syntactic processing, suggesting that the same mechanisms used for handling syntactic dependencies also transmit bias. Bias effects are sparse, with a handful of heads or neurons reproducing the full impact, while gender-neutral forms like singular they are poorly represented and more diffusely encoded across layers. Overall, the results show that Transformer models store and propagate bias through concentrated, syntax-linked pathways, raising challenges for debiasing without disrupting linguistic competence

title: What if This Modified That? Syntactic Interventions via Counterfactual Embeddings
abstract: Neural language models exhibit impressive performance on a variety of tasks, but their internal reasoning may be difficult to understand. Prior art aims to uncover meaningful properties within model representations via probes, but it is unclear how faithfully such probes portray information that the models actually use. To overcome such limitations, we propose a technique, inspired by causal analysis, for generating counterfactual embeddings within models. In experiments testing our technique, we produce evidence that suggests some BERT-based models use a tree-distance-like representation of syntax in downstream prediction tasks.
specific_phenomena: structural ambiguity and tree-distance-like syntactic representations:  coordination ambiguity (clause vs. noun phrase conjunction) and NP/Z ambiguity (where a word’s grammatical category resolves clause vs. object attachment); relative clause (RC) attachment ambiguity (whether a clause modifies one or both noun phrases) and NP/VP ambiguity (prepositional phrase attachment to a verb phrase vs. a noun phrase).
experimental_materials_comment: controlled, syntactically ambiguous stimuli and naturalistic language for probe training:  Coordination Corpus (243 sentences testing clause vs. noun phrase conjunction via singular/plural verb agreement) and an NP/Z Corpus (60 sentences testing clause vs. object attachment via masked word category); an RC Corpus (192 sentences testing whether a relative clause modifies one or both noun phrases) and an NP/VP Corpus (144 sentences testing prepositional phrase attachment to a verb phrase vs. a noun phrase). For probe training and evaluation, they used 5,000 training entries and ~4,000 validation/test entries from the Penn Treebank,
interp_method: gradient-based algorithm to generate counterfactual embeddings. They also describe it as a new technique for generating counterfactual embeddings or more generally as a technique for generating counterfactual embeddings within models, inspired by causal analysis.
main_findings: used a gradient-based causal analysis with counterfactual embeddings to test whether BERT-based models actually use the syntactic information they encode. It found that the masked word prediction model (Mask BERT) actively leverages a distance-based syntactic representation—counterfactual manipulations consistent with plural or singular parses reliably shifted its predictions—while depth-based syntax had little effect. In contrast, the question-answering BERT showed no clear evidence of using syntactic knowledge, with changes in outputs driven more by embedding layer choice than by syntactic structure. The work also showed that multi-layer, non-linear distance probes outperform simpler linear probes, challenging the assumption that probe simplicity is always preferable.

title: Learning Which Features Matter: RoBERTa Acquires a Preference for Linguistic Generalizations (Eventually)
abstract: One reason pretraining on self-supervised linguistic tasks is effective is that it teaches models features that are helpful for language understanding. However, we want pretrained models to learn not only to represent linguistic features, but also to use those features preferentially during fine-turning. With this goal in mind, we introduce a new English-language diagnostic set called MSGS (the Mixed Signals Generalization Set), which consists of 20 ambiguous binary classification tasks that we use to test whether a pretrained model prefers linguistic or surface generalizations during finetuning. We pretrain RoBERTa from scratch on quantities of data ranging from 1M to 1B words and compare their performance on MSGS to the publicly available RoBERTa_BASE. We find that models can learn to represent linguistic features with little pretraining data, but require far more data to learn to prefer linguistic generalizations over surface ones. Eventually, with about 30B words of pretraining data, RoBERTa_BASE does consistently demonstrate a linguistic bias with some regularity. We conclude that while self-supervised pretraining is an effective way to learn helpful inductive biases, there is likely room to improve the rate at which models learn which features matter.
model_name: [{'string': 'robertabase pretrained by liu et al.', 'family': 'BERT', 'category': 'Enc-Only', 'size': 'base', 'model': ''}, {'string': '12 other robertas pretrained from scratch', 'family': 'BERT', 'category': 'Enc-Only', 'model': ''}]
model_name_comment: RoBERTaBASE pretrained by Liu et al. (2019b), 12 other RoBERTas pretrained from scratch
syntactic_phenomena: Argument Structure and other Constructions, Agreement and feature-checking
specific_phenomena: relative clauses, control and raising constructions, syntactic category distinctions (e.g., presence of an adjective), syntactic position (e.g., main verb in “-ing” form, often within embedded clauses), irregular past tense verbs, subject–auxiliary inversion in question formation, and agreement phenomena.
fine_tuning_materials: MSGS
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli for fine-tuning and testing: MSGS (Mixed Signals Generalization Set), a template-generated dataset that precisely manipulates grammatical and surface features while preserving well-formedness, even if sentences are semantically odd. MSGS includes 20 ambiguous binary classification tasks and 9 unambiguous control tasks, with a 2×2×2 design (linguistic feature × surface feature × domain) to test whether models prefer true linguistic generalizations over superficial cues. Training and test sets come from different in-domain and out-of-domain templates (and lexicons when relevant) to ensure that success reflects generalization rather than memorization. Targeted features span morphology, syntactic category, syntactic construction, and syntactic position, alongside five surface features such as length, lexical content, and orthography.
interp_method: poverty of the stimulus design, testing models with the Mixed Signals Generalization Set (MSGS) through three experiment types: (1) Unambiguous control experiments to check if models can represent basic linguistic and surface features; (2) Fully ambiguous experiments where training equally supports a linguistic and a surface generalization, with testing revealing which is chosen; and (3) Partially ambiguous inoculation experiments that add tiny amounts (0.1–1%) of disambiguating data to otherwise ambiguous sets to see how easily a surface bias can be shifted toward a linguistic generalization.
main_findings: while language models like RoBERTa can represent syntactic features (e.g., syntactic category, control vs. raising constructions, verb position) with relatively little pretraining, preferring these linguistic generalizations over surface correlations requires far more data. Models pretrained on under 100M words struggle even to represent certain complex syntactic features, but once pretraining exceeds ~1B words, a consistent linguistic bias emerges—reducing the amount of extra “inoculating” data needed to favor syntactic over superficial cues. RoBERTaBASE, with 30B words of pretraining, shows the strongest bias, reliably ignoring spurious correlations in favor of abstract grammatical patterns that depend on tense, inflection, parts of speech, hierarchical syntax, and constructions like control and raising. The results suggest a data threshold—between 1B and 30B words—where models shift from merely recognizing syntactic features to actively prioritizing them for generalization.

title: Investigating Novel Verb Learning in BERT: Selectional Preference Classes and Alternation-Based Syntactic Generalization
abstract: Previous studies investigating the syntactic abilities of deep learning models have not targeted the relationship between the strength of the grammatical generalization and the amount of evidence to which the model is exposed during training. We address this issue by deploying a novel word-learning paradigm to test BERT’s few-shot learning capabilities for two aspects of English verbs: alternations and classes of selectional preferences. For the former, we fine-tune BERT on a single frame in a verbal-alternation pair and ask whether the model expects the novel verb to occur in its sister frame. For the latter, we fine-tune BERT on an incomplete selectional network of verbal objects and ask whether it expects unattested but plausible verb/object pairs. We find that BERT makes robust grammatical generalizations after just one or two instances of a novel word in fine-tuning. For the verbal alternation tests, we find that the model displays behavior that is consistent with a transitivity bias: verbs seen few times are expected to take direct objects, but verbs seen with direct objects are not expected to occur intransitively.
syntactic_phenomena: Argument Structure and other Constructions, Agreement and feature-checking
specific_phenomena: verbal alternation classes (e.g., Causative/Inchoative, Dative, Spray/Load, Benefactive, Material/Product, and various reciprocal, reflexive, and prepositional alternations, spanning changes in transitivity, multi-argument transitive patterns, and oblique-subject alternations. ) and selectional preferences: assess whether BERT can generalize a verb’s semantic restrictions on its objects—such as requiring animacy, inanimacy, location, or material—based on limited, indirect evidence
fine_tuning_materials: fine-tune BERT with its masked-language modeling objective to predict each of the novel verb tokens in the training data (exp. material)
experimental_materials_comment: controlled, artificial stimuli:  novel, non-existent verbs and objects (e.g., dax, blicket) into templated sentences that strictly controlled grammatical context. During fine-tuning, all non-target open-class words were masked, forcing BERT to rely on syntactic cues like word order and function words. For selectional preference tests, training data consisted of simple transitive sentences (“The [MASK] [Verb] the [Noun]”), while alternation tests used sentence frames based on Levin’s (1993) verb classifications, with attested verbs replaced by novel tokens. Test sets were similarly crafted to compare attested, plausible, and implausible pairings or to evaluate verbs in sister vs. unrelated frames.
interp_method: two evaluation methods—Psycholinguistic Generalization Test and Embedding Classification Test—both inspired by novel word learning studies in psycholinguistics. They adapt this paradigm to neural models by fine-tuning BERT on sentences with novel verbs and objects, then testing how well it generalizes the learned grammatical patterns.
main_findings: finds that BERT can make strong syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure, showing human-like learning behavior. After seeing just one or two examples of a novel verb, BERT generalizes its grammatical patterns, including selectional preferences—predicting plausible verb–object pairings from both direct and indirect evidence—and verbal alternation classes, where it often extends a verb’s usage to related syntactic frames. The model exhibits a transitivity bias, expecting verbs to take direct objects and struggling most when generalizing from transitive to intransitive frames. Overall, BERT achieved 82% accuracy on alternation tests, with near-perfect scores in about half the cases, though performance was lower for alternations involving changes in transitivity.

title: Attention Can Reflect Syntactic Structure (If You Let It)
abstract: Since the popularization of the Transformer as a general-purpose feature encoder for NLP, many studies have attempted to decode linguistic structure from its novel multi-head attention mechanism. However, much of such work focused almost exclusively on English — a language with rigid word order and a lack of inflectional morphology. In this study, we present decoding experiments for multilingual BERT across 18 languages in order to test the generalizability of the claim that dependency syntax is reflected in attention patterns. We show that full trees can be decoded above baseline accuracy from single attention heads, and that individual relations are often tracked by the same heads across languages. Furthermore, in an attempt to address recent debates about the status of attention as an explanatory mechanism, we experiment with fine-tuning mBERT on a supervised parsing objective while freezing different series of parameters. Interestingly, in steering the objective to learn explicit linguistic structure, we find much of the same structure represented in the resulting attention patterns, with interesting differences with respect to which parameters are frozen.
specific_phenomena: specific syntactic relations from Universal Dependencies, focusing on amod (adjectival modifiers), det (determiners), nsubj (core subjects), and obj (objects), while also analyzing a broader set including advcl, advmod, aux, case, cc, conj, csubj, mark, nmod, obl, and punct, in the context of subject–verb relations and full dependency tree structures.
languages_tested_comment: 18: ar (Arabic), cs (Czech), de (German), en (English), es (Spanish), fi (Finnish), fr (French), hi (Hindi), id (Indonesian), it (Italian), ja (Japanese), ko (Korean), pl (Polish), pt (Portuguese), ru (Russian), sv (Swedish), tr (Turkish), zh (Chinese)
fine_tuning_materials: fine-tuned multilingual BERT by replacing the biaffine parser’s usual BiLSTM encoder with the full mBERT network, keeping the biaffine decoder to predict dependency arcs and labels. Training used concatenated Parallel Universal Dependencies (PUD) treebanks for all 18 languages (excluding Thai), ran for 20 epochs with Adam at a learning rate of 3×10⁻⁵, and evaluated on the largest non-PUD treebank per language.
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language data from the Parallel Universal Dependencies (PUD) treebanks—1,000 professionally translated news and Wikipedia sentences across multiple languages—and evaluated the fine-tuned parser on the largest non-PUD treebank test set for each language
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Fine-tuning, Activation Patching (Ablation), Attention Analysis
interp_method: decoding dependency trees from mBERT's attention heads, they apply the Chu-Liu-Edmonds maximum spanning tree algorithm.• For fine-tuning mBERT on a supervised parsing objective, they employ the graph-based decoding algorithm of the biaffine parser introduced by Dozat and Manning (2016)
main_findings: pretrained multilingual BERT (mBERT) already encodes some syntactic structure in single attention heads, with certain relations like adjectival modifiers and determiners being easier to decode than subjects and objects, and some languages showing higher decodability than others due to morphological and tokenization factors. Fine-tuning on an explicit parsing task greatly improved syntactic decodability (up to ~30% UUAS gains), especially in higher layers, with Value (V) parameters carrying the most faithful structural information, Dense layers aiding arc labeling, and Key/Query parameters contributing surprisingly little; however, decoding remained more challenging for languages like Japanese, Korean, Chinese, French, and Turkish. (decoding experiments for mBERT across 18 languages have been presented. The purpose of theseexperiments is testing if dependency syntax is reflected in attention patterns. In particular, the main aim is to confirm that theattention patterns of BERT-based models can capture structural features across typologically diverse languages, as observed inEnglish; )

title: Pretraining with Artificial Language: Studying Transferable Knowledge in Language Models
abstract: We investigate what kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language. We design artificial languages with structural properties that mimic natural language, pretrain encoders on the data, and see how much performance the encoder exhibits on downstream tasks in natural language. Our experimental results show that pretraining with an artificial language with a nesting dependency structure provides some knowledge transferable to natural language. A follow-up probing analysis indicates that its success in the transfer is related to the amount of encoded contextual information and what is transferred is the knowledge of position-aware context dependence of language. Our results provide insights into how neural network encoders process human languages and the source of cross-lingual transferability of recent multilingual language models.
specific_phenomena: latent dependency structures. They compare a Flat Dependency structure, where tokens are arranged randomly with crossing arcs (non-projective), to a Nesting Dependency structure, which enforces hierarchical, non-crossing arcs—found to transfer better to natural language. Their Dependency languages encode head–tail relations with distinct tokens (e.g., <4543 and 4543>), making them more naturalistic than previously studied Parenthesis languages, which use identical tokens for both ends.
fine_tuning_materials: . Fine-tuning and evaluation (L2) employed the English Penn Treebank for causal language modeling (CLM) and the English EWT dataset from UD v2.8 for dependency parsing under a masked language modeling (MLM) paradigm.
experimental_materials_comment: artificial languages were hand-crafted to probe structural knowledge transfer, using integer-based vocabularies unrelated to real words. Unstructured languages modeled token distributions: Uniform (equal probability per token), Zipf (Zipfian frequency distribution), and Log-linear (statistical cooccurrence patterns for sentence coherence). Structured languages modeled latent dependency structures, often with Zipf sampling: Flat Dependency (crossing arcs, distinct head/tail tokens), Nesting Dependency (hierarchical, non-crossing arcs, distinct head/tail tokens), Flat Parenthesis (crossing arcs, identical head/tail tokens), and Nesting Parenthesis (hierarchical nesting, identical head/tail tokens).
interp_method: Test for Inductive Bias via Language Model Transfer (TILT) framework, originally introduced by Papadimitriou and Jurafsky (2020), to evaluate knowledge transfer. In TILT, an encoder is first pretrained on a source language (L1)—in this study, hand-crafted artificial languages with specific structural properties—then transferred to a target natural language (L2) for a downstream task. During transfer, L1 embeddings are replaced with L2 vocabulary embeddings, while encoder parameters remain frozen, allowing the researchers to measure how well the structural knowledge learned in L1 generalizes to L2 processing
main_findings: neural LMs can transfer structural knowledge from artificial languages to natural language tasks, especially when the artificial languages mimic natural language properties like token distributions and dependency structures. Nesting dependency structures—closer to natural language syntax—consistently outperform flat structures in language modeling, masked language modeling, and dependency parsing, with Transformers benefiting more than LSTMs. Statistical dependencies, as in Log-linear languages, also provide a useful inductive bias by encouraging models to preserve contextual information, particularly local context crucial for predicting syntactic roles. While natural language pretraining still yields the best results, structured artificial languages enable meaningful transfer, whereas unstructured token distributions harm performance by discouraging contextual learning.

title: Limits for Learning with Language Models
abstract: With the advent of large language models (LLMs), the trend in NLP has been to train LLMs on vast amounts of data to solve diverse language understanding and generation tasks. The list of LLM successes is long and varied. Nevertheless, several recent papers provide empirical evidence that LLMs fail to capture important aspects of linguistic meaning. Focusing on universal quantification, we provide a theoretical foundation for these empirical findings by proving that LLMs cannot learn certain fundamental semantic properties including semantic entailment and consistency as they are defined in formal semantics. More generally, we show that LLMs are unable to learn concepts beyond the first level of the Borel Hierarchy, which imposes severe limits on the ability of LMs, both large and small, to capture many aspects of linguistic meaning. This means that LLMs will continue to operate without formal guarantees on tasks that require entailments and deep linguistic understanding.
model_name_comment: BERT-large, RoBERTa-large,  GPT-3.5 davinci, and ChatGPT
specific_phenomena: word order, sentence structure, needed to identify string segments consistent with universal quantification; order of arguments in a logical operator,; and negation sign pairing, where correct placement of negation with its predicate (e.g., “not blue”) is vital for accurate interpretation and logical consistency.
fine_tuning_materials: BERT-large and RoBERTa-large further fine-tuned on the CoQA conversational QA dataset
experimental_materials_comment: The controlled stimuli were hand-crafted to directly test concepts like universal quantification, word order, and argument order in logical operators. Tests for quantification used finite sequences of descriptive formulas (e.g., “a1 is blue, a2 is red…”) and varied consistent/inconsistent cases across object counts, along with challenge examples like the “hats” and “fifteen hearts” scenarios. Word order tests instructed models to produce sentences with strict positional constraints (e.g., ending in “house”), while argument order tests used logical prompts such as “If p then q. q, therefore p.”
interp_method: continuation semantics: They introduce this as a framework in Section 3 of their paper. The authors adapt notions central to truth-conditional semantics to LLMs by representing models as strings, which is enabled by continuation semantics. In this framework, the meaning of a string is defined in terms of its possible continuations—the set of longer strings that contain it. They explicitly state that they capture semantic entailments within the semantic framework of LLMs using continuation semantics.
main_findings: argues that LLMs have fundamental theoretical and empirical limitations in linguistic understanding, especially with semantic entailment and syntax. It proves that LLMs cannot master universal quantification (e.g., the meaning of “every”) or concepts beyond the first level of the Borel Hierarchy, which blocks them from fully learning many everyday expressions and from guaranteeing sound reasoning. This inability undermines tasks like entailment recognition and consistency checking, contributing to errors such as hallucinations. Syntactically, the work shows that correct reasoning with quantifiers requires precise word order, but empirical tests—including with GPT-3.5 and ChatGPT—reveal that LLMs often mishandle sentence order, argument positions in logic, and even simple constraints like ending a sentence with a specific word. These findings suggest that LLMs may learn only approximate or permuted representations of strings, making robust reasoning with order-dependent arguments extremely difficult.

title: Assessing the Generalization Capacity of Pre-trained Language Models through Japanese Adversarial Natural Language Inference
abstract: Despite the success of multilingual pre-trained language models, it remains unclear to what extent these models have human-like generalization capacity across languages. The aim of this study is to investigate the out-of-distribution generalization of pre-trained language models through Natural Language Inference (NLI) in Japanese, the typological properties of which are different from those of English. We introduce a synthetically generated Japanese NLI dataset, called the Japanese Adversarial NLI (JaNLI) dataset, which is inspired by the English HANS dataset and is designed to require understanding of Japanese linguistic phenomena and illuminate the vulnerabilities of models. Through a series of experiments to evaluate the generalization performance of both Japanese and multilingual BERT models, we demonstrate that there is much room to improve current models trained on Japanese NLI tasks. Furthermore, a comparison of human performance and model performance on the different types of garden-path sentences in the JaNLI dataset shows that structural phenomena that ease interpretation of garden-path sentences for human readers do not help models in the same way, highlighting a difference between human readers and the models.
syntactic_phenomena: Hierarchical structure, negation and NPIs, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: garden-path sentences with noun-modifying clauses (GP-double-o, GP-punctuation, GP-selectional, GP-wa, GP-scrambling, and standard garden-path cases), as well as scrambling (particle-swapping), passive, causative, factive adverbs, factive verbs, modal expressions, negation, NP-coordination, sentence-subordination (because- and if-clauses), and sentence-coordination (conjunction and disjunction)
fine_tuning_materials: fine-tuned on 2 Japanese NLI datasets: JSICK, JSNLI
experimental_materials_comment: Naturalistic/controlled: Japanese Adversarial NLI (JaNLI) dataset, inspired by HANS and designed to expose model weaknesses through synthetically generated examples targeting 11 Japanese linguistic phenomena, including multiple garden-path sentence types, scrambling, passive, causative, factive adverbs and verbs, modal expressions, negation, NP-coordination, and sentence-level subordination and coordination. Using 144 fixed templates for premise–hypothesis pairs instantiated 100 times each, JaNLI totals 14,400 examples with lexical items selected for plausibility from existing corpora. The naturalistic component consists of JSICK, a manual expert translation of the English SICK dataset with re-annotated gold labels, and JSNLI, an automatic translation of SNLI, both originally derived from Flickr image caption data. T
interp_method: Data Augmentation: To investigate whether a small amount of targeted data could improve performance on linguistically diverse phenomena, a small subset of the JaNLI dataset (700 examples) was added to the basic training datasets (JSICK or JSNLI) during the fine-tuning process for some experiments. This added subset had no overlap in (P, H) pairs with the JaNLI test set.
main_findings: finds that pre-trained Japanese and multilingual BERT models show poor out-of-distribution generalization in NLI, performing near chance on the JaNLI dataset and often failing badly on non-entailment cases, where accuracy can approach zero despite near-perfect performance on entailment cases. Unlike humans, the models gain little benefit from structural cues that ease the interpretation of garden-path sentences, and they fail to improve significantly on challenging constructions—such as passive, causative, factive adverbs, and scrambling—even when given targeted data augmentation. The results highlight persistent word order insensitivity in Japanese, a language with flexible syntax, and show that human annotators vastly outperform the models, achieving 94% accuracy across all phenomena. Overall, the work underscores a substantial gap between human and model syntactic understanding and the limitations of current LMs in resisting misleading heuristics in Japanese NLI.

title: Shaking Syntactic Trees on the Sesame Street: Multilingual Probing with Controllable Perturbations
abstract: Recent research has adopted a new experimental field centered around the concept of text perturbations which has revealed that shuffled word order has little to no impact on the downstream performance of Transformer-based language models across many NLP tasks. These findings contradict the common understanding of how the models encode hierarchical and structural information and even question if the word order is modeled with position embeddings. To this end, this paper proposes nine probing datasets organized by the type of \emph{controllable} text perturbation for three Indo-European languages with a varying degree of word order flexibility: English, Swedish and Russian. Based on the probing analysis of the M-BERT and M-BART models, we report that the syntactic sensitivity depends on the language and model pre-training objectives. We also find that the sensitivity grows across layers together with the increase of the perturbation granularity. Last but not least, we show that the models barely use the positional information to induce syntactic trees from their intermediate self-attention and contextualized representations.
syntactic_phenomena: word order, Dependency parsing and constituency
specific_phenomena: dependency relations, syntax tree depth, and top constituents
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic sentences from the CoNLL 2017 Shared Task (covering English, Swedish, and Russian, which vary in word order flexibility) with controlled syntactic perturbations: . Nine probing datasets were created using three perturbation types: NgramShift (local reordering of 2–4 word n-grams within syntactic phrases), ClauseShift (distant reordering by rotating syntactic subtrees around the root), and RandomShift (global shuffling of all words). Each dataset contains 10,000 original–perturbed sentence pairs, with perturbations crafted using language-specific heuristics to ensure syntactic control.
Mechanistic_method: parameter-free probing, representation analysis, acceptability judgments based on pseudo-perplexity
interp_method: Self-Attention Probing treats attention weights as graphs to see if attention heads capture full syntactic trees; Token Perturbed Masking measures how masking one token affects prediction of another, yielding an “impact matrix” of inter-word relationships; Token Identifiability (TI) gauges similarity in token representations between original and perturbed sentences; Self-Attention Distance (SAD) compares attention patterns across perturbations using Jensen–Shannon Divergence; and Pseudo-perplexity (PPPL), with its variants MeanLP and PenLP, estimates sentence probabilities in a masked LM, correlating with human acceptability judgments.
main_findings: show that LMs’ syntactic knowledge is limited and varies by model, language, and perturbation type. M-BERT and M-BART detect large-scale word order changes (RandomShift) better than local (NgramShift) or clause-level (ClauseShift) perturbations, with sensitivity improving in higher layers. They rely little on explicit positional embeddings for building syntactic trees, and performance differs across languages—M-BART restoring structure better in Swedish, but both struggling in Russian’s freer word order. Pre-training objectives matter: M-BART’s sentence-shuffling pre-training yields greater syntactic robustness than M-BERT’s MLM+NSP setup. Overall, while transformer LMs encode some syntactic and hierarchical information, they still have notable difficulty with long-distance dependencies.

title: Unnatural Languages Are Not Bugs but Features for LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been observed to process non-human-readable text sequences, such as jailbreak prompts, often viewed as a bug for aligned LLMs. In this work, we present a systematic investigation challenging this perception, demonstrating that unnatural languages - strings that appear incomprehensible to humans but maintain semantic meanings for LLMs - contain latent features usable by models. Notably, unnatural languages possess latent features that can be generalized across different models and tasks during inference. Furthermore, models fine-tuned on unnatural versions of instruction datasets perform on-par with those trained on natural language, achieving 49.71 win rates in Length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 in average across various base models. In addition, through comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs process unnatural languages by filtering noise and inferring contextual meaning from filtered words.
model_name_comment: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1, Vicuna-7B-v1.5, Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Gemma2-9B-Instruct, Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct, GPT-3.5-turbo, and GPT-4o
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, word order
specific_phenomena: dependency structure and word arrangement abilities
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic: QA datasets (SynContextQA, SimGSM8K), EN_EWT corpus for dependency parsing; Controlled stimuli comprised manipulated versions of natural language, primarily unnatural languages—semantically equivalent to the originals but syntactically distorted into forms unreadable to humans—created via a gradient-based stochastic sampling method to ensure models could still recover their meaning. Unnatural contexts, instructions, and GSM8K problems tested model comprehension and instruction-following with such inputs. Additional baselines included Shuf-Inj (shuffled words with random tokens), random or empty instructions, and dropping-token methods like pure_topX.X (keeping top influential tokens) and random_injection_topX.X (adding random tokens alongside top tokens) to systematically compare how models process degraded or noisy language.
interp_method: modified structural probing approach, they trained a linear head on a frozen pre-trained model (e.g., Llama-3-8B) to predict dependency syntax trees from the EN_EWT Universal Dependencies dataset, then applied it to unnatural sentences.
main_findings: found that LLMs can comprehend “unnatural languages”—text sequences meaningless to humans but semantically interpretable to the models—by leveraging them as latent features rather than treating them as noise. These features generalize across models, tasks, and datasets, enabling high accuracy recovery in QA tasks and on-par performance with natural language when fine-tuned on unnatural data. Even without alignment training, base models showed substantial success in understanding such inputs. Analysis revealed that LLMs filter out irrelevant tokens, extract key terms, and can reorganize shuffled keywords to match natural language order. Crucially, using structural probing, the authors showed that LLMs can detect and reproduce dependency structures in unnatural sentences, indicating that syntactic understanding extends beyond human-intelligible language.

title: Detecting Syntactic Change with Pre-trained Transformer Models
abstract: We investigate the ability of Transformer-based language models to find syntactic differences between the English of the early 1800s and that of the late 1900s. First, we show that a fine-tuned BERT model can distinguish between text from these two periods using syntactic information only; to show this, we employ a strategy to hide semantic information from the text. Second, we make further use of fine-tuned BERT models to identify specific instances of syntactic change and specific words for which a new part of speech was introduced. To do this, we employ an automatic part-of-speech (POS) tagger and use it to train corpora-specific taggers based only on BERT representations pretrained on different corpora. Notably, our methods of identifying specific candidates for syntactic change avoid using any automatic POS tagger on old text, where its performance may be unreliable; instead, our methods only use untagged old text together with tagged modern text. We examine samples and distributional properties of the model output to validate automatically identified cases of syntactic change. Finally, we use our techniques to confirm the historical rise of the progressive construction, a known example of syntactic change.
specific_phenomena: Changes in a word’s part of speech, Historical rise of the progressive construction
experimental_materials_comment: Naturalistic but controlled: British Hansard corpus,  controlled stimuli from naturalistic text using a semantic masking procedure: all open-class words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) were replaced with their POS tags, which were then substituted with common English words typically bearing those tags, producing grammatically plausible but semantically nonsensical sentences (e.g., “colorless green ideas” instead of “JJ JJ NNS”). Closed-class words such as auxiliaries, prepositions, and determiners were left intact to preserve syntactic scaffolding. To control for confounders, they matched sentence lengths across historical periods and created shuffled-input controls, where POS tag sequences were scrambled to remove real syntactic order.
interp_method: employed several targeted methods to detect syntactic change and assess their models. To show that BERT can distinguish 1830s from 1990s English based purely on syntax, they used a semantic-masking approach—replacing open-class words with substitutes tied to their POS tags to remove semantic cues. For pinpointing specific changes, particularly shifts in part of speech, they used two main techniques: Tagging Disagreements, which flagged cases where a 1990s-trained POS tagger agreed with ground truth but an 1830s-trained tagger disagreed; and Masking and Confusion, where a word was masked in context to see if the older model tagged the sentence correctly only when the word was hidden, indicating confusion over its modern use. The masking strategy proved more effective than tagging disagreements. They also introduced a confusion score, quantifying how much a model’s syntactic predictions improved when a given word was masked—applied at both word and sentence levels—to capture how atypical or new usages disrupted the model’s understanding.
main_findings: found that fine-tuned Transformer models, such as BERT, possess strong syntactic knowledge, enabling them to distinguish English from the early 1800s and late 1900s with over 90% accuracy even when semantic information was removed by replacing open-class words with POS-tag-associated substitutes. Performance improved when the true order of POS tags was preserved, showing reliance on genuine syntactic structure rather than simple tag counts. The models also identified specific historical syntactic changes—most notably shifts in part of speech for words like co-operative (noun → adjective) and material (adjective → noun)—using methods based on tagging disagreements and masking strategies, with the latter proving more effective. Additionally, they confirmed the historical rise of the progressive construction (be + verb-ing), with the 1830s model showing marked difficulty in handling these forms compared to the 1990s model. Overall, the results demonstrate that modern language models can detect and characterize syntactic change over time independently of semantic cues.

title: Linguistic Blind Spots of Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are the foundation of many AI applications today. However, despite their remarkable proficiency in generating coherent text, questions linger regarding their ability to perform fine-grained linguistic annotation tasks, such as detecting nouns or verbs, or identifying more complex syntactic structures like clauses in input texts. These tasks require precise syntactic and semantic understanding of input text, and when LLMs underperform on specific linguistic structures, it raises concerns about their reliability for detailed linguistic analysis and whether their (even correct) outputs truly reflect an understanding of the inputs. In this paper, we empirically study the performance of recent LLMs on fine-grained linguistic annotation tasks. Through a series of experiments, we find that recent LLMs show limited efficacy in addressing linguistic queries and often struggle with linguistically complex inputs. We show that the most capable LLM (Llama3-70b) makes notable errors in detecting linguistic structures, such as misidentifying embedded clauses, failing to recognize verb phrases, and confusing complex nominals with clauses. Our results provide insights to inform future advancements in LLM design and development.
model_name_comment: GPT-3.5 (Ouyang et al., 2022; gpt-3.5-0613), Gemini-Pro 1.0 (Team et al., 2023), Llama 3 (7B, 13B, 70B) (Touvron et al., 2023), Llama 2 (7B, 13B, 70B), and Mistral (7B, 8×7B) (Jiang et al., 2023, 2024)
specific_phenomena: dependency relations, focusing on both full dependency trees and individual grammatical relations. adjectival modifiers, determiners, core subjects (nsubj) and objects, Universal Dependencies (e.g., advcl, aux, conj, nmod, obl, punct
experimental_materials_comment: CoNLL 2000 subset of the Penn Treebank corpus
interp_method: zero-shot prompting approach, where models must identify specific linguistic structures in a question–answer format without prior examples, this approach is compared to alternatives such as chain-of-thought and structured prompting. To ensure a reliable evaluation, they design a data sampling strategy that groups samples into eight levels of increasing linguistic complexity and apply a Uniform sampling method to reduce biases typically present in traditional NLP datasets that use Random sampling. Additionally, the study measures linguistic complexity using external tools—the lexical complexity analyzer and syntactic complexity analyzer from Lu (2012)—and frames the evaluation as a set of fine-grained linguistic annotation tasks.
main_findings: shows they perform poorly on fine-grained linguistic annotation tasks that require precise syntactic understanding. Their performance is notably better for simple word-level structures (e.g., nouns or verbs) but drops dramatically for phrase- and sentence-level structures such as verb phrases, complex nominals, dependent clauses, and T-units, where models often achieve near-zero F1 scores. These failures suggest that LLMs lack compositional syntactic knowledge—the ability to combine simpler elements into more complex structures—and instead rely largely on surface-level statistical patterns. As a result, they frequently miss valid structures, produce false positives, or misidentify clauses and verb phrases, with prompt engineering offering only minimal improvement. Performance also declines as linguistic complexity increases, indicating that earlier evaluations using simpler datasets likely overestimated model capabilities. Among the models tested, Llama3-70B performed best and GPT-3.5 followed, but both remained significantly less accurate than smaller traditional NLP systems, while scaling model size produced only modest gains and did not resolve these fundamental syntactic limitations.

title: When does word order matter and when doesn't it?
abstract: Language models (LMs) may appear insensitive to word order changes in natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. In this paper, we propose that linguistic redundancy can explain this phenomenon, whereby word order and other linguistic cues such as case markers provide overlapping and thus redundant information. Our hypothesis is that models exhibit insensitivity to word order when the order provides redundant information, and the degree of insensitivity varies across tasks. We quantify how informative word order is using mutual information (MI) between unscrambled and scrambled sentences. Our results show the effect that the less informative word order is, the more consistent the model's predictions are between unscrambled and scrambled sentences. We also find that the effect varies across tasks: for some tasks, like SST-2, LMs' prediction is almost always consistent with the original one even if the Pointwise-MI (PMI) changes, while for others, like RTE, the consistency is near random when the PMI gets lower, i.e., word order is really important.
specific_phenomena: word order, case markers, grammatical agreement (e.g., subject–verb agreement), and animacy, all of which can help LMs infer syntactic roles even when order is altered. determine subjecthood/objecthood — often via grammatical agreement and animacy — emerges as a key factor enabling LMs to handle scrambled sentences in certain cases
experimental_materials_comment: both naturalistic and controlled stimuli to investigate LMs’ sensitivity to word order. For naturalistic language, a Reordering Model (RM), based on T5, was trained on 100,000 English Wikipedia sentences scrambled at the unigram level with six random seeds, yielding 600,000 training and validation pairs. RoBERTa was then evaluated on a diverse set of popular binary NLU benchmarks—SST-2, MRPC, QQP, RTE, COPA, BoolQ, and WinoGrande—covering tasks from sentiment analysis to commonsense reasoning. For controlled stimuli, the authors created context-free grammar (CFG) datasets to isolate the effect of linguistic redundancy, with two sentence types: Type A, where grammatical agreement or animacy could reveal subjecthood/objecthood, and Type B, where only word order could determine roles. Each set had 1,000 sentences scrambled six times.
interp_method: redundancy effect, the idea that LMs may not rely heavily on word order in NLU tasks when other linguistic cues (e.g., case markers, agreement, animacy) provide the same information. To measure this redundancy, they estimate how informative word order is using mutual information (MI) between unscrambled and scrambled sentences, approximated via a variational method with a Reordering Model (RM) and a pre-trained LM (T5). They then analyze the relationship between Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) — a sentence-level measure of redundancy — and the consistency of LM predictions across scrambled vs. original inputs, using a Bayesian mixed-effect logistic model.
main_findings: Linguistic redundancy helps explain why LMs sometimes appear insensitive to word order in NLU tasks — other cues such as case marking, agreement, and animacy often duplicate the information that order provides. This redundancy effect allows LMs to handle scrambled sentences well when alternative cues can replace word order. The authors quantified redundancy using Mutual Information (MI) and Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) to measure how much information order contributes, with higher PMI indicating that order is less critical. Evidence from a Reordering Model (RM) showed that for sentences with strong cues (“Type A”), original order could be restored with very high accuracy (0.948), while for sentences lacking strong cues (“Type B”), accuracy fell to near chance (0.506). RoBERTa NLU experiments revealed low order dependence for tasks like SST-2 and MRPC, where bag-of-words cues suffice, and high order dependence for RTE, BoolQ, and COPA, where performance dropped sharply with low PMI. In low-PMI cases, LMs often produced grammatical but semantically incorrect sentences, reflecting biases toward common syntactic patterns, such as turning questions into statements. Overall, LMs have syntactic and semantic knowledge enabling them to use non-order cues for understanding, but their reliance on word order varies by task and the availability of alternative cues.

title: Unnatural language processing: How do language models handle machine-generated prompts?
abstract: Language model prompt optimization research has shown that semantically and grammatically well-formed manually crafted prompts are routinely outperformed by automatically generated token sequences with no apparent meaning or syntactic structure, including sequences of vectors from a model's embedding space. We use machine-generated prompts to probe how models respond to input that is not composed of natural language expressions. We study the behavior of models of different sizes in multiple semantic tasks in response to both continuous and discrete machine-generated prompts, and compare it to the behavior in response to human-generated natural-language prompts. Even when producing a similar output, machine-generated and human prompts trigger different response patterns through the network processing pathways, including different perplexities, different attention and output entropy distributions, and different unit activation profiles. We provide preliminary insight into the nature of the units activated by different prompt types, suggesting that only natural language prompts recruit a genuinely linguistic circuit.
specific_phenomena: Function elements/words, Inflected verbs, Modifiers
experimental_materials_comment: Naturalistic language consisted of human-crafted, semantically and grammatically well-formed prompts drawn from an augmented version of the PARAREL dataset (itself built from LAMA, LPAQA, and Wikipedia patterns), further expanded and cleaned by experts for use with auto-regressive LMs—for example, "[X] belongs to the continent of [Y]". Controlled stimuli, termed “unnatural language,” were machine-generated prompts lacking meaning or syntactic structure, produced in two forms: discrete prompts (M-disc), generated via AutoPrompt as short (N=5) sequences of vocabulary tokens (e.g., "[X] Antarctica = sequelsStationrough [Y]"), and continuous prompts (M-cont), generated via Optiprompt as N=5 learned continuous vectors in embedding space with no direct vocabulary correspondence.
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Activation Analysis, Attention Analysis
interp_method: For prompt generation, they use AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) to produce discrete prompts (M-disc) via gradient-guided token search in the LM’s vocabulary, and OptiPrompt (Zhong et al., 2021) to create continuous prompts (M-cont) by optimizing vectors in the embedding space. For analysis, they measure Knowledge Neuron Activation Overlap (Geva et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022) to see which intermediate feed-forward units are engaged, and quantify Attention Distribution following Ramsauer et al. (2021) to assess how attention is spread across tokens. They also use the Local Mutual Information score (Evert, 2005) to identify vocabulary items most distinctively associated with each prompt type, and apply diagnostic classifiers—specifically L1-regularized logistic regression (Pedregosa et al., 2011)—to model activations at each layer, enabling them to distinguish activation patterns across prompt types.
main_findings: LMs process human-crafted and machine-generated prompts through fundamentally different internal pathways. Human prompts engage a “linguistic circuit” that activates units tied to syntactic features like function words, inflected verbs, and modifiers. In contrast, effective machine-generated prompts—often nonsensical, code-like, or symbol-heavy—lack syntactic structure yet can outperform natural prompts in zero-shot tasks. These prompts trigger distinct activation patterns: higher perplexity, concentrated attention on fewer tokens, low overlap in “knowledge neuron” activations with human prompts, and stronger activation in the first and last layers. Units activated by machine prompts are typically linked to coding terms, punctuation sequences, or non-linguistic characters, suggesting LMs can leverage entirely different, non-linguistic circuits to arrive at correct answers—possibly through distributed activation that incidentally steers outputs toward the right semantic fields.

title: Does Incomplete Syntax Influence Korean Language Model? Focusing on Word Order and Case Markers
abstract: Syntactic elements, such as word order and case markers, are fundamental in natural language processing. Recent studies show that syntactic information boosts language model performance and offers clues for people to understand their learning mechanisms. Unlike languages with a fixed word order such as English, Korean allows for varied word sequences, despite its canonical structure, due to case markers that indicate the functions of sentence components. This study explores whether Korean language models can accurately capture this flexibility. We note that incomplete word orders and omitted case markers frequently appear in ordinary Korean communication. To investigate this further, we introduce the Syntactically Incomplete Korean (SIKO) dataset. Through SIKO, we assessed Korean language models' flexibility with incomplete syntax and confirmed the dataset's training value. Results indicate these models reflect Korean's inherent flexibility, accurately handling incomplete inputs. Moreover, fine-tuning with SIKO enhances the ability to handle common incomplete Korean syntactic forms. The dataset's simple construction process, coupled with significant performance enhancements, solidifies its standing as an effective data augmentation technique.
specific_phenomena: word order and case markers
fine_tuning_materials: SIKO
experimental_materials_comment: both naturalistic language and controlled, syntactically incomplete stimuli. For the naturalistic language component, the researchers used well-established Korean benchmark datasets that reflect real-world usage. These included the KLUE Benchmark—specifically, KLUE-TC (45,680 news headlines, where case marker omission is common) and KLUE-NLI (23,000 standard literary-style entries)—as well as the AI-Hub Korean Dialogue Dataset (279,992 colloquial dialogues from messaging platforms, frequently featuring syntactic incompleteness). Initial analyses confirmed the prevalence of incomplete syntax, with case marker omission in 97.4% of KLUE-TC examples and non-canonical word order in 35% of AI-Hub dialogues. For the controlled stimuli, the authors created the Syntactically Incomplete Korean (SIKO) dataset by systematically introducing syntactic incompleteness into complete sentences drawn from the naturalistic benchmarks. SIKO included four key transformation methods: Case Marker Deletion (CMdel), which removed all case markers; Semantic-Preserving Shuffling (ShufSem.Presrv), which reordered words while maintaining original meaning; Semantic Non-Preserving Shuffling (ShufSem.Non.Presrv), which randomly rearranged words regardless of meaning; and Mixed Application, combining shuffling with case marker removal to maximally reduce syntactic cues. From the original corpora, 22,000 instances were sampled to produce five SIKO variants, with 20,000 used for fine-tuning and 2,000 for inference testing.
interp_method: method for generating syntactically incomplete Korean data is called SIKO (Syntactically Incomplete Korean). Within this framework, they created several variants to simulate different forms of syntactic incompleteness for fine-tuning LMs: CMdel, which removes all case markers and is noted for being cost-efficient; ShufSem.Presrv, which reorders words while preserving meaning (initially generated by ChatGPT and then human-verified); ShufSem.Non.Presrv, which randomly shuffles words without preserving meaning; and Mixed Application methods that combine shuffling with case marker deletion—specifically, ShufSem.Presrv&CMdel and ShufSem.Non.Presrv&CMdel. The authors present SIKO and its variants as an effective, low-cost approach to data augmentation for modeling Korean’s syntactic flexibility.
main_findings: Korean LMs already reflect the syntactic flexibility of Korean, handling incomplete or altered sentence structures with minimal performance loss, especially when case markers are deleted. While Natural Language Inference tasks remain sensitive to word order changes, other tasks like text classification and dialogue are largely unaffected, showing LMs’ ability to extract meaning from grammatically varied input. Fine-tuning with the Syntactically Incomplete Korean (SIKO) dataset further boosts robustness: case-marker-deletion data (CMdel) improves handling of missing markers, while word-order-shuffling data aids in processing reordered input. SIKO outperforms standard data augmentation methods and is cost-efficient, though excessive syntactic noise can reduce benefits. Larger models inherently show greater syntactic adaptability, but fine-tuning brings both large and small models to similar performance ceilings. Overall, Korean LMs prove resilient to syntactic incompleteness, and targeted fine-tuning can optimize them for real-world Korean usage.

title: Local Structure Matters Most in Most Languages
abstract: Many recent perturbation studies have found unintuitive results on what does and does not matter when performing Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks in English. Coding properties, such as the order of words, can often be removed through shuffling without impacting downstream performances. Such insight may be used to direct future research into English NLP models. As many improvements in multilingual settings consist of wholesale adaptation of English approaches, it is important to verify whether those studies replicate or not in multilingual settings. In this work, we replicate a study on the importance of local structure, and the relative unimportance of global structure, in a multilingual setting. We find that the phenomenon observed on the English language broadly translates to over 120 languages, with a few caveats.
specific_phenomena: coding properties—features of language such as word order and the presence of grammatical cues; “local” versus “global” structural reliance
fine_tuning_materials: finetuned on the English version of the dataset
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language from eight widely used cross-lingual tasks—such as PAWS-X, XNLI, QAM, QADSM, WPR, XCopa, BUCC, and Tatoeba—covering over 120 languages and sourced from benchmarks like XTREME, XGLUE, and Ponti et al. (2020); controlled stimuli through systematic perturbations designed to manipulate local and global structure. These include full shuffling (complete randomization of subword or character order), neighbor flipping (swapping adjacent subwords or characters with a controllable probability ρ to disrupt local structure), and phrase shuffling (randomly grouping and reordering phrases of a controllable average length to change absolute positions with minimal local disruption). In total, 43 perturbation settings, including unaltered text, are tested for each task and language to probe the models’ reliance on different structural properties of language.
interp_method: methodology of systematically perturbing text to compare the effects of altering local structure (e.g., character order) versus global structure (e.g., word order) on NLU task performanc
main_findings: NLU tasks across more than 120 languages, neural language models rely heavily on local structure—such as character order—while showing comparatively little dependence on global structure, like overall word order. Performance degradation is tightly correlated with the degree of local perturbation, and this holds even when controlling for vocabulary loss or using vocabulary-free models, confirming that the effect stems from local structure disruption itself. Global structure, by contrast, generally contributes less, and shuffling words often leaves task performance largely intact, suggesting that syntax in the sense of strict word order is not universally critical. Notable exceptions include the PAWS-X paraphrase task, where precise grammatical relationships are essential, and Chinese character script languages, which show greater resilience to local perturbations due to the semantic richness of individual characters. These findings imply that while English-based NLP insights about local structure generalize widely, task-specific and language-specific differences—especially for grammar-sensitive problems or character-based scripts—must be accounted for in multilingual model design.

title: A logical-based corpus for cross-lingual evaluation
abstract: At present, different deep learning models are presenting high accuracy on popular inference datasets such as SNLI, MNLI, and SciTail. However, there are different indicators that those datasets can be exploited by using some simple linguistic patterns. This fact poses difficulties to our understanding of the actual capacity of machine learning models to solve the complex task of textual inference. We propose a new set of syntactic tasks focused on contradiction detection that require specific capacities over linguistic logical forms such as: Boolean coordination, quantifiers, definite description, and counting operators. We evaluate two kinds of deep learning models that implicitly exploit language structure: recurrent models and the Transformer network BERT. We show that although BERT is clearly more efficient to generalize over most logical forms, there is space for improvement when dealing with counting operators. Since the syntactic tasks can be implemented in different languages, we show a successful case of cross-lingual transfer learning between English and Portuguese.
specific_phenomena: Simple Negation (¬, “not”), Boolean Coordination (∧, “and”), Quantification (∀ “for every” and ∃ “some”), Definite Description (ι “the” plus equality ‘=’), Comparatives (e.g., testing binary relation properties like transitivity with ‘>’), and Counting (generalized counting quantifier ∃=n, “exactly n”).
fine_tuning_materials: BERTmulti to the Portuguese version of the dataset
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli derived from a newly proposed synthetic Contradiction Detection (CD) dataset, designed explicitly to minimize reliance on world knowledge and isolate structural reasoning. The dataset is generated by first defining sentence pairs in a formal language and then realizing them in natural languages (English and Portuguese) through structurally dependent rules. This process ensures the focus remains on structural inference—the interpretation of logical connectives and invariant properties—rather than on lexical or common-knowledge cues. The dataset is organized hierarchically into tasks, each introducing a new logical or syntactic construct, including Simple Negation (¬, “not”), Boolean Coordination (∧, “and”), Quantification (∀ “for every,” ∃ “some”), Definite Description (ι, “the,” plus equality ‘=’), Comparatives (e.g., transitivity via ‘>’), and Counting (∃=n, “exactly n”). To test generalization rather than memorization, distinct realization functions are applied so that names and entities differ entirely between training and test sets, allowing for a clearer assessment of a model’s competence in handling logical forms across languages.
interp_method: Cross-Lingual Contradiction Detection (CLCD) as both a method and dataset framework for evaluating structural inference capabilities in language models. CLCD comprises a suite of small, synthetically generated datasets specifically designed to test contradiction detection in controlled syntactic settings. These datasets focus on structural inferences rather than relying on lexical or statistical shortcuts, ensuring that success requires understanding the underlying grammatical and logical relationships. The framework includes a synthetic Contradiction Detection (CD) dataset, a structure-oriented CD dataset, and carefully crafted templates to cover various syntactic patterns.
main_findings: finds that pre-trained Transformer models, particularly BERT, are highly effective at capturing syntactic regularities and logical patterns in Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks, outperforming recurrent models in structural inference. BERTeng (trained on English) was notably efficient at generalizing over most logical forms, solving tasks like simple negation, Boolean coordination, and definite description with minimal training data, and achieving near-perfect accuracy. However, it struggled with tasks involving quantifiers and especially counting operators, revealing limitations in numerical reasoning. Importantly, BERT’s strong performance was not due to memorizing superficial patterns, as it failed when premise-hypothesis structures were disrupted or labels randomized, indicating genuine structural learning. The research also demonstrated successful cross-lingual transfer, with multilingual BERT and even BERT trained on unrelated languages (e.g., Chinese) learning certain structural patterns in Portuguese, despite tokenizer noise and grammatical differences. Overall, the findings highlight BERT’s superiority in syntactic and logical inference but also point to the need for improvements in handling complex quantitative reasoning.

title: Lower Perplexity is Not Always Human-Like
abstract: In computational psycholinguistics, various language models have been evaluated against human reading behavior (e.g., eye movement) to build human-like computational models. However, most previous efforts have focused almost exclusively on English, despite the recent trend towards linguistic universal within the general community. In order to fill the gap, this paper investigates whether the established results in computational psycholinguistics can be generalized across languages. Specifically, we re-examine an established generalization —the lower perplexity a language model has, the more human-like the language model is— in Japanese with typologically different structures from English. Our experiments demonstrate that this established generalization exhibits a surprising lack of universality; namely, lower perplexity is not always human-like. Moreover, this discrepancy between English and Japanese is further explored from the perspective of (non-)uniform information density. Overall, our results suggest that a cross-lingual evaluation will be necessary to construct human-like computational models.
specific_phenomena: syntactic category—including nominal, verbal, modifier, and other types; anti-locality effect, a hallmark of hierarchical syntax in head-final languages, is examined
experimental_materials_comment: The Dundee Corpus for English, The BCCWJ-EyeTrack for Japanese, which provides gaze duration annotations for phrasal units. This corpus is explicitly described as containing data from "naturally occurring Japanese texts"
interp_method: nan
main_findings: challenges the universality of the common assumption that lower perplexity (PPL) makes language models more human-like in predicting human reading behavior. In English, this correlation holds strongly (Spearman’s ρ = –0.87), but in Japanese, the trend reverses for LMs with PPL below 400, where better next-word prediction actually reduces psychometric predictive power (ρ = 0.53). The authors attribute this discrepancy to differences in uniform information density (UID): English exhibits more uniform processing difficulty, while Japanese shows greater variability and sentence-final speed-ups in gaze duration. LM training to minimize PPL enforces uniform surprisals, aligning well with English but conflicting with Japanese’s less uniform patterns. Probing syntactic factors, they find that in Japanese, human gaze duration is most influenced by syntactic category, with human-like models reflecting this non-uniformity—until PPL drops too low, at which point it disappears. In contrast, low-PPL Japanese LMs show stronger anti-locality effects, consistent with hierarchical syntax in head-final languages. Overall, the findings stress the need for cross-lingual evaluation and caution against blindly optimizing for lower PPL, which in some languages may make models less human-like while also inflating computational costs.

title: Transformer Grammars: Augmenting Transformer Language Models with Syntactic Inductive Biases at Scale
abstract: We introduce Transformer Grammars (TGs), a novel class of Transformer language models that combine (i) the expressive power, scalability, and strong performance of Transformers and (ii) recursive syntactic compositions, which here are implemented through a special attention mask and deterministic transformation of the linearized tree. We find that TGs outperform various strong baselines on sentence-level language modeling perplexity, as well as on multiple syntax-sensitive language modeling evaluation metrics. Additionally, we find that the recursive syntactic composition bottleneck which represents each sentence as a single vector harms perplexity on document-level language modeling, providing evidence that a different kind of memory mechanism—one that is independent of composed syntactic representations—plays an important role in current successful models of long text.
specific_phenomena: 31 syntactic generalization test suites from Hu et al. (2020) eg., Licensing, which tests constraints between word pairs that are linearly distant but structurally close via c-command relationships, and Gross Syntactic State, which requires tracking whether an opening clause is subordinate (needing a main clause to follow) or a main clause (allowing the sentence to end).
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic data, the authors used the Penn Treebank (PTB), a small parsed sentence-level corpus of about 1 million words, and BLLIP-LG, a medium-scale 40-million-word dataset with parse trees from Hu et al. (2020); controlled stimuli, they employed the 31 syntactic generalization test suites from Hu et al. (2020); for ablation experiments, they created syntactically transformed parse trees—binary left-branching, binary right-branching, and reversed trees—to keep the same terminal words but alter the syntactic structure, allowing the researchers to test how crucial correct syntax is for Transformer Grammars’ performance.
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Activation Patching (Ablation), Regression Analysis
interp_method: novel class of Transformer language models that integrate recursive syntactic compositions through a special attention mask and deterministic transformation of the linearized tree
main_findings: Transformer Grammars (TGs) are a class of Transformer language models that integrate recursive syntactic composition into the Transformer architecture via a special attention mask and deterministic transformation of linearized parse trees, enabling joint modeling of syntactic phrase-structure trees and word strings. The study finds that TGs outperform syntax-free baselines like Transformer-XL (terminals) and even strong tree-aware models like TXL (trees) in sentence-level perplexity, syntactic generalization, and parse reranking, while also training faster than batched RNNGs. Their recursive syntactic compositions provide a powerful inductive bias, producing explicit constituent representations and enabling superior performance on syntax-sensitive benchmarks—even surpassing much larger non-syntactic models such as GPT-2, Gopher, and Chinchilla. However, TGs struggle with document-level language modeling due to their sentence-level vector bottleneck, and their restricted attention mechanism, while beneficial for syntax learning, reduces lexical copying ability and rare token prediction. Ablation experiments confirm that TGs depend heavily on correct syntactic structures, and probing shows that they excel at encoding hierarchical constituent information but are weaker at retaining lexical context compared to TXL (trees). Overall, TGs demonstrate that explicit recursive syntactic modeling is a valuable inductive bias for human-like syntactic competence, though it trades off some performance on long-form text.

title: Do LLMs learn a true syntactic universal?
abstract: Do large multilingual language models learn language universals? We consider a candidate universal much-discussed in the linguistics literature, the Final-over-Final Condition (Sheehan et al., 2017b). This Condition is syntactic in the sense that it can only be stated by reference to abstract sentence properties such as nested phrases and head direction. A study of typologically diverse “mixed head direction” languages confirms that the Condition holds in corpora. But in a targeted syntactic evaluation, Gemini Pro only seems to respect the Condition in German, Russian, Hungarian and Serbian. These relatively high-resource languages contrast with Basque, where Gemini Pro does not seem to have learned the Condition at all. This result suggests that modern language models may need additional sources of bias in order to become truly human-like, within a developmentally-realistic budget of training data.
specific_phenomena: Final-over-Final Condition (FOFC)—a proposed syntactic universal stating that a head-final superphrase cannot contain a head-initial subphrase,  including head direction patterns—head-initial, head-final, and mixed-headedness—and their role in headed phrase structure trees of depth two. It examines dependencies such as syntactic complements, extended projections, and frameworks like X-bar theory, as well as structural representations through Universal Dependencies (UD) and Surface UD (SUD) graphs. The authors refer to grammatical categories like auxiliaries, verbs, objects, tense, nouns, determiners, and complementizers, alongside word order configurations, distinguishing harmonic (consistent head direction) from disharmonic patterns, and noting specific orders like V<O vs. O<V or Aux<VP vs. VP<Aux. Several syntactic movement phenomena are also addressed, including topicalization, VP-fronting, verb-second movement, extraposition, and relativization, which can influence FOFC applicability
experimental_materials_comment: created controlled minimal pairs by transforming attested sentences from C4/multilingual data. This transformation involved reordering dependency sub-trees to produce disharmonic word orders while preserving sentence length, lexical items, and grammatical relations. The minimal pairs were then used to compare model-assigned log-probabilities for FOFC-respecting versus FOFC-violating sentences, providing a focused test of the models’ syntactic understanding of the FOFC.
interp_method: targeted syntactic analysis method they used to test whether LLMs obey the Final-over-Final Condition (FOFC).
main_findings: whether LLMs learn the Final-over-Final Condition (FOFC)—a proposed syntactic universal stating that a head-final superphrase cannot contain a head-initial subphrase. A large-scale corpus analysis of typologically diverse languages (Hungarian, Basque, Russian, Serbian, German) confirmed that FOFC holds in human language data, with rare apparent violations largely explained by parser errors or linguistic phenomena. When evaluated using minimal-pair syntactic tests, Gemini Pro and PaLM successfully learned FOFC patterns in high-resource languages (German, Russian, Hungarian, Serbian) but failed in Basque, assigning higher probability to FOFC-violating sentences despite the universal holding in the corpus. The authors attribute this to data scarcity—Basque had the smallest training set (153M tokens), close to a human-like developmental exposure (~100M tokens), and unlike Serbian, lacked benefits from related-language transfer. Model size increases yielded only marginal improvements, suggesting that massive data exposure, rather than architectural sophistication alone, drives FOFC learning in LLMs. The findings imply that current models require superhuman amounts of text to acquire some universals, supporting the view that additional inductive biases—such as parser-like mechanisms or curriculum learning—may be necessary for human-like syntactic competence under realistic training conditions.

title: Extracting structure from an LLM - how to improve on surprisal-based models of Human Language Processing
abstract: Prediction and reanalysis are considered two key processes that underly humans’ capacity to comprehend language in real time. Computational models capture it using Large Language Models (LLMs) and a statistical measure known as ‘surprisal’. Despite successes of LLMs, surprisal-based models face challenges when it comes to sentences requiring reanalysis due to pervasive temporary structural ambiguities, such as garden path sentences. We ask whether structural information can be extracted from LLM’s and develop a model that integrates it with their learnt statistics. When applied to a dataset of garden path sentences, the model achieved a significantly higher correlation with human reading times than surprisal. It also provided a better prediction of the garden path effect and could distinguish between sentence types with different levels of difficulty.
specific_phenomena: pervasive temporary structural ambiguities that challenge current surprisal-based models. Their primary case study involves garden path sentences: NP/S sentences, NP/Z sentences (where a verb may have no complement at all (Z for zero))
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli, specifically the Sturt et al. (1999) dataset, which was carefully designed for investigating garden path effects. This dataset includes 32 ambiguous NP/S sentences (e.g., “The traveller heard the clock had woken everybody up”) and 32 ambiguous NP/Z sentences (e.g., “Before the traveller packed the clock had woken everybody up”), each paired with an unambiguous control, for a total of 128 sentence. All sentences were divided into four equal-sized regions, and self-paced reading times were collected for each region from 24 participants
interp_method: structure-aware measure of sentence processing difficulty called Incompatibility Fraction (IF), which quantifies the mismatch between predicted and actual probability distributions while incorporating grammatical structure.
