Additionally, models with lower perplexity tended to show better syntactic performance, indicating a link between predictive certainty and syntactic knowledge. JBLiMP’s minimal-pair design allowed for these fine-grained analyses, revealing both the strengths and limitations of current language models in representing human-like syntactic knowledge.

title: Language Models Learn Rare Phenomena from Less Rare Phenomena: The Case of the Missing AANNs
abstract: Language models learn rare syntactic phenomena, but the extent to which this is attributable to generalization vs. memorization is a major open question. To that end, we iteratively trained transformer language models on systematically manipulated corpora which were human-scale in size, and then evaluated their learning of a rare grammatical phenomenon: the English Article+Adjective+Numeral+Noun (AANN) construction (“a beautiful five days”). We compared how well this construction was learned on the default corpus relative to a counterfactual corpus in which AANN sentences were removed. We found that AANNs were still learned better than systematically perturbed variants of the construction. Using additional counterfactual corpora, we suggest that this learning occurs through generalization from related constructions (e.g., “a few days”). An additional experiment showed that this learning is enhanced when there is more variability in the input. Taken together, our results provide an existence proof that LMs can learn rare grammatical phenomena by generalization from less rare phenomena. Data and code: https://github.com/kanishkamisra/aannalysis.
specific_phenomena: Article+Adjective+Numeral+Noun (AANN) construction e.g., "a beautiful five days,"
experimental_materials_comment: controlled, templatically generated AANN sentences from Mahowald (2023), totaling 12,960 items, with 3,420 having human acceptability ratings. All training-set AANN instances were excluded from testing, ensuring generalization assessment. Each acceptable AANN example was paired with corrupted variants (e.g., altered word order or missing elements), and model knowledge was measured by its preference for well-formed over corrupted versions.
interp_method: "filtered pretraining" method. This approach involves training Language Models (LMs) on systematically manipulated corpora . The authors highlight that this method is becoming fruitful for providing causal answers to questions about syntactic learning in LMs. In their study, they systematically manipulated the 100M-word BabyLM corpus, by removing and replacing elements, to explore how frequent and related phenomena during training facilitate generalization behavior in LMs.
main_findings: findings show that language models can acquire syntactic knowledge of rare constructions like the Article+Adjective+Numeral+Noun (AANN) pattern without direct exposure, generalizing from related and more frequent linguistic phenomena rather than relying solely on memorization. Even when trained with no AANN examples, models achieved well-above-chance accuracy and displayed human-like preferences for acceptable adjective types, outperforming perturbed variants of the construction. Crucially, related patterns—such as measure noun phrases with plural nouns after indefinite articles—played a key role in enabling this generalization, while removing them caused large performance drops. Variability in lexical items within construction slots also boosted productivity, and these effects were absent in shallow n-gram models, suggesting that deeper linguistic pattern learning, not just surface statistics, underlies the models’ success.

title: Injecting structural hints: Using language models to study inductive biases in language learning
abstract: Both humans and transformer language models are able to learn language without explicit structural supervision. What cognitive inductive biases make this learning possible? Here, we examine the effect of different inductive learning biases by actively controlling the inductive biases of artificial learners: we structurally bias models by pretraining on synthetic formally-structured data, and evaluate these structural biases by fine-tuning on three typologically-distant human languages: English, Japanese, and Basque. We investigate the effect on downstream language perplexity of three types of inductive bias: 1) recursive, hierarchical processing 2) unrestricted token-token dependencies that can’t be modeled by context-free grammars, and 3) a Zipfian power-law vocabulary distribution. We show that complex, non-context-free interactions between tokens form the best inductive biases. Our study leverages the capabilities of transformer models to run controlled language learning experiments that are not possible to run on humans, and surfaces hypotheses about the structures that facilitate language learning in both humans and machines.
specific_phenomena: recursive, hierarchical processing—modeled by the NEST formal language, which mirrors center-embedding structures in natural languages and can be captured by context-free grammars—and crossing token-token relationships—modeled by the CROSS formal language, which exhibits non-context-free, context-sensitive dependencies such as Swiss German cross-serial dependencies, gapping, and crossing discourse anaphora.
fine_tuning_materials: For fine-tuning,  transformer language models were trained on three typologically diverse natural languages—English (wikitext-103, 103M tokens), Japanese (Wikipedia corpus, 129M tokens), and Basque (Wikipedia corpus, 63M tokens)—to test whether inductive bias effects generalized cross-linguistically.
experimental_materials_comment: nan
interp_method: method of structural injection, causally intervene in transformer language models and manipulate their structural inductive biases, before training on natural language; testing how language learning proceeds under different conditions, influence, rather than measure, the inductive bias of transformers
main_findings: examines what inductive biases make language learning possible for both humans and large language models, using GPT-2–sized transformer LMs pretrained on synthetic, structurally organized languages before fine-tuning on typologically diverse natural languages (English, Japanese, Basque). The experiments reveal that structural inductive biases greatly enhance downstream language learning compared to unstructured data, with non-context-free crossing dependencies (CROSS) outperforming purely recursive hierarchical structures (NEST) across all languages. Even minimal inclusion of crossing dependencies into a recursive bias (1–10%) significantly boosts performance, supporting the idea that “mildly context-sensitive” biases better reflect human-like language learning conditions. Additionally, a Zipfian vocabulary distribution serves as a beneficial inductive bias, improving generalization even without token overlap between pretraining and fine-tuning, though its combination with grammatical biases yields mixed results. Overall, the findings indicate that complex token-token interactions—especially crossing dependencies—are a more powerful foundation for syntactic knowledge in LMs than recursion alone, offering insights into possible structural predispositions in human language acquisition.

title: The Effects of Corpus Choice and Morphosyntax on Multilingual Space Induction
abstract: In an effort to study the inductive biases of language models, numerous studies have attempted to use linguistically motivated tasks as a proxy of sorts, wherein performance on these tasks would imply an inductive bias towards a specific linguistic phenomenon. In this study, we attempt to analyse the inductive biases of language models with respect to natural language phenomena, in the context of building multilingual embedding spaces.We sample corpora from 2 sources in 15 languages and train language models on pseudo-bilingual variants of each corpus, created by duplicating each corpus and shifting token indices for half the resulting corpus. We evaluate the cross-lingual capabilities of these LMs, and show that while correlations with language families tend to be weak, other corpus-level characteristics, such as type-token ratio, tend to be more strongly correlated. Finally, we show that multilingual spaces can be built, albeit less effectively, even when additional destructive perturbations are applied to the training corpora, implying that (effectively) bag-of-words models also have an inductive bias that is sufficient for inducing multilingual spaces.
specific_phenomena: analyzing language model inductive biases and multilingual space induction, particularly word order, morphological information, and grammar. Word order is examined through “shuffling” perturbations that remove sequential context, revealing that models may rely more heavily on ordering cues when morphological information is stripped away via lemmatisation. Morphology is targeted through lemmatisation, which eliminates inflectional forms by reducing words to their base forms, and through the measurement of “counting complexity” (the number of distinct morphological features) using UniMorph.
languages_tested_comment: Arabic, Czech, Danish, German, English, Spanish, Finnish, French, Hebrew, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic, and controlled: Common Crawl in 15 languages (including Indo-European and non-Indo-European varieties) selected for their diversity in head-dependent entropy, each parsed into Universal Dependencies and sampled into matched training/validation sets.  . Two tokenisation schemes were used: BPE and UD-style. To create controlled stimuli, the authors generated synthetic “pseudo-bilingual” variants by duplicating each monolingual corpus and shifting vocabulary indices in one half to ensure no lexical overlap, producing structurally identical but lexically distinct “languages.” They then applied three destructive perturbations—shuffling (removing word-order context), lemmatisation (removing morphological variation), and corruption (both shuffling and lemmatising)—to isolate the contributions of syntax, morphology, and bag-of-words information in multilingual space induction.

This yields “pseudo-bilingual variants” for training. They also use Dufter & Schütze’s (2021) BERT variant as the architecture for their lower-capacity models and employ the same evaluation metrics—word translation and sentence retrieval—to assess the quality of the induced multilingual spaces.

main_findings: investigates the inductive biases of masked language models (MLMs) in constructing multilingual embedding spaces, focusing on whether a language’s grammar meaningfully impacts alignment when training on multiple languages. The authors find that MLMs remain surprisingly robust to destructive perturbations such as lemmatisation (removing morphology) and shuffling (removing word order), with many corrupted-data models still achieving over 50% retrieval/translation accuracy. This suggests that even bag-of-words-like models can induce multilingual spaces, challenging prior claims about the necessity of position embeddings. Performance correlates only weakly with language family but more strongly with corpus-level statistics such as type–token ratio, hapax legomena frequency, average token length, and morphological counting complexity, even when morphology is absent. Additionally, lexical and subword-level features—like non-initial subwords, digits, and single-letter tokens—appear to act as anchors for cross-lingual transfer. Overall, the results indicate that MLMs rely more on surface-level distributional cues than on deep syntactic or morphological structures for multilingual alignment.

title: Subword models struggle with word learning, but surprisal hides it
abstract: We study word learning in subword and character language models with the psycholinguistic lexical decision task. While subword LMs struggle to discern words and non-words with high accuracy, character LMs solve this task easily and consistently. Furthermore, when comparing word learning and syntactic learning, both processes are separable in character LM where word learning predates syntactic learning, whereas these processes are simultaneous in subword LM. This raises questions about the adequacy of subword LMs for modeling language acquisition and positions character LMs as a viable alternative.

In character LMs, word learning happens early and separately from syntax learning, producing a human-like trajectory where vocabulary knowledge develops before grammatical understanding. In contrast, subword (BPE) LMs show tightly intertwined word and syntax learning—words are recognized reliably only in plausible syntactic contexts, and gains in lexical and syntactic performance occur simultaneously. This entanglement is confirmed by high correlations between BPE lexical performance and many BLiMP syntactic phenomena. While character models excel at context-independent word recognition and maintain clear separation between lexical and syntactic development, BPE models achieve stronger overall syntactic benchmark performance, especially in smaller architectures. However, their reliance on syntactic context to identify words raises questions about their suitability as cognitive models of human language acquisition.

title: Learning Non-linguistic Skills without Sacrificing Linguistic Proficiency
abstract: The field of Math-NLP has witnessed significant growth in recent years, motivated by the desire to expand LLM performance to the leaning of non-linguistic notions (numerals, and subsequently, arithmetic reasoning). However, non-linguistic skill injection typically comes at a cost for LLMs: it leads to catastrophic forgetting of core linguistic skills, a consequence that often remains unaddressed in the literature. As Math-NLP has been able to create LLMs that can closely approximate the mathematical skills of a grade schooler or the arithmetic reasoning skills of a calculator, the practicality of these models fail if they concomitantly shed their linguistic capabilities. In this work, we take a closer look into the phenomena of catastrophic forgetting as it pertains to LLMs and subsequently offer a novel framework for non-linguistic skill injection for LLMs based on information-theoretic interventions and skill-specific losses that enable the learning of strict arithmetic reasoning. Our model outperforms the state-of-the-art both on injected non-linguistic skills and on linguistic knowledge retention, and does so with a fraction of the non-linguistic training data (1/4) and zero additional synthetic linguistic training data.

interp_method: Skill-LM: This model is designed for non-linguistic skill injection into Large Language Models (LLMs) while simultaneously preserving their linguistic proficiency.
main_findings: demonstrates that LLMs face catastrophic forgetting of linguistic skills, particularly syntactic knowledge, when trained on non-linguistic tasks like arithmetic reasoning. For example, BERT fine-tuned on arithmetic showed severe degradation on CoLA, a task measuring grammatical acceptability, while other tasks such as WNLI were less affected. This forgetting arises from parameter sharing, as certain parameters are critical for both linguistic and non-linguistic tasks. To address this, the study proposes Skill-LM, which uses a multi-task skill-injection loss alongside Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) to preserve parameters important for linguistic proficiency while learning new skills. Skill-LM achieves superior retention of linguistic abilities and strong non-linguistic performance with only a fraction of the additional training data required by prior methods like GenBERT. Overall, the findings show that LLMs can acquire quantitative reasoning without compromising existing linguistic knowledge, including syntax, by carefully balancing skill learning through multi-task training and weight regularization.

title: What BERT Is Not: Lessons from a New Suite of Psycholinguistic Diagnostics for Language Models
abstract: Pre-training by language modeling has become a popular and successful approach to NLP tasks, but we have yet to understand exactly what linguistic capacities these pre-training processes confer upon models. In this paper we introduce a suite of diagnostics drawn from human language experiments, which allow us to ask targeted questions about information used by language models for generating predictions in context. As a case study, we apply these diagnostics to the popular BERT model, finding that it can generally distinguish good from bad completions involving shared category or role reversal, albeit with less sensitivity than humans, and it robustly retrieves noun hypernyms, but it struggles with challenging inference and role-based event prediction— and, in particular, it shows clear insensitivity to the contextual impacts of negation.
specific_phenomena: Negation, sensitivity to grammaticality and cues, such as using determiners ("a" vs. "an"); but lots of Semantics: Commonsense/pragmatic inference, Semantic roles and event knowledge, Category membership semantic roles derived from sentence syntax and noun position/word order (e.g., ROLE-88)
experimental_materials_comment: controlled psycholinguistic stimul: test sets include CPRAG-102 for commonsense and pragmatic inference, ROLE-88 for semantic roles and event knowledge, and NEG-136 for category membership and negation, with each designed to reveal model insensitivities observed in human brain patterns.
interp_method: "suite of psycholinguistic diagnostics," a set of targeted tests derived from human psycholinguistic experiments. These diagnostics are carefully controlled to probe specific linguistic capabilities and are designed to evaluate language models (LMs) through their word predictions in context without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike prior LM evaluations that focus mainly on syntax, this suite extends to higher-level capacities such as commonsense and pragmatic inference, semantic roles and event knowledge, category membership, and negation. The tests are specifically chosen to reveal insensitivities in models, reflecting patterns observed in human brain responses, providing a more nuanced assessment of LMs’ linguistic understanding.
main_findings: introduces psycholinguistic diagnostics to evaluate BERT’s linguistic capacities, revealing a nuanced profile of its strengths and weaknesses. Overall, BERT can distinguish between good and bad completions, retrieve noun hypernyms, and leverage word order and grammatical cues, such as determiners, indicating strong syntactic competence. Diagnostics like ROLE-88 show that BERT can detect role reversals and use noun positions to interpret sentence structure, suggesting that failures in these tasks stem from weak event knowledge rather than syntactic misunderstanding. However, BERT struggles with complex inference, role-based event prediction, and exhibits a pronounced insensitivity to negation, often misassigning probabilities in negative statements. While its predictions are generally grammatical and structurally sound, its semantic and pragmatic reasoning abilities remain limited, highlighting that its linguistic strengths lie primarily in syntax and lexical relationships rather than deeper contextual understanding.

title: Ling-CL: Understanding NLP Models through Linguistic Curricula
abstract: We employ a characterization of linguistic complexity from psycholinguistic and language acquisition research to develop data-driven curricula to understand the underlying linguistic knowledge that models learn to address NLP tasks. The novelty of our approach is in the development of linguistic curricula derived from data, existing knowledge about linguistic complexity, and model behavior during training. Through the evaluation of several benchmark NLP datasets, our curriculum learning approaches identify sets of linguistic metrics (indices) that inform the challenges and reasoning required to address each task. Our work will inform future research in all NLP areas, allowing linguistic complexity to be considered early in the research and development process. In addition, our work prompts an examination of gold standards and fair evaluation in NLP.

experimental_materials_comment: Naturalistic datasets include SNLI, SST-2, and RTE, which involve tasks such as sentence entailment and sentiment classification and are derived from real-world text, allowing the analysis of linguistic complexity in typical language use. Controlled-stimuli datasets include CoLA (grammatical acceptability), AN-Pairs (adjective-noun usage), GED (grammatical error detection), and ANLI (adversarially constructed NLI examples designed to challenge models).
interp_method: Ling-CL, is a curriculum learning approach that leverages human-verified linguistic complexity information to evaluate the difficulty of text data for NLP models. Ling-CL constructs linguistic curricula by combining both the intrinsic complexity of the data and the model’s behavior during training, with the goal of revealing the underlying linguistic knowledge models acquire for NLP tasks. The method identifies the most influential linguistic complexity indices that contribute to learning and can apply different curriculum strategies—such as sigmoid, negative-sigmoid, and Gaussian weighting—while aggregating indices using either weighted average or max-index methods.
main_findings: how NLP models acquire and utilize linguistic knowledge by explicitly incorporating linguistic complexity into the training process through data-driven curricula. The framework identifies key linguistic indices that measure task-specific difficulty, quantifying their influence with weight factors (ρi) derived from model performance. Ling-CL improves model accuracy, especially on linguistically challenging samples, and enables more nuanced evaluation by grouping test data by linguistic complexity. Optimization methods for index aggregation and selection—focusing on a subset of critical indices like Type-Token Ratio, verb/noun ratios, and clauses per sentence—outperform simpler approaches, revealing that different indices are important for different tasks and that top indices remain stable across training. Regarding syntactic knowledge, Ling-CL uses 23 syntactic indices capturing clausal and sentential length, subordination, coordination, morphological variation, and other structural properties. Across tasks, the model’s learning dynamics highlight how syntactic complexity affects performance: for AN-Pairs, sentence length and adverbs influence adjective-noun agreement; for GED, noun variation drives syntactic consistency; and for CoLA, function words, conjunctions, and T-units underpin sentence structure and coherence. Overall, Ling-CL provides a systematic methodology for uncovering how models learn syntactic and other linguistic patterns over training.

title: Prompting Language Models for Linguistic Structure
abstract: Although pretrained language models (PLMs) can be prompted to perform a wide range of language tasks, it remains an open question how much this ability comes from generalizable linguistic understanding versus surface-level lexical patterns. To test this, we present a structured prompting approach for linguistic structured prediction tasks, allowing us to perform zero- and few-shot sequence tagging with autoregressive PLMs. We evaluate this approach on part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and sentence chunking, demonstrating strong few-shot performance in all cases. We also find that while PLMs contain significant prior knowledge of task labels due to task leakage into the pretraining corpus, structured prompting can also retrieve linguistic structure with arbitrary labels. These findings indicate that the in-context learning ability and linguistic knowledge of PLMs generalizes beyond memorization of their training data.
specific_phenomena: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, Sentence chunking is also examined, where models identify non-overlapping spans reflecting syntactic relationships, evaluated on the CONLL2000 dataset using BIO tagging. While Named Entity Recognition (NER) is included as a structured prediction task, it primarily assesses semantic rather than syntactic knowledge; however, the BIO tagging framework still probes the model’s ability to handle structural span prediction.
experimental_materials_comment: English sequence tagging tasks using naturalistic language datasets—POS tagging (English UD, GUM corpus), sentence chunking (CONLL2000), and NER (CONLL2003)—which reflect real-world text. In addition, the authors use controlled stimuli for labels by varying how classes are represented: original task labels, shuffled labels, arbitrary proxy labels, and semantically meaningful "words" labels. These manipulations test the models’ ability to extract linguistic structure beyond memorizing standard label forms,
interp_method: structured prompting: This new paradigm is proposed for iteratively prompting autoregressive Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) to probe for word- and span-level linguistic structures in sequence tagging tasks, allowing for zero- and few-shot sequence tagging without additional finetuning.
main_findings: demonstrates that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) inherently capture and utilize linguistic structure, which can be effectively probed using a method called structured prompting. This approach iteratively prompts autoregressive PLMs to recover word- and span-level linguistic structures in sequence tagging tasks such as POS tagging, NER, and sentence chunking, without additional finetuning or parameters. PLMs exhibit a strong understanding of syntactic knowledge, generalizing beyond memorization of training data, and can even handle arbitrary or descriptive labels while maintaining high accuracy, indicating internalized mappings between linguistic categories and concepts. Performance improves with larger model size and more demonstrations, and while pretraining contributes to task knowledge, it is not the sole source, as PLMs can override provided label mappings that conflict with their prior knowledge. Overall, structured prompting reveals that PLMs possess robust, generalizable linguistic capabilities that extend beyond rote learning.

title: Interpreting Language Models with Contrastive Explanations
abstract: Model interpretability methods are often used to explain NLP model decisions on tasks such as text classification, where the output space is relatively small. However, when applied to language generation, where the output space often consists of tens of thousands of tokens, these methods are unable to provide informative explanations. Language models must consider various features to predict a token, such as its part of speech, number, tense, or semantics.Existing explanation methods conflate evidence for all these features into a single explanation, which is less interpretable for human understanding.To disentangle the different decisions in language modeling, we focus on explaining language models contrastively: we look for salient input tokens that explain why the model predicted one token instead of another. We demonstrate that contrastive explanations are quantifiably better than non-contrastive explanations in verifying major grammatical phenomena, and that they significantly improve contrastive model simulatability for human observers. We also identify groups of contrastive decisions where the model uses similar evidence, and we are able to characterize what input tokens models use during various language generation decisions.
model_name_comment: GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and GPT-Neo (Black et al., 2021)
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, negation and NPIs
specific_phenomena: Anaphor Agreement, Argument Structure, Determiner-Noun Agreement,  NPI Licensing, Subject-Verb Agreement
experimental_materials_comment: used WikiText-103 to obtain “confusion scores” for word pairs in the human user study and to generate contrastive explanations for the 10 most frequent words in each major part of speech; controlled stimuli, the BLiMP dataset provided minimally different English sentence pairs targeting specific grammatical phenomena (e.g., Anaphor Agreement, Argument Structure, Determiner-Noun Agreement, NPI Licensing, Subject-Verb Agreement), with custom rules to pinpoint the tokens enforcing grammatical acceptability. Additionally, for the human simulatability study, 20 highly confusable word pairs were used—half drawn from BLiMP paradigms (e.g., actor/actress, herself/himself), and half selected from WikiText-103 based on high confusion scores (e.g., black/green, son/brother)
interp_method: Contrastive Explanations, identifies input tokens that explain why a language model chose one token (the target) over another (the foil). They extend three saliency-based methods to operate in this contrastive framework: Contrastive Gradient Norm, which measures how strongly an input token pushes the model toward the target while away from the foil; Contrastive Gradient × Input, which computes the dot product between the contrastive gradient and the token’s embedding; and Contrastive Input Erasure, which quantifies how removing a token increases the foil’s likelihood while decreasing the target’s likelihood. This method aims to produce more fine-grained, linguistically meaningful explanations of model predictions.
main_findings: shows that contrastive explanations—which highlight why a model predicts one token instead of another—offer clearer, more linguistically aligned insights into language model behavior than traditional explanations. Applied to GPT-2 and GPT-Neo, they better identify evidence relevant to syntactic phenomena, even when the cues are far from the target token, and consistently align with known grammatical rules such as anaphor agreement, subject–verb agreement, and determiner–noun agreement, as tested with the BLiMP dataset. Clustering these explanations reveals that models use distinct contextual features to make fine-grained linguistic distinctions, like contrasting singular vs. plural forms or animate vs. inanimate nouns. Analysis also uncovers the types of features models rely on for different parts of speech and how these features sometimes lead to errors. Importantly, contrastive explanations improve human simulatability, enabling people to predict model outputs more accurately and find the reasoning process more useful, thereby deepening interpretability for complex syntactic decisions.

title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train -sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of  we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With , we localize individual neurons that are highly relevant for a particular feature and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs.  In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.
specific_phenomena: part-of-speech (POS), grammatical dependencies, and morphological features of individual tokens. The POS features include categories like AUX, VERB, NOUN, ADJ, PRON, and PUNC, among others. Grammatical dependencies studied include aux:pass, nsubj, obj, amod, acl, ccomp, punct, and many more. Morphological features cover aspects such as verb forms (Inf, Part, Fin, Ger), tense (Past), person (1, 2, 3), gender (Fem, Masc, Neut), number (Plur), voice (Pass), and pronoun types (Dem, Prs, Rel, Art). Beyond token-level features, the study also examined higher-level contextual features, such as whether a sequence is Python code or French, identifying monosemantic neurons that activate specifically for these contexts. Additionally, refined analyses of neurons for features like is_passive_verb and is_verb revealed that probes can uncover both more granular and broader representations than initially assumed,

interp_method: sparse probing, which trains k-sparse linear classifiers on LLM neuron activations to predict specific input features. By adjusting the sparsity parameter k, the method identifies which neurons are most relevant, even when features are distributed across polysemantic or superposed neurons. Within this framework, the authors introduce two refinements: Optimal Sparse Probing (OSP), which finds a provably optimal k-sparse classifier but is computationally intensive for large k, and Adaptive Thresholding, which iteratively reduces k by retraining probes using only the highest-magnitude neurons from the previous step. Sparse probing is particularly effective for localizing neurons associated with specific linguistic or contextual features and for analyzing how representations are distributed across layers.
main_findings: investigates how large LMs internally represent human-interpretable features, using k-sparse linear probes across 100+ features in 7 Pythia models (70M–6.9B parameters). The main findings reveal a structured, interpretable organization of neurons: early layers often represent features in superposition, where polysemantic neurons activate for multiple unrelated n-grams, while middle layers contain seemingly monosemantic neurons encoding high-level linguistic and contextual features such as part-of-speech, morphological traits, or programming language indicators. Sparse probing effectively identifies these neurons and avoids confounding correlations. The study also highlights scaling dynamics: some features develop dedicated neurons as model size grows, others split into finer-grained features, and some remain constant. Regarding syntactic and linguistic knowledge, neurons specialized for grammatical, morphological, and contextual features were identified, with ablation experiments showing their causal role in performance and token disambiguation. Detailed analysis of precision and recall further reveals that neuron-level representations do not always align with human categorizations, emphasizing the nuanced and distributed nature of LLMs’ linguistic feature encoding. Overall, the research demonstrates that LLMs learn a diverse hierarchy of linguistic representations, from low-level superposed features to high-level monosemantic syntactic and contextual features.

title: Dissecting Contextual Word Embeddings: Architecture and Representation
abstract: Contextual word representations derived from pre-trained bidirectional language models (biLMs) have recently been shown to provide significant improvements to the state of the art for a wide range of NLP tasks. However, many questions remain as to how and why these models are so effective. In this paper, we present a detailed empirical study of how the choice of neural architecture (e.g. LSTM, CNN, or self attention) influences both end task accuracy and qualitative properties of the representations that are learned. We show there is a tradeoff between speed and accuracy, but all architectures learn high quality contextual representations that outperform word embeddings for four challenging NLP tasks. Additionally, all architectures learn representations that vary with network depth, from exclusively morphological based at the word embedding layer through local syntax based in the lower contextual layers to longer range semantics such coreference at the upper layers. Together, these results suggest that unsupervised biLMs, independent of architecture, are learning much more about the structure of language than previously appreciated.

main_findings: Research on contextual word embeddings derived from pre-trained bidirectional language models (biLMs) shows that these representations substantially advance performance across a variety of NLP tasks, typically reducing relative error by 10–25% compared to traditional embeddings like GloVe. All major architectures—LSTM, CNN, and self-attention—learn high-quality contextual vectors, though trade-offs exist between speed and accuracy, with LSTMs generally achieving the highest accuracy and Transformers or Gated CNNs offering faster computation. Deep biLMs develop a hierarchical representation of language structure: the initial word embedding layer encodes primarily morphological information, lower contextual layers capture local syntactic structure such as part-of-speech and short-range dependencies, while upper layers encode longer-range semantic information, including coreference relationships. Contextual vectors also support span-based syntactic representations, effectively clustering phrasal units by chunk type. Probing experiments reveal that POS information is captured early in the network, whereas constituency parsing benefits from higher layers, highlighting a gradient from token-level to phrasal-level syntax. When applied via ELMo-style weighted layer combinations, biLMs learn to mix contextual information optimally for downstream tasks, with middle layers providing the most transferable representations. Overall, these findings indicate that unsupervised biLMs, regardless of architecture, learn rich syntactic and semantic structures, functioning as general-purpose feature extractors for natural language.

title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.
syntactic_phenomena: negation and NPIs, Argument Structure and other Constructions

experimental_materials_comment: Controlled stimuli consisted of curated datasets of simple, unambiguous true/false statements designed with fixed templates but allowing inter-dataset variations. Structural manipulations included negation (e.g., “The city of [city] is not in [country]”) and logical conjunctions/disjunctions (e.g., “It is the case both that s1 and that s2”). Datasets included examples such as cities, neg cities, sp en trans, larger than, smaller than, and conjunction/disjunction variations. These controlled statements ensured interpretability analyses focused specifically on truth representation rather than general LLM performance. Naturalistic language came from uncurated datasets to validate whether truth representations generalize to more complex and realistic statements. Examples include companies true/false (claims about companies), common claim true/false (GPT-3-davinci-002 or human-labeled claims), counterfact true/false (factual recall statements), and a likely dataset of nonfactual text where the final token varied in predicted likelihood.
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Activation Patching, Feature Visualization (PCA)
interp_method: introduce mass-mean probing, which uses mass-mean probes as a simple, optimization-free method for identifying feature directions in model representations. The approach defines a probe vector as the difference between the mean of the false data and the mean of the true data (i.e., a difference-in-means direction). When applied to independent and identically distributed (IID) evaluation data, a correction is added to account for interference from non-orthogonal features, effectively performing linear discriminant analysis. Compared to methods like logistic regression (LR) and contrast-consistent search (CCS), mass-mean probing identifies directions that are more causally implicated in model outputs, even though classification accuracy is similar for larger models.
main_findings: LLMs develop a linear and generalizable representation of truth that emerges across layers and scales with model size. Visualizations of true/false statement embeddings reveal clear linear separation, with true statements distinguished from false ones in the top principal components. Importantly, LLMs handle structural and syntactic diversity, such as negations or logical conjunctions, by gradually forming an abstract concept of truth: early layers may represent surface correlations, while later layers encode a more robust, generalized notion of truth. Misalignments, such as orthogonal separations between original and negated statements, diminish in deeper layers, and including structurally diverse data in probe training improves generalization. The representations are localized in a small set of hidden states, often at the final token or punctuation, indicating a “summarization” of the statement’s truth. Overall, the findings suggest that LLMs encode truth in a way that generalizes across syntactic variation and becomes increasingly abstract with depth and model scale.

title: Backpack Language Models
abstract: We present Backpacks: a new neural architecture that marries strong modeling performancewith an interface for interpretability and control. Backpacks learn multiple non-contextual sense vectors for each word in a vocabulary, and represent a word in a sequence as a context-dependent, non-negative linear combination ofsense vectors in this sequence. We find that, after training, sense vectors specialize, each encoding a different aspect of a word. We can interpret a sense vector by inspecting its (non-contextual, linear) projection onto the output space, and intervene on these interpretable hooks to change the model’s behavior in predictable ways. We train a 170M-parameter Backpack language model on OpenWebText, matching the loss of a GPT-2 small (124Mparameter) Transformer. On lexical similarity evaluations, we find that Backpack sense vectors outperform even a 6B-parameter Transformer LM’s word embeddings. Finally, we present simple algorithms that intervene on sense vectors to perform controllable text generation and debiasing. For example, we can edit the sense vocabulary to tend more towards a topic, or localize a source of gender bias to a sense vector and globally suppress that sense.

interp_method: The name "Backpack" is inspired by the analogy that "a backpack is like a bag—but more orderly". This reflects its design, where a Backpack representation is a sum of non-contextual senses, but the weights in this sum depend on the ordered sequence, providing more structure than a simple bag-of-words model. Backpack Language Model (Backpack LM). This architecture is built around two key components: sense vectors, which are multiple learned, non-contextual vectors for each word that capture different aspects or potential roles of that word, and contextualization weights, which are generated by a separate network—often a Transformer—based on the full input sequence to determine how the sense vectors should be linearly combined into a context-specific representation. By separating word meaning into interpretable sense vectors and context-dependent weighting, Backpacks provide “interpretable hooks,” enabling interventions that have predictable global effects across contexts. Examples include sense-controlled generation for topic control and sense vector ablation (such as “Remove-Sense10”) for mitigating gender bias
main_findings: research on Backpack Language Models (LMs) highlights their competitive performance, interpretability, and controllability, alongside some limitations in linguistic competence. Despite having more parameters than comparable Transformers (e.g., 170M vs. 124M in GPT-2 small), Backpack LMs match GPT-2’s OpenWebText perplexity, outperform it on LAMBADA and Wikitext, but lag behind on BLiMP, suggesting weaker performance on fine-grained linguistic competence. A key innovation is their use of multiple non-contextual sense vectors per word, which specialize to encode different predictive roles—such as Sense 12 for general relatedness (“synonyms”), Sense 14 for syntactic/argument structure (verb objects, noun modifiers), Sense 3 for bigram patterns, and Sense 7 for proper noun associations. This specialization enables interpretability and direct manipulation of model behavior: topic steering via sense reweighting, gender bias mitigation by downscaling stereotype-linked senses, and knowledge editing through proper noun sense adjustments. Backpacks also achieve state-of-the-art-like performance on lexical similarity tasks, outperforming even much larger Transformer embeddings. While their ability to capture certain syntactic relations emerges through specialized senses like Sense 14, their underperformance on BLiMP marks a current gap compared to Transformers.

title: Transformer visualization via dictionary learning: contextualized embedding as a linear superposition of transformer factors
abstract: Transformer networks have revolutionized NLP representation learning since they were introduced. Though a great effort has been made to explain the representation in transformers, it is widely recognized that our understanding is not sufficient. One important reason is that there lack enough visualization tools for detailed analysis. In this paper, we propose to use dictionary learning to open up these ‘black boxes’ as linear superpositions of transformer factors. Through visualization, we demonstrate the hierarchical semantic structures captured by the transformer factors, e.g., word-level polysemy disambiguation, sentence-level pattern formation, and long-range dependency. While some of these patterns confirm the conventional prior linguistic knowledge, the rest are relatively unexpected, which may provide new insights. We hope this visualization tool can bring further knowledge and a better understanding of how transformer networks work. The code is available at: https://github.com/zeyuyun1/TransformerVis.
specific_phenomena: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, syntactic dependency, word-level polysemy disambiguation (e.g., "left" as a verb, "mind" as a noun, "park" as a noun, "light" as a noun), sentence-level pattern formation (consecutive adjectives, consecutive nouns, unit exchanges like "56 inches (140 cm)," and “city, state” structures), and long-range dependency.

Mechanistic_method: dictionary learning, Feature Visualization, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations)
interp_method: use dictionary learning to interpret transformer networks, representing contextualized embeddings as a sparse linear combination of transformer factors. This method aims to visualize the hierarchical semantic and syntactic structures captured by transformers by factorizing embeddings into elementary semantic components.
main_findings: research on transformer visualization via dictionary learning reveals that transformer factors capture hierarchical semantic and syntactic structures, showing low-level word-level polysemy disambiguation, mid-level sentence-level patterns, and high-level long-range dependencies. Syntactic knowledge is particularly evident in early layers, where factors progressively disambiguate word senses and parts-of-speech, as demonstrated with the word “left,” achieving high accuracy in POS tagging. Mid-level factors capture phrase and sentence structures, such as consecutive adjectives or enumerated nouns, while high-level factors detect long-range dependencies that have syntactic implications. These findings indicate that transformers learn low-level syntactic features in early layers and more abstract, structural patterns in later layers, and the patterns are validated through adversarial text experiments.

Grammatical categories allow humans to infer the type of new words and apply rules to novel contexts without lexical overlap. The findings show that BERT-large achieves partial success in abstracting over categories and generalizing to novel words, with all tested category pairs performing significantly above chance. The methodology involved a novel probing task inspired by infant language acquisition: BERT’s masked language model was finetuned on signal contexts that clearly indicated a word’s grammatical category, and then tested on novel contexts using [unusedn] tokens to represent new words. title: Controlled Evaluation of Grammatical Knowledge in Mandarin Chinese Language Models
abstract: Prior work has shown that structural supervision helps English language models learn generalizations about syntactic phenomena such as subject-verb agreement. However, it remains unclear if such an inductive bias would also improve language models’ ability to learn grammatical dependencies in typologically different languages. Here we investigate this question in Mandarin Chinese, which has a logographic, largely syllable-based writing system; different word order; and sparser morphology than English. We train LSTMs, Recurrent Neural Network Grammars, Transformer language models, and Transformer-parameterized generative parsing models on two Mandarin Chinese datasets of different sizes. We evaluate the models’ ability to learn different aspects of Mandarin grammar that assess syntactic and semantic relationships. We find suggestive evidence that structural supervision helps with representing syntactic state across intervening content and improves performance in low-data settings, suggesting that the benefits of hierarchical inductive biases in acquiring dependency relationships may extend beyond English.

main_findings: examines the grammatical knowledge of Mandarin Chinese language models, comparing LSTMs, RNNGs, Transformers, and PLMs trained on datasets of different sizes, with a focus on the effects of structural supervision. Overall, structural supervision improves models’ representation of syntactic state, particularly in low-data settings, helping them maintain performance across complex intervening content and achieve more human-like processing of garden-path sentences. RNNGs and PLMs were more robust to long or syntactically complex modifiers than LSTMs and vanilla Transformers, while syntactic dependencies were generally easier to learn than semantic ones. Data size influenced performance for Transformers but had less clear effects for other models, with issues like segmentation and parsing errors in the Xinhua corpus potentially limiting gains from supervision. Baseline n-gram models performed poorly, highlighting the importance of structured learning. Although the benefits of structural supervision in Mandarin were smaller than in English, the findings emphasize its value for grammatical generalization, especially in low-resource contexts and for handling complex syntactic dependencies.

title: Learning Syntax Without Planting Trees: Understanding When and Why Transformers Generalize Hierarchically
abstract: Transformers trained on natural language data have been shown to exhibit hierarchical generalization without explicitly encoding any structural bias. In this work, we investigate sources of inductive bias in transformer models and their training that could cause such preference for hierarchical generalization. We extensively experiment with transformers trained on five synthetic, controlled datasets using several training objectives and show that while objectives such as sequence-to-sequence modeling, classification, etc., often failed to lead to hierarchical generalization, language modeling objective consistently led to transformers generalizing hierarchically. We then study how different generalization behaviors emerge during the training by conducting pruning experiments that reveal joint existence of subnetworks within the model implementing different generalizations. Finally, we take a Bayesian perspective to understand transformers' preference for hierarchical generalization: We establish a correlation between whether transformers generalize hierarchically on a dataset and if the simplest explanation of that dataset is provided by a hierarchical grammar compared to regular grammars exhibiting linear generalization. Overall, our work presents new insights on the origins of hierarchical generalization in transformers and provides a theoretical framework for studying generalization in language models.

main_findings: shows that transformers can acquire and generalize hierarchical syntactic structures even without explicit architectural biases. A key finding is that the language modeling objective uniquely encourages hierarchical generalization, unlike other objectives such as sequence-to-sequence modeling or classification. Transformers trained on this objective achieved high accuracy across tasks like question formation, tense reinflection, and agreement, sometimes reaching 100%. Additionally, models trained on ambiguous data often develop multiple subnetworks that encode both hierarchical and linear rules, coexisting throughout training; this phenomenon disappears when the data is disambiguated. From a Bayesian perspective, hierarchical generalization is favored due to a “simplicity bias”: hierarchical grammars provide a simpler and better-fitting explanation of diverse datasets, leading LMs to adopt hierarchical rules when they best balance simplicity and fit, whereas low-diversity data does not produce a strong preference. Overall, hierarchical generalization emerges from a combination of the language modeling objective, data diversity, and inherent simplicity biases in transformers.

title: Feature Interactions Reveal Linguistic Structure in Language Models
abstract: We study feature interactions in the context of feature attribution methods for post-hoc interpretability. In interpretability research, getting to grips with feature interactions is increasingly recognised as an important challenge, because interacting features are key to the success of neural networks. Feature interactions allow a model to build up hierarchical representations for its input, and might provide an ideal starting point for the investigation into linguistic structure in language models. However, uncovering the exact role that these interactions play is also difficult, and a diverse range of interaction attribution methods has been proposed. In this paper, we focus on the question which of these methods most faithfully reflects the inner workings of the target models. We work out a grey box methodology, in which we train models to perfection on a formal language classification task, using PCFGs. We show that under specific configurations, some methods are indeed able to uncover the grammatical rules acquired by a model. Based on these findings we extend our evaluation to a case study on language models, providing novel insights into the linguistic structure that these models have acquired.
specific_phenomena: CoLA task, focusing on linguistic acceptability—determining whether a sentence is grammatically correct—and syntactic dependency structure, specifically evaluating how well FIDAMs align the interaction of each token with its parent in the dependency parse tree.
fine_tuning_materials: Roberta fine-tuned on the CoLA task
experimental_materials_comment: controlled formal languages and naturalistic language from the CoLA task. For the controlled stimuli, small-scale formal languages—Identity Rule, Dyck-2, and Palindrome—are used to train models (LSTMs and Transformers) to classify strings as well-formed or corrupted, ensuring they learn the underlying grammatical rules. Positive examples are generated from probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs), and negative examples are created by minimally corrupting these strings. In contrast, the naturalistic CoLA task evaluates a RoBERTa-base model fine-tuned to classify the linguistic acceptability of real sentences. The dataset is filtered to ensure alignment with syntactic dependency trees (using spaCy) and limited to sentences of 14 tokens or fewer. Feature interactions are analyzed between each token and its parent in the dependency tree, with interventional baselines derived from count-based distributions over 100,000 Google Books sentences.
interp_method: "grey box methodology" to systematically evaluate the faithfulness of Feature Interaction Detection and Attribution Methods (FIDAMs) in revealing linguistic structure within language models. Their approach begins by characterizing FIDAMs along two dimensions: how features are removed (e.g., replaced with a static baseline or sampled from a background distribution) and how the effect of this removal is quantified (e.g., output difference or Shapley values), allowing both categorization of existing methods and creation of novel variants. They focus primarily on pairwise interactions, incorporating methods such as Group Ablation, Archipelago, Shapley Interaction Index (SII), Shapley-Taylor Interaction Index (STII), Hessian, Hessian × Input, and Integrated Hessians (IH). In controlled stimuli experiments with formal languages, they generate corpora using Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs), train small LSTMs and Transformers to 100% accuracy on binary classification tasks, and extract feature interactions using the FIDAMs. The performance is quantified using Average Relative Rank (ARR), measuring how well the extracted interactions match the known grammatical dependencies, with baselines including zero-valued, fixed mapping, or sampled distributions. For natural language, they extend this methodology to RoBERTa-base fine-tuned on the CoLA task, evaluating FIDAM alignment with syntactic dependency structures by computing ARR between each token and its parent in the dependency parse tree, using spaCy for parsing and count-based distributions from the Google Books corpus for interventional baselines. Computational constraints limit sentence length to 14 tokens and filter out multi-subword tokens.
main_findings: examine how Feature Interaction Detection and Attribution Methods (FIDAMs) can uncover linguistic structure within language models. On formal language tasks using Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs), certain FIDAM and baseline combinations (e.g., Group Ablation, SII, STII) perfectly recovered grammatical dependencies, achieving maximum Average Relative Rank (ARR) scores. In a case study on RoBERTa-base fine-tuned on the CoLA linguistic acceptability task, FIDAMs showed partial alignment with syntactic dependency structures, with ARR scores above chance but never perfect. Notably, alignment decreased with longer sentences, and structural information only weakly correlated with the model’s acceptability predictions. The study identifies an Attribution Generalisation problem, where FIDAM performance on controlled formal languages does not reliably predict performance on complex natural language tasks. Despite this, the research shows that, under certain configurations, feature interactions can meaningfully reveal syntactic structures in language models, offering a more direct alternative to methods like Structural Probes, though the degree of alignment depends on task and method choice.

title: Filtered Corpus Training (FiCT) Shows that Language Models can Generalize from Indirect Evidence
abstract: This paper introduces Filtered Corpus Training, a method that trains language models (LMs) on corpora with certain linguistic constructions filtered out from the training data, and uses it to measure the ability of LMs to perform linguistic generalization on the basis of indirect evidence. We apply the method to both LSTM and Transformer LMs (of roughly comparable size), developing filtered corpora that target a wide range of linguistic phenomena. Our results show that while transformers are better qua LMs (as measured by perplexity), both models perform equally and surprisingly well on linguistic generalization measures, suggesting that they are capable of generalizing from indirect evidence.
specific_phenomena: Blimp, subject–verb agreement with intervening distractors—such as PP-modified subjects (AGR-PP-MOD), relative clauses in subject position (AGR-REL-CL), and agreement with both regular and irregular plurals (AGR-RE-IRR-SV). Negative polarity items (NPIs) were targeted in contexts like after “only” (NPI-ONLY), under sentential negation (NPI-SENT-NEG), and in certain questions (NPI-SIM-QUES). Quantifier-related phenomena included superlative quantifiers that cannot appear under negation (QUANTIFIER-SUPERLATIVE) and weak quantifiers in existential there constructions (QUANTIFIER-EXISTENTIAL-THERE). Binding Theory (Principle A) was addressed via filters on c-command relations (BINDING-C-COMMAND), case (BINDING-CASE), binding domains (BINDING-DOMAIN), and reconstruction (BINDING-RECONSTRUCTION). Determiner–noun agreement was tested in cases with and without an intervening adjective (DET-ADJ-NOUN, DET-NOUN), and passive constructions (PASSIVE) were evaluated for proper transitivity.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled syntactic tests from the Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs (BLiMP), which contains 67 benchmarks with 1,000 minimal pairs each, targeting phenomena across morphology, syntax, semantics, and the syntax–semantics interface. In each pair, one sentence is grammatical and the other ungrammatical (e.g., “A sketch of lights doesn’t appear” vs. “A sketch of lights don’t appear”), and models were evaluated using the full-sentence method—assigning higher probability to the grammatical form.
interp_method: Filtered Corpus Training (FiCT). This methodology involves training language models (LMs) on corpora where certain linguistic constructions have been filtered out from the training data.
main_findings: applying the Filtered Corpus Training (FiCT) methodology finds that both LSTM and Transformer language models can form sophisticated linguistic generalizations from indirect evidence, even when specific constructions are removed from training data, showing that their success is not purely due to memorization. While Transformers achieve lower perplexity than LSTMs, this does not translate into superior linguistic generalization, as measured by accuracy delta and probability delta—both architectures perform comparably on grammaticality judgments when generalization is required. Notably, LSTMs exhibit greater robustness in their judgments, with higher correlations in probability deltas before and after filtering, suggesting they are less affected by data removal than Transformers. Applied across a broad set of syntactic and semantic phenomena from BLiMP, the findings confirm that LMs can generalize without direct exposure, and they highlight a dissociation between traditional LM performance metrics (perplexity) and genuine syntactic generalization ability.

title: Probing for Incremental Parse States in Autoregressive Language Models
abstract: Next-word predictions from autoregressive neural language models show remarkable sensitivity to syntax. This work evaluates the extent to which this behavior arises as a result of a learned ability to maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures. We extend work in syntactic probing to the incremental setting and present several probes for extracting incomplete syntactic structure (operationalized through parse states from a stack-based parser) from autoregressive language models. We find that our probes can be used to predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes and causally intervene on model representations and steer model behavior. This suggests implicit incremental syntactic inferences underlie next-word predictions in autoregressive neural language models.
specific_phenomena: filler–gap dependency contexts
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic data, the probes were trained and evaluated on ground-truth action trajectories from the Penn Treebank (PTB), a widely used corpus of English text, with parsing performance assessed on the PTB test split. For controlled stimuli, the authors focused on NP/Z syntactic ambiguities, using shared sentence prefixes (e.g., “Even though the band left the party”) that allow multiple parses until a disambiguating continuation is observed. They expanded on a prior NP/Z dataset (Futrell et al., 2019) with continuations targeting Zero-complement, NP-complement, both, or neither parses. Additional controls involved manipulating verb transitivity in NP/Z prefixes to test ALMs’ sensitivity to syntactic cues in next-word predictions. For counterfactual analyses, specific sentences from this modified NP/Z dataset were used to generate embeddings that causally intervene on model representations, demonstrating the influence of incremental syntactic states on model behavior.
interp_method: several methods to probe syntactic representations in pretrained autoregressive language models (ALMs). Initially, they apply the structural probe from Hewitt and Manning (2019), which learns a distance function over hidden states to approximate word distances in dependency trees, successfully recovering gold tree structures. Building on this, they introduce a suite of incremental-parse probes designed to decode incremental syntactic belief states using the stack-based representations of shift-reduce parsers and the generative arc-standard dependency formalism. These include the Geometric Action Probe (GAP), which links syntactic distances and depths to action probabilities using the geometry of embeddings; the MLP Action Probe (MAP), which relaxes GAP’s assumptions with a learned multilayer perceptron while still employing an explicit stack; and the No-Stack Action Probe (NAP), which removes assumptions about both the stack and the linking function, attending over the entire prefix to predict action sequences.
main_findings: finds that autoregressive language models (ALMs) like GPT2 demonstrate strong syntactic knowledge, showing sensitivity to incremental syntactic structures in next-word predictions. GPT2 can recover correct parses even for ambiguous prefixes, dynamically updating inferred dependencies as sentences unfold. To probe this, researchers developed three incremental-parse probes: the Geometric Action Probe (GAP), MLP Action Probe (MAP), and No-Stack Action Probe (NAP). MAP, which explicitly uses a stack, outperforms GAP and captures stack-like representations, suggesting that ALMs internally maintain stack-based syntactic structures. Probes can predict model behavior in ambiguous contexts, with MAP showing strong alignment between hidden states and next-word predictions. Counterfactual analysis confirms that perturbing embeddings toward specific parses causally alters ALM predictions, demonstrating that these stack-like representations mediate behavior. Overall, ALMs learn and utilize incremental, interpretable syntactic representations that enable them to approximate global parsing performance despite being unidirectional models.

title: A Targeted Assessment of Incremental Processing in Neural Language Models and Humans
abstract: We present a targeted, scaled-up comparison of incremental processing in humans and neural language models by collecting by-word reaction time data for sixteen different syntactic test suites across a range of structural phenomena. Human reaction time data comes from a novel online experimental paradigm called the Interpolated Maze task. We compare human reaction times to by-word probabilities for four contemporary language models, with different architectures and trained on a range of data set sizes. We find that across many phenomena, both humans and language models show increased processing difficulty in ungrammatical sentence regions with human and model ‘accuracy’ scores a la Marvin and Linzen (2018) about equal. However, although language model outputs match humans in direction, we show that models systematically under-predict the difference in magnitude of incremental processing difficulty between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences. Specifically, when models encounter syntactic violations they fail to accurately predict the longer reading times observed in the human data. These results call into question whether contemporary language models are approaching human-like performance for sensitivity to syntactic violations.
