syntactic_phenomena: Ellipsis and filler-gap dependencies, Agreement and feature-checking
specific_phenomena: These included Wh-cleft structures (Cleft), three types of filler–gap dependencies—subject gap (FGD-subj), object gap (FGD-obj), and prepositional phrase gap (FGD-pp)—and the main verb/reduced relative clause gardenpath construction (MVRR). They also examined four NPI licensing contexts involving any and ever in both subject relative clause modifiers (NPL-any-src, NPL-ever-src) and object relative clause modifiers (NPL-any-orc, NPL-ever-orc). Subject–verb number agreement was tested in three modifier contexts—subject relative clause (SVNA-src), object relative clause (SVNA-orc), and prepositional phrase (SVNA-pp). Finally, reflexive anaphora was probed for masculine and feminine pronouns in both subject (RNA-m-src, RNA-f-src) and object relative clause modifiers (RNA-m-orc, RNA-f-orc).
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli, 16 syntactic test suites adapted from Hu et al. (2020), each targeting a specific structural phenomenon in English. Each suite was designed to probe a specific syntactic phenomenon—such as cleft structures, filler-gap dependencies, main verb/reduced relative clause gardenpaths, NPI licensing, subject–verb number agreement, and reflexive anaphora—using 20–25 carefully constructed items. Every item appeared in four conditions (two grammatical and two ungrammatical), with sentence regions deliberately manipulated to create these contrasts and “critical regions” marked to indicate where the syntactic manipulation occurred.
interp_method: collected human reaction time data using the Interpolated Maze task (I-Maze), a novel online adaptation of the traditional Maze task that blends elements from the Grammatical-Maze (G-Maze) and Lexical-Maze (L-Maze) variants. In the I-Maze, participants make word-by-word choices to progress through a sentence, but in critical regions where one condition might be ungrammatical, L-Maze distractors—non-English nonce words—are used. This ensures that participants must choose real English words over nonce words, making the correct choice unambiguous while allowing the task to capture reaction time differences in both grammatical and ungrammatical contexts.
main_findings: compared humans and neural language models (LMs) in incremental syntactic processing, revealing qualitative alignment but quantitative mismatch. Both humans and LMs found ungrammatical sentence regions more difficult, with similar accuracy scores and strong correlations between model and human preferences across syntactic test suites. However, LMs systematically under-predicted the magnitude of difficulty humans experienced, especially in critical regions with syntactic violations, showing an average reaction time gap of 95–126 ms and larger residual errors for ungrammatical conditions. This reduced sensitivity challenges single-stage processing theories, as word surprisal alone could not fully explain human slowdowns; models would require surprisal values in ungrammatical contexts to be about ten times larger to match human behavior. Among the four tested models—JRNN, GRNN, GPT-2, and RNNG—GPT-2 and RNNG most closely matched human-like patterns despite RNNG’s smaller training corpus. Human data came from a new Interpolated Maze task, and model evaluation covered sixteen syntactic phenomena, including cleft structures, filler-gap dependencies, garden-path sentences, NPI licensing, subject–verb agreement, and reflexive anaphora.

title: CausalGym: Benchmarking causal interpretability methods on linguistic tasks
abstract: Language models (LMs) have proven to be powerful tools for psycholinguistic research, but most prior work has focused on purely behavioural measures (e.g., surprisal comparisons). At the same time, research in model interpretability has begun to illuminate the abstract causal mechanisms shaping LM behavior. To help bring these strands of research closer together, we introduce CausalGym. We adapt and expand the SyntaxGym suite of tasks to benchmark the ability of interpretability methods to causally affect model behaviour. To illustrate how CausalGym can be used, we study the pythia models (14M--6.9B) and assess the causal efficacy of a wide range of interpretability methods, including linear probing and distributed alignment search (DAS). We find that DAS outperforms the other methods, and so we use it to study the learning trajectory of two difficult linguistic phenomena in pythia-1b: negative polarity item licensing and filler--gap dependencies. Our analysis shows that the mechanism implementing both of these tasks is learned in discrete stages, not gradually.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, Hierarchical structure, Ellipsis and filler-gap dependencies, Binding and Coreference, Negation and NPIs
specific_phenomena: Agreement category, tasks test subject-verb and reflexive number agreement across subject-relative clauses, object-relative clauses, and prepositional phrases, including the novel agr_gender task. The Licensing category focuses on Negative Polarity Item (NPI) licensing, examining whether "any" or "ever" is correctly licensed by negated subjects or objects in relative clauses. Garden path effects test syntactic ambiguities, including Main Verb/Reduced Relative ambiguities and Noun Phrase/Z-clause ambiguities with or without modifiers, for both object and transitive verb contexts. The Gross Syntactic State category evaluates subordination processing, with variations across subject-relative clauses, object-relative clauses, and prepositional phrases. Finally, Long-Distance Dependencies assess filler-gap constructions and cleft sentences, including multiple levels of embedding, hierarchy tests, and extraction from objects, subjects, or prepositional phrases.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled to isolate specific linguistic phenomena. They are adapted and expanded from SyntaxGym, which uses templated, targeted syntactic evaluation benchmarks. Central to CausalGym are minimal pairs—sentences that differ along only a single linguistic feature, such as number agreement or filler-gap dependencies, while keeping other features constant. To generate sufficient examples for training supervised interpretability methods, the authors employ templatic generation, using aligned slots that can be combinatorially mixed to produce many minimal pairs. The materials focus exclusively on grammatical sentences, with any ambiguously grammatical examples manually removed, ensuring the benchmark tests how models implement mechanisms for converting feature alternations
interp_method: describe several methods for identifying features and modifying activations to causally influence model behavior, categorized as supervised or unsupervised. Supervised methods include Distributed Alignment Search (DAS), which optimizes an intervention direction across multiple neurons to maximize the output probability of a counterfactual label and is the only method with a causal training objective; Linear Probing, where a classifier predicts a distribution over classes from neural representations; Difference-in-means, which calculates differences in per-class mean activations to control or erase linear features; and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), which assumes Gaussian-distributed classes with shared covariance. Unsupervised methods include Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which intervenes along the first principal component to capture maximal variance, and K-means clustering, where the feature direction is defined by the difference between centroids of two clusters. Random vectors serve as an unsupervised baseline. Additionally, the Vanilla Interchange Intervention, though not a feature-finding method, is included as a non-learned baseline, fully replacing the activation of a component in the base input with that from a source input.
main_findings: the CausalGym study introduces a benchmark to evaluate how well interpretability methods can causally influence LM behavior on linguistic tasks, with a particular focus on syntactic knowledge. It benchmarks supervised methods such as Distributed Alignment Search (DAS), linear probing, and difference-in-means, finding that DAS consistently identifies the most causally-efficacious features, though its apparent advantage may partly stem from access to model outputs during training. Unsupervised methods like PCA and k-means performed substantially worse, and LDA barely exceeded random baselines. Using tasks adapted from SyntaxGym, the study examined specific syntactic phenomena, including Negative Polarity Item (NPI) licensing and filler-gap dependencies, revealing that the underlying causal mechanisms emerge in discrete stages rather than gradually. These mechanisms involve multi-step information movement across layers, such as negation features moving through intermediate tokens for NPI prediction or filler information propagating for wh-extraction. The findings suggest that LMs do not learn syntactic mechanisms uniformly but instead build them progressively through distinct stages. CausalGym emphasizes understanding internal causal mechanisms, moving beyond input-output behavior, and provides a framework for psycholinguistic insights into how models encode complex syntactic knowledge, although the results are currently limited to English models in the Pythia series and methods restricted to one-dimensional linear subspaces.

title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how \textit{universal} circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLP layers. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. Finally, we demonstrate this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English examples.
specific_phenomena: Subject-Verb Agreement (SVA)
experimental_materials_comment: uses controlled experimental materials rather than naturalistic language, focusing on contrastive sentence pairs to test subject-verb agreement (SVA). For English, the dataset from Arora et al. (2024), based on SyntaxGym, features pairs differing only in subject number, allowing creation of “clean” and “corrupted” sentences (e.g., “The executive that embarrassed the manager has” vs. “The executives that embarrassed the manager”). For Spanish, a similar approach was applied: GPT-4 generated verbs and nouns, multi-subword tokens were filtered, and contrastive pairs were constructed (e.g., “El ingeniero que ayudó al cantante era” vs. “Los ingenieros que ayudaron al cantante”).
Mechanistic_method: Direct Logit Attribution, Attention Analysis, activation patching (steering)
interp_method: mechanistic interpretability (MI) to reverse-engineer model algorithms, circuit analysis to locate and explain the roles of key components, direct logit attribution (DLDA) to measure components’ effects on logits, denoising activation patching to intervene with activations from clean inputs, attention pattern analysis to examine head behavior, and activation steering to test the causal effect of identified directions like the ‘subject number’ signal.
main_findings: The study on the Gemma 2B language model reveals that the circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement (SVA) are largely consistent across English and Spanish, showing that the model implements similar solutions for the same task in different languages. A key attention head, L13H7, transfers subject information to the last residual stream by writing a language-independent ‘subject number’ signal, which is then read by a small set of final MLP neurons—most notably MLP13 and its neuron 2069, whose activation determines whether singular or plural verb forms are predicted. Principal Component Analysis confirms that this signal is encoded in a one-dimensional subspace, and interventions demonstrate its causal effect, allowing predictions to be flipped across languages. Minor differences appear in Spanish, such as greater contributions from MLP17 and activation of non-English-specific neurons like neuron 1138, but overall, the model exhibits a universal, causally effective syntactic representation for SVA.

title: A polar coordinate system represents syntax in large language models
abstract: Originally formalized with symbolic representations, syntactic trees may also be effectively represented in the activations of large language models (LLMs). Indeed, a 'Structural Probe' can find a subspace of neural activations, where syntactically related words are relatively close to one-another. However, this syntactic code remains incomplete: the distance between the Structural Probe word embeddings can represent the existence but not the type and direction of syntactic relations. Here, we hypothesize that syntactic relations are, in fact, coded by the relative direction between nearby embeddings. To test this hypothesis, we introduce a 'Polar Probe' trained to read syntactic relations from both the distance and the direction between word embeddings. Our approach reveals three main findings. First, our Polar Probe successfully recovers the type and direction of syntactic relations, and substantially outperforms the Structural Probe by nearly two folds. Second, we confirm that this polar coordinate system exists in a low-dimensional subspace of the intermediate layers of many LLMs and becomes increasingly precise in the latest frontier models. Third, we demonstrate with a new benchmark that similar syntactic relations are coded similarly across the nested levels of syntactic trees. Overall, this work shows that LLMs spontaneously learn a geometry of neural activations that explicitly represents the main symbolic structures of linguistic theory.

experimental_materials_comment: The naturalistic dataset was drawn from the English Web Treebank (EWT), containing 254,820 words across 16,622 sentences from diverse web genres such as weblogs, newsgroups, emails, and reviews. All sentences were manually annotated according to the Universal Dependencies framework, with sentences containing emails or web addresses filtered out. The dataset was split into training (11,827 sentences), validation (1,851), and test (1,869) sets, and was used to train the Polar Probe on neural activations from Mistral-7B-v0.1 and Llama-2-7b-hf to evaluate its ability to identify dependency types. The controlled stimuli dataset, called the Long-Nested Sentence Dataset, comprised 100 linguistically well-designed sentences with long-nested structures, including variations such as short sentences, relative clauses, and long-nested constructions. This dataset was used to precisely evaluate how the Polar Probe reconstructs complex syntactic trees, assess whether embeddings of syntactically identical sentences map to consistent latent positions, and disentangle word position from syntactic role, confirming that the probe reliably represents dependency structures and types even in complex sentences.
interp_method: Unlike the earlier Structural Probe, which only captured the existence of syntactic links via distance, the Polar Probe reads syntactic relations from both the distance and direction between word embeddings [1, 3, 4, 5C]. It is implemented as a single linear transformation optimized jointly with an Angular objective (to capture direction and type of syntactic relations) and a Structural objective (to capture distances in the dependency tree).
main_findings: demonstrates that syntactic knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is represented in a low-dimensional polar coordinate system within intermediate layer activations, where distances encode the existence of syntactic relations and angles encode their type and direction. The Polar Probe, which leverages both distance and direction, substantially outperforms the traditional Structural Probe, achieving 95% AUC for dependency type classification and high Labeled Attachment Scores while maintaining syntactic distance performance. This representation is compact, with an optimal dimensionality of 128, precise in state-of-the-art models, and consistent across syntactic levels, sentence structures, and different LLMs, including Mistral-7B-v0.1, Llama-2-7b-hf, and BERT-large. Remarkably, raw LLM activations already encode syntactic types above chance, but training a Polar Probe requires rich, pre-trained representations, indicating that LLMs spontaneously learn structured, symbolic-like syntactic geometry. These findings provide evidence that neural networks internally represent the key symbolic structures of linguistic theory, offering a framework for connecting connectionist and symbolic approaches in cognitive science.

title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language Models
abstract: Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate the magnitude of models’ preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across architectures and model sizes—notably, that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

experimental_materials_comment: controlled, synthetically generated stimuli: generated sentence prompts from a predefined vocabulary and templates to avoid confounds from token collocations in the models’ training data. These prompts were designed to test specific subject-verb agreement structures: simple agreement and within relative clause (RC) cases with adjacent subject-verb pairs, across one or two distractors to examine adverbial interference, and across prepositional phrase (PP) or RC constructions to test effects of intervening nouns or verbs. For each structure, 300 prompts were randomly sampled from all possible noun-verb combinations, focusing on third-person singular/plural verb distinctions.
interp_method: causal mediation analysis. More precisely, they apply the "behavioral-structural method of causal mediation analysis", based on Pearl’s (2001) framework, to identify which internal components of neural language models—such as individual neurons—mediate syntactic agreement behavior. Within this framework, they use two key metrics. The Total Effect (TE) measures the model’s overall preference for the grammatically correct form by intervening on a prompt, for example by changing the grammatical number of the subject, and observing the resulting change in output probabilities. The Natural Indirect Effect (NIE) isolates the contribution of a specific model component by assigning that component the value it would have taken under the intervention while leaving the rest of the prompt unchanged. Together, these measures allow the authors to quantify both the overall impact of an intervention and the role of particular internal components in producing the model’s syntactic behavior.
main_findings: the study on causal analysis of syntactic agreement mechanisms in neural language models (LMs) revealed that these models, including GPT-2, Transformer-XL, and XLNet, can reliably perform subject-verb agreement even in complex contexts, correctly predicting grammatical tokens across constructions like filler-gap dependencies and reflexive anaphora. Using causal mediation analysis, the researchers quantified the models’ preferences for correct verb inflections through the total effect (TE), showing strong grammatical preferences that do not consistently scale with model size. Adverbial distractors unexpectedly increased TEs, whereas attractors like prepositional phrases or relative clauses reduced them. The grammaticality margin indicated that plural subjects are easier for GPT-2 to agree with than singular ones, with attractor type more influential than distance. Natural indirect effect (NIE) analysis revealed distinct mechanisms: for adjacent subject-verb pairs, NIEs increased in higher layers, while for separated pairs, they peaked in lower and upper-middle layers before decreasing, reflecting distributed syntactic encoding. XLNet, in contrast, used a unified mechanism across structures. Neuron overlap analysis showed that GPT-2 and Transformer-XL share high-NIE neurons across syntactically similar structures, while XLNet exhibits more specialized neurons, despite using a unified mechanism. Attention head analysis indicated that lower-layer heads may encode lexical information, whereas structural information is distributed across upper layers. Finally, the presence or absence of the complementizer ‘that’ had minimal effect on TE and NIE, suggesting that agreement mechanisms remain robust across minor structural variations.

title: Not all layers are equally as important: Every Layer Counts BERT
abstract: This paper introduces a novel modification of the transformer architecture, tailored for the data-efficient pretraining of language models. This aspect is evaluated by participating in the BabyLM challenge, where our solution won both the STRICT and STRICT-SMALL tracks. Our approach allows each transformer layer to select which outputs of previous layers to pro- cess. The empirical results verify the potential of this simple modification and show that not all layers are equally as important
model_name_comment: LTG-BERT (Samuel et al., 2023), ELC-BERT. OPT125m, RoBERTabase, T5base)
specific_phenomena: BLiMP and MSGS, Anaphor Agreement (AA), ensuring reflexive pronouns match their antecedents; Argument Structure (AS), evaluating verb-argument compatibility; Binding (B), focusing on pronoun-antecedent relationships; Control/Raising (CR), testing predicates embedding infinitival VPs; Determiner-Noun Agreement (DNA) for number agreement between determiners and nouns; Ellipsis (E), especially noun phrase ellipsis; Filler-Gap (FG) dependencies from phrasal movement; Irregular Forms (IF), such as past participles; Island Effects (IE), restricting filler-gap placements; NPI Licensing (NL), covering distribution constraints of negative polarity items; Quantifiers (Q), examining restrictions on quantifier distribution; and Subject-Verb Agreement (SVA) for present-tense number agreement. In MSGS, which tests a model’s preference for linguistic over spurious features, linguistic features include Main Verb (MV) in "-ing" form, Control/Raising (CR) constructions, and Syntactic Category (SC) such as adjectives. For comparison, MSGS also incorporates surface-level features like Lexical Content (LC), e.g., presence of "the," and Relative Token Position (RTP), assessing the order of "the" and "a."
fine_tuning_materials: GLUE and SuperGLUE
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli for evaluating specific linguistic capabilities. controlled stimuli: BLiMP benchmark evaluates syntactic knowledge through zero-shot preferences over minimal pairs, testing phenomena such as anaphor agreement (AA), argument structure (AS), binding (B), control/raising (CR), determiner-noun agreement (DNA), ellipsis (E), filler-gap dependencies (FG), irregular forms (IF), island effects (IE), NPI licensing (NL), quantifiers (Q), and subject-verb agreement (SVA). The MSGS benchmark examines a model’s bias toward linguistic versus surface explanations, including surface features like lexical content (LC) and relative token position (RTP), and linguistic features such as main verb (MV), control/raising (CR), and syntactic category (SC). W
Mechanistic_method: analysis of learnable layer weight, Feature Visualization (heatmaps), Activation Patching (Ablation)
interp_method: Every Layer Counts BERT (ELC-BERT) This name was chosen because the model allows each transformer layer to selectively process outputs from previous layers, leading to the finding that not every layer is of equal significance to the following layers, thus highlighting that "every layer counts" in a flexible way, a modified transformer architecture that adds layer weighting to improve how information is propagated through the model. Unlike traditional residual connections, which treat all previous layers equally, ELC-BERT allows each layer to process a convex combination of outputs from all preceding layers, enabling more selective use of prior representations. The method is presented as a generalization of the ReZero transformer, because it lets each layer individually weight contributions from earlier layers rather than simply scaling its own output. To keep computational costs manageable, the approach removes residual connections inside all multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules.
main_findings: findings regarding ELC-BERT and its syntactic knowledge in language models are as follows: ELC-BERT introduces a novel transformer modification allowing each layer to selectively process outputs from previous layers, challenging the traditional assumption that all layers are equally important. In the BabyLM challenge, ELC-BERT excelled in both STRICT (100M words) and STRICT-SMALL (10M words) tracks, achieving top scores on BLiMP, GLUE, and overall benchmarks. On BLiMP, which measures syntactic understanding, ELC-BERT generally outperformed baselines, though slightly underperformed its LTG-BERT base in some cases; a “weighted output” variant improved its performance. On MSGS, assessing preference for linguistic over spurious features, ELC-BERT significantly outperformed LTG-BERT, indicating stronger reliance on genuine linguistic cues. GLUE evaluations showed modest but consistent improvements, with certain architectural variants providing notable gains. Analysis of learned layer weights revealed a complex inter-layer hierarchy: early layers (1–5) focus on surface-level embedding information, middle layers (6–10) emphasize linguistic features while selectively ignoring lower layers, and later layers (11–12) reintegrate surface-level information for the language modeling head. These results demonstrate that not all layers contribute equally, and ELC-BERT’s selective layer processing enhances both syntactic and general language understanding.

title: Mitigating Frequency Bias and Anisotropy in Language Model Pre-Training with Syntactic Smoothing
abstract: Language models strongly rely on frequency information because they maximize the likelihood of tokens during pre-training. As a consequence, language models tend to not generalize well to tokens that are seldom seen during training. Moreover, maximum likelihood training has been discovered to give rise to anisotropy: representations of tokens in a model tend to cluster tightly in a high-dimensional cone, rather than spreading out over their representational capacity.Our work introduces a method for quantifying the frequency bias of a language model by assessing sentence-level perplexity with respect to token-level frequency. We then present a method for reducing the frequency bias of a language model by inducing a syntactic prior over token representations during pre-training. Our Syntactic Smoothing method adjusts the maximum likelihood objective function to distribute the learning signal to syntactically similar tokens. This approach results in better performance on infrequent English tokens and a decrease in anisotropy. We empirically show that the degree of anisotropy in a model correlates with its frequency bias.
model_name_comment: small 8-layer encoder-style RoBERTa model , OPT-125M , t5. , RoBERTa-base (Liu et al., 2019)
specific_phenomena: Part-of-Speech (POS) tags, Blimp, function words (e.g., determiners, prepositions, conjunctions) are also considered, given their syntactic importance
experimental_materials_comment: BLIMP, COLA (Warstadt et al., 2019) and SST-2 (Socher et al., 2013), as well as two language inference, tasks, MNLI (Williams et al., 2018) and QNLI (Rajpurkar et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018)
interp_method: Syntactic Smoothing: This method is designed to reduce the frequency bias and anisotropy in language models by adjusting the maximum likelihood objective function during pre-training. It achieves this by distributing the learning signal to syntactically similar tokens, using part-of-speech (POS) tag distributions as a coarse proxy for syntactic similarity
main_findings: highlight that language models (LMs) exhibit a frequency bias due to their maximum likelihood pre-training objective, causing infrequent tokens to cluster tightly in representation space (anisotropy) and hindering generalization. To address this, the research introduces Syntactic Smoothing, which imposes a syntactic prior over token representations by distributing training updates to syntactically similar tokens, measured via POS tag cosine similarity. Key findings show that Syntactic Smoothing significantly reduces frequency bias and anisotropy, with stronger smoothing and paced variants achieving greater improvements. The method enhances representations of infrequent tokens, improves performance on linguistic benchmarks like BLiMP, and does not degrade downstream NLU tasks—in some cases, performance even improves. Furthermore, results are robust to alternative syntactic similarity metrics, demonstrating that integrating syntactic knowledge into training objectives can improve model generalization without compromising overall language understanding.

title: Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects: Discrepancy in Performance and Competence for Form and Meaning
abstract: This study investigates the linguistic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding signifier (form) and signified (meaning) by distinguishing two LLM assessment paradigms: psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic. Traditional psycholinguistic evaluations often reflect statistical rules that may not accurately represent LLMs' true linguistic competence. We introduce a neurolinguistic approach, utilizing a novel method that combines minimal pair and diagnostic probing to analyze activation patterns across model layers. This method allows for a detailed examination of how LLMs represent form and meaning, and whether these representations are consistent across languages. We found: (1) Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct; (2) Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence; (3) Instruction tuning won't change much competence but improve performance; (4) LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning. Additionally, we introduce new conceptual minimal pair datasets for Chinese (COMPS-ZH) and German (COMPS-DE), complementing existing English datasets.
specific_phenomena: Syntax sub-category [Figure 3]: These include argument structure, ellipsis, filler–gap dependencies, and island effects
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli in the form of minimal pair datasets to rigorously evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) on linguistic form and meaning. These stimuli consist of carefully constructed sentence pairs where one sentence is grammatically or conceptually acceptable and the other minimally violates the relevant property. For form (grammaticality) assessment, the datasets include BLiMP for English (67,000 pairs across 13 phenomena), CLiMP for Chinese (16,000 pairs across 9 phenomena), and DistilLingEval for German (82,711 pairs across 8 phenomena). For meaning (conceptuality) assessment, the study uses COMPS for English (49,340 pairs testing taxonomy, property norms, co-occurrence, and random relationships), as well as COMPS-ZH and COMPS-DE, which are translated and human-verified versions for Chinese and German.
interp_method: neurolinguistic assessment method as “minimal pair probing”, or simply “Neuro”. This approach combines a minimal pair design with diagnostic probing to analyze internal activation patterns across model layers, enabling evaluation of how Large Language Models (LLMs) represent both linguistic form (syntax, morphology) and meaning.
main_findings: LLMs exhibit a stronger and earlier mastery of linguistic form (syntax, morphology, and the syntax-semantics interface) than of conceptual meaning. By distinguishing between psycholinguistic (performance-based) and neurolinguistic (competence-based) assessment paradigms, the research shows that LLMs’ underlying syntactic competence often exceeds what is observable in output-based evaluations, with neurolinguistic measures reaching up to 97% accuracy on syntax tasks. Layer-wise analyses indicate that grammatical features are encoded progressively, forming clearer clusters in deeper layers, and that form stabilizes earlier than meaning. Instruction fine-tuning (chat versions) improves performance in metalinguistic settings without fundamentally changing competence, reducing the gap between observable performance and underlying knowledge. Across multiple languages, LLMs consistently perform better on form than on meaning, though low-resource languages like German show weaker performance. The study also finds a positive correlation between form and meaning competence, suggesting that LLMs’ understanding of meaning is largely anchored to their formal representations, which may contribute to confidently incorrect outputs or hallucinations. Overall, LLMs internally structure grammatical knowledge robustly and encode syntax more effectively than semantic content.

title: On the Cross-lingual Transferability of Monolingual Representations
abstract: State-of-the-art unsupervised multilingual models (e.g., multilingual BERT) have been shown to generalize in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting. This generalization ability has been attributed to the use of a shared subword vocabulary and joint training across multiple languages giving rise to deep multilingual abstractions. We evaluate this hypothesis by designing an alternative approach that transfers a monolingual model to new languages at the lexical level. More concretely, we first train a transformer-based masked language model on one language, and transfer it to a new language by learning a new embedding matrix with the same masked language modeling objective, freezing parameters of all other layers. This approach does not rely on a shared vocabulary or joint training. However, we show that it is competitive with multilingual BERT on standard cross-lingual classification benchmarks and on a new Cross-lingual Question Answering Dataset (XQuAD). Our results contradict common beliefs of the basis of the generalization ability of multilingual models and suggest that deep monolingual models learn some abstractions that generalize across languages. We also release XQuAD as a more comprehensive cross-lingual benchmark, which comprises 240 paragraphs and 1190 question-answer pairs from SQuAD v1.1 translated into ten languages by professional translators.
syntactic_phenomena: Agreement and feature-checking, binding and coreference
specific_phenomena: subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora, categories are derived from the Marvin and Linzen (2018) dataset
experimental_materials_comment: tested on controlled benchmarks and probing datasets that target specific linguistic abilities. Cross-lingual classification benchmarks include XNLI (Natural Language Inference), MLDoc (document classification), and PAWS-X (paraphrase identification), while cross-lingual question answering is assessed using XQuAD, a new dataset with professionally translated SQuAD v1.1 paragraphs spanning ten languages. For linguistic probing, semantic knowledge is evaluated via WiC and SCWS, and syntactic knowledge is assessed using the Marvin and Linzen (2018) dataset, which tests phenomena like subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora through minimally different English sentence pairs.
interp_method: MONOTRANS, a method for transferring a monolingual model to new languages at the lexical level. In MONOTRANS, a transformer-based masked language model is first pre-trained on a source language (L1). To adapt it to a target language (L2), a new embedding matrix is learned for L2 while all other model parameters remain frozen. This method does not require a shared subword vocabulary or joint multilingual training
main_findings: investigates cross-lingual transfer of monolingual representations, with a focus on syntactic knowledge in language models. It challenges the common belief that a shared subword vocabulary and joint multilingual training are essential for zero-shot cross-lingual generalization, showing that MONOTRANS, which transfers monolingual models to new languages via a new embedding matrix while freezing other parameters, performs competitively with multilingual BERT (mBERT) on benchmarks like XNLI, MLDoc, PAWS-X, and XQuAD. The study highlights that deep monolingual models capture linguistic abstractions that can generalize across languages, and that effective vocabulary size per language is more critical than shared vocabulary or joint training. However, probing experiments reveal that syntactic abstractions transfer less robustly than semantic ones: while monolingual semantic knowledge learned in non-English languages transfers well to English, syntactic tasks such as subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora show significant accuracy drops (e.g., 86.5% vs. 58–64% for agreement), indicating that syntactic knowledge is more challenging to transfer across languages.

title: Probing Linguistic Features of Sentence-Level Representations in Neural Relation Extraction
abstract: Despite the recent progress, little is known about the features captured by state-of-the-art neural relation extraction (RE) models. Common methods encode the source sentence, conditioned on the entity mentions, before classifying the relation. However, the complexity of the task makes it difficult to understand how encoder architecture and supporting linguistic knowledge affect the features learned by the encoder. We introduce 14 probing tasks targeting linguistic properties relevant to RE, and we use them to study representations learned by more than 40 different encoder architecture and linguistic feature combinations trained on two datasets, TACRED and SemEval 2010 Task 8. We find that the bias induced by the architecture and the inclusion of linguistic features are clearly expressed in the probing task performance. For example, adding contextualized word representations greatly increases performance on probing tasks with a focus on named entity and part-of-speech information, and yields better results in RE. In contrast, entity masking improves RE, but considerably lowers performance on entity type related probing tasks.
specific_phenomena: syntactic information” tasks, which evaluate how well sentence encoders capture various syntactic features relevant to relation extraction. These include Tree Depth (TreeDepth), measuring the depth of the longest path from root to leaf in a parse tree; Shortest Dependency Path Tree Depth (SDPTreeDepth), testing whether embeddings retain the depth of the dependency path between relation arguments; and Argument Ordering (ArgOrd), assessing whether the encoder captures the sequence of head and tail arguments. Additionally, four tasks probe the part-of-speech (POS) of tokens surrounding arguments—PosHeadL, PosHeadR, PosTailL, and PosTailR—to evaluate sensitivity to local syntactic context. Finally, Grammatical Role tasks (GRHead, GRTail) examine the syntactic function of relation arguments by predicting their dependency labels,
experimental_materials_comment: used TACRED and SemEval 2010 Task 8 to train relation extraction models and probe learned sentence representations. TACRED contains 106,264 sentences with entity mention pairs collected from TAC KBP evaluations, annotated with person- and organization-oriented relation types (e.g., per:title, org:founded), negative examples, and typed entities. The study also utilized TACRED’s provided named entity, part-of-speech, and dependency parsing information. SemEval 2010 Task 8, a benchmark for binary relation classification, includes 8,000 training and 2,717 testing sentences annotated with pairs of untyped nominals and one of nine directed semantic relation types plus an undirected “Other” type, totaling 19 relation types; sentences were parsed with the Stanford Parser for linguistic features. Both datasets consist of real-world text,
interp_method: introduced 14 probing tasks tailored to RE, covering surface-level features like argument distance, syntactic properties such as parse tree depth and argument ordering, and semantic features like entity types. To support this work, they provided an open-source RE framework built on AllenNLP and REval, an extension of the SentEval toolkit, specifically designed to implement these probing tasks.
main_findings: demonstrates that contextualized word representations like ELMo and BERT significantly enhance the encoding of syntactic and semantic information, improving both probing-task and Relation Extraction (RE) performance. Syntactic knowledge, probed via tasks such as Tree Depth, Shortest Dependency Path, POS tagging near arguments, and grammatical roles, shows that CNNs, BiLSTMs, and GCNs capture local and dependency-based structures effectively, while Self-Attention models, despite lower probing scores, achieve superior RE performance by capturing deeper, more abstract linguistic patterns. Encoder architecture strongly shapes learned features: local/recency biases benefit POS and argument-related tasks, GCNs excel at tree-structured syntactic tasks, and entity masking encourages models to focus on context rather than literal mentions. Overall, syntactic knowledge is valuable, but high probing-task performance does not guarantee better downstream results; deep contextual models with attention mechanisms best leverage both syntactic and semantic cues for effective RE.

title: Can neural networks understand monotonicity reasoning?
abstract: Monotonicity reasoning is one of the important reasoning skills for any intelligent natural language inference (NLI) model in that it requires the ability to capture the interaction between lexical and syntactic structures. Since no test set has been developed for monotonicity reasoning with wide coverage, it is still unclear whether neural models can perform monotonicity reasoning in a proper way. To investigate this issue, we introduce the Monotonicity Entailment Dataset (MED). Performance by state-of-the-art NLI models on the new test set is substantially worse, under 55%, especially on downward reasoning. In addition, analysis using a monotonicity-driven data augmentation method showed that these models might be limited in their generalization ability in upward and downward reasoning.
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Negation and NPIs
specific_phenomena: monotonicity operators and their arguments, which models must detect within the syntactic structure. These operators include determiners (e.g., every, all, some, a few, few, most), negation (not, never), verbs (deny, prohibit, avoid), nouns (absence of, lack, prohibition), adverbs (scarcely, hardly, rarely), prepositions (without, except, but), and conditionals (if, when, unless), all of which can create downward-entailing contexts within their scope and upward-entailing contexts outside it. Phrase replacements are another key phenomenon, often involving conjunctions, disjunctions, modifiers (e.g., replacing “person” with “young person”), relative clauses, and comparatives, used to generate inference problems in controlled syntactic positions. The dataset also captures embedding and scopal relations, including “reverse” cases where polarity is flipped due to nested downward-entailing contexts. Additionally, negative polarity items (NPIs) such as any, ever, at all, and non-constituents—added phrases that do not form syntactic constituents with the premise—are highlighted, as they challenge models to correctly handle non-monotone or complex monotone inferences.
fine_tuning_materials: GLUE
experimental_materials_comment: combine naturalistic language and controlled stimuli to comprehensively evaluate NLI models’ syntactic reasoning. The naturalistic component was created through crowdsourcing, drawing sentences from the Parallel Meaning Bank (PMB) and having workers generate hypotheses by making polarized parts of sentences more specific, producing naturally occurring monotonicity inference problems. The controlled stimuli component was collected from manually curated datasets such as FraCaS and the GLUE diagnostic set, as well as 11 linguistics publications, providing expert-designed examples targeting specific linguistic phenomena.
interp_method: primary method for analyzing syntactic knowledge in language models is the Monotonicity Entailment Dataset (MED), which, although a dataset, embodies a specific methodology for probing models. MED was created using a human- and linguistics-oriented approach: first, a two-step crowdsourcing process generates monotonicity inference problems, where workers replace polarized parts of sentences with more specific phrases (hypothesis creation) and then validate premise-hypothesis pairs for entailment and naturalness. This process incorporates polarity computation based on syntactic structures using the ccg2mono system. Additionally, MED integrates monotonicity problems from previous curated datasets like FraCaS and the GLUE diagnostic set, as well as examples from 11 linguistics publications. This methodology allows the dataset to systematically evaluate and analyze whether NLI models capture the structural and syntactic properties necessary for monotonicity reasoning.
main_findings: highlight significant challenges in monotonicity reasoning. Neural network models, including state-of-the-art NLI models like BERT, perform poorly on the Monotonicity Entailment Dataset (MED), especially for downward reasoning, often falling below the majority baseline. Monotonicity reasoning requires models to capture the interaction between lexical items and syntactic structures, such as detecting monotonicity operators (e.g., “all,” “not”) and understanding the polarity of phrases in context. Analyses indicate that models struggle to generalize: training on upward inferences improves performance on that direction but harms downward inference accuracy, suggesting that models fail to internalize structural relations between operators and their arguments. BERT, for instance, often cannot distinguish downward operators like “few” from upward operators like “a few,” and fails to recognize conditional contexts where polarity changes inside versus outside the conditional scope. Non-lexical inferences, which rely more on structural understanding than lexical knowledge, remain particularly difficult. Moreover, previous datasets like FraCaS and GLUE were limited in both monotonicity coverage and syntactic variety, while crowdsourced datasets such as SNLI and MultiNLI contain hidden biases and very few downward inferences. The MED dataset was specifically designed to address these limitations by providing broader monotonicity coverage and detailed linguistic annotations, emphasizing the need for syntactic awareness in language models to handle complex reasoning.

title: Do Neural Models Learn Systematicity of Monotonicity Inference in Natural Language?
abstract: Despite the success of language models using neural networks, it remains unclear to what extent neural models have the generalization ability to perform inferences. In this paper, we introduce a method for evaluating whether neural models can learn systematicity of monotonicity inference in natural language, namely, the regularity for performing arbitrary inferences with generalization on composition. We consider four aspects of monotonicity inferences and test whether the models can systematically interpret lexical and logical phenomena on different training/test splits. A series of experiments show that three neural models systematically draw inferences on unseen combinations of lexical and logical phenomena when the syntactic structures of the sentences are similar between the training and test sets. However, the performance of the models significantly decreases when the structures are slightly changed in the test set while retaining all vocabularies and constituents already appearing in the training set. This indicates that the generalization ability of neural models is limited to cases where the syntactic structures are nearly the same as those in the training set.
specific_phenomena: syntactic phenomena and structural changes, particularly in the context of monotonicity inference. These included adding adverbs or short prepositional phrases at the beginning of sentences, performing replacements in object positions, and testing inferences across varying embedding depths—from simple non-embedded clauses to deeply nested multi-level embeddings. They also examined peripheral- and center-embedded clauses and compared model performance on syntactic structures closely matching the training set versus slightly altered ones.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled, systematically generated stimuli designed to evaluate monotonicity inference and compositional generalization in neural models. These synthesized datasets are created using context-free grammar rules and lexical entries to generate premise sentences, followed by “replacement functions” to produce hypotheses. The authors carefully control which semantic and syntactic patterns appear in training versus test sets, allowing targeted assessment of systematicity and productivity. Variations include unseen combinations of quantifiers and predicate replacements, slight syntactic changes (e.g., adding adverbs or prepositional phrases), replacements in object positions, and varying embedding depths to test productivity and local interpretation. Gold labels are automatically assigned via monotonicity calculus and validated using logical formulas and a theorem prover. While the primary focus is on these controlled stimuli, the authors also include a naturalistic dataset (MultiNLI) in a supplementary experiment to examine the transferability of their findings to conventional NLI corpora.
interp_method: an evaluation protocol designed to test whether neural models can learn the systematicity of monotonicity inference in natural language. This protocol involves synthesizing training instances from sampled sentences and systematically controlling the training/test split to determine which semantic and syntactic patterns the models encounter during training and which remain unseen. By doing so, the protocol assesses the models’ ability to generalize to novel combinations of semantic properties, providing a structured way to evaluate their inferential systematicity on monotonicity tasks.
main_findings: indicate that neural models in natural language inference (NLI) exhibit fragile generalization abilities with respect to syntactic structures. While models like BERT, LSTM, and TreeLSTM can learn certain systematic patterns combining lexical and logical phenomena, their performance drops sharply when tested on sentences with even slight syntactic variations from the training set, such as added adverbs or short prepositional phrases. Models also struggle with productivity, failing to generalize systematically to embedded clauses beyond one level deeper than their training, and they show poor local interpretation, performing at chance on simpler inferences despite being trained on complex embeddings. Regarding systematicity, BERT initially generalized to unseen predicate replacements and reached high accuracy with increased training, while LSTM and TreeLSTM showed partial success. However, all models failed to generalize to unseen combinations of embedding quantifiers. Model-specific patterns emerged: BERT benefited from mixing synthetic and naturalistic training data, TreeLSTM generalized slightly better to deeper embeddings, and LSTM and BERT underperformed on downward inferences. Overall, the results reveal that neural NLI models’ ability to capture syntactic knowledge and compositional structure is limited, highly sensitive to training structures, and often unable to systematically handle deeper or varied syntactic embeddings.

title: Assessing Monotonicity Reasoning in Dutch through Natural Language Inference
abstract: In this paper we investigate monotonicity reasoning in Dutch, through a novel Natural Language Inference dataset. Monotonicity reasoning shows to be highly challenging for Transformer-based language models in English and here, we corroborate those findings using a parallel Dutch dataset, obtained by translating the Monotonicity Entailment Dataset of Yanaka et al. (2019). After fine-tuning two Dutch language models BERTje and RobBERT on the Dutch NLI dataset SICK-NL, we find that performance severely drops on the monotonicity reasoning dataset, indicating poor generalization capacity of the models. We provide a detailed analysis of the test results by means of the linguistic annotations in the dataset. We find that models struggle with downward entailing contexts, and argue that this is due to a poor understanding of negation. Additionally, we find that the choice of monotonicity context affects model performance on conjunction and disjunction. We hope that this new resource paves the way for further research in generalization of neural reasoning models in Dutch, and contributes to the development of better language technology for Natural Language Inference, specifically for Dutch.
model_name_comment: BERTje, Roberta-based model for Dutch, mBert
specific_phenomena: Monotonicity reasoning, in particular, relies on subtle aspects of syntax and the correct interpretation of syntactic constituents. Models struggle with long-distance dependencies and show poor sensitivity to negation, especially in downward entailing contexts, where double negation or “reverse” cases arise. Conjunctions and disjunctions interact with monotonicity in complex ways: conjunctions are harder than disjunctions in downward contexts, reversing the pattern seen in upward contexts. Conditionals and Negative Polarity Items (NPIs), which depend heavily on their syntactic and semantic environments, also present challenges
experimental_materials_comment: MED-NL, is a controlled stimuli set explicitly designed to test monotonicity reasoning in Dutch. It was created by translating the English Monotonicity Entailment Dataset (MED), preserving entailment/neutral labels based on monotonicity properties, and carefully controlling for specific linguistic phenomena through annotated features like lexical changes, conjunction, disjunction, conditionals, NPIs, and double negation. MED-NL focuses on how particular lexical items license inferences in upward or downward contexts, offering precise, targeted evaluation. For model fine-tuning, the study also used SICK-NL, a standard Dutch NLI benchmark derived from the English SICK dataset.
interp_method: focuses on evaluating monotonicity reasoning, a type of inference that tests both lexical and syntactic knowledge, using Natural Language Inference (NLI) as the framework. To this end, the authors created the MED-NL dataset, specifically designed to probe models’ ability to handle monotonicity. Their procedural approach involved standard language model fine-tuning: models such as BERTje, RobBERT, and multilingual BERT were trained on the SICK-NL dataset and subsequently tested on MED-NL to assess their reasoning capabilities.
main_findings: finds that monotonicity reasoning poses significant challenges for Dutch language models, revealing clear limitations in their syntactic knowledge. Both monolingual models (BERTje and RobBERT), even when fine-tuned on Dutch NLI data, struggle with downward entailing contexts, largely due to poor sensitivity to negation. Model performance is also affected by monotonicity context: in upward entailing contexts, disjunctions, conditionals, NPIs, and reverse cases are hardest, while in downward entailing contexts, conjunctions become more difficult than disjunctions. Multilingual BERT, despite weaker exposure to Dutch training data, outperformed the monolingual models on overall MED-NL performance and specific linguistic features. The research also confirms prior findings that LMs encode some syntactic structure but fail to generalize systematically across NLI tasks, especially for long-distance dependencies and complex embedding patterns. Overall, while Dutch LMs capture certain aspects of syntax, their ability to leverage this knowledge for rigorous monotonicity reasoning and compositional inference remains severely limited.

title: Do Syntax Trees Help Pre-trained Transformers Extract Information?
abstract: Much recent work suggests that incorporating syntax information from dependency trees can improve task-specific transformer models. However, the effect of incorporating dependency tree information into pre-trained transformer models (e.g., BERT) remains unclear, especially given recent studies highlighting how these models implicitly encode syntax. In this work, we systematically study the utility of incorporating dependency trees into pre-trained transformers on three representative information extraction tasks: semantic role labeling (SRL), named entity recognition, and relation extraction. We propose and investigate two distinct strategies for incorporating dependency structure: a late fusion approach, which applies a graph neural network on the output of a transformer, and a joint fusion approach, which infuses syntax structure into the transformer attention layers. These strategies are representative of prior work, but we introduce additional model design elements that are necessary for obtaining improved performance. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that these syntax-infused transformers obtain state-of-the-art results on SRL and relation extraction tasks. However, our analysis also reveals a critical shortcoming of these models: we find that their performance gains are highly contingent on the availability of human-annotated dependency parses, which raises important questions regarding the viability of syntax-augmented transformers in real-world applications.
specific_phenomena: Bert base on argument structure
experimental_materials_comment: utilizes naturalistic language data drawn from established NLP corpora, with no use of controlled stimuli. For Semantic Role Labeling (SRL), it employs the CoNLL-2005 corpus (featuring Wall Street Journal articles and the out-of-domain Brown corpus) and the CoNLL-2012 OntoNotes dataset, which includes PropBank-style annotations. For Named Entity Recognition (NER), it uses the OntoNotes 5.0 dataset, covering 18 named entity types. For Relation Extraction (RE), it relies on a corrected version of the TACRED dataset, which includes 41 relation types plus a "no_relation" class. The dependency parses applied to them varied in quality, ranging from human-annotated (gold) to both in-domain and off-the-shelf automated parses.
interp_method: 2 methods for incorporating dependency syntax into pre-trained transformer models, referred to as Late Fusion and Joint Fusion. In the Late Fusion approach, a syntax-aware graph neural network (syntax-GNN) processes the output of a transformer model, with a Highway Gate used to adaptively select useful syntactic representations. In contrast, Joint Fusion embeds syntactic information directly into the transformer’s self-attention layers, integrating syntax during the model’s internal computations. Collectively, these models are termed Syntax-Augmented BERT (SA-BERT), highlighting their aim to enhance BERT with syntactic structure for improved language understanding.
main_findings: show that latent tree learning models, particularly ST-Gumbel, fail to capture conventional syntactic phenomena. While traditional TreeRNNs rely on constituency to represent meaningful sentence units, these models often ignore it, instead creating unorthodox structures such as initial or final two-word constituents and systematically pairing negation words with the following word, producing implausible phrases. They also handle function words and modifiers inconsistently, failing to form proper noun phrases with determiners, misattaching prepositions, and generating odd adverbial constituents. Overall, the models do not recover core syntactic units like noun or prepositional phrases, suggesting that their learned grammars diverge significantly from formal syntactic structures.

title: Assessing the syntactic capabilities of transformer-based multilingual language models
abstract: Multilingual Transformer-based language models, usually pretrained on more than 100 languages, have been shown to achieve outstanding results in a wide range of cross-lingual transfer tasks. However, it remains unknown whether the optimization for different languages conditions the capacity of the models to generalize over syntactic structures, and how languages with syntactic phenomena of different complexity are affected. In this work, we explore the syntactic generalization capabilities of the monolingual and multilingual versions of BERT and RoBERTa. More specifically, we evaluate the syntactic generalization potential of the models on English and Spanish tests, comparing the syntactic abilities of monolingual and multilingual models on the same language (English), and of multilingual models on two different languages (English and Spanish). For English, we use the available SyntaxGym test suite; for Spanish, we introduce SyntaxGymES, a novel ensemble of targeted syntactic tests in Spanish, designed to evaluate the syntactic generalization capabilities of language models through the SyntaxGym online platform.
specific_phenomena: within the SyntaxGym (English) and SyntaxGymES (Spanish); phenomena include grammatical dependencies such as subject-verb agreement, long-distance dependencies (LDDs), garden path effects, reflexive anaphora, and negative polarity items, along with Spanish-specific constructions like determiner/adjective agreement, subjunctive mood licensing, subject pro-drop, and flexible word order. Each circuit targets a distinct class of syntactic behavior—such as Agreement, Licensing, Center Embedding, Gross Syntactic Expectation, and Garden Path Effects—with multiple test suites capturing variations and complexity (e.g., with and without modifiers). Linearization circuit is introduced for Spanish to probe its flexible syntax
experimental_materials_comment: controlled linguistic stimuli: employ SyntaxGym (for English) and SyntaxGymES (for Spanish), which are collections of targeted syntactic tests specifically designed to probe language models’ syntactic generalization. These tests consist of carefully crafted items that vary systematically across predefined grammatical conditions, allowing for precise evaluation based on the notion of surprisal—i.e., how (un)expected a word is given the preceding context. Many items include modifiers to increase linear distance and syntactic complexity, and the suites feature both grammatical and ungrammatical constructions,
interp_method: evaluate syntactic knowledge in language models using SyntaxGym (for English) and SyntaxGymES (for Spanish), both comprising targeted syntactic test suites designed to probe specific grammatical phenomena. Their methodology closely follows that of Hu et al. (2020a) and relies on the principle of surprisal, where models are expected to assign lower surprisal (i.e., higher probability) to grammatically correct continuations. For Spanish, they introduce SyntaxGymES, which includes adaptations of 11 English test suites and 15 newly developed ones, including a unique Linearization circuit addressing Spanish-specific word order flexibility. To assess probability in bidirectional models like BERT and RoBERTa, the authors use the sequential sampling procedure proposed by Wang and Cho (2019), allowing them to simulate left-to-right prediction despite the models' original bidirectional design.
main_findings: show that syntactic generalization varies significantly by language and model type. Monolingual models like RoBERTa outperform multilingual models in English, while in Spanish, multilingual models like XLM-R perform better than monolingual BETO, likely due to differences in training data size. The performance of multilingual models is not uniform—XLM-R excels in Spanish but underperforms in English compared to mBERT. All models struggle with complex syntactic phenomena, especially long-distance dependencies and agreement in English, though Spanish’s richer morphology aids generalization. A newly introduced Linearization test highlights challenges with Spanish word order flexibility. The training objective also matters: models using Next Sentence Prediction (NSP), like BERT and mBERT, better capture clause-level syntax. Finally, the study introduces SyntaxGymES, a benchmark for Spanish syntactic evaluation, underscoring the need for multilingual syntactic testing to assess generalization more comprehensively.

title: Interpreting Language Models Through Knowledge Graph Extraction
abstract: Transformer-based language models trained on large text corpora have enjoyed immense popularity in the natural language processing community and are commonly used as a starting point for downstream tasks. While these models are undeniably useful, it is a challenge to quantify their performance beyond traditional accuracy metrics. In this paper, we compare BERT-based language models through snapshots of acquired knowledge at sequential stages of the training process. Structured relationships from training corpora may be uncovered through querying a masked language model with probing tasks. We present a methodology to unveil a knowledge acquisition timeline by generating knowledge graph extracts from cloze "fill-in-the-blank" statements at various stages of RoBERTa's early training. We extend this analysis to a comparison of pretrained variations of BERT models (DistilBERT, BERT-base, RoBERTa). This work proposes a quantitative framework to compare language models through knowledge graph extraction (GED, Graph2Vec) and showcases a part-of-speech analysis (POSOR) to identify the linguistic strengths of each model variant. Using these metrics, machine learning practitioners can compare models, diagnose their models' behavioral strengths and weaknesses, and identify new targeted datasets to improve model performance.
model_name_comment: RoBERTa pretrained and from scratch, pretrained BERT-base-cased, DistilBERT
specific_phenomena: primarily analyzed through the POSOR (Part-of-Speech Overprediction Rate) framework.  Part-of-speech understanding is a major focus, covering verbs, nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, adpositions, conjunctions, determiners, cardinal numbers, particles, punctuation, and articles, with examples showing improved grammatical predictions over training.
experimental_materials_comment: combines naturalistic language and controlled stimuli to probe the syntactic and semantic knowledge of language models. Naturalistic materials come from datasets like SQuAD and Google-RE, both derived from Wikipedia, ensuring that sentences reflect real-world language and factual structures; the models themselves are trained on large text corpora, including Wikipedia, supporting their natural language processing capabilities. Controlled stimuli are implemented through cloze-style “fill-in-the-blank” queries, including a subset of context-insensitive SQuAD questions manually converted into cloze form and template-based sentences from Google-RE (e.g., “[S] was born in [O]…”).
interp_method: introduce POSOR (Part-of-Speech Overprediction Rate) as a specific metric within their broader pipeline for analyzing language model performance. POSOR compares the frequency of each part of speech in a model’s extracted knowledge graph relations against a ground truth knowledge graph, revealing whether the model overpredicts or underpredicts particular grammatical categories. This metric is embedded in a larger methodology that uses knowledge graph extraction (via Graph Edit Distance and Graph2Vec) from cloze-style statements to trace a model’s knowledge acquisition over time and identify its linguistic strengths,
main_findings: introduces a novel pipeline for extracting and comparing knowledge graphs (KGs) from masked language models, providing fine-grained diagnostics beyond traditional accuracy metrics. By quantitatively comparing models using metrics like Graph Edit Distance and Graph2Vec, the study shows that models trained from scratch gradually acquire knowledge closer to pretrained models like RoBERTa, BERT, and DistilBERT. Focusing on linguistic and syntactic knowledge, the research tracks how models learn grammatical structures over training, using a Part-of-Speech Overprediction Rate (POSOR) metric to analyze relation triples. Results demonstrate that as training progresses, models improve in syntactic prediction—for example, refining article and noun usage and better representing adverbs—while pretrained models exhibit consistent strengths, such as RoBERTa’s superior pronoun prediction. Overall, the study provides a diagnostic framework that enhances interpretability of language model behavior, highlighting when and how linguistic and syntactic knowledge is acquired and identifying areas for targeted improvement.

title: An information theoretic view on selecting linguistic probes
abstract: There is increasing interest in assessing the linguistic knowledge encoded in neural representations. A popular approach is to attach a diagnostic classifier – or ”probe” – to perform supervised classification from internal representations. However, how to select a good probe is in debate. Hewitt and Liang (2019) showed that a high performance on diagnostic classification itself is insufficient, because it can be attributed to either ”the representation being rich in knowledge”, or ”the probe learning the task”, which Pimentel et al. (2020) challenged. We show this dichotomy is valid information-theoretically. In addition, we find that the ”good probe” criteria proposed by the two papers, *selectivity* (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) and *information gain* (Pimentel et al., 2020), are equivalent – the errors of their approaches are identical (modulo irrelevant terms). Empirically, these two selection criteria lead to results that highly agree with each other.
specific_phenomena: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language corpora. They used the Universal Dependencies (UD) dataset (Zeman et al., 2019), accessed through the Flair toolkit (Akbik et al., 2018), focusing on English, French, and Spanish. For their probing task, they employed Part-of-Speech (POS) labels from SpaCy.
interp_method: refer to three specific methodological terms in the sources: Hewitt and Liang’s (2019) “selectivity” criterion, which uses a control task; Pimentel et al.’s (2020) “information gain” criterion, which uses a control function; and, more generally, the paper advocates for using “control mechanisms” as an umbrella term that encompasses both approaches for selecting effective probes. They compare two main methods for selecting high-quality probes: the Selectivity Criterion, introduced by Hewitt and Liang (2019), which uses a control task to determine whether probe performance reflects the representation itself or merely the probe’s ability to learn the task; and the Information Gain (or Gain) Criterion, proposed by Pimentel et al. (2020), which uses a control function to measure the reduction in cross-entropy from randomized representations. The authors group these approaches under the broader term “control mechanisms” and argue that, when randomization is properly implemented, the two methods are equivalent for probe selection. They also provide the code used in their experiments through the InfoProbe repository.
main_findings: examine the assessment of linguistic knowledge—particularly syntactic knowledge—encoded in neural representations, with a focus on selecting effective diagnostic classifiers, or probes. A key insight is the validity of the probing dichotomy: high probe performance can indicate either that the representations are inherently rich in information or that the probe itself is effectively learning the task. Information-theoretically, these interpretations are both plausible. The study shows that two popular probe selection criteria—Hewitt and Liang’s selectivity and Pimentel et al.’s information gain—are equivalent when randomization is ideal, and empirically they strongly agree across POS tagging tasks in multiple languages. The recommended approach is to employ control mechanisms, either by randomizing targets or representations, rather than relying solely on raw probe accuracy. Practical rules of thumb for probe training include using small probes with modest weight decay and ensuring sufficient training (e.g., beyond four epochs) without excessive overfitting. Regarding syntactic knowledge in mBERT, the study confirms that contextual embeddings encode rich linguistic information: probes trained on mBERT substantially outperform FastText in POS tagging, indicating that syntactic features are well-represented in its contextualized vectors.

title: When Your Language Model Cannot Even Do Determiners Right: Probing for Anti-Presuppositions and the Maximize Presupposition! Principle
abstract: The increasing interest in probing the linguistic capabilities of large language models (LLMs) has long reached the area of semantics and pragmatics, including the phenomenon of presuppositions. In this study, we investigate a phenomenon that, however, has not yet been investigated, i.e., the phenomenon of anti-presupposition and the principle that accounts for it, the Maximize Presupposition! principle (MP!). Through an experimental investigation using psycholinguistic data and four open-source BERT model variants, we explore how language models handle different anti-presuppositions and whether they apply the MP! principle in their predictions. Further, we examine whether fine-tuning with Natural Language Inference data impacts adherence to the MP! principle. Our findings reveal that LLMs tend to replicate context-based n-grams rather than follow the MP! principle, with fine-tuning not enhancing their adherence. Notably, our results further indicate a striking difficulty of LLMs to correctly predict determiners, in relatively simple linguistic contexts.
specific_phenomena: determiners, anti-presupposition triggers,
fine_tuning_materials: GLUE only for Eng
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli, designed for a precise linguistic diagnostic using minimal pair analysis. These stimuli contrasted nearly identical items differing in only one key feature, making them ideal for probing anti-presuppositions. The materials were grounded in psycholinguistic data from Schneider et al. (2019), which examined the Maximize Presupposition! (MP!) principle with definite and indefinite determiners in visualized story contexts. Researchers constructed prompts by masking determiners in context sentences, carefully controlling sentence structure (e.g., pairing specific fruit types with feminine determiners) to prevent early disambiguation. Additionally, supplementary conditions incorporated the anti-presupposition triggers “beide” (both) and “alle” (all) within the same minimal pair framework, maintaining controlled sentence structure and masked token placement.
interp_method: refer to minimal pair analysis as their methodological approach. This controlled linguistic diagnostic involves comparing two nearly identical linguistic items that differ in only one specific aspect, making it well-suited for probing anti-presuppositions. Minimal pair analysis is a well-established technique for diagnosing syntactic knowledge in LLMs and has been shown to effectively reveal how models process subtle linguistic contrasts.
main_findings: examined whether large language models (LLMs) follow the Maximize Presupposition! (MP!) principle by analyzing their predictions for masked tokens involving anti-presupposition triggers. The findings reveal that LLMs largely fail to adhere to this principle, instead relying on replicating words from the immediate context. They show striking difficulty with determiners, such as "the" versus "a/an," even in simple contexts, indicating challenges with fundamental grammatical roles that reflect aspects of syntactic knowledge. For triggers like "both" and "all," models often predicted numerals incorrectly, suggesting limitations in understanding basic word meanings and presuppositions. Fine-tuning on NLI datasets had minimal effect, as models continued to over-rely on context-based replication without truly capturing underlying linguistic principles. Overall, the study highlights that LLMs struggle with core elements of linguistic reasoning, including the syntactic handling of function words, revealing broader limitations in their grammatical and syntactic competence.

title: Linguistic Frameworks Go Toe-to-Toe at Neuro-Symbolic Language Modeling
abstract: We examine the extent to which, in principle, linguistic graph representations can complement and improve neural language modeling. With an ensemble setup consisting of a pretrained Transformer and ground-truth graphs from one of 7 different formalisms, we find that, overall, semantic constituency structures are most useful to language modeling performance -- outpacing syntactic constituency structures as well as syntactic and semantic dependency structures. Further, effects vary greatly depending on part-of-speech class. In sum, our findings point to promising tendencies in neuro-symbolic language modeling and invite future research quantifying the design choices made by different formalisms.
specific_phenomena: hierarchically nested syntactic constituents and phrase structure, as specified in PTB trees, along with functional labels in the PTB-fxn formalism. They address syntactic dependencies, particularly in Universal Dependencies (UD), including forward-pointing dependencies, and structural features like deep NP nesting, VP-nesting, verb attachment, and modifiers, which can influence a model’s ability to utilize nouns, verbs, and adjuncts. Other discussed phenomena include subject-verb agreement, grammatical relations, and word order patterns, all of which are encoded to varying degrees in SLRs.
