Finally, the authors define structural relative types for slicing—parents, siblings, grandparents, parents’ siblings, children, and coparents—to capture context relevant for next-token prediction within the graph-structured representations.
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language dataset consists of sentences from the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), representing authentic, domain-specific English text, specifically in the financial news domain. These sentences are annotated with syntactic and semantic formalisms from the Penn Treebank (PTB) and the MRP 2019 & 2020 shared tasks.
interp_method: present it as a “computationally inexpensive method for statically and deterministically projecting slices into a high-dimensional space by vector concatenation.” Second, when comparing to an R-GCN baseline, they refer to it as “concatenation-based slice vector encoding.” More generally, the method is framed as a “framework-agnostic neural encoding scheme” for linguistic graphs, emphasizing its flexibility across different graph formalisms and neural architectures.
main_findings: indicate that symbolic linguistic representations (SLRs), particularly those capturing syntactic and semantic structure, significantly enhance neural language modeling performance. Incorporating ground-truth linguistic graphs into GPT-2 yields substantial gains across metrics like perplexity, accuracy, and confidence, demonstrating that base models trained on raw text alone do not fully internalize these structures. Among SLR formalisms, semantic constituency graphs were most effective, outperforming syntactic constituency and dependency-based representations, likely because constituency graphs leverage higher-level structural relations beyond immediate token dependencies. Word-class analyses revealed nuanced effects: SLRs improved modeling for most parts of speech, but nouns were an exception, with some syntactic constituency graphs even harming performance due to nested structures and slicing limitations. Dependency structures (UD) were especially useful for verbs, while constituency representations (PTB, PTG) helped with adpositions and subordinating conjunctions. Ablation studies confirmed that models rely heavily on the structural arrangement of graph nodes and anchoring of tokens, with shuffled or perturbed graphs drastically reducing performance. Overall, the findings suggest that while pretrained LMs encode shallow syntactic knowledge, explicit symbolic representations—particularly those capturing deeper and more abstract structural and semantic relations—provide critical complementary information, enhancing next-word prediction and reinforcing the importance of structured linguistic guidance in neural language modeling.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP models with CheckList
abstract: Although measuring held-out accuracy has been the primary approach to evaluate generalization, it often overestimates the performance of NLP models, while alternative approaches for evaluating models either focus on individual tasks or on specific behaviors. Inspired by principles of behavioral testing in software engineering, we introduce CheckList, a task-agnostic methodology for testing NLP models. CheckList includes a matrix of general linguistic capabilities and test types that facilitate comprehensive test ideation, as well as a software tool to generate a large and diverse number of test cases quickly. We illustrate the utility of CheckList with tests for three tasks, identifying critical failures in both commercial and state-of-art models. In a user study, a team responsible for a commercial sentiment analysis model found new and actionable bugs in an extensively tested model. In another user study, NLP practitioners with CheckList created twice as many tests, and found almost three times as many bugs as users without it.
syntactic_phenomena: POS, Binding and coreference, negation and NPIs, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: part-of-speech (POS) understanding; Named Entity Recognition (NER), Coreference resolution, Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) including active/passive alternations. Logic tests further probe understanding of relationships like symmetry and conjunctions, reflecting syntactic and semantic comprehension, Negation
fine_tuning_materials: BERT-large finetuned on SQuAD
experimental_materials_comment: Controlled stimuli are generated through templates and Minimum Functionality Tests (MFTs), which create simple, targeted examples to evaluate specific capabilities, such as negation. For instance, a template like "I {NEGATION} {POS_VERB} the {THING}" can be systematically filled with words from pre-built lexicons to generate numerous controlled test cases, ensuring focused assessment of model behavior. On the other hand, naturalistic language is leveraged through perturbation-based tests applied to real-world data, such as unlabeled airline tweets. Invariance (INV) and Directional Expectation (DIR) tests introduce controlled changes to these naturally-occurring inputs, allowing evaluation on realistic language while retaining systematic testing benefits.
interp_method: task-agnostic methodology for testing Natural Language Processing (NLP) models. It is also referred to as a new evaluation methodology and accompanying tool for comprehensive behavioral testing of NLP models. introduce CheckList, a task-agnostic methodology and software tool for comprehensively testing the behavior of Natural Language Processing (NLP) models. Inspired by software engineering’s black-box testing approach, CheckList evaluates a model’s input-output behavior without requiring knowledge of its internal architecture. The methodology is organized around a conceptual matrix that assesses different linguistic capabilities—such as negation, vocabulary, and named entity recognition (NER)—through three types of tests: Minimum Functionality Tests (MFTs), which target specific behaviors with simple unit-test-like examples; Invariance Tests (INVs), which apply label-preserving perturbations to check whether predictions remain stable; and Directional Expectation Tests (DIRs), which introduce changes expected to alter predictions in a known direction.
main_findings: CheckList, a task-agnostic methodology for evaluating NLP models, revealed that even state-of-the-art language models like BERT and RoBERTa exhibit significant limitations in core linguistic capabilities despite high benchmark accuracy. In terms of syntactic knowledge, these models struggled with negation, failing simple Minimum Functionality Tests in sentiment analysis and machine comprehension, particularly when negation occurred at the end of a sentence or was separated from sentiment-bearing words. Coreference resolution was also weak, as models often misidentified pronouns such as “he/she” or “his/her,” highlighting gaps in syntactic and semantic understanding. Semantic role labeling posed challenges, with BERT and RoBERTa unable to reliably track agents, predicates, or active/passive alternations. Temporal distinctions such as “before” versus “after” were frequently misinterpreted, and models showed high sensitivity to minor perturbations like typos or added URLs, indicating reliance on surface patterns. Additionally, finetuned BERT models displayed errors in named entity recognition and struggled with vocabulary, part-of-speech distinctions, and taxonomic reasoning, failing to account for modifiers, synonyms, or antonyms. Overall, these results indicate that high accuracy on standard benchmarks often masks deficiencies in fundamental syntactic and semantic processing, with models relying on shortcuts rather than a genuine understanding of language structure.

title: Intermediate-Task Transfer Learning with Pretrained Models for Natural Language Understanding: When and Why Does It Work?
abstract: While pretrained models such as BERT have shown large gains across natural language understanding tasks, their performance can be improved by further training the model on a data-rich intermediate task, before fine-tuning it on a target task. However, it is still poorly understood when and why intermediate-task training is beneficial for a given target task. To investigate this, we perform a large-scale study on the pretrained RoBERTa model with 110 intermediate-target task combinations. We further evaluate all trained models with 25 probing tasks meant to reveal the specific skills that drive transfer. We observe that intermediate tasks requiring high-level inference and reasoning abilities tend to work best. We also observe that target task performance is strongly correlated with higher-level abilities such as coreference resolution. However, we fail to observe more granular correlations between probing and target task performance, highlighting the need for further work on broad-coverage probing benchmarks. We also observe evidence that the forgetting of knowledge learned during pretraining may limit our analysis, highlighting the need for further work on transfer learning methods in these settings.
syntactic_phenomena: Argument Structure and other Constructions, POS, Hierarchical structure, benchmark, Dependency parsing and constituency
specific_phenomena: SentEval, Acceptability Judgment (AJ), and Edge-Probing (EP) tasks. Key phenomena include:, General Grammaticality/Acceptability:, AJ-CoLA (Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability): Assesses a model’s understanding of general grammaticality., AJ-EOS (End of Sentence): Tests the ability to identify grammatical sentences without standard indicators like punctuation or capitalization., Specific Syntactic Features and Structures:, AJ-WH (Wh-word Detection): Evaluates detection of swapped wh-words and the model’s ability to link wh-words to their antecedents., AJ-Def (Definite/Indefinite Articles): Checks if the model can detect swapped definite/indefinite articles., AJ-Coord (Coordinating Conjunctions): Assesses understanding of relationships between clauses via conjunctions., EP-POS (Part-of-Speech Tagging): Measures the ability to assign correct syntactic categories to words., EP-Const (Constituent Labeling): Tests classification of spans into phrases like noun or verb phrases., EP-UD (Dependency Labeling): Evaluates understanding of functional relationships between tokens., SE-TreeDepth (Tree Depth): Measures ability to estimate maximum depth of a sentence’s constituency parse tree., SE-TopConst (Top Constituents): Tests identification of high-level syntactic structure via constituent sequences., SE-BShift (Bigram Shift): Evaluates detection of reordered consecutive tokens., SE-CoordInv (Coordination Inversion): Checks if coordinating clauses have been swapped., SE-Tense (Past-Present): Assesses identification of main verb tense., SE-SubjNum (Subject Number) & SE-ObjNum (Object Number): Test classification of singular vs. plural subjects or direct objects., Metadata-level Phenomena Related to Syntax:, SE-SentLen (Sentence Length): Evaluates the ability to classify sentence length., SE-SOMO (Odd-Man-Out): Measures detection of random replacements of content words with others of the same part of speech.
fine_tuning_materials: SuperGLUE
experimental_materials_comment: combine naturalistic language and controlled stimuli; Naturalistic language is drawn from diverse real-world sources across intermediate tasks (e.g., QAMR, CommonsenseQA, SciTail, Cosmos QA, SocialIQA, CCG, QA-SRL, SST-2, QQP, MNLI), target tasks (e.g., SuperGLUE benchmarks like CB, COPA, RTE, MultiRC, WiC, BoolQ, ReCoRD), and probing tasks (e.g., Edge-Probing and SentEval tasks), reflecting authentic language use. Controlled stimuli or modified naturalistic language are used to test narrow behaviors or introduce specific challenges, such as HellaSwag’s adversarially filtered examples, Winograd Schema Challenge items requiring world knowledge, Acceptability Judgment tasks (AJ-CoLA, AJ-WH, AJ-Def, AJ-Coord, AJ-EOS) with swapped function words or removed cues, Edge-Probing tasks targeting difficult cases like definite pronoun resolution, and SentEval “input noising” tasks (SE-BShift, SE-CoordInv, SE-SOMO) that manipulate sentence structure or content.
interp_method: refer to the method for improving pretrained models as STILTs, which stands for Supplementary Training on Intermediate Labeled-data Tasks. This approach involves first fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task and then fine-tuning it again on the target task of interest. The process is also generally described as intermediate-task training or intermediate-task transfer learning.
main_findings: examined when and why intermediate-task training benefits Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks using pretrained RoBERTa across 110 intermediate–target task combinations and 25 probing tasks. Overall, intermediate tasks requiring high-level inference, such as NLI and commonsense QA (e.g., MNLI, CommonsenseQA, HellaSwag, Cosmos QA), were most effective, whereas tasks like SocialIQA, CCG, and QQP often led to negative transfer. Focusing on syntactic knowledge, intermediate-task training had little to no impact on SentEval probing tasks, which assess low-level syntactic skills such as sentence length, tree depth, top constituents, bigram shifts, coordination inversion, main verb tense, and subject/object number. Improvements were somewhat observed for acceptability judgment tasks (AJ-WH, AJ-Def, AJ-Coord, AJ-EOS), though these gains generally did not correlate with target-task performance, except for AJ-CoLA. Edge-Probing tasks revealed that higher-level semantic abilities—coreference, semantic proto-role labeling, and relation classification—were more predictive of target-task success than low-level syntactic skills. Additionally, intermediate-task training sometimes caused catastrophic forgetting, particularly for probing tasks similar to RoBERTa’s masked language modeling objective (SE-BShift, SE-SOMO, SE-CoordInv), indicating that negative transfer may partially result from loss of pretraining knowledge. Overall, while intermediate-task training can modestly improve certain syntactic capabilities, these gains do not appear to strongly influence downstream NLU performance

title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the linguistic similarity and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory.
model_name_comment: 104 LLMs: llama2, llama3, TinyLlama, yi, olmo, qwen, SeaLLMs, SmolLM, gemma, gpt2, gpt-Neo, opt, InternLM-2.5, phi, pythia, distilbert
specific_phenomena: BLiMP, include argument structure (e.g., passive, transitive), ellipsis, filler-gap dependencies, island effects, S-selection, binding (Principle A cases), and control raising. In Chinese (SLING), phenomena span alternative questions, anaphors, anaphor agreement, argument structure, aspect, floating quantifier agreement, government, negation, noun phrase agreement, relative clauses, reflexives, and subject-predicate agreement. Russian (RuBLiMP) includes anaphor agreement, floating quantifier agreement, government, negation, noun phrase agreement, and subject-predicate agreement.
experimental_materials_comment: controlled linguistic minimal pairs, which are sentence pairs differing in only a single word or phrase, with one sentence grammatical and the other ungrammatical. This design ensures that differences in LLM activations for each pair primarily reflect the model’s representation of the specific linguistic phenomenon, minimizing the influence of other factors such as topic or semantic meaning. The study draws on three established datasets: BLiMP for English, SLING for Chinese, and RuBLiMP for Russian, encompassing a total of 150,000 minimal pairs across 67 English, 38 Chinese, and 45 Russian linguistic phenomena, with approximately 1,000 pairs per phenomenon.
interp_method: refer to their method as linguistic similarity, which uses linguistic minimal pairs to probe how Large Language Models (LLMs) internally represent linguistic phenomena. The process involves three main steps: first, extracting the model’s hidden activations for each sentence in a minimal pair; second, computing the activation differences between the paired sentences, isolating the representation of the specific linguistic phenomenon while canceling out other content; and third, measuring the similarity between these activation differences—using cosine similarity—to quantify how similarly the model represents different linguistic phenomena.
main_findings: probe the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By subtracting the models’ hidden activations for each pair and comparing the resulting differences via cosine similarity, the researchers derived a measure of linguistic similarity across phenomena. Key findings include: consistency in linguistic similarity is strongly influenced by training data exposure, with higher-resource languages like English showing greater alignment than Chinese or Russian; LLMs’ representations align closely with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories, especially for syntactic and syntax-semantics phenomena, although this alignment weakens at broader hierarchical levels; some phenomena exhibit high similarity even across theoretical category boundaries, suggesting linguistic similarity can refine our understanding of language structure; linguistic similarity is only weakly correlated with semantic similarity, indicating context-dependent representations; and in multilingual LLMs, phenomena cluster primarily by language but show cross-lingual “attraction” for corresponding phenomena, indicating partial alignment across languages. The experiments span over 100 LLMs and 150,000 minimal pairs across English, Chinese, and Russian.

title: Syntactic Inductive Bias in Transformer Language Models: Especially Helpful for Low-Resource Languages?
abstract: A line of work on Transformer-based language models such as BERT has attempted to use syntactic inductive bias to enhance the pretraining process, on the theory that building syntactic structure into the training process should reduce the amount of data needed for training. But such methods are often tested for high-resource languages such as English. In this work, we investigate whether these methods can compensate for data sparseness in low-resource languages, hypothesizing that they ought to be more effective for low-resource languages. We experiment with five low-resource languages: Uyghur, Wolof, Maltese, Coptic, and Ancient Greek. We find that these syntactic inductive bias methods produce uneven results in low-resource settings, and provide surprisingly little benefit in most cases.
specific_phenomena: direct objects, subjects, sibling and child tokens, and syntactically local tokens—defined by proximity in dependency parse trees. main clause's predicate and its arguments, are also highlighted as crucial syntactic dependencies. syntactic structures, including subtrees, with a focus on short subtrees (limited to three nodes in SynCLM), phrase-level constituents like noun phrases, and broader clausal and inter-clausal dependencies. The concept of the lowest common ancestor in parse trees is central to defining positive training samples for the phrase-guided contrastive objective in SynCLM.
languages_tested_comment: Uyghur, Wolof, Maltese, Coptic, Ancient Greek
experimental_materials_comment: combination of naturalistic language data and controlled stimuli to evaluate syntactic knowledge in Transformer Language Models (TLMs). Naturalistic data includes corpora such as Wikipedia, Universal Dependencies treebanks, WikiAnn, AMALGUM, the English Web Treebank, and a subset of BERT’s pretraining data. These sources provide real-world text for pretraining and evaluation. In contrast, the PrOnto benchmark serves as a more controlled stimulus, constructed through aligned and annotated New Testament verses to probe specific linguistic phenomena.
Mechanistic_method: Inductive Bias, manipulate model architecture, Modified Self-Attention
interp_method: explores several specific methods aimed at integrating Syntactic Inductive Bias (SIB) into Transformer Language Models (TLMs), particularly for improving performance in low-resource language settings. The key methods include SynCLM (Syntax-guided Contrastive Language Model), which combines two novel contrastive loss functions—phrase-guided and tree-guided objectives—to guide models toward syntactic structure during training, and SLA (Syntax-aware Local Attention), which restricts attention to syntactically local tokens based on dependency parses. These approaches are implemented within MicroBERT, a compact BERT-like model designed for experimentation with various combinations of syntax-related enhancements. Model variants (e.g., µB-MP, µB-MPT-SLA, µB-MXPT) combine different configurations of loss functions, SLA, and auxiliary tasks like part-of-speech tagging. While the study benchmarks these against baselines like MBERT and MBERT-VA, it finds that SIB methods yield limited and inconsistent improvements, especially in low-resource languages, prompting a call for future work to focus on higher-level syntactic representations.
main_findings: evaluates the effectiveness of syntactic inductive bias (SIB) methods—SynCLM and SLA—in enhancing syntactic knowledge in Transformer Language Models (TLMs), particularly in low-resource language settings. Contrary to expectations, the results show limited and inconsistent benefits of these SIB methods. In low-resource scenarios, SIB did not significantly improve performance on syntactic tasks like Universal Dependencies parsing and only offered modest gains in Named Entity Recognition (NER), primarily when not combined with part-of-speech tagging. In the PrOnto benchmark, improvements were similarly inconsistent. The research also found that SIB methods were more sensitive to data quantity than to parse quality or model size, offering some gains in low-data English settings but degrading performance in higher-data ones. While self-attention mechanisms in TLMs show syntactic sensitivity, the inductive biases applied here—focused on low-level syntactic structures (e.g., phrases)—may be insufficient, as TLMs might already capture such information without guidance. The authors suggest that future SIB methods should target higher-level syntactic structures, such as clause-level dependencies, to more effectively support syntactic learning in low-resource contexts.

title: Analyzing Redundancy in Pretrained Transformer Models
abstract: Transformer-based deep NLP models are trained using hundreds of millions of parameters, limiting their applicability in computationally constrained environments. In this paper, we study the cause of these limitations by defining a notion of Redundancy, which we categorize into two classes: General Redundancy and Task-specific Redundancy. We dissect two popular pretrained models, BERT and XLNet, studying how much redundancy they exhibit at a representation-level and at a more fine-grained neuron-level. Our analysis reveals interesting insights, such as i) 85% of the neurons across the network are redundant and ii) at least 92% of them can be removed when optimizing towards a downstream task. Based on our analysis, we present an efficient feature-based transfer learning procedure, which maintains 97% performance while using at-most 10% of the original neurons.
specific_phenomena: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, CCG super tagging, and syntactic chunking
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language: for general redundancy analysis, they employed the Penn Treebank development set (~44,000 tokens). For task-specific analysis, they considered two main categories: sequence labeling (core linguistic tasks) and sequence classification tasks. Sequence labeling tasks included POS tagging (Penn TreeBank), CCG super tagging (CCGBank), semantic tagging (Parallel Meaning Bank), and syntactic chunking (CoNLL 2000). Sequence classification tasks were drawn from the GLUE benchmark, including SST-2 (sentiment analysis), MRPC (semantic equivalence), MNLI and QNLI (natural language inference), QQP (question pair similarity), RTE (textual entailment), and STS-B (semantic textual similarity).
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Activation Patching (Ablation), Centered Kernel Alignment
interp_method: method for efficient feature-based transfer learning, structured into three steps. Step 1, called LayerSelector (LS), uses task-specific layer classifiers to identify the lowest layer that maintains oracle performance. Steps 2 and 3 are combined into CCFS (Correlation Clustering + Feature Selection): Step 2 employs Correlation Clustering (CC) to remove generally redundant neurons, while Step 3 applies Linguistic Correlation Analysis (Feature Selection, FS) to identify a minimal set of task-specific neurons required for optimal performance. This three-step procedure systematically reduces both layer- and neuron-level redundancy while preserving task accuracy.
main_findings: investigates redundancy in large pretrained transformers such as BERT and XLNet, categorizing it into general and task-specific redundancy at both the layer and neuron levels. Their analysis reveals extremely high neuron-level redundancy, with up to 85% of BERT neurons and 92% of XLNet neurons being removable without accuracy loss, most of which occurs within the same or neighboring layers. Layer-level analysis shows adjacent layers are highly similar, except for the final layers, which are more task-specific. Task-specific pruning can remove over 92% of neurons for downstream tasks, with XLNet generally more redundant than BERT. Core language tasks, particularly syntactic ones like POS tagging, CCG super tagging, and chunking, require more neurons and utilize lower layers, whereas sequence-level tasks can perform well with very few neurons and layers. Leveraging these insights, the authors propose an efficient transfer learning method that prunes redundant neurons and layers, reducing feature sets to fewer than 100 neurons while maintaining over 97% of original performance and achieving up to 6.2× speedups, with recommendations for pyramid-style architectures featuring wider lower layers and narrower higher layers to optimize efficiency.

title: Not All Models Localize Linguistic Knowledge in the Same Place: A Layer-wise Probing on BERToids' Representations
abstract: Most of the recent works on probing representations have focused on BERT, with the presumption that the findings might be similar to the other models. In this work, we extend the probing studies to two other models in the family, namely ELECTRA and XLNet, showing that variations in the pre-training objectives or architectural choices can result in different behaviors in encoding linguistic information in the representations. Most notably, we observe that ELECTRA tends to encode linguistic knowledge in the deeper layers, whereas XLNet instead concentrates that in the earlier layers. Also, the former model undergoes a slight change during fine-tuning, whereas the latter experiences significant adjustments. Moreover, we show that drawing conclusions based on the weight mixing evaluation strategy -- which is widely used in the context of layer-wise probing -- can be misleading given the norm disparity of the representations across different layers. Instead, we adopt an alternative information-theoretic probing with minimum description length, which has recently been proven to provide more reliable and informative results.
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Binding and coreference, Argument Structure and other Constructions
specific_phenomena: Dependency Labeling, Named Entity Recognition (NER), Semantic Role Labeling (SRL), Coreference Resolution, and Relation Classification
fine_tuning_materials: MNLI
experimental_materials_comment: relied on datasets of naturalistic language rather than controlled stimuli, though they do not explicitly frame them as such. For probing pretrained representations across NLP tasks like dependency labeling, named entity recognition (NER), semantic role labeling (SRL), coreference resolution, and relation classification, the authors used OntoNotes 5.0 (NER, SRL, coreference), the English Web Treebank (dependencies), and SemEval 2010 Task 8 (relation classification). For computing representation norms and conducting Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), samples of 500 tokens or 5,000 sentences from OPUS were used. For fine-tuning and evaluating models, MNLI was the primary dataset, with CoLA and SST-2 included for complementary result
interp_method: use Minimum Description Length (MDL) probing for their layer-wise analysis, an information-theoretic method designed to measure how much linguistic knowledge is encoded in model representations and how much effort is needed to extract it. Proposed by Voita and Titov (2020), MDL probing addresses limitations of conventional "weight mixing" probes, which can be misleading due to layer-wise norm disparities, and provides more interpretable and reliable results by probing each layer separately. The authors implement the online coding method, where the probe is progressively trained on varying amounts of data and the cross-entropy for each portion is summed to compute the final codelength. They use compression (c), defined as the uniform codelength divided by the MDL, as the evaluation metric, with higher values indicating better encoding. MDL probing is applied to pre-trained and fine-tuned BERT, XLNet, and ELECTRA across core NLP tasks, including Dependency Labeling, Named Entity Recognition, Semantic Role Labeling, Coreference Resolution, and Relation Classification.
main_findings: examines how BERT, XLNet, and ELECTRA encode and distribute linguistic knowledge, including syntactic information, across their layers and how fine-tuning affects this distribution. Encoding behaviors differ across models: ELECTRA encodes linguistic and syntactic knowledge in deeper layers and achieves the highest compression scores, XLNet concentrates it in earlier layers, and BERT accumulates it in middle layers. These patterns are influenced by pre-training objectives—ELECTRA’s replaced token detection encourages deeper, context-aware representations, whereas BERT and XLNet’s token recovery objective leads to diminished linguistic information in final layers. Fine-tuning effects vary: XLNet undergoes larger representational changes in higher layers, making it more prone to forgetting linguistic knowledge but allowing more task-specific adaptation; ELECTRA changes minimally, reflecting its robust pre-trained encoding. Across models, fine-tuning often shifts information toward earlier layers as final-layer linguistic knowledge is replaced by task-specific features. The study also critiques conventional layer-wise probing, favoring Minimum Description Length (MDL) probing for more reliable evaluation. Focusing on syntactic knowledge via Dependency Labeling using the English Web Treebank, layer-wise MDL results confirm model-specific patterns: XLNet peaks in early layers, BERT in middle layers, and ELECTRA in deeper layers, with ELECTRA showing the highest overall quality for syntactic encoding.

title: Emergent Linguistic Structures in Neural Networks are Fragile
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been reported to have strong performance on natural language processing tasks. However, performance metrics such as accuracy do not measure the quality of the model in terms of its ability to robustly represent complex linguistic structures. In this paper, focusing on the ability of language models to represent syntax, we propose a framework to assess the consistency and robustness of linguistic representations. To this end, we introduce measures of robustness of neural network models that leverage recent advances in extracting linguistic constructs from LLMs via probing tasks, i.e., simple tasks used to extract meaningful information about a single facet of a language model, such as syntax reconstruction and root identification. Empirically, we study the performance of four LLMs across six different corpora on the proposed robustness measures by analysing their performance and robustness with respect to syntax-preserving perturbations. We provide evidence that context-free representation (e.g., GloVe) are in some cases competitive with context-dependent representations from modern LLMs (e.g., BERT), yet equally brittle to syntax-preserving perturbations. Our key observation is that emergent syntactic representations in neural networks are brittle. We make the code, trained models and logs available to the community as a contribution to the debate about the capabilities of LLMs.
specific_phenomena: dependency reconstruction, POS tagging, root identification, and tree-depth estimation, often reducing results to near-random levels. Deeper latent features do not confer additional robustness, and subtle perturbations with minimal representational distance can severely impair syntactic understanding.
fine_tuning_materials: SST-2
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language and controlled stimuli. Naturalistic language consists of datasets from the English Universal Dependencies collection, which represent real-world linguistic input annotated with syntactic information such as POS tags and dependency relations. Controlled stimuli are systematic perturbations designed to evaluate the robustness of linguistic representations. These include: (1) Consistent POS Substitution (coPOS), which replaces words with synonyms while preserving syntactic roles to maintain the dependency structure; (2) Context Consistent Substitution (coCO), which uses GPT-2 to generate semantically consistent word substitutions that may not fully preserve syntax; and (3) Baseline perturbations, which replace words randomly without regard for syntactic structure.
interp_method: 3 perturbation methods to evaluate syntactic robustness: coPOS (Consistent POS Substitution): Replaces words with synonyms that maintain the original word’s part-of-speech (POS), preserving the sentence’s syntactic structure. WordNet synonyms are chosen to maximize Hamming distance (number of words changed) while minimizing syntactic disruption. Misclassifications under this method indicate weaknesses in the model’s syntactic representation. coCO (Context Consistent Substitution): Uses a generative model (e.g., GPT-2) to replace words with contextually appropriate alternatives that maintain semantic meaning but do not strictly preserve syntactic coherence. Baseline Perturbation: Randomly substitutes words from the English vocabulary without regard for syntactic or semantic consistency, serving as a control to measure the effect of unconstrained perturbations.
main_findings: demonstrates that syntactic knowledge in language models (LLMs) is highly fragile. Both context-dependent models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) and context-free embeddings (e.g., GloVe, Word2Vec) show brittle representations of complex syntax, challenging the assumption that contextual embeddings inherently capture syntax better. Even syntax-preserving perturbations, such as coPOS substitutions, drastically degrade performance on dependency reconstruction, POS tagging, root identification, and tree-depth estimation, often reducing accuracy to near-random levels. Deeper layers do not guarantee more robustness, and even subtle local changes can severely disrupt syntactic understanding. Context-aware perturbations (coCO) have similarly disruptive effects. Fine-tuning generally weakens syntactic performance, and counter-fitting for context-free embeddings fails to improve robustness. The findings suggest that syntactic structures in LLMs emerge from fitting sentences to their syntax trees but collapse under word substitutions, a shift that humans easily handle. Traditional metrics like Spearman correlation are unreliable, as they can indicate high similarity even when syntactic structures are significantly altered.

title: Holmes A Benchmark to Assess the Linguistic Competence of Language Models
abstract: We introduce Holmes, a new benchmark designed to assess language models’ (LMs’) linguistic competence—their unconscious understanding of linguistic phenomena. Specifically, we use classifier-based probing to examine LMs’ internal representations regarding distinct linguistic phenomena (e.g., part-of-speech tagging). As a result, we meet recent calls to disentangle LMs’ linguistic competence from other cognitive abilities, such as following instructions in prompting-based evaluations. Composing Holmes, we review over 270 probing studies and include more than 200 datasets to assess syntax, morphology, semantics, reasoning, and discourse phenomena. Analyzing over 50 LMs reveals that, aligned with known trends, their linguistic competence correlates with model size. However, surprisingly, model architecture and instruction tuning also significantly influence performance, particularly in morphology and syntax. Finally, we propose FlashHolmes, a streamlined version that reduces the computation load while maintaining high-ranking precision.

Controlled stimuli involve minimal pairs and targeted datasets to test specific linguistic phenomena: BLiMP provides 67 tasks on morphology, syntax, and semantics (e.g., island effects); Zorro contributes 21 tasks for validating linguistic contrasts; oLMpics generates lexical reasoning probes; Context Probes assess knowledge of word properties (e.g., animacy, verb dynamics); and negation datasets evaluate understanding of negation cues and scope. T
interp_method: benchmark FlashHolmes is introduced as a benchmark for assessing a model’s linguistic competence—its implicit understanding of language—independently from its observable performance, while FlashHolmes offers a computationally cheaper version that preserves ranking precision by omitting selected samples. A central technique within Holmes is classifier-based probing, also called diagnostic classifiers, where simple linear probes are trained on a model’s internal representations to predict linguistic features such as part-of-speech tags. The sources also discuss CheckList, a task-agnostic behavioral testing framework for NLP models that uses Minimum Functionality Tests (MFT) to check specific capabilities, Invariance Tests (INV) to verify that label-preserving input changes do not alter predictions, and Directional Expectation Tests (DIR) to confirm that perturbations influence outputs in predictable ways. Finally, information-theoretic probing evaluates how clearly linguistic information is encoded in internal representations by applying concepts such as minimum description length and compression.
main_findings: introduce Holmes, a benchmark for assessing the linguistic competence of language models (LMs), along with FlashHolmes, a computationally efficient version that maintains high ranking precision. Holmes reveals that LMs exhibit strong competence in morphology and syntax, likely due to their reliance on local word neighborhoods during pre-training, whereas performance is weaker on semantic, reasoning, and discourse phenomena. Linguistic competence generally scales with model size, with noticeable gains beyond 0.5–1.0 billion parameters, and is strongly influenced by model architecture: encoder-only LMs (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) outperform decoder-only models (e.g., GPT-2, LLaMA-2), even at much larger scales, due to their bidirectional token encoding. Instruction tuning improves morphology and syntax performance (+10% and +5%, respectively), though effects on other phenomena are mixed, suggesting superficial alignment. Holmes employs classifier-based probing to reliably measure linguistic knowledge, avoiding conflation with instruction-following behavior typical of prompting-based evaluations. The benchmark covers 75 syntactic tasks, including POS and constituent labeling, dependency labeling, bigram shifts, tree-depth, top-constituent tasks, subject- and object-number, alternations, binding, control/raising, negative polarity item licensing, island effects, argument structure, ellipsis, and filler-gap phenomena, providing a comprehensive view of syntactic competence in LMs.

title: Sneaking Syntax into Transformer Language Models with Tree Regularization
abstract: While compositional accounts of human language understanding are based on a hierarchical tree-like process, neural models like transformers lack a direct inductive bias for such tree structures. Introducing syntactic inductive biases could unlock more robust and data-efficient learning in transformer language models (LMs), but existing methods for incorporating such structure greatly restrict models, either limiting their expressivity or increasing inference complexity. This work instead aims to softly inject syntactic inductive biases into given transformer circuits, through a structured regularizer. We introduce TreeReg, an auxiliary loss function that converts bracketing decisions from silver parses into a set of differentiable orthogonality constraints on vector hidden states. TreeReg integrates seamlessly with the standard LM objective, requiring no architectural changes. LMs pre-trained with TreeReg on natural language corpora such as WikiText-103 achieve up to 10% lower perplexities on out-of-distribution data and up to 9.5 point improvements in syntactic generalization, requiring less than half the training data to outperform standard LMs. TreeReg still provides gains for pre-trained LLMs: Continued pre-training of Sheared Llama with TreeReg results in improved syntactic generalization, and fine-tuning on MultiNLI with TreeReg mitigates degradation of performance on adversarial NLI benchmarks by 41.2 points. We release all code to guide future research.
specific_phenomena: Licensing, Gross Syntactic State, Garden Path Effects, Center Embedding, Agreement, Long Distance Dependencies
fine_tuning_materials: MultiNLI was used for fine-tuning the Sheared Llama-1.3B model.
experimental_materials_comment: For naturalistic corpora, WikiText-103 was used to pre-train GPT-2-small models, particularly in cases where the pre-training and parsed data came from different sources. BLLIP-LG, an already-parsed dataset, was utilized to train 16-layer language models from scratch and for continued pre-training of the Sheared Llama-1.3B model, with its parses also leveraged for TREEREG training when main LM training occurred on WikiText-103. The Penn TreeBank (PTB), a manually annotated corpus, was employed to evaluate out-of-distribution generalization via perplexity and to assess parsing capabilities of TREEREG-trained models. controlled: BLiMP, which presents minimal pairs of grammatical and ungrammatical sentences, and SyntaxGym (SG), which evaluates six syntactic phenomena: Licensing, Gross Syntactic State, Garden Path Effects, Center Embedding, Agreement, and Long Distance Dependencies, using surprisal-based constraints. Adversarial NLI benchmarks such as MoNLI and MED were included to test whether TREEREG fine-tuning mitigates spurious shortcut learning. Finally, the 4000 Questions dataset was employed to evaluate parsing capabilities on a domain distinct from newswire text
Mechanistic_method: Inductive Bias (orthogonality constraints), manipulate model architecture
interp_method: TREEREG is a novel differentiable loss function designed to softly inject syntactic inductive biases into transformer language models (LMs) without requiring any architectural changes. It works by converting bracketing decisions from silver parses into differentiable orthogonality constraints on vector hidden states
main_findings: TREEREG is a differentiable loss function that injects syntactic inductive biases into transformer language models (LMs) without modifying their architecture. By converting constituency bracketing from silver parses into differentiable orthogonality constraints on hidden states, TREEREG enhances syntactic generalization, enabling faster grokking and higher performance on diagnostic sentence transformation tasks like Tense Inflection and Question Formation. It improves scores on syntactic test suites such as BLiMP and SyntaxGym, lowers perplexity on out-of-distribution data, and mitigates adversarial performance degradation. TREEREG also increases sample efficiency, achieving better syntactic generalization with significantly less training data. Additionally, it implicitly encodes constituency parses in hidden states, yielding strong parsing capabilities with emergent syntactic structure across intermediate layers. The benefits rely on alignment with true syntactic parses rather than arbitrary structure, and TREEREG integrates seamlessly with standard LM training, adding modest computational overhead while leaving inference complexity unchanged. Overall, TREEREG effectively enhances transformers’ syntactic competence, generalization, and sample efficiency while preserving their original architecture.

title: Exploring Linguistic Properties of Monolingual BERTs with Typological Classification among Languages
abstract: The impressive achievements of transformers force NLP researchers to delve into how these models represent the underlying structure of natural language. In this paper, we propose a novel standpoint to investigate the above issue: using typological similarities among languages to observe how their respective monolingual models encode structural information. We aim to layer-wise compare transformers for typologically similar languages to observe whether these similarities emerge for particular layers. For this investigation, we propose to use Centered Kernel Alignment to measure similarity among weight matrices. We found that syntactic typological similarity is consistent with the similarity between the weights in the middle layers, which are the pretrained BERT layers to which syntax encoding is generally attributed. Moreover, we observe that a domain adaptation on semantically equivalent texts enhances this similarity among weight matrices.

To control for semantic variability, the study used controlled stimuli in the form of domain adaptation: BERT models were fine-tuned on the EuroParl parallel corpus, which contains semantically equivalent sentences across languages.
interp_method: bidimensional Centered Kernel Alignment (biCKA): This method is described as a variant of the standard Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). While CKA is generally used to compare similarities between activation matrices, the authors introduced biCKA because CKA is not directly suitable for weight matrices, where both rows and columns play crucial roles. BiCKA specifically compares matrices by considering both their rows and columns. The authors explicitly state that biCKA is "our solution to compute the similarity between weight matrices".
main_findings: investigates how monolingual BERT models encode syntactic structure by comparing their layer-wise weight matrices across languages with varying typological similarities. Unlike traditional probing methods, the authors use bidimensional Centered Kernel Alignment (biCKA) to directly measure similarity between weight matrices, correlating these with linguistic typology from WALS. They find that syntactic information is primarily encoded in BERT’s middle layers (4–6), with the attention output dense (OA) and value (V) matrices showing the strongest correlations. Clustered language analyses confirm these results, highlighting features related to word order. Domain adaptation with semantically equivalent parallel corpora further strengthens these correlations, particularly in layers 2–6, while later layers focus more on semantic processing. Overall, the findings suggest that specific attention matrices in middle layers are critical for representing syntactic properties, providing a new, direct method to understand cross-linguistic patterns in BERT’s internal representations and offering potential avenues for explainable and targeted model adaptation.

title: Assessment of Pre-Trained Models Across Languages and Grammars
abstract: We present an approach for assessing how multilingual large language models (LLMs) learn syntax in terms of multi-formalism syn- tactic structures. We aim to recover constituent and dependency structures by casting parsing as sequence labeling. To do so, we select a few LLMs and study them on 13 diverse UD treebanks for dependency parsing and 10 tree- banks for constituent parsing. Our results show that: (i) the framework is consistent across en- codings, (ii) pre-trained word vectors do not favor constituency representations of syntax over dependencies, (iii) sub-word tokenization is needed to represent syntax, in contrast to character-based models, and (iv) occurrence of a language in the pretraining data is more important than the amount of task data when recovering syntax from the word vectors
model_name_comment: mBERT, xlm-roberta, and canine (-c and -s) model
specific_phenomena: constituent and dependency structures. Parsing tasks are cast as sequence labeling problems. dependency parsing: arcs and relations, using three encodings—head-selection, bracketing-based, and transition-based—and measures performance across arcs of different lengths and directions. constituent parsing: assesses common tree levels, lowest non-terminal symbols, leaf unary branches, and span lengths.

fine_tuning_materials: dependency parsing task
experimental_materials_comment: primarily consisted of naturalistic language data, specifically various treebanks: 13 Universal Dependencies (UD 2.9) treebanks in Skolt Sami, Guajajara, Ligurian, Bhojpuri, Kiche, Welsh, Armenian, Vietnamese, Chinese, Basque, Turkish, Bulgarian, Ancient Greek.  Penn Treebank (PTB) and Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB). 8 SPMRL shared task treebanks for rich-resource languages.
interp_method: Multi-paradigm, multilingual, recovery framework – emphasizes that it is the first framework to recover both dependency and constituent structures across multiple languages. Sequence-labeling framework – highlights the core technique, where parsing tasks are cast as sequence labeling problems to extract syntactic structures. Linear probing framework – situates their method within the broader linear probing paradigm, associating word vector sequences with linguistic properties.
main_findings: introduces a framework for evaluating how multilingual LLMs encode syntactic structures—both constituent and dependency—through sequence labeling, enabling a multilingual and multi-paradigm analysis. Key findings include the consistency of syntactic recoverability across different encoding schemes, emphasizing the reliability of the method. The research underscores the critical role of sub-word tokenization, with subword-based models like mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa outperforming character-based ones, especially in syntactic tasks. It also reveals that pretraining data coverage is more influential than task-specific data size: languages absent from pretraining data yielded weaker syntactic recovery, even with large treebanks. Importantly, no strong preference was found between constituent and dependency syntax representations in model encodings. While XLM-RoBERTa typically excels in downstream tasks, mBERT showed stronger frozen representations for syntax and better generalization to unseen languages. Overall, the findings suggest that while fine-tuning improves performance, static representations in LLMs already contain rich syntactic information—particularly when subword tokenization and pretraining coverage are in place.

title: On the utility of enhancing BERT syntactic bias with Token Reordering Pretraining
abstract: Self-supervised Language Modelling (LM) objectives —like BERT masked LM— have become the default choice for pretraining language models. TOken Reordering (TOR) pretraining objectives, beyond token prediction, have not been extensively studied yet. In this work, we explore challenges that underlie the development and usefulness of such objectives on downstream language tasks. In particular, we design a novel TOR pretraining objective which predicts whether two tokens are adjacent or not given a partial bag-of-tokens input. In addition, we investigate the usefulness of Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN), when placed on top of the BERT encoder, in order to enhance the overall model ability to leverage topological signal from the encoded representations. We compare language understanding abilities of TOR to the one of MLM on word-order sensitive (e.g. Dependency Parsing) and insensitive (e.g. text classification) tasks in both full training and few-shot settings. Our results indicate that TOR is competitive to MLM on the GLUE language understanding benchmark, and slightly superior on syntax-dependent datasets, especially in the few-shot setting.
specific_phenomena: word-order/token-order; token positions and neighbor relationships; syntactic cues, abstractions, biases, and language structure; linguistic acceptability, evaluated via the CoLA task which depends on word order; dependency parsing (DP), a syntax-sensitive task; n-gram shuffling, used to test sensitivity to word-order perturbations; pairwise ordering accuracy, measuring models’ ability to correctly predict successive token pairs; and potential future exploration in constituency parsing and syntax-diagnosing benchmarks like SyntaxGym and BLiMP.
fine_tuning_materials: GLUE, dependency parsing task
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language for both pretraining and evaluation—pretraining on the WikiBooks corpus (English Wikipedia + BookCorpus) and fine-tuning on NLU benchmarks like GLUE and dependency parsing datasets (PTB and five UD corpora). To specifically probe syntactic knowledge and word-order sensitivity, the researchers introduced controlled stimuli by modifying naturalistic datasets: n-gram shuffling to disrupt word order, token masking to vary lexical information, and partially/fully masked sequences to test the Token Reordering (TOR) ability.
interp_method: Token Reordering (TOR), a self-supervised pretraining objective to enhance word-order awareness, and Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN), a structure-aware module added on top of BERT—together forming BERT+GIN—to leverage topological signals from encoded representations.
main_findings: shows that incorporating the Token Reordering (TOR) pretraining objective and a Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) module enhances BERT’s syntactic knowledge, particularly for order-sensitive tasks like Dependency Parsing and CoLA. TOR, which reconstructs partially shuffled token sequences, improves word-order awareness and allows larger batch sizes than standard MLM, though full-sequence shuffling harms performance. While TOR is competitive on order-insensitive tasks, it provides substantial gains on syntax-dependent tasks, especially in few-shot settings. The addition of a GIN module further boosts performance by enforcing structure-aware representations during pretraining, even if the GIN is removed during fine-tuning. TOR-trained models are more sensitive to word-order perturbations, and the benefits of TOR and GIN diminish as the amount of labeled fine-tuning data increases, highlighting their particular value in low-resource scenarios. Overall, combining TOR and GIN significantly strengthens BERT’s encoding of syntactic structure and word-order information.

title: Probing BERT on Syntactic Representation Paradigms: Dependency vs Constituency Trees
abstract: On the quest for interpreting deep Neural Language Models (NLMs), linguistically annotated probing sets are essential tools for investigating models' linguistic abilities. Such a line of research is currently dominated by dependency-based syntactic annotation formalisms, and particularly by Universal Dependencies treebanks. In this work, we test whether different Syntactic Representation Paradigms (SRP) have an impact on the performance of NLMs. To this aim, we set up a multilingual study where we compare the scores obtained by BERT on a set of probing tasks performed on 10 treebanks annotated according to two paradigms, i.e. the dependency and the constituency one, which diverges on fundamental annotation principles. Results suggest that BERT performance is minimally but consistently affected by SRPs and that such impact mostly concerns specific linguistic phenomena.
specific_phenomena: dependency- and constituency-based representations; maximum depth (max-depth), the longest path from root to leaf in dependency or phrase structure trees; average length of phrases/dependency links (avg-len), the mean number of words per dependency or phrase; maximum phrase/link length (max-len), the longest dependency link or largest phrase in a sentence; and average clause length (avg-cl-len), the mean number of tokens per clause, calculated differently depending on the annotation paradigm. features were selected to enable multilingual comparison
languages_tested_comment: Catalan, Dutch, French, Icelandic, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, Vietnamese
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language data drawn from 10 typologically diverse languages using existing treebanks annotated under dependency-based (D-SRP, mostly UD) and constituency-based (C-SRP, mostly PTB-like) paradigms, with most texts coming from newspapers to minimize genre effects. To introduce controlled stimuli, the authors created a multilingual set of parallel trees, selecting only sentences annotated in both SRPs with identical segmentation and tokenization to isolate the effect of syntactic representation. They also controlled for sentence length, testing models on subsets of the shortest 10% (“Min”) and longest 10% (“Max”) of sentences to examine length effects. Additionally, some resources, like the Turkish Penn Treebank, imposed pre-existing constraints on sentence length, adding another controlled dimension to the experimental setup.
interp_method: diagnostic probing paradigm. More specifically, they refer to it as the linguistic probing task approach defined in Conneau et al(2018), which is a type of probing classification approach
main_findings: examined whether different Syntactic Representation Paradigms (SRPs) influence BERT’s ability to encode syntactic information. Using a multilingual setup with 10 treebanks annotated in both dependency-based (D-SRP, Universal Dependencies) and constituency-based (C-SRP, Penn Treebank-like) schemes, the study found that BERT’s performance is only minimally affected by SRP, with no consistent preference across all languages and tasks. However, language-specific trends emerged: PST was preferred for Dutch, French, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese, and Vietnamese, while UD was favored for Catalan, Icelandic, Spanish, and Turkish. Differences were most pronounced for features like maximum tree depth (max-depth) and average clause length (avg-cl-len), where representation differences between SRPs influenced BERT’s predictions, while maximum phrase/link length (max-len) showed minimal variation. Sentence length also impacted performance, with longer sentences generally yielding higher probing scores and slightly better results under D-SRP. A key contribution of the work is a publicly available multilingual resource of parallel sentences annotated in both SRPs, enabling reproducibility. The findings highlight that BERT’s encoding of syntax is sensitive to structural representations in nuanced, language-specific ways, and further analysis is needed to fully understand NLMs’ syntactic abilities.

title: LIMIT-BERT : Linguistics Informed Multi-Task BERT
abstract: In this paper, we present Linguistics Informed Multi-Task BERT (LIMIT-BERT) for learning language representations across multiple linguistics tasks by Multi-Task Learning. LIMIT-BERT includes five key linguistics tasks: Part-Of-Speech (POS) tags, constituent and dependency syntactic parsing, span and dependency semantic role labeling (SRL). Different from recent Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks (MT-DNN), our LIMIT-BERT is fully linguistics motivated and thus is capable of adopting an improved masked training objective according to syntactic and semantic constituents. Besides, LIMIT-BERT takes a semi-supervised learning strategy to offer the same large amount of linguistics task data as that for the language model training. As a result, LIMIT-BERT not only improves linguistics tasks performance but also benefits from a regularization effect and linguistics information that leads to more general representations to help adapt to new tasks and domains. LIMIT-BERT outperforms the strong baseline Whole Word Masking BERT on both dependency and constituent syntactic/semantic parsing, GLUE benchmark, and SNLI task. Our practice on the proposed LIMIT-BERT also enables us to release a well pre-trained model for multi-purpose of natural language processing tasks once for all.

fine_tuning_materials: GLUE
experimental_materials_comment: controlled; Part-Of-Speech (POS) tagging; Constituent and dependency syntactic parsing (Penn Treebank, ~50k annotated sentences); Semantic role labeling (Propbank: CoNLL-2005 span style, CoNLL-2009 dependency style); Evaluation benchmarks: GLUE (9 NLU tasks), SNLI
interp_method: Linguistics Informed Multi-Task BERT (LIMIT-BERT), is a multi-task learning framework that enhances language representations by training on multiple linguistic tasks and using Syntactic/Semantic Phrase
main_findings: main findings regarding the integration and impact of syntactic knowledge in LIMIT-BERT indicate that explicitly incorporating linguistic information substantially enhances both syntactic and semantic performance. LIMIT-BERT outperforms the strong baseline BERTWWM across multiple tasks, including dependency and constituent parsing, span- and dependency-based Semantic Role Labeling (SRL), GLUE, and SNLI. Key contributions include the use of Multi-Task Learning (MTL) to retain linguistic knowledge, and Syntactic Phrase Masking (SPM) during pre-training to better capture syntactic structures, both of which improve performance on downstream tasks and natural language understanding benchmarks. LIMIT-BERT also shows notable gains on long sentences, benefiting from semi-supervised training on larger datasets with extended sentence lengths. Interestingly, the model sometimes achieves better syntactic parsing results without fine-tuning, highlighting the effectiveness of the pre-trained syntactic representations learned through the semi-supervised, linguistically informed training procedure.

title: Composition, Attention, or Both?
abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel architecture called Composition Attention Grammars (CAGs) that recursively compose subtrees into a single vector representation with a composition function, and selectively attend to previous structural information with a self-attention mechanism. We investigate whether these components -- the composition function and the self-attention mechanism -- can both induce human-like syntactic generalization. Specifically, we train language models (LMs) with and without these two components with the model sizes carefully controlled, and evaluate their syntactic generalization performance against six test circuits on the SyntaxGym benchmark. The results demonstrated that the composition function and the self-attention mechanism both play an important role to make LMs more human-like, and closer inspection of linguistic phenomenon implied that the composition function allowed syntactic features, but not semantic features, to percolate into subtree representations.

main_findings: highlight that both the composition function and self-attention are essential for making language models (LMs) exhibit human-like syntactic generalization, as demonstrated by Composition Attention Grammars (CAGs). Explicit syntactic supervision consistently improves performance across architectures, with the composition function enabling proper percolation of syntactic features (e.g., agreement) into subtree representations, though semantic features like animacy may not propagate as effectively. CAGs outperform models with dynamic masking or those lacking composition, showing recursive composition offers significant advantages. Self-attention boosts performance when combined with syntactic supervision (as in PLM and CAG), but underperforms without it (as in vanilla Transformers). Notably, CAGs achieved the highest accuracy on SyntaxGym, even surpassing GPT-2, despite smaller training data and model size. The findings also emphasize a dissociation between perplexity and human-like syntactic generalization, as models with lower perplexity do not necessarily perform better syntactically. A key limitation of CAGs is their high computational cost due to recursive training and memory-intensive self-attention.

title: Mechanisms vs. Outcomes: Probing for Syntax Fails to Explain Performance on Targeted Syntactic Evaluations
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a robust mastery of syntax when processing and generating text. While this suggests internalized understanding of hierarchical syntax and dependency relations, the precise mechanism by which they represent syntactic structure is an open area within interpretability research. Probing provides one way to identify the mechanism of syntax being linearly encoded in activations, however, no comprehensive study has yet established whether a model's probing accuracy reliably predicts its downstream syntactic performance. Adopting a "mechanisms vs. outcomes" framework, we evaluate 32 open-weight transformer models and find that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations across English linguistic phenomena. Our results highlight a substantial disconnect between latent syntactic representations found via probing and observable syntactic behaviors in downstream tasks.
model_name_comment: GPT-2, LLaMA (2 and 3), Falcon, Mistral, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, T5, and ELECTRA, Pythia, Gemma, Olmo

For deeper syntactic analysis, the study also examines specific, syntactically complex test suites within Subject-Verb Agreement (e.g., distractor agreement with relational nouns and relative clauses) and Filler-Gap Dependencies (e.g., wh-vs-that contrasts with both short and long-distance gaps)
experimental_materials_comment: combination of naturalistic language and controlled stimuli to evaluate the syntactic knowledge in language models. For the naturalistic component, syntactic probes were trained using dependency parses from the Penn Treebank (PTB), annotated with Stanza Universal Dependencies (UD). This corpus, composed of human-written text, reflects real-world language usage and syntactic patterns. For controlled evaluation, the study used BLiMP (Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for English), which consists of 67 template-generated sub-datasets covering 13 grammatical phenomena. Each sub-dataset includes 1,000 minimal sentence pairs that differ by a single grammatical contrast,
interp_method: Mechanisms vs. Outcomes" framework to investigate the relationship between internal syntactic representations in language models and their actual performance on syntactic tasks. In this framework, "mechanisms" refer to syntactic features extracted from model activations using probing methods—specifically, three types of syntax probes (gstruct_phi, gortho_phi, and ghead_phi), along with a control probe (gctrl_phi). These probes attempt to recover syntactic structures such as dependency trees from hidden states. "Outcomes" denote the models' performance on BLiMP, a benchmark of minimal pairs that test syntactic acceptability. The central aim is to determine whether the syntactic knowledge uncovered by probes correlates with actual syntactic behavior.
main_findings: finds a significant disconnect between the syntactic information extracted through probing methods and actual syntactic performance in downstream tasks. Despite evaluating 32 transformer models using several probing techniques, the study shows that syntactic probes fail to predict models’ accuracy on targeted syntactic benchmarks like BLiMP. While some per-phenomenon correlations (e.g., with anaphor agreement) appeared statistically significant, these were likely spurious or confounded by non-syntactic factors. Probes also performed poorly on critical syntactic phenomena such as subject-verb agreement and filler-gap dependencies. Even when probing recovered syntactically relevant structures like subject-verb dependencies, this did not reliably predict correct model behavior on corresponding evaluations. Overall, the findings challenge the assumption that high probing accuracy reflects genuine syntactic competence, concluding that direct behavioral evaluations remain the most reliable way to assess syntactic knowledge in language models.

title: From Language to Cognition: How LLMs Outgrow the Human Language Network
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable similarity to neural activity in the human language network. However, the key properties of language shaping brain-like representations, and their evolution during training as a function of different tasks remain unclear. We here benchmark 34 training checkpoints spanning 300B tokens across 8 different model sizes to analyze how brain alignment relates to linguistic competence. Specifically, we find that brain alignment tracks the development of formal linguistic competence -- i.e., knowledge of linguistic rules -- more closely than functional linguistic competence. While functional competence, which involves world knowledge and reasoning, continues to develop throughout training, its relationship with brain alignment is weaker, suggesting that the human language network primarily encodes formal linguistic structure rather than broader cognitive functions. We further show that model size is not a reliable predictor of brain alignment when controlling for feature size and find that the correlation between next-word prediction, behavioral alignment and brain alignment fades once models surpass human language proficiency. Finally, using the largest set of rigorous neural language benchmarks to date, we show that language brain alignment benchmarks remain unsaturated, highlighting opportunities for improving future models. Taken together, our findings suggest that the human language network is best modeled by formal, rather than functional, aspects of language
specific_phenomena: BLIMP, SYNTAXGYM; such as subject–verb agreement, anaphora, quantifiers, and island effects, filler–gap dependencies and center embeddings
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language and controlled stimuli: datasets such as BLANK2014, where participants listened to eight stories of approximately five minutes each; the NARRATIVES dataset, which included 27 spoken stories analyzed via fMRI; PEREIRA2018, with short passages presented one sentence at a time across 24 topics; and FUTRELL2018, which used a natural stories corpus to collect behavioral reading times. Controlled stimuli were shorter and specifically designed to test particular linguistic phenomena or grammatical rules. Examples include FEDORENKO2016, which captured ECoG signals from participants reading eight-word sentences, and TUCKUTE2024, where participants read 1,000 six-word sentences covering a broad linguistic space. Additionally, formal linguistic competence was assessed using linguistic benchmarks: BLIMP, which evaluates 67 English grammatical phenomena through 1,000 minimal pairs per task testing syntax, morphology, and semantics, and SYNTAXGYM, consisting of 31 tasks designed to systematically measure syntactic knowledge in LLMs.
interp_method: benchmarks: BLIMP and SYNTAXGYM, evaluates linguistic competence through zero-shot benchmarks that distinguish formal competence, such as grammar and syntax assessed with BLiMP and SyntaxGym, from functional competence, such as reasoning and world knowledge assessed with ARC, Social IQA, PIQA, Winogrande, and HellaSwag. A longitudinal training trajectory analysis tracks 34 checkpoints across eight Pythia model sizes, spanning 300 billion tokens, to determine when brain-like representations emerge relative to linguistic skills.
main_findings: demonstrate that models acquire rule-based syntactic structures early in training, and that this formal competence closely aligns with the human brain's language network. Using two benchmarks—BLiMP and SyntaxGym—to assess knowledge of syntax, morphology, and semantics, the study found that brain alignment strongly correlates with formal linguistic competence, much more than with functional competence (which involves reasoning and world knowledge). Remarkably, formal competence saturates early, around 4 billion tokens, aligning with early brain alignment saturation (~8 billion tokens), while functional competence continues improving throughout training. Even untrained models exhibited above-chance performance on formal tasks, suggesting that architectural inductive biases play a role in encoding syntactic knowledge from the outset. Overall, the findings suggest that the human language network is best modeled by the formal, structural aspects of language, such as syntax, rather than by broader functional or semantic abilities.

title: Interpretability of Language Models for Learning Hierarchical Structures
abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models grasp complex, recursive language structures defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn this CFG language and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm.
