specific_phenomena: Depth and attachment, Context-Free Grammars (CFGs). Key phenomena include complex recursive structures, bracket matching as a simple long-range dependency, and induction heads that perform abstract logic operations beyond token-level copying. Models are tested on logical reasoning tasks, selection of correct tokens (e.g., names), and long-range dependencies spanning hundreds of tokens. The study also emphasizes local ambiguity in “hard CFGs,” where global planning via dynamic programming is required, and implicit CFGs, where terminal symbols represent bags of tokens sharing syntactic or semantic properties. Additionally, the authors investigate robustness to grammar mistakes, showing that models can learn a “mode switch” to correct errors, and explore unbalanced CFGs with length-1 rules (cfg8/9/0 families) that produce globally ambiguous strings, further challenging the models’ hierarchical reasoning.
experimental_materials_comment: uses synthetic Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) as controlled experimental stimuli to investigate how transformers learn complex, recursive language structures. These synthetic CFGs, including families like cfg3b–cfg3f and cfg3e1–cfg3e2, are specifically designed to generate long, locally ambiguous sequences that often require dynamic programming to parse, enabling precise analysis of the models’ hidden-state representations. Additional unbalanced CFG families (cfg8, cfg9, cfg0) explore varied rule types and depths, further challenging model learning. For comparison, the authors also use a simplified naturalistic CFG derived from the Penn TreeBank (PTB). While small GPT-2 models can learn this PTB CFG with high accuracy, its shorter sentences and lower ambiguity make it less suitable for interpretability studies, underscoring the advantage of synthetic CFGs for probing hierarchical reasoning. Implicit CFGs, where terminal symbols represent “bags of words,” demonstrate that adding real-world-like variability does not substantially increase learning difficulty, as this information is encoded in embeddings.
interp_method: "multi-head linear probing method" to analyze transformer representations, demonstrating that the models’ hidden states linearly encode Nonterminal (NT) information, despite CFG structure not being explicitly provided during pre-training. They also identify two key attention patterns: position-based attention, where weights depend on the relative distance between tokens to capture CFG regularities, and boundary-based attention, where tokens at NT-end boundaries preferentially attend to nearby NT-end tokens across levels, supporting the model’s learning of hierarchical and recursive CFG structures.
main_findings: finds that transformer-based generative models like GPT can accurately learn and generate sequences from complex, recursive context-free grammars (CFGs), even when sentences are long, locally ambiguous, and require dynamic programming (DP) to parse. Models with relative or rotary attention (GPTrel, GPTrot) outperform those with absolute or uniform attention, highlighting the importance of positional mechanisms for learning hierarchical structure. GPT hidden states linearly encode nonterminal (NT) ancestor and boundary information, with this information locally concentrated around NT boundaries, whereas encoder models like DeBERTa struggle to capture deep hierarchical information near the CFG root. GPT’s attention patterns mirror dynamic programming operations: position-based attention captures token distance regularities, and boundary-based attention preferentially links NT-end tokens, effectively passing hierarchical information across layers. These mechanisms allow GPT to implicitly implement DP-like reasoning, learning both explicit CFG rules and implicit CFGs where terminals represent token distributions. Finally, GPT models are sensitive to grammatical errors, but robustness improves when pre-training includes corrupted or perturbed data, enabling a “mode switch” that adapts completion behavior depending on input quality.

title: Parallel Trees: a novel resource with aligned dependency and constituency syntactic representations
abstract: The paper introduces Parallel Trees, a novel multilingual treebank collection that includes 20 treebanks for 10 languages. The distinguishing property of this resource is that the sentences of each language are annotated using two syntactic representation paradigms (SRPs), respectively based on the notions of dependency and constituency. By aligning the annotations of existing resources, Parallel Trees represents an example of exploiting pre-existing treebanks to adapt them to novel applications. To illustrate its potential, we present a case study where the resource is employed as a benchmark to investigate whether and how BERT, one of the first prominent neural language models (NLMs), is sensitive to the dependency- and constituency-based approaches for representing the syntactic structure of a sentence. The case study results indicate that the model’s sensitivity fluctuates across languages and experimental settings. The unique nature of the Parallel Trees resource creates the prerequisites for innovative studies comparing dependency and phrase-structure trees, allowing for more focused investigations without the interference of lexical variation.

Although the sentences in Parallel Trees are naturally occurring, the resource functions as controlled stimuli: each sentence is annotated in two syntactic representation paradigms (dependency and constituency), aligned to control for lexical and semantic variation.
interp_method: diagnostic probing approach:  relies on the idea that if a lightweight classifier, known as a probing model, can successfully predict a specific language property using the sentence embeddings from a pre-trained NLM as input, then it can be inferred that the NLM has implicitly encoded that property. This methodology is widely adopted in the literature for interpreting NLMs and assessing their linguistic competencies
main_findings: found that BERT is sensitive to different syntactic representation paradigms (SRPs), encoding constituency-based and dependency-based structures in distinct ways, though differences in probing scores were generally small and variable across languages. BERT’s performance varied with both language and sentence length: dependency-based representations were favored in languages like Icelandic, Spanish, and Catalan, while phrase-based representations performed better in French, Italian, and Vietnamese, with preferences shifting for shortest and longest sentences. The model also showed differential sensitivity to specific linguistic features—such as syntactic tree depth, average clause length, and average phrase/link length—depending on sentence length and SRP. Overall, the results suggest that BERT’s syntactic generalizations are complex and context-dependent, supporting the idea that both constituency- and dependency-based frameworks are important to capture human-like syntactic competence, highlighting an integrative approach for fully modeling syntax in neural language models.

title: Language Models Grow Less Humanlike beyond Phase Transition

experimental_materials_comment: combined naturalistic language data and controlled stimuli to investigate language model behavior. For naturalistic data, pretraining used a 1-billion-token sample from the English CC100 subcorpus, while alignment with human reading behavior (PPP) was evaluated using four corpora: three eye-tracking datasets (Dundee, Provo, MECO) and one self-paced reading dataset (Natural Stories). interp_method: frame their research as a "series of correlational and causal experiments" investigating how pretraining phase transitions affect language models’ alignment with human reading behavior (PPP). They employ several specific methods: PPP is measured via delta log-likelihood (∆LL) comparing models with and without LM surprisals; phase transitions are tracked using Unlabeled Attachment Score (UAS) for syntactic attention structure (SAS) and Prefix-matching Score (PS) for induction heads, with breakthrough points defined when these metrics cross thresholds. Ablation experiments test causal effects by zeroing out attention heads and measuring changes in PPP, using head-specific SAS scores. Regularization techniques—syntactic (LSAS) and copying (LCOPY)—suppress SAS or induction head formation to study their effects, while Gaussian Noise Injection (GNI) serves as a control for model perturbation. These methods together allow the authors to link syntactic attention patterns, induction heads, and learning dynamics to model performance and human alignment.
main_findings: investigates how pretraining phase transitions in language models (LMs), marked by the rapid emergence of specialized attention heads, explain why alignment with human reading behavior—measured as Psychometric Predictive Power (PPP)—reaches a tipping point and may later plateau or degrade. The researchers find that PPP peaks coincide with these phase transitions across models and datasets, supporting the Dynamics Hypothesis: post-transition learning dynamics, rather than persistent circuits, drive PPP degradation. Focusing on syntactic knowledge, they identify the Specialized Attention Structure (SAS) phase transition, where attention patterns suddenly align with syntactic dependency edges, measured via Unlabeled Attachment Score (UAS). The emergence of SAS leads to abrupt improvements in syntactic performance, as shown by BLiMP scores. Applying a syntactic regularizer to suppress SAS delays both the phase transition and the PPP tipping point, supporting the role of learning dynamics. Additionally, SAS consistently precedes induction heads, acting as scaffolding for their development, while induction heads themselves can inhibit SAS. Overall, the study links syntactic attention structures, phase transitions, and learning dynamics to both LM syntactic ability and human-alignment performance.

title: Multilingual Nonce Dependency Treebanks: Understanding how Language Models represent and process syntactic structure
abstract: We introduce SPUD (Semantically Perturbed Universal Dependencies), a framework for creating nonce treebanks for the multilingual Universal Dependencies (UD) corpora. SPUD data satisfies syntactic argument structure, provides syntactic annotations, and ensures grammaticality via language-specific rules. We create nonce data in Arabic, English, French, German, and Russian, and demonstrate two use cases of SPUD treebanks. First, we investigate the effect of nonce data on word co-occurrence statistics, as measured by perplexity scores of autoregressive (ALM) and masked language models (MLM). We find that ALM scores are significantly more affected by nonce data than MLM scores. Second, we show how nonce data affects the performance of syntactic dependency probes. We replicate the findings of Müller-Eberstein et al. (2022) on nonce test data and show that the performance declines on both MLMs and ALMs wrt. original test data. However, a majority of the performance is kept, suggesting that the probe indeed learns syntax independently from semantics.

Key aspects include syntactic argument structure and valency of predicates, which govern how verbs select their subjects and objects, alongside word order and grammatical roles (subject, object, etc.). LMs are evaluated for their understanding of dependency relations/labels (e.g., nsubj, obj, amod, cop) and edge attachment (head prediction) within directed and labeled dependency trees, considering word distances and left/right edge orientation. Morphosyntactic constraints play a major role, encompassing features like adjective suffixes, determiner selection, case marking, and number agreement. POS tags and grammaticality checks
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language and controlled stimuli. Naturalistic language comes from Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks for five languages—Arabic, English, French, German, and Russian—providing grammatically correct sentences that reflect real-world usage. Controlled stimuli are generated using SPUD (Semantically Perturbed Universal Dependencies), which creates grammatical but nonsensical sentences by replacing content words while preserving the original syntactic structure, argument structure, and dependency relations. SPUD ensures grammaticality through language-specific rules, accounting for POS tags, word order, dependency relations, and morphosyntactic constraints (e.g., English “a/an” or French determiners). Human evaluations confirmed that up to 87% of SPUD sentences are rated grammatical, making them reliable for probing syntactic knowledge independently of semantics.
interp_method: PUD (Semantically Perturbed Universal Dependencies), described as a framework  or an algorithm designed for creating nonce treebanks for the multilingual Universal Dependencies (UD) corpora. This framework aims to generate grammatical but nonsensical data by preserving the original syntactic structure of sentences while replacing content words according to language-specific rules.
main_findings: LMs retain substantial syntactic knowledge even when lexical semantics are disrupted. SPUD-generated sentences, which preserve syntax but replace content words, are consistently harder for LMs to predict, particularly for autoregressive LMs (ALMs), whose perplexities increase more than masked LMs (MLMs)’ pseudo-perplexities. Probing experiments reveal that syntax can be learned independently of semantics: while probe performance drops on SPUD data, a majority of syntactic structure is still captured. MLMs (e.g., mBERT, RoBERTa) outperform ALMs (e.g., GPT-2, mGPT) on both original and nonce data, particularly in predicting edge attachments (UAS) rather than relation labels (RelAcc), suggesting attachment requires more contextual information. Overall, MLMs are better at identifying syntactic structure in the absence of lexical co-occurrence, highlighting differences in how model architecture and scoring functions affect syntactic knowledge retention.

title: Syntax-BERT: Improving Pre-trained Transformers with Syntax Trees
abstract: Pre-trained language models like BERT achieve superior performances in various NLP tasks without explicit consideration of syntactic information. Meanwhile, syntactic information has been proved to be crucial for the success of NLP applications. However, how to incorporate the syntax trees effectively and efficiently into pre-trained Transformers is still unsettled. In this paper, we address this problem by proposing a novel framework named Syntax-BERT. This framework works in a plug-and-play mode and is applicable to an arbitrary pre-trained checkpoint based on Transformer architecture. Experiments on various datasets of natural language understanding verify the effectiveness of syntax trees and achieve consistent improvement over multiple pre-trained models, including BERT, RoBERTa, and T5.
model_name_comment: vanilla Transformer, BERT-Base/Large, RoBERTa-Base/Large, and T5-Large
specific_phenomena: sub-networks defined by syntax-based sparse masks: captures ancestor (parent), offspring (child), and sibling relationships, with each type further differentiated by the number of “hops” or distances between tokens in the syntax tree. The parent mask encodes ancestor relationships at a given distance, the child mask encodes offspring relationships, and the sibling mask connects nodes sharing a lowest common ancestor within a specified distance. Additionally, a pairwise mask handles interactions between tokens from different sentences in tasks requiring inter-sentence attention, independent of tree distances.
fine_tuning_materials: Glue
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language datasets: The main datasets included the Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST-1 and SST-2), which contains over 10,000 movie review sentences with corresponding constituency trees, and Natural Language Inference (NLI) datasets such as SNLI and MNLI, which involve determining semantic relationships between premise and hypothesis sentences. Additionally, they evaluated performance on the GLUE benchmark, encompassing single-sentence classification tasks (e.g., CoLA, SST-2), similarity and paraphrase tasks (e.g., MRPC, QQP, STS-B), and pairwise inference tasks (e.g., MNLI, RTE, QNLI, WNLI).
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques, Feature Visualization, Activation Patching (Ablation)
interp_method: nan
main_findings: syntax-BERT is a framework designed to enhance pre-trained Transformer models like BERT, RoBERTa, and T5 by explicitly incorporating syntax trees into their architecture. While standard Transformers capture some syntactic knowledge implicitly, Syntax-BERT bridges the gap to expert-crafted “golden syntax trees” using a novel method that decomposes self-attention into sub-networks reflecting ancestor, offspring, and sibling relationships in syntax trees, with syntax-based sparse masks and a topical attention layer to weight these relationships. This approach improves performance across multiple NLP tasks, including GLUE, CoLA, SST-2, and NLI benchmarks, often with notable gains on smaller datasets, while introducing only minimal additional parameters. Syntax-BERT works in a plug-and-play manner without requiring pre-training from scratch and can be combined with other methods like LISA for further gains. Structural probing confirms that it captures more syntactic information than vanilla models, demonstrating that explicitly modeling syntax can meaningfully enhance Transformer representations, particularly when resources or training data are limited.

title: Constituency Parsing using LLMs
abstract: Constituency parsing is a fundamental yet unsolved natural language processing task. In this paper, we explore the potential of recent large language models (LLMs) that have exhibited remarkable performance across various domains and tasks to tackle this task. We employ three linearization strategies to transform output trees into symbol sequences, such that LLMs can solve constituency parsing by generating linearized trees. We conduct experiments using a diverse range of LLMs, including ChatGPT, GPT-4, OPT, LLaMA, and Alpaca, comparing their performance against the state-of-the-art constituency parsers. Our experiments encompass zero-shot, few-shot, and full-training learning settings, and we evaluate the models on one in-domain and five out-of-domain test datasets. Our findings reveal insights into LLMs' performance, generalization abilities, and challenges in constituency parsing.
model_name_comment: ChatGPT, GPT-4, OPT, LLaMA, and Alpaca, LSTM seq2seq models (Lstms and vanilla Transformer)
specific_phenomena: constituency parsing, which predicts sentence structure according to phrase structure grammar, reformulated as a sequence-to-sequence generation problem: complex and lengthy structures, including long-range nested dependencies, extremely long constituents (spans over 35 tokens), and the structured output of trees; constituent tags across multiple levels, from clauses (e.g., S) to phrases (e.g., ADJP) and words (e.g., CC), reflecting hierarchical syntactic information
fine_tuning_materials: fine-tune LLMs on the full training dataset of the Penn Treebank (PTB), MCTB dataset
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language datasets rather than controlled stimuli. For in-domain evaluation, the Penn Treebank (PTB) dataset, drawn from news text (~40,000 instances), is used. For cross-domain evaluation, the MCTB dataset exposes models to diverse domains, including Dialogue, Forum, Law, Literature, and Review, representing a wide range of naturalistic language styles.
interp_method: Constituency Parsing with LLMs” and frame it as a sequence-based method that treats constituency parsing as a sequence-to-sequence generation problem using generative large language models. Throughout the paper, they also describe their models as LLM-based parsers, emphasizing that this work is the first systematic study of the impact of LLMs on constituency parsing and aims to explore the potential of recent LLMs to tackle this syntactic task.
main_findings: investigates the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in constituency parsing, examining how well these models can predict syntactic tree structures despite being primarily trained on text. The findings indicate that LLMs significantly enhance sequence-based parsing, with large models like LLaMA-65B achieving results competitive with state-of-the-art chart-based parsers. However, open-source LLMs show limited zero- and few-shot transfer, whereas commercial models like ChatGPT and GPT-4 generalize better in low-data scenarios. Instruction tuning can slightly reduce performance in full fine-tuning but helps in few-shot settings. LLM-based parsers face cross-domain generalization challenges, with performance dropping 8.9–17% on out-of-domain datasets, though larger models generalize slightly better. Sequence-based errors, such as invalid trees and hallucinations, are significant issues, especially for long or complex sentences. Data efficiency is limited, with models like LLaMA-7B needing full training data to reach peak performance, although they still outperform smaller models in low-data regimes. Finally, linearization strategies matter: bracket-based methods excel in fine-tuning, while span-based methods are more effective in few-shot settings, and decoding strategy has minimal impact. Overall, LLMs show strong potential for constituency parsing but retain structural limitations inherent to sequence-based modeling.

title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature’s roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
specific_phenomena: Grammatical Number (Singular, Plural), Grammatical Gender (Masculine, Feminine), and Tense (Present, Past). Additional concepts analyzed for cross-lingual feature sharing include Case (Accusative, Dative, Genitive, Nominative), Person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), and Polarity (Negative). These concepts were selected based on their annotation in at least six languages from the Universal Dependencies 2.1 dataset
languages_tested_comment: Arabic, Chinese, Czech, Dutch, English, French, German, Greek, Hebrew, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Persian, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, Ukrainian, and Vietnamese.
experimental_materials_comment: natrual: a multilingual treebank containing dependency-parsed sentences. This corresponds to the 23 languages that Aya-23 was trained on
interp_method: employ several key methods to investigate and manipulate grammatical representations in LLMs. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), specifically Gated SAEs, are used to discover interpretable feature directions in the models’ activations. To test the causal role of these features, they apply causal interventions, including activation patching—an exact but compute-intensive approach—and its faster approximation, attribution patching (AtP), which uses integrated gradients to identify features critical for model behavior. They also use probing classifiers, particularly linear probes, to predict morphosyntactic concepts from intermediate layer activations. Finally, feature steering is applied in machine translation tasks, clamping features to counterfactual values to demonstrate their functional selectivity and causal influence on model outputs.
main_findings: indicate that LLMs develop abstract, cross-lingual representations of grammatical concepts such as number, gender, and tense, which are shared across typologically diverse languages. Studies using sparse autoencoders on models like Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B show up to 50% overlap in features encoding the same grammatical concepts across languages, suggesting that even English-dominated models capture multilingual morphosyntactic abstractions. Causal interventions confirm that these shared multilingual features are crucial: ablating them drastically reduces classifier performance, and a small subset of “massively multilingual features” accounts for most probe behavior. Importantly, these features are human-interpretable, functionally selective, and causally influential; manipulating a single feature can reliably shift predictions toward intended grammatical contrasts, with minimal interference on other concepts. Overall, the research supports the idea that LLMs operate on an internal “lingua franca” of abstract grammatical concepts, enabling robust cross-lingual generalization even when trained primarily on English.

title: Multilingual Alignment of Contextual Word Representations
abstract: We propose procedures for evaluating and strengthening contextual embedding alignment and show that they are useful in analyzing and improving multilingual BERT. In particular, after our proposed alignment procedure, BERT exhibits significantly improved zero-shot performance on XNLI compared to the base model, remarkably matching pseudo-fully-supervised translate-train models for Bulgarian and Greek. Further, to measure the degree of alignment, we introduce a contextual version of word retrieval and show that it correlates well with downstream zero-shot transfer. Using this word retrieval task, we also analyze BERT and find that it exhibits systematic deficiencies, e.g. worse alignment for open-class parts-of-speech and word pairs written in different scripts, that are corrected by the alignment procedure. These results support contextual alignment as a useful concept for understanding large multilingual pre-trained models. Data: [MultiNLI](https://paperswithcode.com/dataset/multinli), [XNLI](https://paperswithcode.com/dataset/xnli)
specific_phenomena: POS: word retrieval POS analysis: distinguish between closed-class POS—determiners, prepositions, conjunctions, pronouns, and auxiliaries—which serve grammatical functions and tend to be more consistently aligned due to their fixed usage patterns, and open-class POS—nouns, adverbs, adjectives, and verbs—which are more semantically rich and substitutable, making them harder to align.
languages_tested_comment: train on English and evaluate on Bulgarian, German, Greek, Spanish, and French
fine_tuning_materials: MultiNLI
experimental_materials_comment: Universal Part-of-Speech Tagset  (Petrov et al., 2012),  composed of naturalistic language: Europarl corpus was used for language pairs involving English and Bulgarian, German, Greek, Spanish, and French, drawing on parliamentary proceedings. The MultiUN corpus supported experiments with Arabic and Chinese, while the Tanzil corpus, consisting of Quranic sentences, was used for Urdu. Additionally, the XNLI dataset, which includes human-translated versions of the English MultiNLI development and test sets, served as the benchmark for zero-shot transfer evaluations. T
Mechanistic_method: Probing Techniques (Contextual Word Retrieval), Feature Visualization (t-SNE), Fine-tuning (Alignment Procedure)
interp_method: Accuracy by part-of-speech tag for non-contextual word retrieval; refer to their method primarily as the fine-tuning-based alignment procedure, which involves fine-tuning mBERT using parallel corpora to improve cross-lingual alignment and downstream performance, particularly in zero-shot transfer settings.
main_findings: highlight the strengths and limitations of mBERT and the effectiveness of a proposed alignment procedure in enhancing its multilingual performance. mBERT, trained on 104 languages with a shared vocabulary, demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer capabilities, particularly due to its partially aligned embeddings, though the reasons for this are not fully understood. However, base BERT shows systematic weaknesses, especially in aligning open-class parts-of-speech and across languages with different scripts or usage frequencies. These issues stem from reliance on co-occurrence statistics during pre-training. The proposed fine-tuning-based alignment method significantly improves both contextual and non-contextual alignment, boosting zero-shot accuracy (e.g., nearly 5% for Bulgarian and Greek), resolving part-of-speech alignment disparities, and requiring only modest amounts of parallel data. The research introduces contextual embedding alignment as a key concept, linking it to downstream performance and demonstrating its effectiveness in disambiguating word meanings. Additionally, while not explicitly focused on syntactic knowledge, the study implicates it through analysis of grammatical word classes, showing that the alignment process enhances the model's understanding of syntactic context and grammatical structure.

title: When Is Multilinguality a Curse? Language Modeling for 250 High- and Low-Resource Languages
abstract: Multilingual language models are widely used to extend NLP systems to low-resource languages. However, concrete evidence for the effects of multilinguality on language modeling performance in individual languages remains scarce. Here, we pre-train over 10,000 monolingual and multilingual language models for over 250 languages, including multiple language families that are under-studied in NLP. We assess how language modeling performance in each language varies as a function of (1) monolingual dataset size, (2) added multilingual dataset size, (3) linguistic similarity of the added languages, and (4) model size (up to 45M parameters). We find that in moderation, adding multilingual data improves low-resource language modeling performance, similar to increasing low-resource dataset sizes by up to 33%. Improvements depend on the syntactic similarity of the added multilingual data, with marginal additional effects of vocabulary overlap. However, high-resource languages consistently perform worse in multilingual pre-training scenarios. As dataset sizes increase, adding multilingual data begins to hurt performance for both low-resource and high-resource languages, likely due to limited model capacity (the "curse of multilinguality"). These results suggest that massively multilingual pre-training may not be optimal for any languages involved, but that more targeted models can significantly improve performance.
specific_phenomena: syntactic similarity of vector representations from lang2vec, a resource based on the World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS)
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language data: compiled a massive dataset from 24 multilingual sources (e.g., OSCAR, Wikipedia), totaling 41.4 billion tokens across 1572 languages, with 252 languages meeting the minimum data threshold for analysis. Employed controlled experimental manipulations—including varying the size of monolingual and multilingual datasets, the syntactic and typological similarity of added languages (using lang2vec and WALS), model size, and tokenizer consistency—to systematically assess how these factors influenced model performance.
interp_method: systematic investigation into the effects of multilingual pre-training on language modeling performance. Their approach involves pre-training over 10,000 monolingual and multilingual GPT-2 models across 252 languages, systematically manipulating four key variables: monolingual dataset size, added multilingual dataset size, linguistic similarity of added languages (with a focus on syntactic similarity), and model size. By evaluating performance changes across this large-scale setup, they provide a fine-grained, quantitative analysis of multilinguality’s impact—particularly in contrast to prior studies that examined only a small number of multilingual models. This large-scale, controlled methodology enables them to isolate the conditions under which multilingual pre-training helps or hinders performance, especially for low-resource languages and syntactic generalization.
main_findings: explore how multilingual pre-training affects language modeling performance across 252 languages. A key finding, especially regarding syntactic knowledge, is that syntactic similarity between languages plays a central role in determining the benefits of multilinguality, particularly for low-resource languages. When low-resource languages are paired with syntactically similar languages during pre-training, performance improves significantly—comparable to increasing monolingual data by up to 33%. Syntactic similarity alone accounts for a large portion (24.2%) of the variance in model gains, outperforming lexical and geographic similarity. However, the benefits plateau quickly, and too much multilingual data can harm performance, even for low-resource languages, due to model capacity limits. For high-resource languages, multilinguality consistently degrades performance—sometimes dramatically, and even more so when added languages are syntactically similar. This counterintuitive finding suggests interference effects and highlights the “curse of multilinguality”: as models are trained on more languages, performance across the board can suffer unless model capacity is sufficiently scaled. Overall, the study demonstrates that while multilingual training can enhance syntactic modeling in low-resource settings—especially with syntactically related languages—it can backfire in high-resource contexts, emphasizing the need for careful multilingual design based on linguistic compatibility and model capacity.

title: Our method allows for fine-grained analysis of the distinctions made by mBERT that disagree with UD, one way of moving past probing’s limitation of detecting only linguistic properties we have training data forrather than properties inherent to the model
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.
specific_phenomena: BLiMP: subject–verb agreement, reflexive binding, wh-islands, polarity licensing, ellipsis, determiner–noun agreement, argument structure, and irregular forms (e.g., irregular verbs like goed/went)
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language for training and controlled stimuli for evaluating syntactic knowledge: use the BLiMP benchmark, a controlled dataset with over 67,000 minimal pairs spanning 13 syntactic phenomena. Each pair contrasts a grammatical sentence with an ungrammatical counterpart differing only in the targeted syntactic feature, enabling precise assessment of syntactic specialization.
Mechanistic_method: Syntactic Sensitivity Index, Activation Patching (Targeted Ablation)
interp_method: whether SSI reflects actual syntactic competence, we examined its correlation with grammaticality judgment accuracy during training for models: a metric to quantify syntax specialization in language models. SSI measures how consistently individual neurons or layers differentiate between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences across various syntactic phenomena, with higher scores indicating stronger specialization. Unlike conventional probing methods, SSI captures structural separation of syntax-sensitive activations without requiring task-specific classifiers. The study validates SSI by showing that layer-wise SSI grows alongside syntax acquisition, predicts grammaticality judgment accuracy better than baseline methods, and that ablating high-SSI neurons significantly increases sentence perplexity, confirming their functional importance for syntactic predictions.
main_findings: mechanistic account of when, where, and how LLMs specialize syntactic structure: demonstrates that syntactic knowledge in LLMs emerges gradually through exposure to data rather than being innate. Syntactic specialization develops unevenly across layers, with different phenomena—such as ellipsis, argument structure, and determiner–noun agreement—peaking at different layers, and exhibits a “critical period” early in training where trajectories initially diverge across random seeds before converging. The authors introduce the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to quantify syntax specialization, showing that high-SSI neurons are functionally necessary for accurate grammatical predictions and strongly correlate with behavioral syntactic competence. Larger models and more extensive training data enhance SSI and layer-localized abstraction, though neuron-level implementation differs across model instances, indicating distributed, non-deterministic representations. Overall, LLMs show emergent, structured syntactic organization with parallels to human language acquisition, including critical periods and staged internal specialization.

title: Amnesic Probing: Behavioral Explanation With Amnesic Counterfactuals
abstract: A growing body of work makes use of probing in order to investigate the working of neural models, often considered black boxes. Recently, an ongoing debate emerged surrounding the limitations of the probing paradigm. In this work, we point out the inability to infer behavioral conclusions from probing results, and offer an alternative method which focuses on how the information is being used, rather than on what information is encoded. Our method, Amnesic Probing, follows the intuition that the utility of a property for a given task can be assessed by measuring the influence of a causal intervention which removes it from the representation. Equipped with this new analysis tool, we can ask questions that were not possible before, e.g. is part-of-speech information important for word prediction?  We perform a series of analyses on BERT to answer these types of questions. Our findings demonstrate that conventional probing performance is not correlated to task importance, and we call for increased scrutiny of claims that draw behavioral or causal conclusions from probing results.
specific_phenomena: coarse and fine-grained part-of-speech tags (c-pos and f-pos, respectively); syntactic dependency labels (dep);  named-entity labels (ner); and syntactic constituency boundaries that mark the beginning and the end of a phrase (phrase start, and phrase end, respectively)
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language English UD Treebank (McDonald et al., 2013) provides coarse-grained Part-of-Speech (c-pos), fine-grained Part-of-Speech (f-pos), and syntactic dependency labels (dep), while English OntoNotes (Weischedel et al., 2013) supplies named-entity labels (ner) and syntactic constituency boundaries (phrase start, phrase end). For training, 100,000 random tokens were sampled from these datasets
interp_method: measuring the influence of a causal intervention that removes it from the representation; Amnesic Probing as a counterfactual approach to assess the utility of a property for a given task. It operates on the intuition that if a property (e.g., part-of-speech) is being used for a task (e.g., language modeling), then its removal should negatively impact the model's ability to perform that task. This method is designed to provide behavioral explanations for how neural models work by measuring the influence of a causal intervention that removes specific information from the representation
main_findings: Amnesic Probing is a method that evaluates the causal importance of specific properties in neural models by removing them from representations and observing the resulting effect on behavior, rather than merely identifying what information is encoded. Using this approach, the study found that conventional probing often overestimates task relevance, as high extractability does not imply actual usage. For BERT, dependency information and coarse/fine Part-of-Speech (POS) labels were crucial for word prediction, while phrase markers were largely unimportant. The impact of removing POS information varied across categories: closed-class words like determiners and conjunctions were heavily affected, whereas open-class words like nouns and verbs were minimally impacted. Differences also emerged between masked and non-masked representations, with different layers showing varying sensitivity to property removal. For instance, c-pos information was most influential in intermediate layers (3, 11–12), and in some cases, removing information improved performance, highlighting nuanced, layer-specific behavior. Overall, Amnesic Probing reveals how syntactic knowledge is causally utilized by neural models, providing a finer-grained understanding than conventional probing.

title: Information Flow Routes: Automatically Interpreting Language Models at Scale
abstract: Information flows by routes inside the network via mechanisms implemented in the model. These routes can be represented as graphs where nodes correspond to token representations and edges to computations. We automatically build these graphs in a top-down manner, for each prediction leaving only the most important nodes and edges. In contrast to the existing workflows relying on activation patching, we do this through attribution: this allows us to efficiently uncover existing circuits with just a single forward pass. Unlike with patching, we do not need a human to carefully design prediction templates, and we can extract information flow routes for any prediction (not just the ones among the allowed templates). As a result, we can analyze model behavior in general, for specific types of predictions, or different domains. We experiment with Llama 2 and show that some attention head roles are overall important, e.g. previous token heads and subword merging heads. Next, we find similarities in Llama 2 behavior when handling tokens of the same part of speech. Finally, we show that some model components can be specialized on domains such as coding or multilingual texts.
specific_phenomena: Parts of Speech (POS) are a primary focus, with function words (e.g., conjunctions, determiners, adpositions, punctuation) showing distinct clustering of component contributions by POS tag, while content words (e.g., nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, numbers) exhibit more mixed patterns influenced by broader context. POS tags are derived using the NLTK universal tagset. Subword structures also influence contributions: model components behave differently depending on whether a token is the first subword or a later subword of a word.
fine_tuning_materials: naturalistic language and controlled stimuli to evaluate Language Model (LM) behavior. For naturalistic language, a subset of 1,000 sentences from the C4 dataset was used to analyze overall patterns in attention head and FFN block importance. Controlled stimuli included several task-specific setups: the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task, where the model predicted indirect objects in sentences with structured templates and contrastive variations; the Greater-than task, which tested numerical prediction in templated sentences with contrastive numbers; and domain-specific evaluations using FLORES-200 multilingual devtest sets (English, Russian, Italian, Spanish), CodeParrot code data, and arithmetic addition/subtraction data to assess component specialization for programming and arithmetic reasoning.
experimental_materials_comment: nan
interp_method: Information Flow Routes, interprets Transformer LM predictions by extracting the most important portion of the network’s information flow. It automatically constructs graphs representing these routes in a top-down manner, keeping only the critical nodes and edges for each prediction. Unlike activation patching, this approach relies on attribution, making it roughly 100× faster and more versatile. The method identifies “important subgraphs” by tracing information through the network, and it evaluates edge importance using ideas from ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-Wise Token-to-Token Interactions), which quantifies each connected node’s contribution based on its proximity to the final output sum. This enables efficient and scalable identification of key computations within the model.
main_findings: introduces Information Flow Routes, a method for interpreting Transformer LMs by automatically constructing graphs that capture the most important computations for a given prediction. This approach is highly efficient—about 100× faster than activation patching—and broadly applicable, allowing analysis of model components across tasks, domains, and predictions without human-designed templates. Experiments on Llama 2 reveal structured bottom-to-top processing: lower layers handle general input processing, while higher layers perform fine-grained, specialized operations, with the last-layer feed-forward network being especially influential. Regarding syntactic knowledge, the study finds that function words elicit distinct component contribution patterns, whereas content words rely on broader contextual reasoning. Subword structure strongly affects information flow, with separate attention heads specialized for previous-token and subword-merging roles, primarily in lower layers. Component contributions depend more on input token POS than output token POS, suggesting early layers handle inputs generically and higher layers refine predictions. Additionally, punctuation shows unique behavior: the first period in a text is largely processed via an "untouched" residual stream, functioning analogously to a Beginning-Of-Sentence token for subsequent tokens. Overall, the findings illuminate how LMs internally route syntactic and subword information during prediction.

title: A Targeted Assessment of the Syntactic Abilities of Transformer Models for Galician-Portuguese
abstract: This paper presents a targeted syntactic evaluation of Transformer models for Galician-Portuguese. We defined three experiments that allow to explore how these models, trained with a masked language modeling objective, encode syntactic knowledge. To do so, we created a new dataset including test instances of number (subject-verb), gender (subject-predicative adjective), and person (subject-inflected infinitive) agreement. This dataset was used to evaluate monolingual and multilingual BERT models, controlling for various aspects such as the presence of attractors or the distance between the dependent elements. The results show that Transformer models perform competently in many cases, but they are generally confounded by the presence of attractors in long-distance dependencies. Moreover, the different behavior of monolingual models trained with the same corpora reinforces the need for a deep exploration of the network architectures and their learning process.
specific_phenomena: syntactic agreement phenomena; number agreement (subject-verb), gender agreement (subject-predicative adjective), and person agreement (subject-inflected infinitive); presence of attractors and distance between dependent elements
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli: created a new dataset, controlled for factors like the presence of attractors and the distance between dependent elements, including sentences without attractors to assess their impact. This design enabled a precise evaluation of how Transformer models encode syntactic knowledge under specific conditions. The dataset is publicly available.
interp_method: targeted syntactic evaluation
main_findings: The targeted syntactic evaluation of Transformer models for Galician-Portuguese shows that these models encode syntactic knowledge with mixed success. They perform competently in many cases but struggle with long-distance dependencies when attractors—distracting elements between dependent words—are present. Differences in performance among monolingual models trained on the same corpora highlight the need for deeper exploration of network architectures and learning dynamics. The study evaluated subject-verb number agreement, subject-predicative adjective gender agreement, and subject-inflected infinitive person agreement using a newly created dataset, controlling for attractors and dependency distance. Both monolingual and multilingual BERT models were tested, while some elements like the formal pronoun “Vostedes” were excluded due to vocabulary limitations, and lower-performing Bertinho models were not discussed.

title: Do Syntactic Probes Probe Syntax? Experiments with Jabberwocky Probing
abstract: Analysing whether neural language models encode linguistic information has become popular in NLP. One method of doing so, which is frequently cited to support the claim that models like BERT encode syntax, is called probing; probes are small supervised models trained to extract linguistic information from another model’s output. If a probe is able to predict a particular structure, it is argued that the model whose output it is trained on must have implicitly learnt to encode it. However, drawing a generalisation about a model’s linguistic knowledge about a specific phenomena based on what a probe is able to learn may be problematic: in this work, we show that semantic cues in training data means that syntactic probes do not properly isolate syntax. We generate a new corpus of semantically nonsensical but syntactically well-formed Jabberwocky sentences, which we use to evaluate two probes trained on normal data. We train the probes on several popular language models (BERT, GPT-2, and RoBERTa), and find that in all settings they perform worse when evaluated on these data, for one probe by an average of 15.4 UUAS points absolute. Although in most cases they still outperform the baselines, their lead is reduced substantially, e.g. by 53% in the case of BERT for one probe. This begs the question: what empirical scores constitute knowing syntax?
specific_phenomena: syntactic structure of a sentence, focusing on syntactic distance between word pairs and the identification of unlabeled undirected parse trees
experimental_materials_comment: English EWT Universal Dependency (UD; Nivreet al., 2016) treebank and substitute words (randomly) with our pseudowords whenever we have one available with matching fine-grained part-of-speech annotation
interp_method:
evaluate the structural probe on DSpr, introduced in Hewitt and Manning(2019)—it is the S pearman correlation between the actual and predicted syntactic distances between each pair of words. We evaluate the perceptron probe using the unlabeled undirected attachment; score (UUAS), which is the percentage of correctly identified edges. These different metrics reflect differences in the probe designs, which are elaborated in Hall Maudslay et al. (2020);
Jabberwocky probing is a method that evaluates syntactic probes by using a corpus of semantically nonsensical but syntactically correct sentences, inspired by Carroll’s (1871) verse of pseudowords, to help distinguish a language model’s understanding of syntax from its reliance on semantics.
main_findings: indicate that current syntactic probes often rely on semantic cues rather than isolating syntax, as evidenced by substantial performance drops on semantically nonsensical but syntactically correct Jabberwocky sentences; while models like BERT, GPT-2, and RoBERTa (BERToids) still generally outperform simple baselines, their advantage is greatly reduced, suggesting previous studies may have overestimated their syntactic abilities. The study highlights that existing probes, which extract only simplified undirected unlabeled parse trees, may conflate syntax with semantics and be misled by statistical confounds, and it urges more careful evaluation, including the development of artificial treebanks and controlled datasets, to properly assess LMs’ syntactic knowledge.

title: Intrinsic Probing through Dimension Selection
abstract: Most modern NLP systems make use of pre-trained contextual representations that attain astonishingly high performance on a variety of tasks. Such high performance should not be possible unless some form of linguistic structure inheres in these representations, and a wealth of research has sprung up on probing for it. In this paper, we draw a distinction between intrinsic probing, which examines how linguistic information is structured within a representation, and the extrinsic probing popular in prior work, which only argues for the presence of such information by showing that it can be successfully extracted. To enable intrinsic probing, we propose a novel framework based on a decomposable multivariate Gaussian probe that allows us to determine whether the linguistic information in word embeddings is dispersed or focal. We then probe fastText and BERT for various morphosyntactic attributes across 36 languages. We find that most attributes are reliably encoded by only a few neurons, with fastText concentrating its linguistic structure more than BERT.
specific_phenomena: morphosyntactic attributes, including PERSON, TENSE, NUMBER, GENDER, CASE, ASPECT, VOICE, Animacy, Definiteness, Mood, Comparison, Polarity, Finiteness, and Possession
languages_tested_comment: 36: Afrikaans, Arabic, Belarusian, Bulgarian, Catalan, Czech, Danish, German, English, Estonian, Basque, Persian, Finnish, French, Irish, Hebrew, Hindi, Croatian, Hungarian, Italian, Latin, Latvian, Lithuanian, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Slovak, Slovenian, Spanish, Serbian, Swedish, Turkish, Ukrainian, and Urdu...
experimental_materials_comment: morphosyntactic attributes rather than purely syntactic structures like parse trees. The specific attributes analyzed include PERSON, TENSE, NUMBER, GENDER, CASE, ASPECT, VOICE, Animacy, Definiteness, Mood, Comparison, Polarity, Finiteness, and Possession. These features are probed across 36 languages from the Universal Dependencies treebanks, with a detailed breakdown of which attributes were analyzed for each language provided in the paper. The authors emphasize that their investigation extends beyond simple features like number and tense to a broader set of morphological and morphosyntactic properties.
interp_method: decomposable multivariate Gaussian probe, sometimes shortened to a decomposable probe. It leverages the decomposability of the multivariate Gaussian distribution to efficiently evaluate which dimensions encode linguistic information. This probe is applied within a broader framework called dimension selection, which systematically identifies the most informative neurons or embedding dimensions for a given morphosyntactic attribute.
main_findings: investigates how linguistic or morphosyntactic knowledge is encoded in language models, distinguishing intrinsic probing, which analyzes how information is structured within representations, from traditional extrinsic probing that only measures extractability. Using a decomposable multivariate Gaussian probe, the study examines morphosyntactic attributes (e.g., tense, number, gender, case, aspect, voice) across 36 languages. Results show that in fastText, linguistic information is highly focal, concentrated in a small number of dimensions (≈10 per attribute), whereas in BERT it is more dispersed (≈35 dimensions per attribute). Despite BERT’s broader distribution, even a few neurons can partially separate features like tense. Overall, fastText often encodes morphosyntactic attributes more effectively than BERT in low-dimensional projections, though BERT closes the gap as more dimensions are considered. Limitations include the Gaussian assumption of embeddings, which may imperfectly reflect real representations, but the lower-bound mutual information estimates provide a reliable minimum of encoded information.

title: Empowering Cross-lingual Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with Typological Feature
abstract: A challenge towards developing NLP systems for the world’s languages is understanding how they generalize to typological differences relevant for real-world applications. To this end, we propose M2C, a morphologically-aware framework for behavioral testing of NLP models. We use M2C to generate tests that probe models’ behavior in light of specific linguistic features in 12 typologically diverse languages. We evaluate state-of-the-art language models on the generated tests. While models excel at most tests in English, we highlight generalization failures to specific typological characteristics such as temporal expressions in Swahili and compounding possessives in Finish. Our findings motivate the development of models that address these blind spots.
model_name_comment: mT5-XXL (13B), PaLM-S (8B), PaLM-M (62B), PaLM-L (540B), and PaLM 2
specific_phenomena: language-agnostic and language-specific syntactic phenomena include negation, numerals, spatial expressions, temporal expressions, and comparatives, capturing patterns common across multiple languages but realized differently depending on morphology or syntax. Language-specific challenges include Swahili time expressions, which follow a sunrise/sunset system; compounding possessives in Finnish, involving complex morphological rules and 15 cases; Mandarin Chinese measure words, where over 150 words must match object types; and Russian motion verbs, which have distinct perfective and imperfective forms for unidirectional versus habitual motion.
languages_tested_comment: 12: English, Spanish, Italian, French, German, Swedish, Finnish, Slovak, Russian, Swahili, Mandarin Chinese, and Arabic
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli generated using the M2C (Multilingual Morphological Checklist) framework, which is designed for systematic behavioral testing of NLP models. M2C uses template-based generation with placeholders for morphological features, ensuring grammatical correctness and allowing tests in morphologically rich languages. The framework targets both general linguistic phenomena—such as negation, numerals, spatial and temporal expressions, and comparatives—and language-specific features, including Swahili time expressions, Mandarin measure words, Finnish compounding possessives, and Russian motion verbs. Tests are structured in a question-answering format (context, question, answer) and are scalable, with up to 2,000 examples per template
interp_method: M2C (Multilingual Morphological Checklist), a morphologically-aware framework for behavioral testing of NLP models. M2C is designed to systematically generate high-quality, controlled tests across a wide range of languages, including those with rich morphology. It enables targeted evaluation of language-specific capabilities, supports investigation of cross-lingual differences in practical scenarios, and allows large-scale, systematic assessment of models’ morphological and syntactic knowledge.
main_findings: indicate that while large language models like PaLM 2 perform very well on English, they face substantial challenges generalizing to typologically diverse languages, with smaller models often passing less than half of non-English tests. Language-agnostic features such as numerals, comparatives, negation, and spatial/temporal expressions remain difficult, especially for smaller models, though robust reasoning emerges at larger scales. Models also struggle with language-specific typological phenomena, including Finnish compounding possessives, Swahili time expressions, Chinese measure words, and Russian motion verbs. Many errors are directly tied to morphological and syntactic knowledge gaps, such as incorrect case, number, gender agreement, or diacritics, highlighting limitations in handling rich morphology, particularly for subword-based models. Model scale improves performance substantially, but even the largest models still leave room for improvement in certain languages. One-shot evaluation provides some gains, mainly for smaller models, but does not fully overcome persistent difficulties with numerals, comparatives, and typologically complex features, showing that multilingual generalization remains a key challenge.

title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the *observational mode*, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the *intervention mode*, we construe E as a claim that neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.
specific_phenomena: targeted syntactic features include: verb tense, transitive vs. intransitive verbs, gender agreement involving names and pronouns, and plural inflection, such as subject-verb agreement and noun-pronoun agreement.
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language and controlled stimuli, depending on the evaluation mode. In observational mode, naturalistic sentences from GPT-2 XL’s training corpus are used to identify neuron activation patterns, while controlled stimuli are introduced to assess prediction errors: sentences are constructed using GPT-3.5-turbo to probe Type I errors (false positives relative to the explanation) and Type II errors (false negatives), with regex programs used for explanations based on formal features like spelling. In intervention mode, the authors rely entirely on template-based controlled stimuli to rigorously test whether a neuron causally mediates a concept. These templates target specific linguistic or factual phenomena (e.g., verb tense, plural inflection, numerical comparison), and are filled with fixed, curated sets of concept instances.
Mechanistic_method: Causal Mediation Analysis (Interchange Interventions), Probing Techniques (linear)
interp_method: introduced by Bills et al. (2023), titled "Language models can explain neurons in language models." This approach leverages GPT-4 to generate natural language explanations for 300,000 individual neurons in the GPT-2 XL model, representing the largest-scale automated effort to interpret LLM internals at the time. The method involves prompting GPT-4 to describe what each neuron responds to in human-readable terms, aiming to make the internal representations of LLMs more interpretable. The current paper rigorously assesses this approach and finds that, despite its scale and accessibility, the generated explanations lack faithfulness and causal validity, especially for syntactic and grammatical functions.
main_findings: presents a critical evaluation of GPT-4-generated natural language explanations for individual neurons in GPT-2 XL, revealing significant shortcomings in their faithfulness and causal utility. Using a novel two-part evaluation framework—observational mode (which tests alignment between neuron activations and explanation-derived predictions) and intervention mode (which tests whether neurons causally mediate the explained concepts)—the authors find that even highly rated explanations perform poorly. In observational mode, explanations showed limited precision and recall (F1 = 0.56), while in intervention mode, they had no meaningful causal impact, performing on par with random baselines across most tasks. Syntax-related evaluations, such as verb tense and agreement, confirmed this pattern, with no evidence that explained neurons were causally responsible for grammatical behavior. The findings also highlight issues with using natural language explanations due to their ambiguity and raise doubts about individual neurons being meaningful units for causal interpretation, as many activations seem to reflect shared linguistic structures rather than isolated semantic concepts.

title: Which sentence embeddings and which layers encode syntactic structure?
abstract: Recent models of language have eliminated syntactic-semantic dividing lines. We explore the psycholinguistic implications of this development by comparing different types of sentence embeddings in their ability to encode syntactic constructions. Our study uses contrasting sentence structures known to cause syntactic priming effects, that is, the tendency in humans to re- peat sentence structures after recent exposure. We compare how syntactic alternatives are captured by sentence embed- dings produced by a neural language model (BERT) or by the composition of word embeddings (BEAGLE, HHM, GloVe). Dative double object vs. prepositional object and active vs. passive sentences are separable in the high-dimensional space of the sentence embeddings and can be classified with a high degree of accuracy. The results lend empirical support to the modern, computational, integrated accounts of semantics and syntax, and they shed light on the information stored at different layers in deep language models such as BERT.
specific_phenomena: dative double object (DO) sentences (e.g., “The sailor mailed his sweetheart a letter”), dative prepositional object (PO) sentences (e.g., “The sailor mailed a letter to his sweetheart”), active voice, and passive voice.
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language and controlled stimuli: For dative double object (DO) and prepositional object (PO) sentences, the researchers used controlled stimuli derived from a syntactic priming experiment based on Bock (1986) and Branigan et al. (1995). Amazon Mechanical Turk participants completed partial sentence prompts biased toward eliciting either DO or PO constructions, producing 11,520 unique sentences (2,607 DO, 2,441 PO, and 1,816 “neither” sentences after filtering). This controlled setup allowed the collection of materials reflecting actual sensitivity to priming. For active versus passive voice, the study relied on naturalistic sentences sampled from the Europarl corpus. Sentences contained a single verb and were filtered to match the vocabularies of BEAGLE and GloVe embeddings. This corpus included 1,303 passive and 20,124 active sentences, noted for their length and low-frequency words, representing challenging, naturally occurring language.
interp_method: describe several methods for creating and evaluating sentence embeddings. Simple techniques include summing, which combines word embeddings by summing or averaging, and random embeddings, which serve as a baseline. Permutation-based methods encode word order: absolute position assigns a unique permutation to each word based on its position, while relative position encodes words relative to a sliding window. Convolution-based methods (circular convolution) form n-gram associations to preserve order. Neural embeddings are obtained from BERT, averaging hidden states from specific layers (e.g., Layer 4 or 7). Other models for word embeddings include BEAGLE, HHM, and GloVe. To evaluate embeddings, the authors measure spatial separability using the sensitivity index (d′) and perform classification with generalized linear models, assessing how well sentence embeddings distinguish syntactic distinctions.
main_findings: investigates how sentence embeddings encode syntactic structures, providing insights into both language models and psycholinguistic theories. Results show that syntactic distinctions—such as dative double object (DO) versus prepositional object (PO) and active versus passive sentences—are separable in high-dimensional sentence embedding spaces, supporting integrated accounts of syntax and semantics. In BERT, mid-layer representations (Layers 4–7) are most effective for capturing these distinctions, achieving high classification accuracy for sentence type (85–87% for active/passive, 96–98% for PO/DO). Different embedding combination methods affect syntactic sensitivity: summing word embeddings is least effective, permutation by relative position is robust, and convolution with holographic vectors like HHM captures abstract syntactic relationships well. Lexical semantics further aids detection of certain structures, while distributional semantic models such as BEAGLE and HHM offer comparable performance to BERT with lower computational cost. Overall, the findings demonstrate that sentence embeddings in modern models encode syntactic knowledge in a distributed, layer-specific manner, with methods for combining word embeddings influencing the preservation of syntactic information.

title: Evidence of Hierarchically-Complex Syntactic Structure Within BERT’s Word Representation
abstract: Our research provides empirical support that LLM’s contextualized word embeddings have captured deep and hierarchical syntactic structure. In 2019, Hewitt and Manning found evidence that LLMs have captured features of structural dependency parses within their word representations; we extend this work by deploying their methodology on sentence structures that are differentiated only in a constituency-based account like Minimalism rather than a dependency-based account. Our novel work creates a dataset containing several carefully selected sentence structures whose dependency parses are identical, but whose constituency trees differ due to to the size of the complement (vP versus TP versus CP). We find differences in the probe's predicted distances that can only be explained if the embeddings have indeed captured some Minimalist structural difference between these sentence types. The impact of our work helps to realize Linzen's (2019) argument that linguists can further the study and understanding of LLMs and that the field of NLP provides novel tools for further linguistic research.
specific_phenomena: hierarchical syntactic structure as described by Constituency Grammar, particularly within a Minimalist framework, contrasting this with the flatter structures typical of Dependency Grammar. Key constructions examined include sentences differentiated by complement size, ranging from bare vPs (perception and causative verbs) to TPs (ECM constructions) and CPs (finite clauses). The dataset leverages wh-question formation and filler-gap dependencies to vary hierarchical distances while keeping dependency distances constant, and includes double-nested complements (double-nested ECMs and CPs) to probe recursion. The study also considers finiteness, the operations of Merge and Move, and the argument-adjunct distinction, aiming to determine whether LLMs encode complex hierarchies and subsurface constituency structures
experimental_materials_comment: controlled stimuli: constructing a novel dataset of 18,252 sentences designed to probe five specific syntactic constructions reflecting different hierarchical structures in a Minimalist framework. The materials were carefully crafted to target constituency differences while keeping dependency parses identical, using wh-question formation to manipulate hierarchical distances without changing head-dependent distances in a Dependency Grammar account. Complement sizes were varied systematically, including bare vP complements, single TP complements (ECM verbs), and single CP complements, as well as double-nested ECMs and double-nested full CP complements to increase hierarchical complexity. The linear distance between wh-constituents and embedded verbs was also varied by changing subjects and adding adverbs, preventing the model from relying solely on linear cues. the structural probe itself was pre-trained on naturalistic dependency parses
interp_method: refer to the structural probe developed by Hewitt and Manning (2019). They describe their work as extending this method by applying it to specific sentence structures and explicitly note that they are “utilizing a probe method developed by (Hewitt and Manning, 2019)”, referring to it as the “structural probe of Hewitt and Manning” or the “original Hewitt and Manning (2019) structural probe”. For their experiments, they used the best-performing pretrained probe from the original study.
main_findings: provides strong evidence that LLMs like BERT encode hierarchically complex syntactic structure within their contextualized embeddings, extending the work of Hewitt and Manning (2019) by focusing on constituency-based distinctions rather than dependency alone. Key findings indicate that the models’ embeddings reflect differences in complement size (vP, TP, CP), with predicted distances from a dependency-trained structural probe correlating with hierarchical depth: CP complements showed the largest distances, followed by TP (ECM verbs) and then vP (perception verbs). This suggests that BERT captures Minimalist-like constituency information, even though the probe was trained only on dependency structures, and implies that nested hierarchies may be implicitly encoded within dependency representations. The results favor a vP analysis for perception verbs over a bare TP account, and although finiteness contributes, significant distinctions between non-finite complements indicate that constituency size is the primary factor. Methodologically, using a probe trained on dependency parses ensures that the observed sensitivity is not simply due to the probe learning the task, lending confidence to the conclusion that LLMs implicitly encode subsurface hierarchical syntax, potentially reducing the need for explicit, dense constituency representations in NLP applications.

title: Reconstruction Probing
abstract: We propose reconstruction probing, a new analysis method for contextualized representations based on reconstruction probabilities in masked language models (MLMs). This method relies on comparing the reconstruction probabilities of tokens in a given sequence when conditioned on the representation of a single token that has been fully contextualized and when conditioned on only the decontextualized lexical prior of the model. This comparison can be understood as quantifying the contribution of contextualization towards reconstruction—the difference in the reconstruction probabilities can only be attributed to the representational change of the single token induced by contextualization. We apply this analysis to three MLMs and find that contextualization boosts reconstructability of tokens that are close to the token being reconstructed in terms of linear and syntactic distance. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to finer-grained decomposition of contextualized representations, and we find that these boosts are largely attributable to static and positional embeddings at the input layer.
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Hierarchical structure, word order, Agreement and feature-checking
specific_phenomena: relations between SOURCE and RECON tokens, including subword relations (e.g., “Bud” and “##dy”), head-dependent relations (single dependency arcs), ancestor-descendant relations (multiple dependency arcs excluding direct dependents), and cases with no syntactic relation. They also analyze finer-grained syntactic properties, such as dependency relations by label, where ROOT and PRT (particle) arcs show consistently high reconstructability, and functional relations between functional heads and content-word dependents, including auxiliary-verb (“aux”/“auxpass”) and complementizer-verb (“mark”) relations, with morphological agreement suggested as a factor enhancing reconstructability in auxiliary-verb pairs. Finally, they consider distance measures, both linear distance (token index difference) and structural distance (number of arcs along the dependency path between SOURCE and RECON).
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language drawn from 10,000 premise sentences sampled from the non-spoken genres of the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI) dataset. These sentences are considered naturalistic because they originate from naturally-occurring text across diverse domains and vary in length, reflecting the types of data the models were trained on. Spoken data was excluded due to its atypicality, and hypothesis sentences were omitted since they were crowd-sourced rather than naturally occurring.Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI; Williams et al. 2018), excluded spoken data,
interp_method: reconstruction probing: a technique for analyzing contextualized representations in masked language models (MLMs). It works by comparing the reconstruction probabilities of tokens when conditioned on a fully contextualized token representation versus a decontextualized lexical prior, thereby quantifying how much contextualization affects predictions for co-occurring tokens. The method is both causal, since it examines the effect of contextual information through input-level intervention, and behavioral, because it leverages the model’s existing reconstruction objective rather than relying on specialized probes. This allows researchers to measure directly how contextual embeddings encode syntactic and semantic information.
main_findings: uses reconstruction probing to quantify how much contextualized embeddings contribute to token reconstruction, focusing on syntactic knowledge in masked language models (BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT). It finds that contextualized representations encode abstract syntactic information rather than exact co-occurring token identities, with reconstruction boosts strongest for syntactic neighbors—subwords, head-dependent pairs, and ancestor-descendant relations—especially in BERT. Finer-grained analyses reveal that functional dependencies (e.g., auxiliary-verb) are highly reconstructable, while complementizer-verb relations are less so.
