Learnable importance scores demonstrate that downstream tasks benefit meaningfully from syntactic integration. Overall, dependency trees are preferred over constituency trees for their conciseness and direct reflection of head-dependent relationships, effectively linking syntax and semantics.

exclusion_grounds: NMT experiment but focus on Bert representations too
title: Dependency-based syntax-aware word representations
abstract: Dependency syntax has been demonstrated highly useful for a number of natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Typical approaches of utilizing dependency syntax include Tree-RNN and Tree-Linearization, both of which exploit explicit 1-best tree outputs from a well-trained parser as inputs. However, these approaches may suffer from error propagation due to the inevitable errors contained in the 1-best tree outputs. In this work, we propose a novel approach to integrate dependency syntax without using the discrete tree outputs. The key idea is to use the intermediate hidden representations of a well-trained encoder-decoder dependency parser, which are referred to as Dependency-based Syntax-Aware Word Representations (Dep-SAWRs). Then, we simply concatenate such Dep-SAWRs with the conventional context-insensitive word embeddings to compose input word representations, without requiring to modify the model architecture of the downstream tasks. We evaluate the proposed method on four kinds of typical NLP tasks, including sentence classification, sentence matching, sequence labeling and machine translation. Experimental results show that the proposed approach is highly promising. On the one hand, it can utilize dependency syntax effectively, bringing consistently better performance on the four tasks compared with baselines without using syntax. On the other hand, the proposed method can outperform the Tree-RNN and Tree-Linearization approaches in most settings, and meanwhile are highly efficient in syntax integration. In addition, the proposed method would be easily extendable to encoding other structural attributes of language.
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Hierarchical structure, word order
specific_phenomena: bilexical syntactic relations, dependency labels, dependency-head pairs, and high-frequency subtrees; legal word orders (tested via Bigram Shift), hierarchical sentence structure (Tree Depth), and top constituent sequences (Top Constituent). The role of syntax in capturing long-distance but closely related word dependencies and possessive relationships
fine_tuning_materials: Dep-SAWRs
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language data from a variety of benchmark NLP datasets across multiple tasks—such as sentence classification, sentence matching, sequence labeling, and machine translation—in English, Chinese, and German. These datasets include real-world texts, with no mention of artificially constructed or manually controlled stimuli. However, to assess syntactic understanding in a more targeted way, the authors employ three syntax probing tasks—Bigram Shift (BS), Tree Depth (TD), and Top Constituent (TC)—which act as controlled assessments focused on specific linguistic properties like word order, sentence hierarchy, and syntactic structure. In addition to standard context-insensitive embeddings (e.g., GloVe, fastText) and contextualized embeddings (ELMo, BERT), the authors train language-specific BiAffine dependency parsers using established treebanks to produce Dependency-based Syntax-Aware Word Representations (Dep-SAWRs). These syntactic embeddings are then used in downstream tasks. The study also employs Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to handle subword-level translation tasks and ensures syntax representation consistency at that level.
interp_method: Dependency-based Syntax-Aware Word Representations (Dep-SAWRs). It is presented as a novel, implicit syntax encoding approach that derives hidden vectorial features from a neural dependency parser, bypassing the use of discrete syntactic tree outputs. Dep-SAWR serves as an efficient and effective alternative to traditional syntax integration methods.
main_findings: reveal that integrating syntactic knowledge, particularly through dependency syntax, significantly enhances performance across various NLP tasks. Traditional methods like Tree-RNN and Tree-Linearization suffer from error propagation and inefficiency due to reliance on discrete 1-best parse trees and structural heterogeneity. The proposed Dependency-based Syntax-Aware Word Representations (Dep-SAWRs) address these issues by implicitly encoding syntax from a neural dependency parser’s hidden representations, avoiding explicit trees and improving both accuracy and efficiency. Dep-SAWR consistently outperforms earlier methods and remains effective even when used alongside contextualized embeddings like ELMo and BERT, which already capture some syntax implicitly. However, syntax integration brings diminishing returns when stronger baselines like BERT are used, though Dep-SAWR still provides notable improvements. Syntax helps especially with longer sentences and benefits from accurate parsers, while freezing parser parameters yields better outcomes than fine-tuning. Finally, combining Dep-SAWR with other syntax integration methods in heterogeneous ensembles proves especially effective, demonstrating their complementary strengths.

title: Unveiling Linguistic Regions in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable cross-lingual alignment and generalization ability. Current research primarily focuses on improving LLMs’ cross-lingual generalization capabilities. However, there is still a lack of research on the intrinsic mechanisms of how LLMs achieve cross-lingual alignment. From the perspective of region partitioning, this paper conducts several investigations on the linguistic competence of LLMs. We discover a core region in LLMs that corresponds to linguistic competence, accounting for approximately 1% of the total model parameters. Removing this core region by setting parameters to zero results in a significant performance decrease across 30 different languages. Furthermore, this core region exhibits significant dimensional dependence, perturbations to even a single parameter on specific dimensions leading to a loss of linguistic competence. Moreover, we discover that distinct monolingual regions exist for different languages, and disruption to these specific regions substantially reduces the LLMs’ proficiency in those corresponding languages. Our research also indicates that freezing the core linguistic region during further pre-training can mitigate the issue of catastrophic forgetting (CF), a common phenomenon observed during further pre-training of LLMs. Overall, exploring the LLMs’ functional regions provides insights into the foundation of their intelligence.
specific_phenomena: grammatical structures, Sentence structure and constituents, cross-linguistic syntactic differences
languages_tested_comment: 30: Arabic, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese
fine_tuning_materials: further pre-training; They also experimented with and compared their methods to "full-scale fine-tuning". A key aspect of their methodology involved "Freeze Core Regions Fine-tuning," where the "Top 5%" core language area was frozen during further pre-training to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. For instance, LLaMA-2-7B was subjected to further pre-training on 100,000 Arabic sentences. They also trained on Chinese Zhihu corpus to evaluate reacquisition of competence
experimental_materials_comment: For naturalistic data, LLaMA-2-7B/13B models were further pre-trained on diverse sources including Chinese platforms (Zhihu, WeChat), English sources (Arxiv, Falcon), and books in 28 additional languages, covering a total of 30 languages. Six languages—Arabic, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese—were selected for targeted pre-training and region localization, with 100,000 samples each, and all 30 languages were used for evaluation using perplexity (PPL) as the metric. Controlled stimuli included structured benchmark tasks such as MMLU (English) and ArabicMMLU, as well as specific prompt-based tests like “There are 365 days in a year and 12,” translated across languages to probe model output after monolingual region removal. The study also implicitly assessed syntactic processing by analyzing how removing regions for Russian affected Ukrainian due to shared sentence structure and constituents.
interp_method: Parameter Importance Estimation, which uses a first-order Taylor expansion to measure parameter sensitivity—the degree to which removing a parameter increases prediction loss. Building on this, they introduce Structured Removal, a method for systematically zeroing out rows or columns in model matrices, focusing particularly on "Top" dimensions that contain high concentrations of important parameters. To probe the fine-grained impact of individual elements, they conduct Single Dimension Perturbation and Single Parameter Perturbation experiments. For addressing catastrophic forgetting during continued pretraining, the authors propose Freeze Core Regions Fine-tuning, which involves freezing the most critical 5% of language-related parameters to preserve prior linguistic competence. More broadly, the study is framed as an exploration of LLMs’ linguistic capabilities from a parameter partitioning or region partitioning perspective, emphasizing the existence of functionally distinct regions—such as core linguistic and monolingual zones—within the model's parameter space.
main_findings: highlight critical insights into how LLMs internalize and localize linguistic competence through specialized parameter regions. Most notably, they identify a "core linguistic region," comprising about 1% of the model’s parameters, that is essential for general linguistic ability and cross-lingual alignment. Zeroing out this region leads to a dramatic loss of performance across 30 languages, and attempts to relearn language rules elsewhere are ineffective, emphasizing its centrality. This core region also shows strong dimensional dependence, where perturbing even individual high-importance dimensions severely degrades linguistic performance. In addition to this shared core, the study uncovers distinct monolingual regions that encode language-specific knowledge—disrupting these leads to impaired performance in the associated language(s), with spillover effects observed between typologically similar languages like Russian and Ukrainian. These monolingual zones are particularly tied to grammatical and syntactic structures. The findings also show that freezing the core linguistic region during further pretraining can reduce catastrophic forgetting, preserving prior linguistic knowledge while learning new languages. Overall, the research underscores that both syntactic knowledge and broader linguistic competence are not uniformly distributed across LLMs but are concentrated in identifiable, highly sensitive parameter regions.

title: Do Transformers Parse while Predicting the Masked Word?
abstract: Pre-trained language models have been shown to encode linguistic structures, e.g. dependency and constituency parse trees, in their embeddings while being trained on unsupervised loss functions like masked language modeling. Some doubts have been raised whether the models actually are doing parsing or only some computation weakly correlated with it. We study questions: (a) Is it possible to explicitly describe transformers with realistic embedding dimension, number of heads, etc. that are capable of doing parsing -- or even approximate parsing? (b) Why do pre-trained models capture parsing structure? This paper takes a step toward answering these questions in the context of generative modeling with PCFGs. We show that masked language models like BERT or RoBERTa of moderate sizes can approximately execute the Inside-Outside algorithm for the English PCFG [Marcus et al, 1993]. We also show that the Inside-Outside algorithm is optimal for masked language modeling loss on the PCFG-generated data. We also give a construction of transformers with 50 layers, 15 attention heads, and 1275 dimensional embeddings in average such that using its embeddings it is possible to do constituency parsing with >70% F1 score on PTB dataset. We conduct probing experiments on models pre-trained on PCFG-generated data to show that this not only allows recovery of approximate parse tree, but also recovers marginal span probabilities computed by the Inside-Outside algorithm, which suggests an implicit bias of masked language modeling towards this algorithm.
syntactic_phenomena: Dependency parsing and constituency, Hierarchical structure
specific_phenomena: parsing and constituency structures: constituency parse trees, whose hierarchical structures are captured in the models’ representations; dependency parse trees, acknowledged as encoded in prior work; Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs), used to generate synthetic pre-training data and isolate syntactic information; marginal span probabilities, representing the likelihood of specific word spans forming constituents and computed via the Inside-Outside algorithm; and relative depth of common ancestors,
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language from the Penn Treebank (PTB) and controlled synthetic stimuli generated via a Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG). The PTB provided real English text for training probes, evaluating parsing performance, and analyzing attention patterns, while the PCFG-generated synthetic data allowed the authors to pre-train RoBERTa models and probe them in a way that isolates syntax from semantics. This synthetic dataset was used for tasks such as confirming constituency parse tree encoding, predicting marginal span probabilities, 1-masking perplexity evaluation, and attention pattern analysis. An out-of-distribution setup—training probes on synthetic data and testing on naturalistic PTB text—ensured that syntactic knowledge observed in the models was intrinsic rather than driven by semantic correlations.
interp_method: that transformer-based masked language models (MLMs) implicitly approximate during pre-training is the Inside-Outside algorithm. This algorithm computes marginal probabilities in Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs), and the study demonstrates that MLMs of moderate size can execute it approximately for English PCFGs. Importantly, the Inside-Outside algorithm is shown to be optimal for the MLM loss on PCFG-generated data, indicating an inherent bias of MLM training toward learning this parsing procedure. While the Labelled-Recall algorithm is mentioned as a probe for extracting unlabelled parse trees from contextual embeddings, the Inside-Outside algorithm remains the primary method associated with the transformer's implicit syntactic computation
main_findings: finds that transformer-based masked language models (MLMs) like BERT and RoBERTa can implicitly perform parsing by approximating the Inside-Outside algorithm for English Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs). This implicit bias arises because MLM training aligns with minimizing loss on PCFG-generated data. While an exact implementation requires unrealistically large models, transformers of moderate size can approximate the algorithm, achieving over 70% F1 on constituency parsing. Pre-training on synthetic PCFG data confirms that these models intrinsically encode syntactic structures, as probes generalize well to out-of-distribution datasets like the Penn Treebank. Model representations also predict marginal span probabilities with high correlation to the algorithm, and attention analyses reveal that lower layers focus on local spans while higher layers process longer spans. Overall, MLM pre-training drives transformers to acquire robust syntactic knowledge, encoding constituency structures and span probabilities in their contextual embeddings, independent of semantic cues.

title: How Well Do Large Language Models Understand Syntax? An Evaluation by Asking Natural Language Questions
abstract: While recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) bring us closer to achieving artificial general intelligence, the question persists: Do LLMs truly understand language, or do they merely mimic comprehension through pattern recognition? This study seeks to explore this question through the lens of syntax, a crucial component of sentence comprehension. Adopting a natural language question-answering (Q&A) scheme, we craft questions targeting nine syntactic knowledge points that are most closely related to sentence comprehension. Experiments conducted on 24 LLMs suggest that most have a limited grasp of syntactic knowledge, exhibiting notable discrepancies across different syntactic knowledge points. In particular, questions involving prepositional phrase attachment pose the greatest challenge, whereas those concerning adjectival modifier and indirect object are relatively easier for LLMs to handle. Furthermore, a case study on the training dynamics of the LLMs reveals that the majority of syntactic knowledge is learned during the initial stages of training, hinting that simply increasing the number of training tokens may not be the `silver bullet' for improving the comprehension ability of LLMs.
model_name_comment: 24 LLMs from 6 distinct families: Mistral, Baichuan2, Falcon, LLaMA, LLaMA2, and ChatGPT
specific_phenomena: grammatical relations and ambiguity resolution: Grammatical Subject (GS), Subject Complement (SC), Direct Object (DO), Indirect Object (IO), Main Verb Phrase (MVP), Adjectival Modifier (ADJ) – including post-modifiers such as relative clauses and reduced relative clauses, Adverbial Modifier / Adjunct (ADV), Coordination (CO), Prepositional Phrase Attachment (PPA), The framework emphasizes functional structure (f-structure),
experimental_materials_comment: extract syntactic information from the Penn Treebank:  Naturalistic sentences are drawn from the Penn Treebank (PTB), ensuring that models are tested on authentic English text, with answers expected to be direct phrases or words from these sentences. To introduce control, the authors designed syntactic patterns for the nine targeted knowledge points and generated questions and answers automatically using templates filled with extracted syntactic information. The evaluation employs three question formats—True/False, Multiple Choice, and Fill in the Blank—to probe different comprehension facets. A balanced down-sampling of over 3.5 million generated questions produced a final set of 3,170 items, ensuring equitable representation across all syntactic phenomena. This setup emphasizes grammatical relations (subjects, objects, complements) and syntactic ambiguity resolution (coordination and prepositional phrase attachment), providing a controlled yet realistic assessment of the LLMs’ sentence comprehension abilities.
interp_method: question-answering (Q&A) paradigm. comprehension aspect of syntax: select nine syntactic knowledge to evaluate: refer to the natural language question-answering (Q&A) paradigm as their method for evaluating syntactic knowledge in LLMs. This approach involves posing syntactically focused questions in natural language to the models and assessing their responses. It is designed to be LLM-friendly and captures the models’ ability to understand and apply syntactic rules in sentence comprehension. The evaluation uses three question formats: True/False, Multiple Choice, and Fill in the Blank, allowing a comprehensive assessment of the models’ grasp of syntax.
main_findings: evaluated 24 LLMs across nine syntactic knowledge points and found that most models demonstrate only a partial grasp of syntax, with notable variability across syntactic phenomena. Larger models (>1B parameters) show basic syntactic understanding, but overall accuracy remains limited. GPT-4 consistently outperforms all other models, even in zero-shot settings. Certain knowledge points, like prepositional phrase attachment (PPA), are particularly challenging, while adjectival modifiers (ADJ) and indirect objects (IO) are easier. Case studies (e.g., Baichuan2) indicate that most syntactic knowledge is acquired early in training, suggesting diminishing returns from further token exposure. Chat or instruction fine-tuned models often improve PPA performance, highlighting the importance of syntax in conversational tasks. Syntactic knowledge does not generalize consistently across question types (True/False, Multiple Choice, Fill in the Blank), and while larger models within a family tend to perform better, cross-family comparisons do not always follow this trend. Finally, few-shot prompting usually improves performance, though some models and knowledge points, like IO, can be misled by in-context examples.

title: CxGBERT: BERT meets Construction Grammar
abstract: While lexico-semantic elements no doubt capture a large amount of linguistic information, it has been argued that they do not capture all information contained in text. This assumption is central to constructionist approaches to language which argue that language consists of constructions, learned pairings of a form and a function or meaning that are either frequent or have a meaning that cannot be predicted from its component parts. BERT’s training objectives give it access to a tremendous amount of lexico-semantic information, and while BERTology has shown that BERT captures certain important linguistic dimensions, there have been no studies exploring the extent to which BERT might have access to constructional information. In this work we design several probes and conduct extensive experiments to answer this question. Our results allow us to conclude that BERT does indeed have access to a significant amount of information, much of which linguists typically call constructional information. The impact of this observation is potentially far-reaching as it provides insights into what deep learning methods learn from text, while also showing that information contained in constructions is redundantly encoded in lexico-semantics.
model_name_comment: BERT-base-cased, CxGBERT, BERT Base Clone, BERT Random, and BERT Plus CxG
specific_phenomena: parts of speech (PoS), tense, entire parse trees, syntactic properties of constructions, syntactic dependency labels, subject-verb agreement, and non-terminal constituents; ditransitive construction (“She gave me a book”), the Xer the Yer construction (“The more I think about it, the less I like it”), plural noun + -s, Personal Pronoun + didn’t + V + how, AUX + not (negative construction), MODAL + BE + Past-Participle, the caused-motion construction (“She sneezed the foam off the cappuccino”), and the resultative construction (“Sarah hammered the metal flat,” or idiomatic instances like “drive someone crazy”)
fine_tuning_materials: construction-specific dataset (small amount of training data: 100, 500, 1000, and 5000 examples)
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language for their experimental materials, drawing from large existing corpora rather than using carefully controlled or artificially constructed stimuli. The main sources include the WikiText-103 corpus, from which sentences are grouped into “documents” based on the constructions they instantiate using a modified grammatical induction algorithm, resulting in the CxG WikiText dataset, and original Wikipedia articles and the Book Corpus for comparison. Examples of constructions extracted from these corpora include patterns like “Personal Pronoun + didn’t + V + how,” the caused-motion construction, resultative constructions (e.g., “drive someone X” or “X MAKES Y Z”), plural nouns (Noun + -s), ditransitive constructions, and MODAL + BE + Past-Participle.
interp_method: several methods and approaches in their study: CxGBERT, a BERT variant trained on “CxG WikiText” with sentences clustered by constructions rather than documents (including Lower and Upper variants); BERTology, the NLP subfield focused on understanding BERT’s internal knowledge; probing, a technique to test whether a sentence encoding contains specific information; edge probing, a probing method for evaluating syntactic and semantic representations at the sub-sentence level; inoculation by fine-tuning, where the model is exposed to a small amount of task-specific data to reveal latent knowledge; and the grammatical induction algorithm, adapted from Dunn (2017), used to identify which constructions sentences instantiate in WikiText-103.
main_findings: finds that BERT inherently captures substantial syntactic knowledge, including parts of speech, tense, and even parse tree structures, reflecting its ability to encode core lexico-semantic information. A novel insight is that BERT also possesses access to constructional information—patterns of sentence structures known as constructions. To test this, the authors created CxGBERT, a BERT variant pre-trained on sentences clustered by constructions rather than traditional documents. Adding constructional information had minimal impact on downstream task performance compared to standard BERT, indicating that construction-based clustering conveys similar information as topical clustering. BERT also demonstrates an impressive ability to identify constructions: it can distinguish whether two sentences instantiate the same construction with nearly 90% accuracy after training on just 500 examples. This knowledge is embedded in internal layers, as freezing the model reduces performance, while fine-tuning (“inoculating”) unlocks constructional understanding. Semantically specific constructions are easier for BERT to identify than more general ones, highlighting that exposure to lexico-semantic patterns allows BERT to implicitly learn constructional information alongside syntactic structures.

title: Does Typological Blinding Impede Cross-Lingual Sharing?
abstract: Bridging the performance gap between high- and low-resource languages has been the focus of much previous work. Typological features from databases such as the World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS) are a prime candidate for this, as such data exists even for very low-resource languages. However, previous work has only found minor benefits from using typological information. Our hypothesis is that a model trained in a cross-lingual setting will pick up on typological cues from the input data, thus overshadowing the utility of explicitly using such features. We verify this hypothesis by blinding a model to typological information, and investigate how cross-lingual sharing and performance is impacted. Our model is based on a cross-lingual architecture in which the latent weights governing the sharing between languages is learnt during training. We show that (i) preventing this model from exploiting typology severely reduces performance, while a control experiment reaffirms that (ii) encouraging sharing according to typology somewhat improves performance.
specific_phenomena: syntactic features from the World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS), • Word order features: The study used a set of 33 word order features performance across four tasks (POS tagging, NER, XNLI, and PAWS-X)
languages_tested_comment: 40 languages: f, ar, bg, bn, de, el, en, es, et, eu, fa, fi, fr, he, hi, hu, id, it, ja, jv, ka, kk, ko, ml, mr, ms, my, nl, pt, ru, sw, ta, te, th, tl, tr, ur, vi, yo, and zh.
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic language data from real-world NLP benchmarks (e.g., POS tagging, NER, XNLI, PAWS-X
interp_method: measuring the impact of typology on cross-lingual sharing performance in a direct manner as part of the model architecture. They achieved this by:  Blinding the model to typological information using adversarial techniques based on gradient reversal, preventing it from exploiting these features
main_findings: blinding mBERT to it impedes successful cross-lingual transfer: Blinding mBERT to syntactic typological features led to significant performance drops on syntax-reliant tasks such as POS tagging, XNLI, and PAWS-X, confirming that syntactic knowledge is crucial for these tasks. In contrast, exposing the model to syntactic features by predicting them slightly improved performance. The blinding also disrupted the model’s internal parameter sharing between syntactically similar languages, while exposing restored alignment with linguistic similarity.

title: Neural Networks as Cognitive Models of the Processing of Syntactic Constraints
abstract: Languages are governed by syntactic constraints—structural rules that determine which sentences are grammatical in the language. In English, one such constraint is subject-verb agreement, which dictates that the number of a verb must match the number of its corresponding subject: “the dogs run”, but “the dog runs”. While this constraint appears to be simple, in practice speakers make agreement errors, particularly when a noun phrase near the verb differs in number from the subject (for example, a speaker might produce the ungrammatical sentence “the key to the cabinets are rusty”). This phenomenon, referred to as agreement attraction, is sensitive to a wide range of properties of the sentence; no single existing model is able to generate predictions for the wide variety of materials studied in the human experimental literature. We explore the viability of neural network language models—broad-coverage systems trained to predict the next word in a corpus—as a framework for addressing this limitation. We analyze the agreement errors made by Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and compare them to those of humans. The models successfully simulate certain results, such as the so-called number asymmetry and the difference between attraction strength in grammatical and ungrammatical sentences, but failed to simulate others, such as the effect of syntactic distance or notional (conceptual) number. We further evaluate networks trained with explicit syntactic supervision, and find that this form of supervision does not always lead to more human-like syntactic behavior. Finally, we show that the corpus used to train a network significantly affects the pattern of agreement errors produced by the network, and discuss the strengths and limitations of neural networks as a tool for understanding human syntactic processing.
specific_phenomena: subject-verb agreement and agreement attraction: Attractors in Prepositional Phrases (PP) vs. Relative Clauses (RC), Number asymmetry, Syntactic distance effects, Linear distance effects, Argument status (Core vs. Oblique Arguments), Grammaticality asymmetry
experimental_materials_comment: controlled experimental stimuli from six human psycholinguistic experiments on subject-verb agreement and agreement attraction, designed to manipulate specific syntactic and semantic factors such as attractor type (PP vs. RC), linear and syntactic distance, notional number, and argument status (core vs. oblique). Sentence completion and self-paced reading paradigms were simulated, and out-of-vocabulary words were occasionally replaced with semantically similar in-vocabulary words, with the verb be commonly used in production tasks. In addition, the neural network language models (LM-ONLY and LM+CCG) were trained on naturalistic corpora, including English Wikipedia (~80M words) and the Wall Street Journal section of the Penn Treebank (~1M words), performing word prediction (and CCG supertagging for LM+CCG).
interp_method: use the ONE-SAMPLE linking function to convert a language model’s output into probabilities for singular versus plural verb forms. This function takes a candidate singular-plural verb pair, computes each form’s probability from the LM’s distribution, and renormalizes them to sum to 1, representing the model’s likelihood of producing each form. Unlike the MAX-PROB method from Linzen et al. (2016), which deterministically selects the higher-probability form, ONE-SAMPLE captures graded, probabilistic behavior, mirroring how humans make non-deterministic agreement errors. "use amnesic probing (Elazar et al., 2021), an approach that uses techniques from the de-biasing literature in Natural Language Processing (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Ravfogel et al., 2020) to identify and remove differences across a linear subspace of a models’ representational space, preventing the model from using particular sources of information."
main_findings: examines how neural network LMs capture human-like syntactic knowledge, focusing on agreement attraction phenomena in English. LM-ONLY models, trained solely on word prediction, successfully replicate some human behaviors such as agreement attraction errors, number asymmetry, linear distance effects, and grammaticality asymmetry, but fail on phenomena tied to hierarchical syntax, including modifier type distinctions (PP vs. RC), syntactic distance effects, conceptual number influences, and argument status. Adding explicit syntactic supervision via CCG supertagging (LM+CCG models) yields mixed results: some aspects, like number asymmetry and linear distance effects, improve, but critical hierarchical distinctions remain largely unmodeled. Training data also affects performance; larger Wikipedia-trained models generally show more human-like agreement patterns than smaller WSJ-trained models, though effects vary by construction frequency. Comparisons with GPT-2 reveal that while transformer architectures achieve lower overall error rates and better capture certain hierarchical effects (e.g., argument status), they still fail to replicate PP vs. RC distinctions and grammaticality asymmetry fully. Overall, neural LMs capture some agreement phenomena but remain limited in modeling hierarchical syntactic sensitivity, with both architecture and training data influencing performance.

title: The Universe of Utterances According to BERT
abstract: It has been argued that BERT “rediscovers the traditional NLP pipeline”, with lower layers extracting morphosyntactic features and higher layers creating holistic sentence-level representations. In this paper, we critically examine this assumption through a principle-component-guided analysis, extracing sets of inputs that correspond to specific activation patterns in BERT sentence representations. We find that even in higher layers, the model mostly picks up on a variegated bunch of low-level features, many related to sentence complexity, that presumably arise from its specific pre-training objectives.
specific_phenomena: imperatives, nominative heading-like constructions
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic: train and development splits of the Georgetown University Multilayer (GUM) corpus, annotated with Universal Dependencies
interp_method: PCA, presenting results under a section titled “Principal Component-based Analysis.” Building on and extending Geva et al. (2021), they replace random neuron inspection with a guided approach that analyzes the major principal components of activation matrices. Specifically, they compute the first five principal components of embedding matrices and extract sentences with maximal and minimal scores for each component, manually identifying recurring patterns or features. This procedure is applied to two key token types: the CLS pseudo-token, which serves as a whole-sentence representation, and the first subword of the root element in sentences annotated with Universal Dependencies. Their distinctive contribution lies in systematically applying PCA to uncover and interpret the dominant features represented within BERT’s internal activations.
main_findings: challenges the assumption that BERT follows a “traditional NLP pipeline” where lower layers extract morphosyntactic features and higher layers form abstract semantic representations, finding instead that even the top layers rely heavily on shallow, low-level features such as sentence length, lexical items, and surface complexity, patterns likely tied to its pre-training objectives (masked-token prediction and next-sentence prediction) rather than deep syntactic understanding. Analyses of the CLS token show strong correlations with length and rare-word frequency, with principal components reflecting contextual or structural patterns (e.g., short quotes, conversational fragments) rather than principled semantics. Root token analyses across layers reveal that lower and middle layers focus largely on lexical and collocational cues, with only occasional morphosyntactic categories (e.g., imperatives), and higher layers continue to be dominated by surface features. Overall, BERT’s internal representations appear to blend lexical, structural, and surface properties without forming clean, high-level grammatical abstractions, suggesting its syntax encoding is shallow and task-specific rather than generalized.

title: Controlled Evaluation of Syntactic Knowledge in Multilingual Language Models
abstract: Language models (LMs) are capable of acquiring elements of human-like syntactic knowledge. Targeted syntactic evaluation tests have been employed to measure how well they form generalizations about syntactic phenomena in high-resource languages such as English. However, we still lack a thorough understanding of LMs’ capacity for syntactic generalizations in low-resource languages, which are responsible for much of the diversity of syntactic patterns worldwide. In this study, we develop targeted syntactic evaluation tests for three low-resource languages (Basque, Hindi, and Swahili) and use them to evaluate five families of open-access multilingual Transformer LMs. We find that some syntactic tasks prove relatively easy for LMs while others (agreement in sentences containing indirect objects in Basque, agreement across a prepositional phrase in Swahili) are challenging. We additionally uncover issues with publicly available Transformers, including a bias toward the habitual aspect in Hindi in multilingual BERT and underperformance compared to similar-sized models in XGLM-4.5B.
model_name_comment: mGPT, BLOOM, XGLM, mBERT, and XLM-RoBERTa
specific_phenomena: auxiliary verb agreement (basque), split ergativity (hindi), noun class agreement (swahili)
fine_tuning_materials: controlled, synthetic experimental materials, aligning with their Targeted Syntactic Evaluation (TSE) methodology. Materials were organized into minimal pairs, each consisting of one grammatical and one ungrammatical sentence differing by a single word, allowing the LM’s ability to detect violations to be assessed. Sentences were artificially generated using an adapted BLiMP approach: a manual vocabulary of ~300 words per language, annotated with syntactic, morphological, and semantic features, was sampled according to predefined sentence templates. Words were grouped semantically to maintain plausibility, and inflections (e.g., Basque case endings) were added via rule-based algorithms or listed exceptions. To ensure validity, a subset of the generated minimal pairs underwent human validation by self-reported L1 speakers, confirming that grammatical contrasts were meaningful.
experimental_materials_comment: nan
interp_method: Targeted Syntactic Evaluation (TSE), a method that compares the probabilities assigned by language models (LMs) to minimally different sequences. TSE allows a fine-grained analysis by isolating a single linguistic phenomenon within a specific sentence structure, making it possible to assess how performance varies with structural complexity. In this study, TSE was used to benchmark open-access Transformer LMs on morphosyntactic phenomena in low-resource languages, specifically auxiliary verb agreement in Basque, split ergativity in Hindi, and noun class agreement in Swahili.
main_findings: assessed the syntactic knowledge of open-access multilingual Transformer language models (LMs) in three low-resource languages: Basque, Hindi, and Swahili, revealing varied capacities across tasks and languages. Overall, LMs performed best on Hindi split ergativity (average accuracy 0.873), followed by Basque auxiliary verb agreement (0.741), and struggled most with Swahili noun class agreement (0.504), with mGPT13B emerging as the top-performing model (0.815 average accuracy). In Basque, errors were mostly linked to indirect objects, reflecting their rarity in corpora, while Hindi LMs generally excelled except for mBERT, which showed a habitual aspect bias. Swahili posed the greatest difficulty, especially with complex intervening phrases containing demonstratives or adjectives. Larger models generally achieved higher accuracy, though XGLM4.5B underperformed due to limited low-resource upsampling and the “curse of multilinguality.” Task complexity affected performance differently: Hindi was robust to intervening material, whereas Swahili performance declined with more complex syntactic structures.

title: Are Structural Concepts Universal in Transformer Language Models? Towards Interpretable Cross-Lingual Generalization
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited considerable cross-lingual generalization abilities, whereby they implicitly transfer knowledge across languages. However, the transfer is not equally successful for all languages, especially for low-resource ones, which poses an ongoing challenge. It is unclear whether we have reached the limits of implicit cross-lingual generalization and if explicit knowledge transfer is viable. In this paper, we investigate the potential for explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages to enhance cross-lingual generalization. Using the syntactic aspect of language as a testbed, our analyses of 43 languages reveal a high degree of alignability among the spaces of structural concepts within each language for both encoder-only and decoder-only LLMs. We then propose a meta-learning-based method to learn to align conceptual spaces of different languages, which facilitates zero-shot and few-shot generalization in concept classification and also offers insights into the cross-lingual in-context learning phenomenon. Experiments on syntactic analysis tasks show that our approach achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods and narrows the performance gap between languages, particularly benefiting those with limited resources.
specific_phenomena: syntactic phenomena, which they call "structural concepts": Word classes (POS tags): These include categories like noun, verb, and other Universal POS (UPOS) tags such as ADJ, ADP, ADV, AUX, CCONJ, DET, INTJ, NUM, PART, PRON, PROPN, PUNCT, SCONJ, SYM, VERB, and X. Grammatical relations (REL): These capture syntactic roles within sentences, such as subject and object.
experimental_materials_comment: For naturalistic language, it uses data from the Universal Dependencies (UD) v2.10 treebanks, which provide parsed corpora from real-world texts across 43 typologically diverse languages. This aligns with the fact that the LLMs studied (mBERT and LLaMA) are pretrained on raw text, allowing them to acquire implicit cross-linguistic knowledge. For controlled stimuli, the researchers focus on structural concepts consistently defined in the UD framework—namely, word classes (e.g., noun, verb) and grammatical relations (e.g., subject, object). These controlled, linguistically defined units enable a systematic and comparable investigation of how LLMs represent and align universal syntactic features across languages.
interp_method: describe their meta-learning-based approach as a framework for explicitly aligning structural concepts across languages to enhance cross-lingual performance. It works by learning a linear transformation of an LLM’s representation space to create a conceptual space where samples are classified based on their distance to concept prototypes. Alignability of these concepts across languages is evaluated using RSA and Procrustes analysis. Through a meta-learning framework, the method learns to align samples from different languages with source language prototypes, enabling effective zero-shot generalization by mapping prototypes into a unified, language-agnostic space. Additionally, the approach improves in-context learning by aligning contextualized representations of query sentences with prototypes derived from demonstration examples, leading to better generalization, especially in low-resource or cross-lingual settings.
main_findings: shows that LLMs implicitly capture universal structural concepts, such as word classes and grammatical relations, across languages, creating a shared conceptual space during pretraining. Analyses across 43 diverse languages revealed that these structural concepts are highly alignable and can be effectively mapped using representation analysis techniques. By introducing a meta-learning approach, the researchers demonstrated that explicit alignment of these concepts significantly boosts zero-shot and few-shot performance, particularly benefiting low-resource languages and narrowing cross-lingual performance gaps. This method also enhances generalization in in-context learning, though challenges remain for unseen sentences and underrepresented languages. Overall, the findings highlight that while LLMs naturally encode cross-linguistic structures, explicitly leveraging this knowledge through alignment methods can greatly improve their adaptability and performance across typologically diverse languages.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models via Linguistic Profiling
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) undergo extensive evaluation against various benchmarks collected in established leaderboards to assess their performance across multiple tasks. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is a lack of comprehensive studies evaluating these models’ linguistic abilities independent of specific tasks. In this paper, we introduce a novel evaluation methodology designed to test LLMs’ sentence generation abilities under specific linguistic constraints. Drawing on the ‘linguistic profiling’ approach, we rigorously investigate the extent to which five LLMs of varying sizes, tested in both zero- and few-shot scenarios, effectively adhere to (morpho)syntactic constraints. Our findings shed light on the linguistic proficiency of LLMs, revealing both their capabilities and limitations in generating linguistically-constrained sentences.
model_name_comment: Gemma (2B and 7B parameters), LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B), and Mistral (7B)
specific_phenomena: define “syntactic properties” as specific linguistic phenomena used to profile and evaluate the sentences generated by LLMs. These properties are organized into three main groups: (1) global and local syntactic tree structure, which includes the depth of the syntactic tree (max_depth) and the length of the longest dependency link (max_link); (2) word order phenomena, such as the distribution of pre-verbal subjects (subj_pre) and post-verbal objects (obj_post); and (3) the use of subordination, which examines the proportion of subordinative clauses in a sentence (subord_prop) as well as their relative position to the main clause, either in pre-verbal (subord_pre) or post-verbal (subord_post) positions.
experimental_materials_comment: naturalistic & controlled: For naturalistic language, the authors used the English Universal Dependency Treebank (EWT, v2.5) as a gold standard to extract authentic linguistic properties, filtering it to sentences of 5–40 tokens, yielding 19,282 examples. These served both to derive representative linguistic distributions and, in few-shot scenarios, to provide five exemplar sentences per prompt. Controlled stimuli consisted of fixed prompts explicitly instructing models to generate sentences with precise linguistic properties, such as “3 verbs” or “1 subordinate clause.” These prompts targeted morpho-syntactic and syntactic properties—including max_depth, max_link, subj_pre, obj_post, subord_prop, subord_pre, and subord_post—and also tested models’ sensitivity to incremental property values, recognizing that LLMs may struggle with exact numerical constraints but can detect relative differences.
interp_method: linguistic profiling' approach: This methodology is a novel evaluation framework designed to test the sentence generation abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) under specific linguistic constraints. It is inspired by the 'linguistic profiling' approach originally proposed by van Halteren (2004). This approach involves using a large number of linguistic feature counts as a "text profile," which allows for computing the distribution of constrained linguistic properties within generated sentences.
main_findings: introduced a method to test LLMs’ ability to generate sentences under specific linguistic constraints, focusing on morpho-syntactic and syntactic properties. Overall, LLMs struggled with generating sentences that met precise numerical constraints (e.g., exactly three verbs) but showed strong sensitivity to incremental variations, indicating an understanding of relative linguistic changes. Mistral performed best in zero-shot scenarios, though Gemma models—especially Gemma-2 and Gemma-7—excelled in few-shot settings, sometimes surpassing Mistral, with larger variants generally outperforming smaller ones. Models adhered more accurately to morpho-syntactic constraints than complex syntactic ones, with depth of syntactic trees and dependency link lengths proving most challenging. Few-shot learning improved performance for most models, especially Gemma variants, though Mistral’s syntactic accuracy declined. Constraining linguistic properties often led to longer sentences in zero-shot conditions, but few-shot learning enabled models to produce more varied and naturalistic outputs, aligning more closely with authentic English structures from the Universal Dependency Treebank dataset.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models through the Lens of Linguistic Proficiency and World Knowledge: A Comparative Study
abstract: The development of sophisticated artificial intelligence systems has rapidly transformed various industries, creating an increased demand for models capable of advanced linguistic processing and comprehensive knowledge integration. Addressing this demand, the presented evaluation explores the capabilities of ChatGPT and Google Gemini through a dual lens of linguistic skill and world knowledge, offering a unique perspective that goes beyond traditional assessments focused solely on language generation or factual recall. Through a carefully structured methodology, which incorporates a range of tasks designed to test syntax, grammar, vocabulary, and logical reasoning, the study provides a comparative analysis of how well each model can manage both linguistic complexity and the retrieval and application of factual information. Results indicate that ChatGPT excels in maintaining grammatical accuracy and consistency, making it particularly suitable for applications requiring rigorous language precision, while Google Gemini demonstrates superior contextual comprehension and logical reasoning abilities, suggesting its efficacy in scenarios where complex understanding and the ability to integrate diverse knowledge are crucial. The insights derived from this evaluation not only highlight the current capabilities and limitations of both models but also provide a foundational understanding that can inform future developments in enhancing language processing and knowledge management within AI systems.
specific_phenomena: covering word and phrase arrangements; grammar, involving rules for correct language use and tasks like grammar correction; and syntactic parsing, where models analyze sentence structures to identify hierarchical relationships. The framework also evaluates models’ ability to detect syntactic errors, maintain grammatical accuracy and consistency, and handle complex linguistic constructs. Additional aspects include understanding sentence structure, manipulating parts of speech, and ensuring cohesion and coherence in longer texts.
experimental_materials_comment: Controlled stimuli are evident in tasks specifically designed to test linguistic skills—such as syntax, grammar, vocabulary, sentence correction, syntactic parsing, sentence completion, and paraphrasing—often using specialized datasets with grammatical errors or syntactic anomalies to challenge the models. World knowledge tasks also employed structured questions, ranging from straightforward factual queries to complex reasoning scenarios. Naturalistic language is reflected in the use of diverse linguistic corpora, containing both formal and informal language, idiomatic expressions, and colloquial usage, allowing assessment of models’ adaptability across registers. Additionally, world knowledge tasks drew from encyclopedic databases, news archives, and specialized knowledge sources, providing realistic language contexts.
interp_method: describe their work as a novel evaluation framework specifically designed to assess both linguistic proficiency and world knowledge in LLMs. Applied to ChatGPT and Google Gemini, the framework provides a structured approach to testing by examining models through a dual lens of linguistic skill and world knowledge. It incorporates a diverse set of tasks targeting syntax, grammar, vocabulary, and logical reasoning, enabling a comprehensive assessment of both structural language competence and contextual understanding.
main_findings: The study evaluating LLMs through linguistic proficiency and world knowledge highlighted key findings regarding syntactic knowledge in ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The research assessed models using tasks targeting grammar, syntax, vocabulary, and logical reasoning, including sentence correction and syntactic parsing, with metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, grammaticality, coherence, and syntactic accuracy. ChatGPT generally outperformed Google Gemini in grammar correction (92% vs. 89% accuracy) and syntactic parsing (87% vs. 85% accuracy), demonstrating strong grammatical consistency, high precision, and recall across diverse linguistic scenarios. Google Gemini, while slightly behind in syntactic accuracy, excelled in handling idiomatic and colloquial language and showed higher performance in sentence completion tasks, reflecting broader contextual and semantic versatility. Overall, ChatGPT’s strengths lie in maintaining rigorous grammatical precision, making it suitable for tasks requiring exact language manipulation, whereas Gemini demonstrates adaptability in more contextually complex or idiomatic settings. Both models, however, faced challenges with ambiguous constructs and complex syntactic arrangements, suggesting that future improvements should focus on richer linguistic datasets and enhanced syntactic parsing and grammar correction algorithms.

title: Interpreting token compositionality in LLMs: A robustness analysis
abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) is integral to enhancing their reliability, interpretability, and inference processes. We present Constituent-Aware Pooling (CAP), a methodology designed to analyse how LLMs process compositional linguistic structures. Grounded in principles of compositionality, mechanistic interpretability, and information theory, CAP systematically intervenes in model activations through constituent-based pooling at various model levels. Our experiments on inverse definition modelling, hypernym and synonym prediction reveal critical insights into transformers' limitations in handling compositional abstractions. No specific layer integrates tokens into unified semantic representations based on their constituent parts. We observe fragmented information processing, which intensifies with model size, suggesting that larger models struggle more with these interventions and exhibit greater information dispersion. This fragmentation likely stems from transformers' training objectives and architectural design, preventing systematic and cohesive representations. Our findings highlight fundamental limitations in current transformer architectures regarding compositional semantics processing and model interpretability, underscoring the critical need for novel approaches in LLM design to address these challenges.
